passages.section: Finite-Time Singularity Formation for the Three-Dimensional Euler Equations
passages.quote: We construct smooth periodic initial data for the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations whose solution blows up in finite time.

anchor.heading: Finite-Time Singularity Formation for the Three-Dimensional Euler Equations

comparisons.note: The paper’s sentence asserts finite-time blow-up from smooth periodic initial data. The formal theorem additionally chooses odd divergence-free data, proves bounded velocity and central vorticity divergence, gives both divergent time integrals, and supplies every off-origin spatial limit. These are stronger conclusions for the same selected solution; they do not apply to every smooth initial datum.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The full existence theorem retains the blow-up claim and supplies the additional conclusions of Theorem 1.1.

audit.reason: The existence theorem contains additional singularity and regularity conclusions beyond this abstract sentence.

explanation.text: There are smooth divergence-free data on the unit torus whose classical Euler solution ceases to be smooth at a finite positive time $T_*$. The construction first produces approximate solutions with summable increments, then identifies their limit as an Euler solution and proves that its vorticity diverges at the origin, in Theorem 7.1 and Propositions 8.1–8.2. This is the existence claim that the remaining argument must establish. The formal theorem asserts the existence of one such datum and solution, representing torus fields by functions on $\mathbb R^3$ invariant under integer translations. Its stronger verdict records additional conclusions for that same solution: oddness, bounded velocity, divergent time integrals of the gradient and vorticity norms, and spatial limits away from the origin.

There is a unique solution on that half-line, with $|Y|\le1$ and $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$ for one function $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$. Its amplitude $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$ equals $\sqrt{\cos\varphi}\exp\int_0^\tau(1+e)\cos\varphi$. passages.quote: The *reference solution* is the solution of the reference system with $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)(0)=(-1,1)$, shown in Figure 1.

comparisons.note: Assume $Y(0)=1$ and define $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$, $U=Ya_{\rm ref}$. The formal statement gives $U(0)=1$, because the integral over $[0,0]$ is zero. In the paper, $U=-\alpha_1$, so the corresponding initial value is $\alpha_1(0)=-1$. This one-coordinate equality is only part of the reference initial data $(-1,1)$; the second component is established separately. No regularity or Riccati equation for $Y$ is needed for this initial-value calculation. The paper’s initial pair is $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(-1,1)$. This formal result gives only $U(0)=1$, assuming $Y(0)=1$, with $U=Ya_{\rm ref}=-\alpha_1$. It supplies the first component after reversing that sign; it does not supply the second component or the evolution.

explanation.text: The reference solution is selected by $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)(0)=(-1,1)$ in (2.5), the growing direction of the initial coefficient matrix. Section 2.2.2 reconstructs it from the Riccati slope by $\alpha_1=-Ya_{\rm ref}$ and $\alpha_2=a_{\rm ref}$, where $Y(0)=1$ and $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$. The two formal initial-value identities give $Ya_{\rm ref}=1$ at zero and $a_{\rm ref}=1$ there, respectively. Their weaker verdicts mean that each supplies one initial component, with the first sign reversed to match $\alpha_1$, and neither alone proves the evolution equation or existence of the reference solution.

Suppose $Y'=s^2(1-\varepsilon x)-2\varepsilon\tau x s^2Y-Y^2$ on $[0,\infty)$. Define $V(\tau)=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$ and $U(\tau)=Y(\tau)V(\tau)$. The formal statement proves $V'=U$ and $U'=s^2(1-\varepsilon x)V-2\varepsilon\tau x s^2U$ for every $\tau\ge0$, with right derivatives at zero. These are (2.5) in the coordinates $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(-U,V)$. No condition $Y(0)=1$ is assumed. The reconstruction always has $V(0)=1$, while the paper’s initial pair $(-1,1)$ additionally requires $Y(0)=1$. Values at negative times are not constrained by the differential-equation hypothesis. Given a solution $Y$ of the Riccati equation on $[0,\infty)$, the formal statement proves that $U=Ya_{\rm ref}$ and $V=a_{\rm ref}$ solve the sign-adjusted linear system. Thus $(-U,V)$ solves (2.5). passages.quote: $$a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp\left(\int_0^\tau Y(\tau')\,d\tau'\right).$$

comparisons.note: For a real function $Y$ and time $\tau$, the formal expression is $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp(\int_0^\tau Y(s)\,ds)$, using the interval integral with its orientation when $\tau<0$. This defines a positive number for every input function. If the integral is not defined by an integrable function on the interval, the formal integral is assigned zero, giving amplitude one; this is not a claim of integrability. In the application, $Y$ solves (2.12) on $[0,\infty)$, hence is continuous there, and the ordinary integral gives the reference amplitude with $a_{\rm ref}(0)=1$ and $a_{\rm ref}'=Ya_{\rm ref}$. This is exactly $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$. The definition accepts arbitrary functions, whereas the paper applies it to the continuous Riccati solution. If an integrand is not integrable, the formal integral is assigned zero; the reference theorem’s regularity avoids that case.

comparisons.note:
Assume a smooth odd unit-periodic solenoidal parent and smooth periodic pressure on $0<T\le1$, with bands $2\mathsf D$ for velocity and $4\mathsf D$ for its odd residual, gradient and both deformation bounds $\mathsf D\ge2$, residual bound $\lambda^{-5/2}$ and $D^2p_U-DR_U\le I$. Put $M=DU\circ X$, $\kappa=DX^{-T}k_*$, $\lambda=|\kappa(t_0,0)|\ge1$ and $0\le t_0<T$. The nonzero central seed solves $\mathbf a_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)M\mathbf a$, is transverse, has $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$, and satisfies $0<\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|\le1$. Every transverse homogeneous solution $\mathbf b$ obeys $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$. For sufficiently small fixed $\ell_*$, the projected seed exists, and every depth $P\ge2$ admits a unique family of retained velocities and normalized pressures satisfying the mean and transverse recursions. For $W=\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)$ and $\mathsf P=\sum_{p=1}^P(\mathsf p_p+\bar q_p)$, $\widetilde{\mathbf d}\cdot W=0$ and the momentum residual is $R_P+R_{\widetilde\chi}$. The oscillations and their sources vanish before activation and outside the envelope; there the remainder is phase independent. Means need not vanish before activation. Smoothness is on the closed slab; no continuation across its endpoints is asserted.

The relevant conclusion is retained for every finite expansion satisfying the recurrence. The formal statement also establishes existence and uniqueness, and admits any smooth periodic pressure with the required residual and coercivity bounds and any nonzero seed with $\gamma\le1$; the paper’s fixed pressure and attained amplitude normalization are included.

comparisons.note: On $[0,T]$, profiles are smooth, one-periodic in $s$, and obey $f(t,a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=f(t,a,s)$. Put $M=DU\circ X$, $\kappa=DX^{-T}k_*$, $\mathbf d=DX^{-T}\nabla_a$, $A_1=g\mathbf aF_h$, and $S=\widetilde\chi'A_1$ in the centered cell. The requirements include $R=R_U\circ X$, $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$, $\mathsf p_1=\widetilde\chi\mathsf p[A_1]$, and $C_1=B_1=\bar q_1=0$. For $1\le p\le P$, $C_{p+1}=\mathbf d\times[-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V_p/|\kappa|^2)]$. For $2\le p\le P$, require $B_{p,t}+MB_p+\mathbf d\bar q_p=-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R$ and $V_{p,t}+MV_p+\kappa\mathsf p_{p,s}=-(H_p-\langle H_p\rangle_s)+f_p^S$. Here $H_p$ is the sum of the preceding linear correction and all lower-level quadratic interactions, with the activation correction subtracted at level two; $f_p^S=-\sum_{i=2}^p(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_s(V_{p+1-i}+C_{p+1-i})$. Means satisfy $B_p=DX\,z_{p,t}$, $\operatorname{div}_az_{p,t}=0$, $z_p(0)=z_p(T)=0$ and zero spatial pressure mean. Transverse velocities are perpendicular to $\kappa$, centered and initially zero, with centered pressure. Finally $V_{P+1}=B_{P+1}=0$. This condition asserts no existence or estimates.

Assume $P\ge2$, a smooth periodic divergence-free parent and its flow, and a constructed family whose leading velocity, pressure and activation contribution vanish before $t_0$ and outside a closed label set $S$. For $W=\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)$ and $\mathsf P=\sum_{p=1}^P(\mathsf p_p+\bar q_p)$, the formal statement gives $\widetilde{\mathbf d}\cdot W=0$ and momentum residual $R_P+R_{\widetilde\chi}$. It also gives all phase-average, support and terminal conventions, and identifies $R_P$ with the final linear terms and quadratic interactions above depth $P$. Outside $S$, the remainder is phase independent. Every profile is smooth on $[0,T]$ and satisfies the phase period and coupled label translations. The construction is an input here, not an existence conclusion.

explanation.text: A bounded differentiable field satisfies $\|v\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le C(\|v\|_\infty+\|\nabla v\|_\infty)$. The derivative bound controls differences at short distances, and the supremum bound controls them at long distances. Lemma 5.7 applies this to spatial derivatives through order $m$, explaining the extra derivative in (5.45). The formal theorem gives the broader statement that if a smooth field on $\mathbb R^3$ has all derivatives through order $m+1$ bounded by $B\ge0$, then its $C^{m,1/2}$ norm is at most $3(m+1)B$. Its stronger verdict records all derivative orders, explicit Hölder regularity and the numerical bound, without a periodicity assumption.

Let $f$ be independent of phase, $\ell_*,h>0$, and $\gamma>0$. Assume finite weighted profile norms at every order and finite order-$j$ coefficient bounds $N_c(j),N_k(j)$ for the label and phase parts of the derivative operator. Given the finite-norm product estimate, the sum of the weighted norms after all ordered sequences of $m$ physical coordinate derivatives is at most $\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}[C_j9N_c(j)\ell_*^{-1}]\,\|f\|_{[m],\gamma}$. The conclusion includes finiteness of all differentiated order-zero norms.

Let $T>0$ and let $f$ be a smooth profile with values in a real normed space, one-periodic in phase and obeying $f(t,a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=f(t,a,s)$. At $t\in[t_0,T]$ let $A(t,\cdot)$ and $B$ be smooth with $B(A(t,x))=D_xA(t,x)$. Require $\ell_*>0$, $\mathsf D,L\ge1$, $\ell_*^{-1}\le\mathsf D^a$, and $\ell_*^j\|D^jB\|_\infty\le L\mathsf D$ for $j\le m+1$. Assume $f$ is phase independent. The formal statement bounds the sum over all ordered coordinate derivatives of length $m$ by $3^mK_m\gamma(t)N_m$, and gives $f^\natural(t)\in C^{m,1/2}$ with norm at most $3(m+1)K_{m+1}\gamma(t)N_{m+1}$. Here $N_j$ sums scaled label and phase derivative suprema through order $j$, each multi-index once. The explicit constants depend on $L$; they are not order-only constants.

This gives the weighted derivative and Hölder estimates for phase-independent profiles under explicit inverse-coefficient bounds. It does not separately assert the operator identity $\widetilde{\mathbf d}g_0=\mathbf dg_0$.

explanation.text: For a phase-independent profile $g_0$, every application of $\widetilde{\mathbf d}$ agrees with application of $\mathbf d$ because $\partial_sg_0=0$. The coefficients of $\mathbf d$ are themselves phase independent, so this remains true after repeated differentiation. This proves the absence of the frequency cost in the mean part of Lemma 5.7. The derivative-iteration result and weighted mean theorem are weaker links because they assume the coefficient bounds and, for the latter, a positive continuous time weight and a smooth inverse label map. The complete formal implication is different in scope because its conclusion is the full derivative-and-Hölder estimate, while the operator simplification occurs within the proof.

explanation.text: For the smooth periodic divergence-free cutoff velocity $u$, the pressure is the periodic solution of $\Delta p=-\operatorname{tr}((\nabla u)^2)$ with zero spatial mean. The source has zero integral because it is the divergence of $(u\cdot\nabla)u$, and the mean normalization removes the additive constant. This choice makes the momentum residual divergence free and distinguishes $p$ from the expansion pressure $\Pi$. The same linked conditions specify this pressure and cutoff, while the proposition and construction establish existence; the cutoff condition alone presupposes a continuous periodic representative of $V$, supplied here by its smooth periodicity. The different uniqueness link proves that any two smooth periodic zero-mean pressures with equal Laplacians coincide, for any common source, and supplies no existence or time regularity by itself.

explanation.text:
For a twice continuously differentiable divergence-free vector field $u$, differentiating the advection term gives $\operatorname{div}((u\cdot
abla)u)=\operatorname{tr}((
abla u)^2)+u\cdot
abla\operatorname{div}u$. The last term vanishes, leaving the identity used to choose the pressure in Proposition 5.11. The square here is matrix composition, so its trace is $\sum_{i,j}\partial_j u_i\,\partial_i u_j$, not the sum of the squared entries of the gradient. The same formal theorem proves this spatial identity at every point under exactly twice continuous differentiability and zero divergence. It needs neither periodicity nor an Euler evolution; those enter only when applying the identity to the cutoff field and solving its Poisson equation.

TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.crossin.text: For positive coupling ratios $\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon_+$, the formalization sets $H=2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$. This is the upper endpoint of the interval in Proposition 2.8, measured in normalized time $\tau=r(t-t_0)$. The definition alone does not assert that a crossing exists or that $H\le T$; those are separate hypotheses and conclusions. It is defined for arbitrary real inputs: the square root of a nonpositive input and division by zero are both taken to be zero, so $H=0$ when $\varepsilon\varepsilon_+\le0$. The crossing theorem assumes positivity and does not use that extension.
TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.crossin.summary: The crossing is sought before this prescribed time

TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.eight_d.text: Assume $\varepsilon>0$, $\varepsilon_+>0$ and $\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$. Then $8/\varepsilon\le2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$. Thus the proposed upper endpoint lies beyond every reference peak with $2/\varepsilon\le\tau_m\le3/\varepsilon$. The paper states the equivalent inequality $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}\ge4/\varepsilon$ in the proof of Proposition 2.8. This is an algebraic comparison of positive numbers; it uses no wave equation and does not itself locate a crossing.
TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.eight_d.summary: The upper endpoint exceeds eight divided by epsilon

TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.exists_.text: Let $\varepsilon>0$, $0<\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$, $2/\varepsilon\le\tau_m\le3/\varepsilon$, and $H=2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}\le T$. Suppose $\rho$ is continuous on $[\tau_m,T]$ and, with $x(\tau)=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, satisfies $1/(4x)\le\rho\le3/(2x)$ there. The formal statement gives a time strictly inside $(\tau_m,H)$ with $\rho=\varepsilon_+$. At every crossing in the larger interval $[\tau_m,T]$, it gives $1/(4\varepsilon_+)\le x\le3/(2\varepsilon_+)$. In the paper $\rho=\eta_+/\nu_+$ and $x=\tan\varphi$. Continuity and the two comparison bounds are assumptions here; the result does not derive them from the wave equations.
TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.exists_.summary: A continuous coupling ratio reaches the successor value

TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.exists_.text: For positive successor ratio at most epsilon divided by 32, a continuous ratio between one half and three halves of the reference cosine crosses that successor value strictly inside the peak-to-horizon interval. Every later crossing also has explicit tangent bounds. The old docstring numbers refer to the earlier manuscript; the current application is Proposition 2.8 using Lemma 2.7.

If a continuous real ratio on $[a,b]$ reaches the next level somewhere, it reaches it at a least time in that interval. The proof makes the level set compact and takes its minimum. It requires neither monotonicity nor uniqueness of crossings, and it does not locate the first crossing outside the chosen interval.
TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.exists_.summary: A nonempty compact crossing set has a first point

TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.x_cross.text: For $\varepsilon>0$ and $\varepsilon_+>0$, put $H=2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$ and $x(\tau)=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$. The formal statement proves $x(H)=2/\varepsilon_+$. Since the reference angle is $\varphi(\tau)=\arctan x(\tau)$, this is exactly the endpoint identity for $\tan\varphi$ used in the proof of Proposition 2.8. It concerns the reference angle, not the angle of a perturbed wave vector, and needs neither the upper bound $\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ nor a wave solution.
TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.x_cross.summary: The endpoint gives an exact value of the tangent

TorusEuler.AuxiliaryTerminalSmoothness.text: The condition asks for one integer $b$, nondecreasing threshold $\mathcal B$ and lower bound $N_1$. For every $N\ge N_1$, it requires stages with $\lambda_0=N$, eventual velocity-residual time bounds, and eventual mixed correction bounds. Their activation times tend to a positive finite $T<S_j$ for every stage. It also requires a smooth odd maximal periodic Euler solution on $[0,T)$ with bounded velocity, $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$, and infinite time integrals of both $\|\nabla u\|_\infty$ and $\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_\infty$. Both $u$ and $\partial_tu$ have every local spatial derivative limit away from $\mathbb Z^3$. The velocity extends periodically and smoothly to all real times off that lattice, with no Euler requirement after $T$. These are required properties, not their existence proof. The displayed condition shares $T$ between stages and solution but does not require $U_j\to u$; the supplied assembly proof uses that actual limit.
TorusEuler.AuxiliaryTerminalSmoothness.summary: One choice of parameters gives a smooth extension

TorusEuler.BoundedSpatialJet.text: An order-$m$ jet is a bounded continuous function of the spatial variable with values in continuous $m$-linear maps. The norm is the uniform operator norm. This type alone does not say that the function is a derivative of any velocity; that compatibility is imposed by later hypotheses.
TorusEuler.BoundedSpatialJet.summary: A uniformly bounded spatial derivative field

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.DeformationOn.text: This proposition packages an actual flow on $[0,T]$, compatibility with all lattice translations, inverse identities, and differentiability with norm bound $C$ for the transitions from and to time zero. The bounds are imposed at every spatial point of the lift. It records geometric regularity of a supplied velocity and flow, without imposing Euler's equation.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.DeformationOn.summary: A periodic flow with bounded forward and inverse deformation

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.DeformationOn.congr.text: A flow certificate for a velocity $u$ on $[0,T]$ with constant $C$ consists of a two-time flow $Y$ of $u$ on $[0,T]$ that commutes with integer translations, whose forward and inverse maps $Y(0,t,\cdot)$ and $Y(t,0,\cdot)$ are mutually inverse and differentiable everywhere with derivative norm at most $C$, for each $t\in[0,T]$. If $u(t,\cdot)=v(t,\cdot)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$, then the same $Y$ is a flow certificate for $v$ on $[0,T]$ with the same constant $C$. Only the trajectory equation is rewritten using the equality of velocities, so no new flow or estimate is introduced.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.DeformationOn.congr.summary: A flow certificate transfers between velocities that agree on the slab

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.DeformationOn.fderi.text: For a flow with bounded deformation on $[0,T]$ and a time $t$ in that slab, the forward derivative at $x$ and reverse derivative at the transported point compose to the identity in both orders. Differentiability and inverse-map identities are already part of the deformation hypothesis. The theorem differentiates those identities, giving actual inverse matrices without any assigned-value inverse construction.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.DeformationOn.fderi.summary: The two deformation matrices are mutual inverses

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.PhaseState.text:
The enlarged particle space is the product of a three-dimensional label and one real phase variable. The phase graph is imposed later; this abbreviation does not restrict points to that graph or quotient the phase modulo one.

The type is an unrestricted Euclidean label and real phase pair. There is no exceptional default or graph membership assertion; phase periodicity and restriction to the transported graph are additional hypotheses or constructions.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.PhaseState.summary: Labels and an independent phase coordinate

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.childVelocity.text: Add to the parent velocity the oscillatory profile evaluated through the reverse parent transition, together with the Eulerian correction $v$. This defines the physical child field used in the deformation theorem. The formula does not itself assert divergence freedom, smoothness, or that the child solves Euler; those require the construction's separate hypotheses.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.childVelocity.summary: The parent velocity with its transported perturbations

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.contDiffOn_pullback.text: The perturbation pulled back by the actual parent flow is jointly smooth.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.contDiffOn_pullback.summary: The pulled-back perturbation is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.defect_scaledField.text: Applying the phase-defect functional to the scaled particle field gives zero when both scales are nonzero. The cancellation is algebraic: the phase velocity is the wave vector paired with the label velocity. This tangency is valid at every enlarged state, so the defect is conserved along the constructed trajectories.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.defect_scaledField.summary: The lifted velocity is tangent to the phase graph

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.defect_scaledGraph.text: When both scaling parameters are nonzero, every point produced by the scaled graph embedding has phase defect zero. The identity records compatibility of the embedded phase with the initial linear phase. It provides the invariant constraint used when a trajectory in the enlarged space is converted back to labels.

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.exists_childFlow_of.text: Given a smooth parent flow, forward and inverse deformation bounds, the twisted divergence identity, phase periodicity, and scaled oscillatory and mean jet bounds, construct the physical child flow with deformation bounded by the specified frequency-quarter-power budget. The numerous smallness and scale hypotheses are explicit inputs; this helper does not establish them for the hierarchy.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.exists_childFlow_of.summary: Child deformation from oscillatory and mean bounds

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.exists_childFlow_of.text: Assume a smooth periodic parent with both Jacobians bounded by $\mathsf D$, positive scales, the prescribed frequency relations, and the explicit step smallness $\Gamma\mathsf D^b\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$. Smooth bounded pullback data with periodic graph field, and first-derivative bounds $B\mathsf D^p\lambda^{-5/4}$ for the scaled label velocity and for its scalar phase velocity, yield a physical child flow with bounded deformation, bound $\Gamma\mathsf D^b\lambda^{1/4}$. The hypotheses carry the profile estimates; this theorem assembles their geometric consequences.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.exists_childFlow_of.summary: Constructing the child flow from scaled derivative bounds

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.graphDerivative_app.text: Let $D:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be linear and continuous. For any $v\in\mathbb R^3$, restricting $D$ to the scaled graph $a\mapsto(a/\ell_*,k_*\cdot a/h)$ gives $D(v/\ell_*,0)+(k_*\cdot v/h)D(0,1)$. This is an algebraic identity for a linear map; it does not assert differentiability of the flow. Applying it to the derivative of the lifted displacement supplies the chain rule in Lemma 5.10. The formal identity allows zero scales, with division by zero defined as zero. The coordinate interpretation in the paper requires $\ell_*,h>0$.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.graphDerivative_app.summary: Separate the scaled label and phase contributions

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.graphField.text: Evaluate the independent-phase field $c$ at the label $a$ and phase $\langle k,a\rangle$. The result is an ordinary time-dependent label velocity. The definition imposes neither periodicity nor divergence freedom; those are proved later from the profile's lattice rule and combined label-phase divergence identity.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.graphField.summary: Restricting the label velocity to its phase graph

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.graphField_pullback.text: A periodic parent flow, periodic Eulerian perturbation, and the skew label-phase lattice rule $W(t,a+n,s+k\cdot n)=W(t,a,s)$ imply spatial periodicity of the graph-restricted pullback velocity. The phase shifts together with the label by the pairing with $k$. No integrality assumption on $k$ is needed because the combined lattice rule handles arbitrary wave vectors.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.graphField_pullback.summary: The profile lattice rule gives a periodic label velocity

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.hasFDerivAt_labelPr.text: For nonzero envelope radius, the derivative of the projected scaled field is exactly the derivative $C$ of the rescaled label velocity. The reciprocal envelope factor in the lifted field cancels with the projection. This preserves the smaller projected-displacement estimate even when the full scaled-field gradient has larger scaling factors.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.hasFDerivAt_labelPr.summary: Projecting removes the envelope reciprocal from the derivative

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.hasFDerivAt_labelTr.text: If the projected displacement of an enlarged transition has derivative $D$ at the embedded label, then the unscaled label transition minus the identity has derivative $D$ composed with the graph slope. Nonzero envelope radius permits cancellation of the initial label. This formula tracks the scale cost before estimating the full transition derivative.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.hasFDerivAt_labelTr.summary: The label displacement derivative factors through the graph

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.hasFDerivAt_scaledF.text: Given derivatives $C$ and $G$ of the rescaled label velocity and scalar phase velocity, the derivative of the lifted field is their product with reciprocal envelope and phase factors. The theorem preserves the separately estimated scalar derivative. It therefore retains the longitudinal cancellation instead of replacing it immediately by a wave-vector norm bound.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.hasFDerivAt_scaledF.summary: The scaled field derivative keeps label and phase separate

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.isLabelFlowOn_label.text: Start with a scaled trajectory family satisfying the initial and trajectory equations, with nonzero label and phase scales. Its projection from the embedded graph is a two-time label flow for the graph-restricted label field on the slab: $Y(s,s,a)=a$ and $\partial_tY(s,t,a)=c(t,Y(s,t,a))$ within the slab. Conservation of phase defect identifies the projected right-hand side, so the result is an actual flow equation on the slab.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.isLabelFlowOn_label.summary: The invariant phase graph produces an actual label flow

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.isLabelFlowOn_physi.text: For a $C^2$ periodic parent and an actual label flow of the graph-restricted pullback field, conjugating by the parent transitions gives a flow of the child velocity (parent velocity plus transported profile and Eulerian correction). The theorem differentiates both the parent trajectory and the evolving label. It proves the correct physical ODE, without asserting that the resulting velocity already satisfies Euler's equation.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.isLabelFlowOn_physi.summary: Conjugating the label flow gives the child flow

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelProjection.text: Multiply the first component of a label-phase state by the envelope radius $\ell$. This continuous linear map returns the physical label from the scaled coordinate when that scale is nonzero and the point lies on the chosen graph. The definition does not inspect the independent phase coordinate.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelProjection.summary: Recovering the label from its scaled coordinate

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelProjection_sca.text: For a state with zero phase defect, projecting the scaled velocity gives the graph-restricted label velocity $c(t,a,\langle k,a\rangle)$ evaluated at its recovered label $a$. Only the envelope radius is assumed nonzero in this identity. It identifies the differential equation satisfied by a projected trajectory once conservation of the defect has placed that trajectory on the graph.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelProjection_sca.summary: On the graph the projected velocity is the label field

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelProjection_sca.text: With nonzero envelope radius $\ell$, sending a label to its scaled graph point and then multiplying the label coordinate by $\ell$ returns the original label. The phase width need not be nonzero because the projection discards the phase component. This identity supplies the correct initial value for the label flow obtained by restricting the enlarged scaled flow.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelProjection_sca.summary: Projecting the scaled graph recovers the label

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelTransition.text: For a transition $\Phi_{s,t}$ on the scaled space $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, define $\mathcal A_{s,t}(a)=\ell_*\,\pi_a\Phi_{s,t}(a/\ell_*,k_*\cdot a/h)$, where $\pi_a$ takes the first three coordinates. With positive scales and the lifted particle flow of Lemma 5.10, $\mathcal A_{0,t}$ is the change of parent labels. The formula also defines the reverse transition. No flow equation, inverse relation, or graph invariance is asserted by this definition; those require separate hypotheses. At zero scale the formula still has a value because a reciprocal of zero is zero, but it no longer describes a change of coordinates.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelTransition.summary: Restrict the lifted transition to the phase graph

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_fderiv_labelTr.text: A derivative bound $B$ on the projected displacement, together with positive scales, gives the derivative of the label transition as the identity plus that displacement derivative composed with the graph slope. Its norm is bounded by $1+(\ell^{-1}+\|k\|h^{-1})B$. The statement supplies both the derivative identity and its quantitative estimate.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_fderiv_labelTr.summary: Projected displacement bounds the full label deformation

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_fderiv_scaledF.text: With positive scales and derivative bounds $A$ and $B$ for the rescaled label and scalar phase velocities, the full scaled-field derivative is bounded by $\ell^{-1}A+h^{-1}B$. That the two given maps $C,G$ are the actual derivatives of these velocities is assumed. This is the quantity made small before applying flow stability.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_fderiv_scaledF.summary: The scaled gradient has two distinct costs

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_fderiv_scaledP.text: For a smooth profile whose weighted coordinate derivatives through order one are bounded by a nonnegative $M$, the derivative after label-phase rescaling has norm at most $4M$. The factor counts the enlarged space's four coordinates. This converts the component estimates supplied by the profile calculus into the operator norm needed for ODE stability.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_fderiv_scaledP.summary: Four weighted coordinates control the first derivative

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_scaledField_le.text: For positive scales, a bound $A$ on the label velocity at the rescaled point controls the enlarged field by $\ell^{-1}A+h^{-1}\|k\|A$. This is a value-level estimate, not a derivative estimate. It supplies the boundedness needed to extend the scaled ODE across the entire time slab.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_scaledField_le.summary: A label-velocity bound also bounds the lifted field

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_scaledGraph_le.text: For positive envelope radius and phase width, the graph embedding has operator norm bounded by $\ell^{-1}+\|k\|h^{-1}$. This is the scale conversion needed to apply a derivative estimate from the enlarged coordinates to the original labels. The theorem itself concerns one fixed linear embedding and makes no flow assumption.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_scaledGraph_le.summary: The graph slope costs envelope and wave-number factors

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseDefect.text: The functional returns the unscaled phase minus the initial wave vector paired with the recovered label. Its zero set is the original phase graph after rescaling, provided both scales are nonzero. Applying it to the lifted particle velocity gives zero, which is the mechanism preserving that graph under the flow.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseDefect.summary: The difference between phase and linear label phase

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseDefect_transit.text: Let $\ell_*,h\ne0$ and let $\Phi_{s,t}$ solve the scaled lifted equation on a closed interval, with $\Phi_{s,s}$ equal to the identity. If its scaled coordinates are $(y,\sigma)$, then $h\sigma-k_*\cdot(\ell_*y)$ is constant along every trajectory. In the unscaled coordinates this is $s-k_*\cdot a$. Hence a trajectory initially on $s=k_*\cdot a$ stays on that graph. The assertion covers either ordering of the two times and uses derivatives from within the closed interval at its endpoints. It proves the invariance used in Lemma 5.10, without requiring a separate uniqueness assertion for the lifted equation.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseDefect_transit.summary: The lifted flow preserves phase minus label phase

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseMean_pullbackF.text: The cutoff tail shifts the phase mean by its label-dependent pullback.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseMean_pullbackF.summary: The cutoff tail changes only the phase mean

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseOscillation_pu.text: The phase-independent cutoff tail contributes no oscillatory term.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseOscillation_pu.summary: The cutoff tail leaves the oscillation unchanged

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition.text: Given parent transitions $X_{s,t}$ and label transitions $\mathcal A_{s,t}$, define $Y_{s,t}(x)=X_{0,t}(\mathcal A_{s,t}(X_{s,0}(x)))$. Thus a physical point is first sent to its label at reference time zero, moved by the label transition, then returned to physical space. If the transitions are flows, the case $s=0$ is $Y(t,a)=X(t,\mathcal A_t(a))$ from Lemma 5.10. The definition accepts arbitrary maps; it does not prove that they are invertible, that $Y$ solves the perturbed velocity equation, or that derivatives exist.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition.summary: Compose parent labels, label motion, and parent flow

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.text: Let $X_{s,t}$ be a parent flow on $[0,T]$ with $0\in[0,T]$. At a fixed time $t$, suppose $X_{0,t}$ and $X_{t,0}$ are differentiable with derivative norm at most $\mathsf D$, and $\mathcal A_{0,t}$ and $\mathcal A_{t,0}$ are differentiable with derivative norm at most $B$. The physical compositions $X_{0,t}\circ\mathcal A_{0,t}$ and $\mathcal A_{t,0}\circ X_{t,0}$ then have derivative norm at most $\mathsf D B$. These are operator norms on $\mathbb R^3$. This supplies the final multiplication of bounds in Lemma 5.10. The result does not by itself assert that the two label transitions are inverse maps.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.summary: Multiply the parent and label deformation bounds

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.text: For a parent flow with time zero in its slab, the physical transition from zero is the parent transition applied after the label transition. The reverse parent map at the initial time becomes the identity. The algebraic formula holds for arbitrary target time $t$; the theorem does not assert a flow equation at that unrestricted time.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.summary: Starting at zero simplifies the physical transition

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.text: When parent and label flows both have uniform spatial Lipschitz bounds, conjugated forward and reverse physical transitions are left and right inverses for every allowed time. The result follows from the restart identities of the two component flows. No derivative estimate or volume-preservation conclusion is part of this statement.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.summary: Reverse physical transitions are two-sided inverses

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.text: The physical transition back to time zero is the reverse label transition applied after the reverse parent transition. The parent transition from zero to zero disappears by the initial-value property. The identity is algebraic for arbitrary $t$; analytic flow and inverse claims later restrict that time to the slab.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.summary: Returning to zero simplifies the inverse transition

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.pullbackField.text: For a parent transition family $X$, a profile $W(t,a,s)$ and a physical perturbation $v(t,x)$, the formal expression is $D(X_{t,0})(X_{0,t}(a))[W(t,a,s)+v(t,X_{0,t}(a))]$. For a differentiable invertible flow this is $c=(D_aX)^{-1}(W+v\circ X)$ in Lemma 5.10. The label $a\in\mathbb R^3$ and phase $s\in\mathbb R$ are kept independent. No smoothness or invertibility is required to form the expression; the derivative is assigned zero where it does not exist. The parent flow hypotheses in the subsequent theorems ensure that it is the usual inverse derivative on the time interval.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.pullbackField.summary: Pull the physical correction back by the parent flow

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.pullbackField_skewP.text: Fix a time and a lattice vector $n\in\mathbb Z^3$. Write $X_f=X_{0,t}$ and $X_r=X_{t,0}$. Assume $X_f(a+n)=X_f(a)+n$, $X_r(x+n)=X_r(x)+n$, $W(a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=W(a,s)$, and $v$ is spatially periodic. Define $c(a,s)=DX_r(X_f(a))[W(a,s)+v(X_f(a))]$. Then $c(a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=c(a,s)$. No differentiability or inverse relation between $X_f,X_r$ is assumed by this translation statement; a derivative at a nondifferentiable point is assigned zero. For the smooth parent flow, $DX_r(X_f(a))=(DX_f(a))^{-1}$, giving the paper's pullback. The conclusion concerns the entire field before subtracting its phase average, and does not require $k_*\in\mathbb Z^3$.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.pullbackField_skewP.summary: The pulled back velocity respects combined translations

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledCutoffTail_ph.text: Let $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and a field of linear maps $G$ be differentiable, with $\|DA(a)\|\le A_1$, $\|G(a)\|\le G_0$ and $\|DG(a)\|\le G_1$ for every $a$, and let $|\ell|\le1$. Suppose $v$ has bounded derivatives and half-Hölder quotients through order two with spatial $C^{2,1/2}$ norm at most $\varepsilon$. Then the phase-independent field $(a,s)\mapsto G(\ell a)\,v(A(\ell a))$ has value and first derivative bounded in operator norm by $\max\{G_0,G_0A_1+G_1\}\varepsilon$. The phase scale $h$ plays no role, since the field does not depend on the phase.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledCutoffTail_ph.summary: A cutoff tail has a controlled first jet after pullback

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledField.text: For any vector field $c(t,a,s)\in\mathbb R^3$, define the lifted field at scaled coordinates $(y,\sigma)$ by $(\ell_*^{-1}c(t,\ell_*y,h\sigma),h^{-1}k_*\cdot c(t,\ell_*y,h\sigma))$. When $\ell_*,h>0$, this is precisely the equation in coordinates $(a/\ell_*,s/h)$ used in Lemma 5.10. The two components come from the same vector $c$, which later yields conservation of $s-k_*\cdot a$. This definition requires neither a divergence condition nor a small gradient. It also accepts zero scales, with reciprocal zero equal to zero; such values have no invertible coordinate interpretation.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledField.summary: Write label and phase velocities in scaled coordinates

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledGraph_labelPr.text: If an enlarged state has zero phase defect and both scales are nonzero, recovering its label and embedding that label again gives the original state. This is the converse of the graph's zero-defect identity. It ensures that preserving the scalar defect keeps a trajectory on the intended graph, rather than merely in a larger constraint set.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledGraph_labelPr.summary: Zero phase defect reconstructs the graph point

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledPerturbation_.text: A phase-independent perturbation costs at most one derivative of the inverse deformation and one derivative of the forward map.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledPerturbation_.summary: The pulled-back tail costs one geometric derivative

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.slope_divergence_pu.text: Let $X$ be the flow of a periodic divergence-free $C^2$ velocity $U$ on $[0,T]$, $T>0$, with a uniform spatial Lipschitz bound. Fix $t\in[0,T]$, a label $a$, and phase $s$, and put $c=(D_aX_{0,t})^{-1}(W+v\circ X_{0,t})$ and $\kappa=(D_aX_{0,t})^{-T}k_*$. Assume $X_{0,t}$ is $C^2$ near $a$, $c$ is differentiable jointly in label and phase there, and $W(t,a,\cdot)$ is differentiable at $s$. If $\operatorname{div}_x[W(t,X_{t,0}(x),s)+v(t,x)]+\kappa\cdot\partial_sW=0$ at $x=X_{0,t}(a)$, then $\operatorname{div}_ac+k_*\cdot\partial_sc=0$ at $(a,s)$. This is the Piola identity with the phase term included. The regularity premise concerns the pulled-back field itself, not merely existence of a derivative of $W$.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.slope_divergence_pu.summary: Incompressibility becomes divergence in label and phase variables

TorusEuler.CommutesTorusLineDerivatives.text: Requires the operator $P$ to preserve every actual derivative relation along each translated torus line $a+s v$: whenever $s\mapsto f(a+sv)$ has derivative $df(a+tv)$ at every $t$, also $s\mapsto Pf(a+sv)$ has derivative $(P\,df)(a+tv)$. The premise and conclusion assert existence of the derivative at every real parameter, not just an equation involving a derivative function defined everywhere. Both the field and its derivative are half-Hölder torus fields.
TorusEuler.CommutesTorusLineDerivatives.summary: Projection commutes with derivatives along torus lines

TorusEuler.CommutesTorusLineDerivatives..text: If $P$ commutes with actual derivatives along all torus lines, its directionwise extension has the same property on linear-map-valued fields. The proof differentiates each coordinate evaluation, applies that commutation hypothesis, and reconstructs the derivative by a finite sum. This lets the same commutation argument be repeated at successive Fréchet derivative orders.

TorusEuler.ComplexEuclideanVec3.text:
This abbreviation is the three-dimensional complex Euclidean target used for Fourier synthesis. Real velocity fields are embedded coordinatewise and recovered by taking their real parts.

This is a type abbreviation for the source type displayed here. It does not by itself assert a PDE, nonvanishing, smoothness or an existence theorem.
TorusEuler.ComplexEuclideanVec3.summary: Complex Euclidean space for Fourier synthesis

TorusEuler.ComplexPressureTensor.text: This finite function type stores the nine complex entries of a three-dimensional tensor. It is the input space for the scalar pressure symbol. The coordinates use the ordinary finite product norm; symmetry and reality are not encoded in the type and are only present for tensors constructed from real velocities.
TorusEuler.ComplexPressureTensor.summary: Complex coordinates for the velocity tensor

TorusEuler.ComplexVec3.text: This abbreviation represents a complex vector as a function from the three coordinate indices to $\mathbb C$, an element of $\mathbb C^3$ with no chosen norm. It is convenient for componentwise Fourier algebra. It is not the Euclidean space with its $L^2$ norm; conversion to that space is made explicitly when orthogonality or contractive operator norms are needed.

TorusEuler.ContinuousOnSlabInSpatialNorm.text: This condition requires $N(f(r)-f(t))\to0$ as $r$ approaches each $t\in[0,T]$ from within $[0,T]$, for a given measurement $N$ of spatial fields. It expresses endpoint continuity using differences of spatial fields. The supplied $N$ is just a real-valued function at this level; its analytic norm properties are not assumed by the definition.
TorusEuler.ContinuousOnSlabInSpatialNorm.summary: Continuity in a spatial norm along a closed slab

TorusEuler.DistinctPairs.text: This subtype consists of pairs whose two coordinates are unequal. It excludes the diagonal before the half-Hölder difference quotient is formed. In a genuine metric space, distinctness makes the distance strictly positive, so its square root has a nonzero reciprocal in the quotient construction.
TorusEuler.DistinctPairs.summary: Pairs of distinct points for difference quotients

TorusEuler.EndpointBoundedTest.text: This subtype packages a measurable scalar function together with existence of a global bound on its norm. It does not demand smoothness or continuity. Such tests can include measurable-set indicators, allowing vanishing integral pairings to detect almost-everywhere zero time means or spatial pairings.

TorusEuler.EndpointCoefficientC1Bound.text: On $I=[0,1]$, a matrix field $K$ is continuous in time in $C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3)$, its periodic lift is differentiable in space, and $\|K(t,a)\|\le C_0$, $\|D_aK(t,a)\|\le C_1$, with $C_0,C_1\ge0$. The torus is $\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$, and matrix norms are operator norms. This is the coefficient hypothesis used by the formal endpoint inverse. It is weaker than the paper's continuity in $C^{1,1/2}$: continuity of the first derivative in that norm is not required. Symmetry, ellipticity and the displacement energy inequality are separate hypotheses.
TorusEuler.EndpointCoefficientC1Bound.summary: Specify the coefficient regularity and two uniform bounds

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexTimeL2.text: The complex time-path space is L² of complex Euclidean three-vectors over the restriction of Lebesgue measure to $(0,T]$. It receives complex extensions of real time-path operators for the Fourier analysis in labels. No frequency, divergence, or zero-mean restriction is built into this abbreviation.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexTimeL2.summary: Complex velocity paths on the restricted time interval

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.text: A complexification consists of a real embedding, real and imaginary projections, compatibility with multiplication by $i$, reconstruction, and a squared-norm splitting identity. These fields are assumptions carried by the structure. They encode the Hilbert-style real/complex relationship needed to extend coefficient operators with unchanged norm.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.summary: Real and imaginary parts reconstruct the complex space

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Package the componentwise extension of a real operator $A$ as a complex continuous linear map. Complex linearity follows from the real and imaginary decomposition of scalars, and continuity uses the original norm bound. The construction applies to any bounded real endomorphism; no coercivity or invertibility is imposed here.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: The real operator extends complex linearly

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Package extension itself as a real continuous linear map from real bounded endomorphisms to complex bounded endomorphisms. Its continuity certificate uses the norm bound one, with exact norm preservation established separately. This lets smoothness and derivative estimates for operator-valued symbols pass through complexification by composition.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: Complex extension is a bounded map between operator spaces

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Applying the bounded linear extension map on operator space to a real operator $A$ gives exactly the complex extension of $A$. This is a definitional compatibility between the continuous-linear-map form of the extension and the previously constructed extension. It lets later smoothness estimates use the bounded map while algebraic proofs continue to use the component formulas.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: The operator space map evaluates to complex extension

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Package extension as a unital ring homomorphism on bounded endomorphisms. It preserves zero, addition, identity, and composition by the previously proved identities. This algebraic form is used to transport units and their inverses; boundedness and smooth dependence are supplied by the separate continuous-linear-map packaging.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: Complex extension preserves the endomorphism ring

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Complex extension commutes with addition of real bounded operators. Both real and imaginary components receive the sum, so linearity of the embedding rearranges the result into two extended operators. This algebraic equality is later bundled as part of a real-linear map between operator spaces.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: Extending a sum adds the extended operators

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Evaluation of the complex-linear extension is the embedding of $A$ applied to the real component plus $i$ times the embedding of $A$ applied to the imaginary component. Although the scalar field has changed from real to complex, the underlying function is the same componentwise construction.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: The complex extension applies the operator to both parts

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Complexifying the real frozen operator $rBr+I-r$ gives the same polynomial expression in the extended projection and coefficient. The identity is algebraic and requires no projection, coercivity, or symmetry assumptions on $r$ and $B$. Those hypotheses enter the later invertibility and norm estimates for this symbol.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: The frozen operator formula survives complexification

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: The extension of $AB$ equals the product of their extensions, where multiplication of endomorphisms means composition. The real and imaginary projection formulas show that applying $B$ then $A$ acts componentwise in the expected order. This property is used in frozen-symbol formulas and inverse compatibility.

Applying the extended complex operator to the embedded real vector $x+i0$ equals embedding $Ax$. The imaginary component of the embedded input is zero, so the extension restricts to the original real action. This is the compatibility used to transfer identities obtained with complex Fourier methods back to the real space.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: The extension agrees on embedded real vectors

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Extending the identity real operator gives the identity complex operator. The proof is precisely the reconstruction property of the complexified space: real part plus $i$ times imaginary part recovers every vector. This identity is required to make extension a unital ring homomorphism on bounded endomorphisms.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: The identity operator remains the identity

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: If $A$ is invertible, extending $A^{-1}$ equals taking the inverse of the extended operator. The proof represents $A$ as an invertible element and maps it through the extension homomorphism. The invertibility assumption is essential: the theorem does not justify interpreting the value assigned to the inverse of a singular operator as a genuine inverse.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: Extension commutes with the inverse of an invertible operator

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: For a real scalar $c$, the extension of $cA$ is $c$ times the extension of $A$. The real scalar restriction matters because the input operator space is over the real field. Combined with additivity and norm preservation, this gives a real continuous linear map on operator spaces.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: Real scalar multiples extend with the same scalar

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.im_e.text: The imaginary projection of the extended operator applied to $z$ is $A$ applied to the imaginary projection of $z$. Thus the same real operator governs both components. This equality supports norm splitting and coercivity arguments without assuming that the complex input itself is the embedding of a real vector.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.im_e.summary: Imaginary projection commutes with the complex extension

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.norm.text: The norm of the complex extension of $A$ equals the norm of $A$. The upper bound follows from squared-norm splitting; the lower bound tests the extended operator on embedded real vectors, whose norms are unchanged. This exact equality keeps frozen-coefficient constants uniform under complexification.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.norm.summary: Complex extension preserves the operator norm exactly

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.norm.text: For any complexification of a real space, the norm of the embedded vector $x+i0$ equals the norm of $x$. Apply the squared-norm splitting and use that its real part is $x$ and imaginary part is zero. This isometry is later used to prove equality, rather than just an upper bound, of extended operator norms.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.norm.summary: Embedding a real vector preserves its norm

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.re_e.text: The real projection of the complex extension of $A$ applied to $z$ is $A(\operatorname{Re}z)$. This identifies the real component of the complex-linear operator with the original real coefficient action. It is later used when transferring Fourier multiplier identities back to real-valued velocities and real test functions.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.re_e.summary: Real projection commutes with the complex extension

TorusEuler.EndpointMeanRecoveredWords.text: Records a finite family of spatial derivative words for the same recovered label velocity $g$. The empty word agrees with $g$ only on the time slab; derivatives and smoothness are required through order $N$. Each word also has a mixed representation fixed by the Leray projection and satisfies its differentiated projected equation, including the coefficient correction.
TorusEuler.EndpointMeanRecoveredWords.summary: Exact spatial derivatives of one recovered velocity

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.text:
Record equality of the labelwise temporal L2 path and the evaluated time curve for almost every label and almost every time. This predicate asserts no time continuity; continuity is supplied when a representative must be unique at every time.

The predicate is only almost-everywhere in both variables. Exceptional-time values can differ; at zero duration it is vacuous. Equality at all times requires a positive duration and continuous representatives.

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.add.text: If two mixed fields represent two time curves, their sum represents the pointwise sum of those curves. The proof intersects the almost-everywhere sets for both input representations with the representative identity for $L^2$ addition. This propagates compatibility through the finite source sums in the differentiated endpoint equation.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.add.summary: Represented fields remain compatible under addition

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.coeff.text: A represented mixed field stays represented after multiplication by compatible mixed and time-slice coefficients. The compatibility hypothesis requires the mixed coefficient's temporal action to equal pointwise multiplication almost everywhere for every input path. Applying it to the path at the current label transfers the representation to the product.

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.eqOn.text: Two continuous time curves representing the same mixed field agree at every time of a positive closed interval. Their primitives agree, and uniqueness of within-interval derivatives identifies their endpoint values as well.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.eqOn.summary: Continuous representatives of one mixed field coincide

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.integ.text: Integrating a mixed field in time represents the primitive of its continuous half-Hölder time curve, provided the duration is nonnegative. The proof uses almost-everywhere equality of the paths, invariance of the primitive under that equality, and commutation of evaluation with integration. This handles the Volterra term in differentiated residuals.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.integ.summary: Time integration preserves the spatial representation

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.norm_.text: If a mixed field represents a continuous half-Hölder time curve bounded by a nonnegative $M$, then its mixed norm is at most $\sqrt T\,M$ for $T\ge0$. The proof constructs the canonical mixed source and identifies it with the given representative through the joint-space embedding. This is a time-$L^2$ conversion, not a pointwise recovery estimate.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.norm_.summary: A continuous source bounds its mixed representative

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.of_sp.text: A continuous half-Holder curve whose L2 image agrees with almost every spatial slice of a mixed field represents that mixed field labelwise almost everywhere. The theorem changes the order of the slice description.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.of_sp.summary: Recovering path representation from spatial slices

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.spati.text: Compatible representatives of lower-order velocity words and coefficient actions give a time-curve representative for the mixed Leibniz correction. The result is assembled from coefficient multiplication and a finite sum.

A continuous time curve representing a mixed field has its L2 value equal to the mixed field's spatial slice for almost every time. The proof constructs a canonical mixed source from the curve and identifies their joint L2 images.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.spati.summary: Spatial slices of a represented mixed field

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.sub.text: The difference of two mixed fields represents the difference of their spatial time curves whenever each original pair satisfies the representation relation. Equality is tracked almost everywhere in both variables rather than assumed pointwise. It supplies compatibility for residuals and commutator corrections containing negative terms.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.sub.summary: Represented fields remain compatible under subtraction

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.zero.text: The zero mixed field represents the identically zero spatial half-Hölder curve. The statement uses the almost-everywhere representative relation in label and time, since even the zero $L^2$ class is compared through its chosen representative. It provides the base case for linear combinations of represented commutator terms.

TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalJets.text: Collects spatial half-Hölder jets for $F^*F$, $F^*(M^*-M)F$ and the source, together with mixed time-path realizations. Proof fields identify their actions almost everywhere, preserve all spatial derivative edges, and give spatial Lipschitz bounds for the zeroth coefficients. The structure contains regularity and compatibility data, not ellipticity, a flow equation or a solution of the endpoint problem.
TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalJets.summary: Compatible physical coefficients and source in both function spaces

TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery.text: Records that a specified label velocity is the lift of one solenoidal curve with the actual kinetic, vorticity and integrated-force jets. It retains recovered words at every finite order, the projected integrated equation, and both coercivity inequalities. This record links later quantitative estimates to the velocity already returned by the existence construction.
TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery.summary: The recovered mean retains its exact derivative data

TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery..text: For a supplied mean recovery, smooth deformation lift, and smooth periodic force, this constructs half Hölder words for the pulled force $F^*f$. The recovered source words equal their negative time primitives. At order $n+1$, the projected kinetic operator acts on the highest derivative of the same recovered velocity, while the right side uses velocity and force only through order $n$, with explicit binomial coefficient terms.
TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery..summary: The recovered mean obeys the higher time equation

TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery..text: Let a recovered physical mean solution on $[0,T]$ with $T\le1$ be given together with its recovered velocity words $v_w(t)$ through length $N$, kinetic coefficient $K$, vorticity coefficient $\Omega$ and source words $S_w$. Suppose $S_w(t)=-\int_0^tg_w$ on $[0,T]$ for continuous $g_w$; $\mu>0$, $L_K\ge0$, $|K(t,a)-K(t,b)|\le L_Kd(a,b)$, $\langle K(t,a)z,z\rangle\ge\mu|z|^2$ and $\|K(t)\|_\infty\le C_K$; $e_S(t)z=\mathbb P(K(t)z)$ with $\|e_S(t)^{-1}\|\le A_s$; $e_M$ is the mixed projection of multiplication by $K-J\Omega$ with $\|e_M^{-1}\|\le A_m$; and the inverse budget is at most $\mathrm{Cap}$. Let $\ell>0$, $K_{\rm cost}\ge0$, $G\ge0$, with $\mathrm{Cap}\cdot\ell^{|w|}\cdot2(\sup_t\|K_w\|+T\sup_t\|\Omega_w\|)\le K_{\rm cost}$ for $1\le|w|\le N$ and $\ell^{|w|}\|g_w(t)\|\le G$ for $|w|\le N$. Then $\ell^{|w|}\|v_w(t)\|\le\mathrm{Cap}(1+2^NK_{\rm cost})^NG$ for every $|w|\le N$ and $t\in[0,T]$. Here order zero refers to the time derivative, not to evaluation at $t=0$.
TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery..summary: The recovered mean has a word bound at time order zero

TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery..text: Reuses every field and every exact jet of a recovered mean while replacing its inverse deformation bound $\mathsf D_0$ by any $\mathsf D\ge\mathsf D_0>0$. Both reciprocal coercivity constants decrease, so their inequalities remain valid. The assumption $L\ge0$ ensures the mixed denominator is positive. No new solution is chosen, which preserves the link between existence and the later estimate.
TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery..summary: Increasing the inverse bound preserves the recovered mean

TorusEuler.EndpointRealTimeL2.text: This abbreviation is the real vector-valued L² space for Lebesgue measure restricted to $(0,T]$. It is the Hilbert space on which mixed endpoint coefficient operators act. The type contains all square-integrable time paths; zero time mean is a separate projection or subspace condition.
TorusEuler.EndpointRealTimeL2.summary: Real velocity paths on the restricted time interval

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.text:
Package the actual spatial derivative words of a periodic lift as half-Holder curves, including smooth time dependence, evaluation identities, spatial derivative relations, and finite uniform norms for each word.

This structure stores actual smooth curves and their compatibility proofs. It does not choose default derivatives; existence for a smooth periodic lift is a separate theorem requiring positive duration. Its fields place no claims outside the closed slab.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.summary: Spatial derivative words as smooth Holder curves

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.ba.text: For a smooth periodic lift on a positive-duration slab and a compatible half-Hölder jet package, the zeroth torus curve has a common spatial Lipschitz bound. Compactness and periodicity first bound the lifted gradient; controlled representatives of two torus points then give the factor-two metric conversion. The constant is existential and depends on the underlying field.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.ba.summary: Smooth periodic data give a uniform spatial Lipschitz bound

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.ev.text: Let $T>0$ and let $f$ be a smooth lifted field, jointly smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, given with its recovered half-Hölder words: torus fields $f_w(t)$, smooth in time on $[0,T]$, whose evaluation at the torus point of $x$ is the spatial derivative word $\partial^wf(t,x)$, with the strong spatial derivative relation between $f_w$ and $f_{jw}$. Then for every time order $i$, every word $w$, every time $t\in[0,T]$ and every $x$, evaluating the $i$th time derivative of the recovered word $f_w$ at the torus point of $x$ gives the actual spatial derivative word $\partial^w$ of the field's Eulerian time derivative $\partial_t^if(t,\cdot)$ at $x$. Both time derivatives are taken within $[0,T]$.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.ev.summary: Time derivatives of recovered Hölder words are derivatives of the lift

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.mu.text: For exact quotient jets of a smooth slab field and a positive label scale, bounds the weighted closed-time half-Hölder norm by $\sqrt2$ times the lifted Hölder jet supremum. The explicit hypothesis that the relevant set of jet values is bounded above prevents using a supremum without finiteness. The jet evaluation identity ensures this estimates the actual spatial derivative word.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.mu.summary: Lifted word bounds control the half Hölder curve

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.mu.text: Let $T>0$, $0<\ell\le1$, and let $f$ be jointly smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$ and periodic in space at each $t\in[0,T]$, with recovered half-Hölder words $f_w(t)$ as above. For every $N$, $i$, every word $w$ of length at most $N$ and every $t\in[0,T]$, $\ell^{|w|}\|\partial_t^if_w(t)\|_{C^{1/2}}\le4R/\sqrt\ell$, where $R=\sum_{|\beta|\le N+1}\ell^{|\beta|}\sup_{r\in[0,T],x}|\partial^\beta\partial_t^if(r,x)|$ is the finite unweighted label norm of order $N+1$, each multi-index counted once.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.mu.summary: The label norm one order higher bounds each recovered time word

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.mu.text: Assume raw derivatives of the selected time derivative have bounds $C(n)AD^{pn}$, with $D\ge1$, nonnegative $A,C$, positive $\ell$, and $\ell D^p\le1$. Then a recovered word of length $n$ has scaled half Hölder norm at most $6(C(n)+C(n+1))AD^p$. The spatial-order dependence is absorbed by the label scale, leaving one fixed parent-scale factor.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.mu.summary: Raw mixed derivative bounds control half Hölder words

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.sl.text: Let $T>0$, $\ell\ge0$, $C\ge0$, and let $f$ be jointly smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$ with recovered half-Hölder words $f_w(t)$. Suppose $\ell^{|w|}\|\partial_t^if_w(t)\|_{C^{1/2}}\le C$ for every word of length at most $n$ and every $t\in[0,T]$. Then the finite unweighted label norm $\sum_{|\beta|\le n}\ell^{|\beta|}\sup_{t,x}|\partial^\beta\partial_t^if|$ is at most $C$ times the number of multi-indices in three variables of order at most $n$.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.sl.summary: Bounds on recovered Hölder words bound the label norm

TorusEuler.EndpointSmoothPotential.text:
Package a real-valued smooth function on Euclidean label space together with lattice periodicity. No zero-mean normalization is part of this structure; only its gradient is relevant to the solenoidal test space.

Smoothness and periodicity are explicit structure fields. Constants and nonzero-mean potentials are allowed; adding a constant does not change the gradient used in the weak solenoidal tests.

TorusEuler.EndpointSobolevEnergyBound.text: For every label $a\in\mathbb T^3$ and every $v\in L^2([0,1];\mathbb R^3)$ with $\int_0^1v=0$, require $\int_0^1(Kv\cdot v+\Omega v\cdot Jv)\,dt\ge\mu\|v\|_{L^2}^2$, where $Jv(t)=\int_0^tv$. Thus $z=Jv$ has both zero endpoint values and ranges over $H^1_0$. This is exactly the test class and energy inequality in (A.2). The condition itself does not require $\mu>0$, coefficient symmetry or pointwise ellipticity; those are imposed separately when applying Theorem A.1.
TorusEuler.EndpointSobolevEnergyBound.summary: Require coercivity for every zero endpoint Sobolev path

TorusEuler.EndpointTorusL2.text:
The joint Hilbert space consists of vector fields square integrable over time restricted to the chosen interval and normalized Haar measure on the label torus. Its elements are almost-everywhere classes.

For nonpositive T the time measure is zero and this L2 space is trivial. Its elements are equivalence classes, so pointwise values must not be interpreted without separate slice or representative lemmas.

TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness.text: For specified $u_0,T_*,u,p$, the formal condition requires $u_0$ to be smooth, odd, divergence free and invariant under integer translations. The periodic Euler solution is smooth and odd on $[0,T_*)$, starts from $u_0$, has mean-zero pressure, and has no smooth continuation to a longer interval. Here $T_*>0$ is a finite real number. Both nonnegative time integrals of $\|\nabla u\|_\infty$ and $\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_\infty$ equal infinity; velocity is uniformly bounded and $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$. Velocity and its time derivative have uniform limits of every spatial derivative on compact sets disjoint from $\mathbb Z^3$. This specifies the required properties; existence is a separate assertion.
TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness.summary: Every conclusion required of the selected Euler solution

TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientCoordinatePo.text: Requires smooth coefficient slices, a positive table of order constants, boundedness of every coordinate-derivative supremum set, and the corresponding power estimate for their finite sum. The explicit boundedness-above clause is part of the mathematical content. It makes this encoding comparable with actual operator-norm derivative bounds under $D\ge1$.
TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientCoordinatePo.summary: Bounded coordinate versions of coefficient powers

TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientMultiIndexPo.text: Let $c(t,a)$ be a phase-independent coefficient with values in a real normed algebra, $a\in\mathbb R^3$ and $t$ in a specified set $I$. This condition requires smoothness in $a$, bounded derivatives of every order uniformly in $(t,a)$, and constants $C_m\ge1$ such that $|c|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^{q(m+1)}$. Here $|c|_m$ sums one supremum for each spatial multi-index of order $m$, and $q$ is a nonnegative integer. The constants are chosen after $\mathsf D$ and $c$ have been fixed. Consequently this condition alone does not state uniformity over a family of parent parameters or coefficients. The paper's real exponent can be enlarged to an integer when $\mathsf D\ge1$.
TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientMultiIndexPo.summary: Bounds all label derivatives with a fixed integer exponent

TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientPower.text: Encodes smoothness of every spatial coefficient slice and one order-indexed table $C_m\ge1$ such that $\|D^mc(t,x)\|\le C_mD^{a(m+1)}$ for all indices and points. The derivative is measured in operator norm. Uniformity is over $t$ and $x$ after $D$, $a$ and $c$ are fixed; the definition alone does not make the table uniform over different families.

TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientPower.mono.text: If the coefficient derivatives of $c$ satisfy $\|D^mc\|\le C_mD^{a(m+1)}$ with smooth slices, then they also satisfy the same condition with exponent $b$ whenever $D\ge1$ and $a\le b$. The same smoothness and prefactor table work. Monotonicity of nonnegative powers supplies the comparison; no new coefficient regularity is constructed.
TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientPower.mono.summary: Coefficient power bounds are monotone in the exponent

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.text:
Package solvers for admissible mean and zero-mean transverse sources, their pressure equations, and a divergence completion preserving zero mean. This is abstract input to the ordered recursion, not a proof of analytic solvability.

Solvers are supplied functions with equations and source admissibility proofs. This structure does not assert their existence for arbitrary analytic data; the physical realization provides them later. Its completion operator need not independently carry a divergence theorem in this abstract structure.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.summary: The mean and transverse solvers for a finite hierarchy

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text:
Construct the finite hierarchy from the supplied mean and transverse solvers, leading wave, completion switch, and phase-independent parent residual. The recursion determines each mean before the corresponding oscillation; positive-depth index behavior is proved separately.

The recursion is defined for every natural depth, including zero. The theorem that profiles vanish at index zero or beyond the retained depth assumes positive depth; the prescribed leading level is treated specially by the recursion. Do not extrapolate the positive-depth zero statement to depth zero.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: The finite profiles produced by ordered solves

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: At every index $p$, the average of the constructed mean $B_p$ equals that mean. The proof reads this off the averaging property stored with the mean at the recursive level. This is an operator-level phase-independence statement; interpreting it as independence of the phase variable uses the concrete periodic profile realization.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Every constructed mean is fixed by averaging

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: At each retained oscillatory level, including the leading level, the constructed completion equals the supplied completion operator applied to that oscillation. The library stores completion at its input level, whereas the paper names the output C at the next level.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Every retained oscillation receives its completion

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: Given a linear divergence operator, assume completed transverse outputs have zero divergence and every mean-solver output does too. The finite constructed velocity then has zero divergence. The theorem uses the actual selected completion at each retained index and treats the leading mean as zero; it does not derive the supplied solver divergence properties.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: The constructed finite velocity is divergence free

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: Assume that the mean and transverse equations have solvers and that the prescribed parent residual is independent of phase. At retained depth $P\ge1$, the constructed oscillatory velocity, mean velocity and two pressures are zero at index zero and at every index greater than $P$. The correction generated by an oscillation is zero at those indices as well. The formal indexing attaches this correction to $V_p$; the paper calls it $C_{p+1}$. Thus the conclusion leaves $C_{P+1}$ in the expansion and sets $C_1=0$. It is a statement about the finite recursive construction, without an assertion that an infinite series converges.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: The finite construction has no profiles beyond its retained depth

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: Fix a finite depth $P$, a leading transverse solution, a phase-independent residual $R$, and solvers for the mean and transverse equations. For $2\le p\le P$, let $H_p$ be the source formed from earlier levels and put $Y_j=V_j+C_j$. In paper notation the two forcings are $-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R$ and $-(H_p-\langle H_p\rangle_s)-\sum_{i=2}^{p}(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_{p+1-i}$. The formal statement proves the corresponding mean and oscillatory equations for the recursively constructed fields. It assumes linear operations for the material derivative, gradients and averaging, and bilinear operations for advection. Interpreting them as $\partial_t+M$, $\mathbf d$, $\kappa\partial_s$ and the displayed products gives the geometric equations, with $R=R_U\circ X$. Their analytic solvers and spatial regularity are inputs, not conclusions of this algebraic result.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Mean and oscillatory corrections satisfy the prescribed recursive equations

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: Given a leading transverse velocity and its phase pressure, a phase-independent parent residual and solvers for the remaining equations, the recursive construction has exactly that velocity and pressure at level one. Its first mean velocity and first mean pressure are zero. The conclusion holds for every nonnegative depth parameter, although the finite sum contains level one only when $P\ge1$. To obtain $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$ in §1.3, the supplied leading velocity must be the activated localized wave. This result does not identify an arbitrary input with that wave, and it does not state $C_1=0$.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: The first oscillation is retained and the first mean vanishes

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: Proves by strong induction that the actual selected finite construction has the velocity and pressure memberships at every index. It requires depth at least one, compatible initial data, operator closure and separate preservation by the chosen mean, transverse and completion solvers. Out-of-range levels use the construction’s proved zero values; retained levels follow the mean-before-transverse order.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Every selected hierarchy level preserves the required classes

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: If every selected mean solve satisfies the supplied seminorm estimate with one additional source derivative, then each constructed level from two through $P$ satisfies the corresponding measured mean bound. The forcing is identified using the actual ordered construction. The theorem transports a solve estimate into level notation rather than proving the analytic inverse bound.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: A selected mean estimate becomes a level estimate

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: Fix a depth $P\ge2$, phase averaging, the linear and quadratic operators of the expansion, and a chosen solution of each mean and transverse equation. For $2\le p\le P$, the recursively constructed pair $(B_p,\bar q_p)$ is the chosen mean solution with source $-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R_U\circ X$. The parent residual is assumed phase independent. This identifies the solution used by the recursion; it does not prove solvability of the endpoint problem from hypotheses on a fluid flow.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: The recursion uses the prescribed endpoint solution
