The threshold depends on the positive strength constant. These bounds supply one common constant $\mathsf D=\mu^9$ for transverse stability and positive coupling.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Both center estimates fit one parent scale

On $[t_0,t_0+\Theta/r]$, consider a supplied growing transverse wave $(\kappa,\mathbf a)$ over $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes\kappa_p+E_c$, starting with covector $\lambda E_3$ and amplitude in the positive direction $-E_1/S+E_2$. The nonzero preceding pair defines its orthonormal frame; freeze $\sigma=|\kappa_p||\mathbf a_p|$ and $

u}$, $S=\sigma/r$, $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$. The preceding pair solves the wave equations over continuous trace-free $B$, with continuous $E_c$ on a compact set containing the interval. For all sufficiently large integers $C_0$, assume $\Theta\ge2$, $\lambda
e0$, $C_0\varepsilon\le1$ and $C_0\Theta^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$. If $\mathsf D\ge252eS$ and $\mathsf D\ge2/(
u\varepsilon)$, every transverse amplitude solution satisfies $|\mathbf b(t)|/|\mathbf a(t)|\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/|\mathbf a(t')|$ for ordered times, and $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$. The seed is nonzero. Scaling both denominators by a positive constant gives (5.5). The defining source for the formal comparison quantity $\delta$ is absent, so its exact correspondence with (2.6) remains unchecked.

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text:
Let $(\kappa,\mathbf a)$ be a supplied growing transverse wave over $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes\kappa_p+E_c$ on $[t_0,t_0+\Theta/r]$, initially with $\kappa=\lambda E_3$ and amplitude in the positive direction $-E_1/S+E_2$. In the preceding wave's orthonormal frame freeze $\sigma=|\kappa_p||\mathbf a_p|$, $
u=E_1\cdot BE_2>0$ and $\eta=E_3\cdot BE_2>0$; put $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $S=\sigma/r$ and $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$. The preceding pair solves the wave equations over continuous trace-free $B$, with continuous $E_c$ on a compact set containing the interval. For every sufficiently large integer $C_0$, assume $\lambda
e0$, $\Theta\ge2$, $C_0\varepsilon\le1$ and $C_0\Theta^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$. For every solution $\mathbf b_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)M\mathbf b$ with $\mathbf b\perp\kappa$, the conclusion is $|\mathbf b(t)|/|\mathbf a(t)|\le252eS|\mathbf b(t')|/|\mathbf a(t')|$ for ordered times in the interval. TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Controls every transverse solution relative to the selected seed

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For a physical growing crossing and sufficiently strong smallness, any two ordered times in its active slab admit a continuous linear equivalence between their transverse planes. Its norm is at most $252eS$ times the ratio of the same growing amplitude’s endpoint norms. For every initial vector the conclusion supplies a full closed-slab amplitude path realizing the equivalence, with transversality throughout.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Physical transport is an equivalence between the transverse planes

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text:
For a nonzero transverse preceding wave, let $E_1=k_p/|k_p|$ and $E_2=\mathbf a_p/|\mathbf a_p|$. The formal object is the scalar $
u=E_1(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$. It is frozen at the activation time, not the time-dependent entry $B_{12}(t)$ elsewhere on the interval. Positivity of this number is required in the amplification data. The same $
u$ is used in $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$ and $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$; the error $\delta$ measures how the time-dependent entry differs from its frozen value.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The first coupling is evaluated at activation

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Given the older gradient $B$, preceding wave vectors $k_p,\mathbf a_p$, and error $E_c$, the formal object is $M(t)=B(t)+\mathbf a_p(t)\otimes k_p(t)+E_c(t)$. Here $(\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p)v=(k_p\cdot v)\mathbf a_p$. For the nonzero transverse preceding wave this equals $B+\sigma_pE_2\otimes E_1+E_c$, as in Section 2.2.1. The matrices are continuous on the prescribed compact set and the preceding vectors satisfy their ordinary differential equations there. This definition does not assert that $M$ itself is a global Euler velocity gradient or that $E_c$ is trace free.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The preceding wave contributes its rank-one gradient

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The formal object is $\sigma=|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|$, the strength of the preceding wave at the new wave’s activation time. Both factors use the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^3$ and are strictly positive under the amplification hypotheses. This is the fixed number denoted $\sigma$ in Section 2.2.1; the evolving strength is $\sigma_p(t)=|k_p(t)||\mathbf a_p(t)|$. Their ratio is estimated separately. The product is the size of the rank-one shear contribution when $k_p$ and $\mathbf a_p$ are perpendicular.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The initial strength fixes the time and shear scales

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The product of the preceding wave-vector and amplitude norms is positive at $t_0$. The proof applies the assumed nonvanishing of the preceding wave vector and amplitude at the activation time $t_0\in I$, so nonvanishing is supplied by the physical assumptions rather than inferred from a norm formula. This positivity is used to define a nonzero growth rate and shear.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The preceding strength is strictly positive at activation

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For the new wave, the formal object is $\eta_+=(\widehat k\times\widehat a)\cdot M\widehat a$, where $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$, $\widehat k=k/|k|$, and $\widehat a=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$. For nonzero perpendicular $k,\mathbf a$ this is the entry $E_{3,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$ used in Lemma 2.7. The definition accepts arbitrary vector functions. A zero vector is normalized to zero, so the formula gives zero if either vector vanishes; the new-wave theorems establish the nonzero transverse setting in which it is an orthonormal-frame coupling. No positivity is contained in this definition.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The coupling uses the full prescribed gradient

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For a new wave vector $k$ and amplitude $\mathbf a$, the formal object is $\nu_+=\widehat k\cdot M\widehat a$, with $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$. When $k,\mathbf a$ are nonzero and perpendicular, their normalized vectors are the first two vectors of the new wave’s frame, and this is exactly $E_{1,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$ in Lemma 2.7. The definition itself imposes neither the wave equations nor positivity. Normalization assigns zero to a zero vector; later positivity conclusions require the hypotheses of the amplification theorem.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The coupling is a scalar entry of the full gradient

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text:
With positive frozen strength $\sigma=|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|$ and coupling $
u=B_{12}(t_0)>0$, the formal object is $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$. It is positive and converts physical time into $	au=r(t-t_0)$. As the paper explains, the exact rate obtained by freezing the initial two-component system is $\sqrt{2
u(\sigma-
u)}$ when $\sigma>
u$. Thus $r$ is the leading strong-shear scale, not that exact frozen growth rate. The two differ by the factor $\sqrt{1-
u/\sigma}$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The scale is the leading strong-shear growth rate

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The record’s activation strength and first coupling are strictly positive, so their growth rate $\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$ is positive. The theorem derives this from the corresponding record facts. It ensures that the physical and normalized clocks are invertible and preserve time order.

The formal object is $\varepsilon=\eta/
u$, where $
u=B_{12}(t_0)>0$ and $\eta=B_{32}(t_0)>0$ are the preceding frame’s frozen entries. Both are evaluated at the activation time, so $\varepsilon$ is constant even when $B$ and the frame evolve. Positivity is part of the data; smallness is an additional hypothesis, imposed through $C_0\varepsilon\le1$. This number determines the reference angle by $	an\varphi=\varepsilon	au^2/2$. It is distinct from the evolving successor ratio $\eta_+/
u_+$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The ratio of positive couplings determines the reference angle

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The frozen ratio is the third coupling divided by the first. Both couplings are assumed strictly positive in the physical amplification data, so the ratio is positive as well. This fact validates the inverse and square-root expressions used for the reference turning interval and the successor crossing horizon.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The frozen coupling ratio is strictly positive

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Given a wave-vector path and amplitude path satisfying the affine equations on the physical set $I$, compose both with the positive clock. Under the hypotheses needed to build the normalized amplification window, they satisfy the corresponding equations on the entire closed normalized interval $[0,T]$. The theorem changes time units and does not assert initial data, transversality or nonvanishing for these new paths.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: A physical wave obeys the normalized equations

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text:
The formal object is $S=\sigma/r$, where $\sigma=|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|>0$ and $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}>0$ with $
u=B_{12}(t_0)$. Therefore $S=\sqrt{\sigma/(2
u)}$. It is the dimensionless scale used in the anisotropic components of the new wave: the $E_2$ component of $k$ and the $E_1,E_3$ components of $\mathbf a$ carry factors $S^{-1}$. Large $S$ describes strong preceding shear. Its positivity follows from the data; quantitative lower bounds such as $S\ge T^2$ require the smallness assumptions.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The shear scale compares shear rate with growth rate

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The frozen shear satisfies $S=r/(2\nu)$, using $r^2=2\sigma\nu$ and the original definition $S=\sigma/r$. The rate and first coupling are positive in the physical model, so division is legitimate. This alternate form is used to compare the center growth constant with the induction parameter.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The shear scale is determined by rate and coupling

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: The map from normalized to physical time is strictly increasing because the rate is positive. The proof divides a strict inequality by the positive rate and adds the activation time. This ensures that the reference turning bracket and the first crossing retain their order after returning to physical time.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The physical clock preserves strict time order

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: Multiplying physical time relative to activation by the positive rate gives a strictly increasing function. This inverse-clock monotonicity converts physical interval memberships and crossing inequalities into normalized ones. The theorem applies to all real times and does not itself state any wave property.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Elapsed normalized time preserves strict order

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For $E_1=k_p/|k_p|$, $E_2=\mathbf a_p/|\mathbf a_p|$ and $E_3=E_1\times E_2$, the formal object is $\eta=E_3(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$. The preceding vectors are nonzero and perpendicular, so this is an entry in an oriented orthonormal frame. The amplification data require $\eta>0$. This fixed value enters $\varepsilon=\eta/\nu$; it is not the time-dependent entry $B_{32}(t)$, whose relative variation contributes separately to the error $\delta$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The second coupling is evaluated in the preceding frame

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: For $T\ge2$ and $C_0\ge240$, this construction reparametrizes the preceding pair by the clock $\tau\mapsto t_0+\tau/r$ and divides both physical strains by the rate $r$. The hypotheses that the clock maps $[0,T]$ into $I$, that $C_0\varepsilon\le1$ for the coupling ratio $\varepsilon$, and that $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$ for the error size $\delta$ supply interval membership and the two smallness inequalities. The output is a normalized amplification window carrying derived coefficient bounds, positive ratio, nonvanishing data, and the normalized wave equations.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The physical assumptions supply a normalized amplification window

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: At a point of the normalized slab, each coupling computed from the normalized gradient equals the corresponding physical frame pairing divided by the frozen first coupling. The identity uses $2S/r=1/\nu$. It accepts arbitrary supplied $k$ and $a$; the separate nonzero transverse hypotheses are needed to call their normalized directions a moving orthonormal frame.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: Normalized couplings equal physical couplings divided by the frozen one

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.text: At a normalized time inside $[0,T]$, the gradient stored in the normalized amplification window equals $r^{-1}$ times the full physical gradient at the clocked time. The proof also matches the preceding-wave rank-one contribution, using nonzero preceding data. This guards against mixing the physical and normalized strain conventions in subsequent coupling estimates.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl.summary: The normalized gradient is the physical gradient divided by rate

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.Q.text:
The coordinate $Q=S(E_2\cdot k)/\lambda$, so the second frame component of $k$ is $\lambda Q/S$. The extra factor $S$ is the scaling used to obtain the reference equation $Q'=-\varepsilon Z$. The definition supplies the coordinate only; orthonormality, nonzero scaling parameters and the wave equation are hypotheses of later lemmas.

The formula contains an inverse or quotient. Its nondegenerate mathematical use requires the denominator conditions in the argument or the calling lemma; totalized inversion alone does not provide them.

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.Space.text:
This abbreviation is three-dimensional real Euclidean space. Its norm is the Euclidean norm; it is distinct from the maximum norm on the auxiliary pair of amplitude coordinates.

This is an abbreviation for a real Hilbert space, with no equation or nonzero-vector condition. The oriented frame lemmas impose perpendicular nonzero data.

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.X.text:
The coordinate $X=(E_1\cdot k)/\lambda$ in the moving frame. The scale $\lambda$ is the positive initial frequency in the comparison theorem. This scalar is defined for arbitrary frame and vector path, so the definition itself imposes no differential equation or nonzero denominator. Those hypotheses enter the decomposition and comparison results that explain how $X$ evolves.

The formula contains an inverse or quotient. Its nondegenerate mathematical use requires the denominator conditions in the argument or the calling lemma; the convention that division by zero gives zero does not provide them.

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.Z.text:
The coordinate $Z=(E_3\cdot k)/\lambda$ in the preceding frame. Initial data $k(t_0)=\lambda E_3(t_0)$ give $Z(t_0)=1$ when the frame is orthonormal and the scale $\lambda$ is nonzero. The amplitude’s third coordinate will divide by $Z$, so Lemma 2.4 subsequently proves that $Z$ stays at least $1/2$ on the comparison interval.

The formula contains an inverse or quotient. Its nondegenerate mathematical use requires the denominator conditions in the argument or the calling lemma; the convention that division by zero gives zero does not provide them.

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.text:
Define the square-root growth rate from the preceding strength and first coupling. It converts physical time to normalized time; strict positivity is proved only under positive physical parameters.

The rate is zero when twice the strength-coupling product is nonpositive, under the real square-root convention. The physically meaningful rescaling assumes both parameters positive, so the rate is nonzero.

Positive preceding strength $\sigma>0$ and positive first coupling $\nu>0$ imply that $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$ is strictly positive. The proof reduces this to positivity of the radicand. This supplies the nonzero denominator required to pass between physical time and normalized time; it does not itself bound the error or construct a wave.
With positive preceding strength and first coupling, squaring the amplification rate gives twice their product. This supplies the scalar cancellation in the normalized model coefficients.

The formal object is $\delta=\sup_I|B_{12}/
u-1|+\sup_I|B_{32}/\eta-1|+r^{-1}\sup_I\|B\|+
u^{-1}\sup_I\|E_c\|$, with entries taken in the preceding wave’s frame and matrix norms the Euclidean operator norms. It agrees with (2.6) when $I=[t_0,t_0+T/r]$. The formalization also allows a larger compact set, measuring all four terms there. The definition accepts arbitrary sets and denominators. Real suprema of empty or unbounded sets are assigned zero, as is division by zero; the amplification hypotheses supply a nonempty compact set, continuity, and positive $
u,\eta,r$, so these exceptional assignments do not enter the estimates.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.summary: Four suprema quantify the departure from the reference setting

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.text:
Let $t_0\le T$. Suppose $B$ is trace free and differentiable in time, and a nonzero perpendicular pair $(\kappa_p,\mathbf a_p)$ solves the wave equations over $B$ on $[t_0,T]$. Assume $\|B\|\le M$, $\|B_t\|\le D$ and $\|E_c\|\le E$ there. Freeze $
u=E_1(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$ and $\eta=E_3(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$, with $0<\eta\le
u$, and take $r>0$. The formal statement gives $\delta\le8[(T-t_0)(M^2+D)/\eta+M/r+E/
u]$, with operator norms and positive denominators. It permits arbitrary valid uniform upper bounds and supplies the explicit constant eight. Here $\delta$ is the paper's expression (2.6), with suprema over $[t_0,T]$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.summary: Bounds comparison error by strain variation and central corrections

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.text: On a nonempty closed interval $[t_0,t_1]$, an orthonormal frame with the stated axis-rate bounds and matrix, derivative, and perturbation bounds controls the physical error $\delta$ by $8[(t_1-t_0)(M^2+D)/\eta+M/r+E_{\max}/\nu]$. The scaling rate is positive and the initial couplings satisfy $0<\eta\le\nu$. These hypotheses make the denominators and real suprema legitimate.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.summary: Frame-rate bounds control the physical comparison error

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.text: If the universal threshold dominates a fixed coefficient and exponent, its finite-smallness inequality bounds that smaller polynomial times delta by epsilon. The horizon must be at least one and the quantities nonnegative.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.summary: A fixed polynomial fits the smallness budget

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.text: A threshold at least two and its product with nonnegative epsilon at most one imply epsilon at most one half. This is a numerical prerequisite for the comparison estimates.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.summary: The epsilon bound from the universal threshold

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.text: Assume $T\ge2$, $\delta,\varepsilon\ge0$, $S>0$, $S^{-1}\le2\delta$, and an integer $C_0\ge240$ with $C_0\varepsilon\le1$ and $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$. Then $\varepsilon\le1/2$, $240\delta T^6\le1$, $T\delta\le1$, and $T^2\le S$. These are the quantitative inequalities needed to absorb polynomial errors and bound the scaled coordinates. The formal exponent $C_0$ is a natural number, so $T^{C_0}$ is an ordinary integer power. This arithmetic implication does not derive $S^{-1}\le2\delta$ from the physical gradients; that estimate is a separate input here.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio.summary: The prescribed smallness supplies four normalized bounds

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.coefficient_.text: The norm of a strain controls each of its orthonormal-frame entries.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.coefficient_.summary: The strain norm controls its frame coefficients

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.continuousOn.text: A jointly smooth parent on a positive closed slab has a continuous spatial gradient at the origin on any comparison interval contained between time zero and the parent endpoint. The proof restricts the joint spatial derivative along the central particle. It does not require that the comparison interval have positive length.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.continuousOn.summary: The actual central gradient is continuous on comparison intervals

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.coordinate_i.text: At the activation time $t_0$, assume an orthonormal frame, a nonzero frequency $\lambda$ and the initial wave vector $k(t_0)=\lambda E_3(t_0)$. The formal statement gives $\zeta_1(t_0)=0$, $\zeta_2(t_0)=0$, $\zeta_3(t_0)=1$, where $\zeta=(E_1\cdot k,SE_2\cdot k,E_3\cdot k)/\lambda$. Under $\tau=r(t-t_0)$ these are precisely $\zeta(0)=(0,0,1)$ after (2.3). The identity does not require $\lambda>0$, any restriction on $S$, or the wave equation. Positivity of the frequency belongs to the later amplification setting.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.coordinate_i.summary: Launching along the third frame vector gives the prescribed initial coordinates

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry.text: For three vectors $E_1,E_2,E_3$ in Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ and a linear map $B$, the formal entry is $E_i\cdot BE_j$. With an orthonormal frame these are the matrix components $B_{ij}$ of Lemma 2.2; in particular $\nu=B_{12}$ and $\eta=B_{32}$. The supplied formula itself does not require orthonormality or trace zero. Its coordinate positions are numbered from zero, so the first, second and third positions correspond to the paper’s subscripts $1,2,3$. No transpose or interchange of row and column is involved.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry.summary: Scalar products express a linear map in the supplied frame

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry_strain.text: In an orthonormal frame $E_1,E_2,E_3$, the frame entries $\langle E_i,ME_j\rangle$ of the strain $M=B+S\sigma\,E_2\langle E_1,\cdot\rangle+E$ are those of $B$ plus those of $E$, plus $S\sigma$ in the single entry $\langle E_2,ME_1\rangle$, row 1 and column 0 when axes are numbered from zero.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry_strain.summary: Only one matrix entry contains the added shear

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.euclidean_er.text: The componentwise estimate gives the Euclidean estimate used in the affine-wave comparison.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.euclidean_er.summary: Component bounds imply the Euclidean error bound

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.exists_frequ.text: There are uniform comparison and initial-frequency thresholds such that every supplied actual parent window satisfying the schedule, strength, coupling, and older-gradient bounds admits a later-wave selection. The output combines the crossing and the center estimates for one trajectory at scale $\lambda_{j+2}$, with $\mathsf D=\mu^9$. The parent window itself remains an explicit input.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.exists_frequ.summary: The schedule constructs a later wave over the actual parent

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.exists_later.text: The actual central gradient splitting constructs a physical amplification window once the preceding cutoff equals one on the new slab. The hypotheses include nonzero perpendicular preceding data, their affine equations, continuous actual gradients, a divergence-free older field, and positive frozen couplings. Continuity of the correction is deduced from the splitting instead of assumed separately.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.exists_later.summary: A completed preceding cutoff yields an actual comparison window

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame.text: Given paths $k_p,\mathbf a_p$ in Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$, the formal frame is $E_1=k_p/|k_p|$, $E_2=\mathbf a_p/|\mathbf a_p|$, $E_3=E_1\times E_2$, as in §1.1 and Lemma 2.2. This definition alone does not assert orthonormality: that requires both vectors to be nonzero and perpendicular. Normalization assigns the zero vector to a zero input, so a vanishing wave vector or amplitude still produces a defined triple but not an orthonormal frame. Its three positions correspond, in order, to the paper’s axes $E_1,E_2,E_3$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame.summary: Nonzero transverse vectors determine the three oriented frame vectors

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.hasDerivWith.text: Let $f$ be a vector-valued path whose derivative at $t_0+\tau/r$, relative to a time set $I$, is $v$. Suppose $s\mapsto t_0+s/r$ maps the chosen normalized time set $J$ into $I$. The formal statement gives derivative $v/r$ for $s\mapsto f(t_0+s/r)$ relative to $J$ at $\tau$. This includes the one-sided derivatives at interval endpoints used in §2.2.1. It does not require $r\ne0$: division by zero is assigned zero, making the reparametrized path constant when $r=0$. The application has $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}>0$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.hasDerivWith.summary: An affine change of time divides the derivative by the growth rate

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.later_compar.text: If the next activation lies within the first old half interval and the new half length is at most one quarter of the old one, the full next comparison slab lies inside the old slab. Nonnegativity of the new half length is explicit. This elementary interval containment allows previous wave equations to be restricted to the next step.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.later_compar.summary: The next comparison interval fits inside its parent

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.mapsTo_ampli.text: For a positive growth rate $r$, sends every $\tau\in[0,T]$ to physical time $t_0+\tau/r$ in $[t_0,t_0+T/r]$. The theorem does not require a separate sign assumption on $T$; when the source interval is empty the mapping assertion is vacuous. In the amplification application, $T\ge2$ supplies the intended nonempty window.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.mapsTo_ampli.summary: The inverse clock preserves the time window

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.mapsTo_inver.text: For a positive rate $r$, every physical time in $[t_0,t_0+T/r]$ maps under $t\mapsto r(t-t_0)$ into $[0,T]$. Positivity allows multiplying both endpoint inequalities without reversing order. No positivity of $T$ is required in the statement; when $T<0$ the source interval is empty.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.mapsTo_inver.summary: Normalized time stays inside the prescribed interval

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.movingFrame_.text: At a time $t$ in a time set $I$, let $B:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ have trace zero. Suppose $\kappa(t),\mathbf a(t)$ are nonzero and perpendicular, with $\kappa_t=-B^T\kappa$ and $\mathbf a_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)B\mathbf a$ there, taking derivatives within $I$. Form $E_1=\kappa/|\kappa|$, $E_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$ and $E_3=E_1\times E_2$. Each $E_i$ has a derivative within $I$ whose Euclidean norm is at most $2\|B\|$. The matrix norm is the operator norm. The statement is pointwise and requires no bound on $B_t$; a uniform bound for $B$ gives the displayed interval estimate in §6.2.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.movingFrame_.summary: Each frame vector has speed bounded by twice the strain

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.moving_waveV.text: Derives the three exact normalized-time equations for $X,Q,Z$ from the preceding affine wave and the new wave-vector equation. The old strain is trace free, the preceding vectors are nonzero and perpendicular, and $\lambda$ and $S$ are nonzero. Both strain operators already use normalized time. The error entries appear with their actual factors of $S$ or $S^{-1}$; this lemma establishes equations, not error bounds.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.moving_waveV.summary: Wave-vector equations in the preceding moving frame

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.moving_waveV.text: For a preceding affine wave and its new wave vector, proves $|X-x|+|Q+\varepsilon t|+|Z-1|\le120\delta T^6\le1/2$. It assumes $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, $T\ge2$, $S\ge1$, nonzero $\lambda$, the normalized strain bounds, correct initial direction, and $240\,\delta\,T^6\le1$. This is the coordinate comparison only; the separate norm comparison and amplitude estimates need further lemmas.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.moving_waveV.summary: The scaled wave vector stays close to the reference

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_a.text: Under the clock mapping hypothesis, composing both wave vectors with the affine normalized clock preserves the ODE form with the strain divided by the rate. The algebraic theorem is total even at rate zero; its physical use has a positive rate.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_a.summary: The affine wave equations after time rescaling

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_c.text:
For any frame family and operator $B$, rewrites $2(\sigma/r)\langle e_i,(B/r)e_jangle$ as $\langle e_i,Be_jangle/
u$. It assumes positive $r,\sigma,
u$ and $r^2=2\sigma
u$. Orthonormality is unnecessary because only bilinearity and the scalar identity are used. This converts the normalized first and third entries into the paper’s relative coupling errors.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_c.summary: A scaled entry becomes a ratio to the coupling

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_n.text: Transforms both new-wave ODEs under $t=t_0+\tau/r$ and rewrites the preceding rank-one shear using normalized frame axes and the relative strength. It requires $r\ne0$, the condition that $\tau\mapsto t_0+\tau/r$ maps the normalized time set into the physical one, and nonzero preceding vectors at activation and the evaluated time. It assumes neither positivity of $r$ nor preceding-wave evolution; those facts are needed by other parts of the amplification argument.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_n.summary: Rescale the wave over the full parent gradient

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r.text: Let $k_p,\mathbf a_p$ be nonzero both at time zero and at time $t$, and let $r\ne0$. Put $\sigma=|k_p(0)||\mathbf a_p(0)|$, $\sigma_p(t)=|k_p(t)||\mathbf a_p(t)|$ and $E_1=k_p/|k_p|$, $E_2=\mathbf a_p/|\mathbf a_p|$. The formal identity is $(\sigma/r)(\sigma_p/\sigma)E_2\otimes E_1=(\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p)/r$. Multiplication by $r$ recovers the preceding-wave term in $M$ in §2.2.1. This algebra does not require perpendicularity or an evolution equation. Time zero here is the chosen base time; the physical application shifts it to $t_0$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r.summary: Normalizing the wave directions preserves the preceding wave’s rank-one gradient

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r.text:
Let $I$ be compact and contain $t_0$, with a continuous frame orthonormal at $t_0$, continuous matrices $B,E_c$, $\sigma>0$, and positive frozen entries $
u=B_{12}(t_0)$, $\eta=B_{32}(t_0)$ satisfying $\eta/
u\le1$. Put $r=\sqrt{2\sigma
u}$, $S=\sigma/r$, and put $\delta=\sup_I|B_{12}/
u-1|+\sup_I|B_{32}/\eta-1|+\sup_I\|B\|/r+\sup_I\|E_c\|/
u$, with $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$. The formal statement proves $\delta\ge0$, $S^{-1}\le2\delta$, and, for every $t\in I$, $\|B/r\|\le\delta$, $\|E_c/r\|\le\delta/S$, $|B_{12}/
u-1|\le\delta$, $|B_{32}/
u-\eta/
u|\le\delta$. Operator norms are Euclidean. No wave evolution is needed for this estimate; compactness and continuity make the suprema finite.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r.summary: The four physical suprema bound the rescaled coefficients

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_s.text: Under positive growth rate and frozen strength and coupling, with $r^2=2\sigma\nu$, identifies $(\sigma/r)\|(1/r)E\|$ with $\|E\|/(2\nu)$. The identity explains the large factor introduced by scaled coordinates. It is an equality for any continuous linear error operator and does not itself impose the small error budget $\delta$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_s.summary: The scaled matrix error is measured against the coupling

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_s.text: The normalization in time divides the full older-plus-wave-plus-error gradient by the rate.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_s.summary: Time normalization divides the full strain by the rate

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_t.text: Multiplying the background operator by the reciprocal rate preserves zero trace. This purely linear identity does not require the rate to be nonzero.

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_w.text: At a time in a set $J$, let $(E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be orthonormal, $b_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$, $d_{ij}=E_i\cdot EE_j$. Assume $E_1'=-b_{12}E_2-b_{13}E_3$, $E_2'=b_{12}E_1-b_{32}E_3$, $E_3'=b_{13}E_1+b_{32}E_2$, and $k'=-M^Tk$, where $M=B+ScE_2\otimes E_1+E$. For $\lambda,S\ne0$, define $(X,Q,Z)=(E_1\cdot k,SE_2\cdot k,E_3\cdot k)/\lambda$. The formal statement gives $X'=-b_{11}X-[c+(b_{21}+b_{12})/S]Q-(b_{31}+b_{13})Z-d_{11}X-d_{21}Q/S-d_{31}Z$, $Q'=-b_{22}Q-2Sb_{32}Z-Sd_{12}X-d_{22}Q-Sd_{32}Z$, and $Z'=-b_{33}Z-(b_{23}-b_{32})Q/S-d_{13}X-d_{23}Q/S-d_{33}Z$. Derivatives are relative to $J$. Here $(X,Q,Z)=\zeta$ in the paper; normalized physical time uses $B/r,E_c/r$ and $c=\sigma_p/\sigma$. The identity assumes no smallness, trace condition or nonvanishing of $k$.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_w.summary: Moving-frame differentiation retains every component of the gradient error

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.physical_aff.text: If normalized paths solve the equations for the strain $M/r$ on $[0,T]$, their compositions with $r(t-t_0)$ solve the physical equations on $[t_0,t_0+T/r]$. The amplitude may also be multiplied by any constant $c$, including zero. The theorem assumes $r>0$ and returns within-set derivatives on the closed slab, without adding a nonvanishing conclusion.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.physical_aff.summary: The inverse clock restores the physical wave equations

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.polynomial_w.text: Let $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, $T\ge2$ and $D\ge0$, with $12DT^3\le1$. On $[0,T]$, suppose $(X,Q,Z)(0)=(0,0,1)$ and $X'=-Q+r_1$, $Q'=-\varepsilon Z+r_2$, $Z'=r_3$, where each $|r_i|\le D(|X|+|Q|+|Z|)$. The formal statement gives $|X-\varepsilon\tau^2/2|+|Q+\varepsilon\tau|+|Z-1|\le24DT^5$ for every $\tau\in[0,T]$. It uses the sum of absolute coordinate errors, which bounds their Euclidean norm. This supplies the perturbative estimate behind (2.10), conditional on these residual bounds; it does not itself obtain them from the physical gradients.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.polynomial_w.summary: Small residuals give an explicit polynomial error from the triangular model

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.scaled_waveV.text: At a fixed time, let $(E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be orthonormal and let $\lambda,S\ne0$. Define the coordinates by $\zeta_1=(k\cdot E_1)/\lambda$, $\zeta_2=S(k\cdot E_2)/\lambda$, $\zeta_3=(k\cdot E_3)/\lambda$. The formal statement proves $k=\lambda(\zeta_1E_1+\zeta_2E_2/S+\zeta_3E_3)$, the wave-vector part of (2.3). The assertion is pointwise linear algebra and includes $k=0$. It neither assumes the wave equation nor constructs an amplitude. Nonzero scales are required because the reconstruction cancels the divisions used in the coordinates.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.scaled_waveV.summary: Projection reconstructs the wave vector in the scaled orthonormal coordinates

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.strain.text:
The normalized strain is B plus the rank-one shear Sσratio e₁⊗e₀ plus E. Orthonormality and evolution of the frame are additional hypotheses when this algebraic expression is used in the amplitude equations.

This is a sum of continuous linear maps for arbitrary data. It imposes neither orthonormality of the frame nor trace or symmetry conditions.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.strain.summary: Older strain plus the leading shear and error

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.strengthRati.text:
The preceding wave strength normalized by its value at activation.

The strength ratio divides by the initial product of vector norms. Nonzero initial wave vector and amplitude are needed for the ratio to be a physical normalization.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.strengthRati.summary: The preceding strength relative to its initial value

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.strengthRati.text: On $[0,T]$, suppose $k_p,\mathbf a_p$ are nonzero, perpendicular paths satisfying $k_p\prime=-B^Tk_p$, $\mathbf a_p\prime=-B\mathbf a_p+2(k_p\cdot B\mathbf a_p)k_p/|k_p|^2$ over trace-free $B$, with Euclidean operator norm $\|B(t)\|\le\delta$ and $T\delta\le1$. The formal statement proves $|\sigma_p(t)/\sigma_p(0)-1|\le2T\delta$, where $\sigma_p=|k_p||\mathbf a_p|$. This is the strength estimate used in Lemma 2.4, after time normalization makes $B$ the physical background divided by $r$. The denominator is positive by the initial nonvanishing assumptions. Only relative derivatives on the interval are needed; smoothness of $B$ is not an additional hypothesis.
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.strengthRati.summary: A small older gradient keeps the preceding strength close to its initial value

TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.waveVector_c.text: Let $0\le\varepsilon\le1/2$, $T\ge2$, $0\le\tau\le T$, and assume $|X-\varepsilon\tau^2/2|+|Q+\varepsilon\tau|+|Z-1|\le1/2$. The formal statement gives $1/2\le Z\le3/2$, $|X|\le T^2$, $|Q|\le T$ and $X^2+Q^2/S^2+Z^2\ge1/4$. These are algebraic consequences of the error bound, before any amplitude equation is used. The conclusion holds for every real $S$, because division by zero is assigned zero and the $Z^2$ term already supplies the lower bound. In the physical application $S>0$ and the last expression is $m$ in (2.3).
TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.waveVector_c.summary: A half-unit coordinate error keeps the third component and norm denominator positive

TorusEuler.Paper.AdmissibleThreshold.text: For a nonnegative integer $b$ and functions $F,\mathcal B$ on the nonnegative integers, the formal condition requires, at positive indices, that $\mathcal B$ be nondecreasing, positive, at least $F$, and satisfy $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$, where $K(s)=320b(s+1)$. Values at zero are unrestricted. The function $F$ is a proposed majorant of the fixed-order analytic constants; the inequality $F(s)\le\mathcal B(s)$ alone does not identify those constants or prove that $F$ bounds them. The condition also does not itself require $b\ge1$. Those facts must be supplied in the application to the parameter choice of §1.5.
TorusEuler.Paper.AdmissibleThreshold.summary: Positive thresholds dominate costs and satisfy the logarithmic floor

TorusEuler.Paper.AmplitudeVector.text: For a prescribed wave vector $k$ on a compact physical time set $I$, the formal condition requires $\mathbf a'=-M\mathbf a+2(k\cdot M\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ and $\mathbf a\cdot k=0$ at every time in $I$, where $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$. Derivatives are taken relative to $I$. This is the amplitude vector of §2.2.1; no initial amplitude or nonvanishing condition is imposed, and the zero solution is allowed. The formula assigns zero to division by zero. Its physical use accompanies a launched wave vector that is nonzero on the active interval, so that convention does not alter the pressure coefficient there.
TorusEuler.Paper.AmplitudeVector.summary: The amplitude solves its linear equation and stays perpendicular to the wave vector

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixB.CutoffSymbol.text: The formal object is a smooth function $\psi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $0\le\psi\le1$, $\psi(\zeta)=1$ for $|\zeta|\le1$, $\psi(\zeta)=0$ for $|\zeta|>2$, and $\psi(-\zeta)=\psi(\zeta)$. Thus its support is compact and contained in the closed ball of radius two. Appendix B assumes radiality; the formal condition requires only evenness, which admits additional symbols. This is a condition on the symbol, not the definition of the operator $S_\Lambda$ or a proof of any operator estimate. No frequency parameter or field is selected here.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixB.CutoffSymbol.summary: Records smoothness, support and evenness of the symbol

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixB.CutoffSymbol..text: Suppose $\psi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ is smooth, takes values in $[0,1]$, equals one on the unit ball, vanishes outside the ball of radius two, and has equal values at points with equal Euclidean norm. The formal statement shows that $\psi$ satisfies the cutoff conditions used in Appendix B. The only deduction is evenness, since $|-\zeta|=|\zeta|$; all other conditions are supplied as hypotheses. It therefore verifies that every radial symbol allowed by the paper is allowed by the formalization, without asserting that an even symbol must be radial.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixB.CutoffSymbol..summary: Derives the formal symbol conditions from radiality

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixB.cutoffSymbol_.text: This theorem shows that the fixed dyadic multiplier cutoff used in the construction is an admissible cutoff symbol in the sense of Appendix B. It gathers the existing smoothness, range, unit-ball and support facts and its symmetry under negation. The paper allows a fixed radial symbol rather than naming this particular object; this is one admissible implementation, not an identification of all choices.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixB.cutoffSymbol_.summary: The fixed cutoff satisfies the appendix hypotheses

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientNo.text:
This requires every coefficient slice $c(t,\cdot)$ to be $C^\infty$ and every unweighted label-jet value set through order $n$ to be bounded above. It is the finiteness condition for all $|c|_m$ with $m\le n$. A companion theorem transfers it to the phase-independent lift for arbitrary weights.

Smoothness rules out derivative defaults, and boundedness above rules out unbounded real suprema. Nonemptiness follows from the inserted zero, including when the time set is empty. The condition asserts no temporal smoothness, no phase dependence and no positivity of external weights. No integral, inverse, square root or conversion from extended nonnegative reals is introduced.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientNo.summary: Smooth coefficient derivatives with finite bounds

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientNo.text: If the coefficient c has smooth bounded label jets through order n, its phase-independent lift has finite mixed norm at the same order for every radius ℓ and phase width h. The proof separates words containing the phase direction, which vanish, from label-only words, whose values are scalar multiples of bounded sets. This supplies the finiteness guard that the companion expression identity does not assume.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientNo.summary: Finite coefficient norms remain finite after adding a phase

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientPo.text: For $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to X$, with $X$ a real normed space, this condition requires smoothness in the label variable, bounded derivatives uniformly over the specified time set $I$, and $|c|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^{q(m+1)}$ for every $m\ge0$. The sequence $(C_m)$ is an explicit input, and $q$ is a nonnegative integer. The quantity $|c|_m$ is the sum of the suprema of the coordinate derivatives with $|\beta|=m$. In Lemma D.2 the output constants are chosen before $I$, $\mathsf D$ and the fields, which supplies the paper's uniformity. This condition by itself imposes no lower bound on $\mathsf D$; the coefficient estimates separately assume $\mathsf D\ge1$.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientPo.summary: Specifies the constants before measuring a coefficient

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientPo.text: For any coefficient $c$ satisfying the power bound (D.6), that is, smooth in $a$ at every time, with bounded coordinate-derivative sets and $|c|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^{a(m+1)}$ for all $m$, and any chosen $n$, this extracts smoothness and the boundedness conditions through order $n$. The conclusion is that $c$ is smooth at every time and every supremum $\sup_{t,a}|\partial_a^\beta c|$ with $|\beta|\le n$ entering $\|c\|_{[n]}$ is finite. It uses the explicit boundedness part of (D.6), not a conclusion inferred from a possibly default-valued real norm inequality. $\mathsf D$ and the coefficient exponent need no extra restriction for this extraction.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.CoefficientPo.summary: Power bounds give finite coefficient norms at every order

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.FieldNormFini.text:
This is the analytic side condition for the finite mixed derivative norm: every time slice is $C^\infty$ in $(a,s)$, and every set of derivative values entering the finite sum is bounded above. It concerns only words of total order at most $n$, although the slice smoothness is unrestricted. It does not itself require phase periodicity or positivity of $\ell$ and $h$; the results using it state those separately where needed.

This condition is the guard, not another numerical norm. Its smoothness clause excludes zero-default derivatives at the measured orders, and boundedness above excludes the default value for an unbounded real supremum. Nonemptiness of each value set already follows from the inserted $0$. If the time set $I$ is empty the conditions are vacuous and all value sets are $\{0\}$; that is an allowed zero-domain convention. Positive $\ell,h$ must still come from the caller.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.FieldNormFini.summary: Smooth mixed jets with bounded supremum sets

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.HolderFieldNo.text:
This requires $C^\infty$ label slices and boundedness of every set of supremum values and half-Hölder quotients through weighted order $n$. It is the finiteness condition paired with the half-Hölder field norm. It imposes no temporal differentiability because the time variable is only an index of a uniform bound.

Smoothness excludes default spatial derivatives; boundedness above excludes unbounded real suprema. The quotient radicand is $|x-y|\ge0$, with zero numerator at $x=y$, so its zero-over-zero diagonal contributes only zero. Each set explicitly includes $0$ and is nonempty. An empty time set is permitted and gives the trivial zero-domain case. No positive radius hypothesis is included here.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.HolderFieldNo.summary: Smooth label jets with bounded Hölder quotients

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.coefficientNo.text:
This sums $\ell^m|c|_m$ for $0\le m\le n$. For a smooth phase-independent coefficient and $\ell\ge0$, a companion identity identifies it with the mixed norm of $(t,a,s)\mapsto c(t,a)$, for any $h$. This definition uses the explicit powers $\ell^m$, so positivity matters if it is to behave as the paper’s norm.

The derivative words use the unrestricted derivative expression and therefore can have the default zero value where differentiability is absent. Smoothness of every spatial slice is part of the corresponding finiteness condition. Each jet-value set contains $0$ by definition, so it is nonempty even for an empty time set. Without boundedness above its real supremum can return the default zero; the finiteness conditions supply exactly that missing guard. The empty time set gives an identically zero norm and is allowed by these general definitions; the paper applications use nonempty slabs. The real suprema are those of the order-$m$ coefficient norms $|c|_m$. A negative $\ell$ can create cancellation between different orders, while $\ell=0$ erases all positive orders; the identity lemmas assume $\ell\ge0$ and the analytic estimates assume $\ell>0$. At $m=0$ the convention $\ell^0=1$ correctly retains the field itself.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.coefficientNo.summary: The weighted finite norm of a phase independent coefficient

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.coefficientNo.text: For a smooth phase-independent coefficient and $\ell\ge0$, the explicit sum $\sum_{m\le n}\ell^m|c|_m$ equals the finite word norm with only label directions. It is the specialization without Hölder quotients of the corresponding identity for label word norms, in the direction useful for replacing a coefficient norm by a word norm. Boundedness is not part of the theorem, so genuine norm interpretation remains a separate finiteness obligation.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.coefficientNo.summary: Coefficient norms equal the weighted label word sum

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.coefficientOr.text: For a phase-independent field $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to X$, this expression is $|c|_m=\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{t\in I,a\in\mathbb R^3}|\partial_a^\beta c(t,a)|$, with the norm of the real normed target space $X$. A sorted list of coordinate differentiations represents each multi-index once. The supremum includes all times in the chosen set, not time derivatives; choosing $I=[t_0,T]$ gives the paper's interval. The expression uses real-valued suprema, so the separate boundedness hypotheses are needed for it to measure the derivatives. It does not assert smoothness or boundedness of an arbitrary coefficient.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.coefficientOr.summary: Sums each spatial multi-index once at a fixed order

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.fieldNorm.text: For $f(t,a,s)$, $a\in\mathbb R^3$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, the expression sums the suprema of $\ell_*^{|\beta|}h^j\partial_a^\beta\partial_s^jf$ over $|\beta|+j\le n$, counting each pair $(\beta,j)$ once. The supremum runs over the entire chosen time set, all labels and all phases. For positive scales and bounded smooth derivatives this is $\|f\|_{[n]}$ in (D.1); for a periodic profile the phase supremum may equivalently be taken over one period. The expression itself neither requires periodicity nor proves boundedness. Smoothness and boundedness are separate assumptions in the estimates that use it, and there are no time derivatives in this norm.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.fieldNorm.summary: Weights label derivatives and phase derivatives separately

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.fieldNorm_pha.text: Let $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to X$ be smooth in its spatial variable at every time, let $\ell_*\ge0$, and let $n\ge0$ be an integer. Regarding $c(t,a)$ as a function of $(t,a,s)$ independent of $s$, the formal statement gives $\|c\|_{[n]}=\sum_{m=0}^n\ell_*^m|c|_m$ for every real phase weight $h$. Every derivative containing a phase differentiation is zero, so only spatial multi-indices remain. This identifies the two expressions used in Appendix D. Boundedness is not a hypothesis of this identity between expressions; it must be supplied separately when interpreting them as finite derivative norms.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.fieldNorm_pha.summary: Identifies the mixed norm of a phase-independent field

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderFieldNo.text: For a phase-independent field $c(t,a)$, this expression is the sum over $|\beta|\le n$ of the uniform-in-time half-Hölder norms of $\ell_*^{|\beta|}\partial_a^\beta c$. Labels range over $\mathbb R^3$ and there is no time differentiation. Each half-Hölder norm is the maximum of the spatial supremum and $\sup_{a\ne b}|g(a)-g(b)|/|a-b|^{1/2}$. The coincident-point quotient is assigned zero. The customary sum of these two quantities is between this maximum and twice it. The paper does not specify that internal convention; the distinction changes constants, not the boundedness class. Boundedness of all quantities entering the expression is a separate hypothesis.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderFieldNo.summary: Uses spatial Hölder bounds uniformly over the time set

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderFieldNo.text: Let $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to X$ be smooth in the label variable, with $X$ a real normed space, and let $\ell_*\ge0$. For every integer $n\ge0$, the formal statement identifies the finite Hölder expression with $\sum_{m=0}^n\ell_*^m|c|_{m,1/2}$. Each multi-index occurs once, and each order uses the supremum over all times in $I$ of the maximum of the spatial supremum and half-Hölder seminorm. The equality is the grouping by order stated in Appendix D. It does not establish finiteness; bounded derivative and difference-quotient families must be assumed when these expressions are used as norms.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderFieldNo.summary: Groups the finite Hölder norm by spatial order

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderOrderNo.text: For a phase-independent field $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to X$, the formal expression sums, over $|\beta|=m$, the supremum in time of the maximum of $\|\partial_a^\beta c(t)\|_\infty$ and its spatial half-Hölder seminorm. Each multi-index is counted once. Difference quotients use Euclidean distances between labels; the quotient at equal labels is assigned zero. The paper's notation $|c|_{m,1/2}$ does not specify whether the two parts of the Hölder norm are added or maximized. Replacing the maximum by their sum changes this quantity by at most a factor two. Smoothness and boundedness are not conclusions of the definition.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.holderOrderNo.summary: Measures each spatial derivative in the maximum Hölder norm

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.jetValues_lab.text: For every smooth coefficient $c$, every word $w$, radius $r\in\mathbb R$ and either choice of Hölder values, the jet-value set in directions $re_i$ is $|r|^{|w|}$ times the set in unit directions, where $|w|$ is the length of the word. This is a set identity before taking any supremum. It holds also for negative $r$ or $r=0$ and does not need boundedness. Spatial smoothness is needed to identify the iterated derivatives with their scaled versions.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.jetValues_lab.summary: A scaled label derivative contributes one radius factor

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.labelPartial.text:
For each time and each index $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, this applies the Fréchet derivative of $f(t,a,s)$ in the label direction $(e_i,0)$. The formalization's indices $0,1,2$ are the paper’s three coordinate labels. Time is a parameter of an arbitrary set $I$ and is not differentiated. The operation is defined on every function; smoothness is supplied by the norm-finiteness hypotheses when it is used analytically.

The phase directional derivative is the unrestricted derivative expression applied to the direction; for a nondifferentiable input it may be the zero default. No differentiability is built into this operation itself. The finiteness condition in Lemma D.1 includes spatial smoothness, and its positive weight makes smoothness of $f/\gamma$ equivalent to that of $f$ at fixed time. No integral, square root, reciprocal or extended-real conversion is introduced here.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.labelPartial.summary: The partial derivative in one label direction

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.labelWordNorm.text: For $\ell\ge 0$ and smooth $c$, this groups the weighted label-word norm by word length. It is $\sum_{m\le n}\ell^m$ times the sum of the unit-direction suprema at order $m$. The same algebraic identity handles ordinary and half-Hölder values. No boundedness is assumed, so the identity remains an identity of the total real-valued expressions even when a constituent supremum is a default; actual norm estimates still require finiteness predicates.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.labelWordNorm.summary: The weighted word sum grouped by derivative order

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.phaseAverage.text:
At each time and label this returns $\int_0^1f(t,a,s)\,ds$, viewed as a profile constant in $s$. It is the paper’s $\langle f\rangle$. The operation uses a vector-valued interval integral and is defined for all functions and real normed target spaces; its analytic interpretation therefore requires integrability and, for nontrivial vector integration, completeness.

A vector-valued integral can return zero if the integrand is not integrable, and the imported integral also uses a zero convention without a complete target. The definition itself assumes neither integrability nor completeness. In the (D.5) clause of the formal statement of Lemma D.1, completeness of the target $E$ is explicit and the finiteness condition with $\gamma>0$ gives smooth, hence continuous, phase slices on every compact interval; these rule out the defaults. Phase periodicity is separately required there. No conversion from extended nonnegative reals occurs.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.phaseAverage.summary: The phase average of a profile

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.phaseInverse.text:
This first forms $s\mapsto\int_0^sf(t,a,\sigma)\,d\sigma$ and then subtracts its average over one phase period. For continuous one-periodic $f$ with zero phase mean, it is the zero-mean periodic primitive denoted $\partial_s^{-1}f$. It is not an algebraic inverse on arbitrary functions; zero mean and periodicity are hypotheses of the analytic primitive clause, not of this definition.

Both the inner primitive and the outer mean are vector-valued interval integrals, so nonintegrability or an incomplete target can collapse them to zero. The formal statement of Lemma D.1 assumes completeness, smooth finite-norm slices, periodicity and zero mean for the inverse bound. These make the integrals genuine and give the intended periodic primitive. Without zero mean the defined primitive need not be periodic, even when all integrals exist. There is no division by the mean.

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.phasePartial.text:
This applies the derivative of $f(t,a,s)$ in the fourth coordinate, the unit $s$ direction. The label and time are held fixed. It is the $\partial_s$ operation appearing in the finite norm and Lemma D.1; the definition itself does not impose periodicity or smoothness.

As for the label partial derivative, the underlying derivative expression is defined for every function and may be zero for a nonsmooth function. The analytic clauses use the finiteness condition, including smoothness in $(a,s)$, and positive $\gamma$ when weighted. Periodicity is separately needed for the phase-average and primitive clauses, not for taking this derivative.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.phasePartial.summary: The phase derivative of a profile

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.weighted.text:
This is $f/\gamma$, implemented as scalar multiplication of each spatial/phase slice by $(\gamma(t))^{-1}$. The weight depends only on time, so label and phase derivatives do not differentiate it. The arbitrary time type permits restriction to any desired slab without changing the definition.

At $\gamma(t)=0$ the inverse is zero, so the whole slice is sent to zero and its weighted norm can vanish for a nonzero field. Positivity of $\gamma$ at every time is an explicit hypothesis of Lemma D.1 and is inherited from the positive seed weight in the applications. The definition alone imposes no guard. No square root or supremum is evaluated here.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.weighted.summary: Division by the time dependent amplitude weight

TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.weightedField.text: For a field $f(t,a,s)$ and a time-dependent scalar $\gamma(t)$, this expression is the mixed finite norm of $f(t,a,s)/\gamma(t)$: it sums $\ell_*^{|\beta|}h^j\sup|\partial_a^\beta\partial_s^j(f/\gamma)|$ over $|\beta|+j\le n$. All suprema include the chosen time set, labels and phases; only labels and phases are differentiated. The paper assumes $\gamma(t)>0$ on $[t_0,T]$, and the numbered estimates impose that assumption. The definition alone allows zero weights: at a time with $\gamma(t)=0$, the normalized field is assigned zero. Thus the expression alone cannot certify the paper's positive-amplitude normalization or the finiteness of its derivative bounds.
TorusEuler.Paper.AppendixD.weightedField.summary: Divides the field by its time-dependent amplitude

TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.MixedIncrementBound.text: Fix a stage $j$ and nonnegative integers $m,q$. Set $w(t,x)=\partial_t^q(U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j)(t,x)$, differentiating at fixed $x$ within $[0,S_j]$. The formal condition requires finiteness of the spatial Hölder measurement, its bound $\|w(t)\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le\lambda_j^{-1}$ for every $t$, and continuity of $t\mapsto w(t)$ in that norm. Thus it includes the meaning of the time-space norm in auxiliary equation (1.2), not merely a pointwise estimate. The spatial norm's defining formula is absent; accompanying comments describe operator norms of spatial derivatives. At $j=0$, the predecessor index is also zero because natural-number subtraction stops at zero. The auxiliary lemma uses this condition only eventually.
TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.MixedIncrementBound.summary: The estimate includes continuity in the spatial norm

TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.Proof.theorem_1_1_o.text: The authors' source records this statement as not proved and outside the main argument; neither formal main theorem uses it. Assume Theorem 7.1, Propositions 8.1, 8.2 and 8.4, Corollary 8.3, and the generalized mixed estimate for every qualifying construction. For each cutoff symbol and integer $a_0$, the conclusion chooses integers $b\ge1$, $a\ge a_0$ and majorants $F,G$. Thresholds satisfying the main conditions for $F$ and $G(7K(s))\le\mathcal B(s)$, with $K(s)=320b(s+1)$, exist; every such threshold yields a solution for all sufficiently large initial frequencies. The solution has bounded velocity, the main vorticity blow-up and integral conclusions, uniqueness among maximal solutions of finite lifespan with the same initial data, and a smooth periodic velocity extension through its terminal time off $\mathbb Z^3$. Euler is imposed only before that time. This is a proved implication. The authors' formalization marks its generalized mixed estimate as not proved; a separate selected construction proves the existence conclusion.
TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.Proof.theorem_1_1_o.summary: The generalized extension follows from stronger hypotheses

TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.Statement.lemma_1_2.text: The authors' source records this statement as not proved and outside the main argument; neither formal main theorem uses it. For each cutoff symbol, the formal statement asks for $a_0$ such that each integer $a\ge a_0$ has a majorant $G$, chosen before the construction. Every sequence satisfying the specified Section 7 step data, strength $18e^3$, and $G(7K(s))\le\mathcal B(s)$ must then satisfy $\|\partial_t^q(U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j)\|_{C([0,S_j];C^{m,1/2})}\le\lambda_j^{-1}$ eventually for every fixed $(m,q)$. Time derivatives fix the physical point; continuity in the spatial norm is included. The majorant also covers the main fixed-order constants used by this argument. This quantifies over every qualifying construction, whereas the paper discusses its selected one. The authors' formalization states this assertion and marks it as not proved; the separately proved selected-construction result has narrower quantifiers.
TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.Statement.lemma_1_2.summary: This assertion is broader than the selected construction

TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.Statement.lemma_1_3.text: The authors' source records this statement as not proved and outside the main argument; neither formal main theorem uses it. For each cutoff symbol and every sufficiently large integer envelope exponent $a$, the formal statement asks for a majorant $G$ chosen before the construction. For every sequence with the specified Section 7 data, strength $18e^3$, and threshold dominating $G(7K(s))$, it then asks that each $q$ admit integers $\psi_q,j_q$ such that, for $j\ge j_q$ and $i\le q$, $\|\partial_t^iU_j\|_{C_tL^\infty}\le\lambda_j^{\psi_q}$ and $\|\partial_t^iR_j\|_{C_tL^\infty}\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-5/2}$. Both time curves must be continuous in the supremum norm on $[0,S_j]$. The exponents and starting indices come after the construction. The authors' formalization marks this universal formulation as not proved; the selected-construction theorem proves the auxiliary estimate with narrower quantifiers.
TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.Statement.lemma_1_3.summary: The exponent follows the construction and time order

TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.Statement.theorem_1.text: The authors' source records this statement as not proved and outside the main argument; neither formal main theorem uses it. For every cutoff symbol and every lower bound on the integer envelope exponent, this formal statement asks for exponents $b,a$ and majorants $F,G$. Suitable thresholds $\mathcal B$ must exist, and every threshold satisfying both majorants must produce, for every sufficiently large initial frequency, a common sequence and a finite-time singular Euler solution. The solution retains bounded velocity, central vorticity divergence, divergent gradient and vorticity integrals, spatial limits off the origin, and uniqueness among maximal solutions of finite lifespan with the same initial data. Its periodic velocity must extend smoothly through the terminal time off $\mathbb Z^3$; Euler is imposed only before it. The authors' formalization marks this generalized assertion as not proved. Its selected-construction existence theorem and the proved main Remark 1.2 establish the required existence of a strengthened solution.
TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.Statement.theorem_1.summary: Every qualifying threshold must yield the strengthened solution

TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.TimeBounds.text: For a specified stage $j$ and nonnegative integers $q,\psi_q$, the condition requires, for every $i\le q$, $|\partial_t^iU_j(t,x)|\le\lambda_j^{\psi_q}$ and $|\partial_t^iR_j(t,x)|\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-5/2}$ on $[0,S_j]\times\mathbb R^3$. It also requires continuity of both time curves in the spatial supremum norm. The fields are periodic lifts, so this is the intended $C([0,S_j];L^\infty)$ meaning of auxiliary equation (1.3). Derivatives fix $x$ and are one-sided at the endpoints. The exponent is an integer, not the cutoff symbol. This condition concerns one stage; it neither selects the exponent nor asserts that the estimates hold eventually.
TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.TimeBounds.summary: The two estimates include supremum-norm continuity

TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.TimeDerivativeThres.text: For a nonnegative integer $b$ and functions $G,\mathcal B$ on the nonnegative integers, the formal condition is $G(7K(s))\le\mathcal B(s)$ for every $s\ge1$, with $K(s)=320b(s+1)$. The argument of $G$ is therefore the largest derivative order and depth admitted by the auxiliary estimate. This condition alone does not require either function to be monotone or positive, and does not assert the main logarithmic lower bound for $\mathcal B$. Those properties enter through separate schedule or admissibility assumptions. The generalized auxiliary statements choose $G$ before the construction; its existence as a suitable analytic majorant is not supplied by this inequality itself.
TorusEuler.Paper.Aux.TimeDerivativeThres.summary: One majorant covers the additional derivative constants

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.CutoffSymbol.eve.text: A radial Fourier symbol is even. The norm is computed before phase substitution. Bounds for weighted profiles require a bounded inverse time weight on the active interval; continuous positivity supplies that bound for the actual central seed.

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsExpansion.eq_c.text: Every expansion is, level by level, the library construction over the solvers chosen from the assumed existence of normalized mean solutions and of zero-start transverse solutions, for the parent residual, activation term and leading pair of the expansion, assuming uniqueness of normalized mean solutions. At level $p$ the mean is solved before the transverse correction, because the new mean transports the leading wave. The finite recursion uses the prescribed mean pressure normalization and a zero-start transverse solution.
TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsExpansion.eq_c.summary: Identify an arbitrary expansion with the chosen recursion

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsExpansion.uniq.text: Uniqueness of the expansion: two families satisfying the defining recursions of the Section 5 expansion for the same parent, cutoff, seed and depth have the same $R$, $S$ and the same levels, assuming uniqueness of normalized mean solutions. The transverse levels are unique by uniqueness of transverse solutions with $V_p(0) = 0$ and zero phase mean of $\mathsf p_p$, the leading level by its cell values, and the recursion propagates the agreement level by level. At level $p$ the mean is solved before the transverse correction, because the new mean transports the leading wave. The finite recursion uses the prescribed mean pressure normalization and a zero-start transverse solution.
TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsExpansion.uniq.summary: The recursive expansion is unique at every retained level

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsSeed.eqOn.text: Uniqueness of the seed: two solutions of (3.2) with the initial data (5.4) agree on $[t_0,T] \times \mathbb R^3$ (linear ODE uniqueness at each label). The seed is the solution of the projected initial-value problem on the active interval. Near-origin quantitative comparison bounds are separate data and are proved later from smallness of the envelope; they are not part of the paper's seed conditions themselves.
TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsSeed.eqOn.summary: The projected initial amplitude determines the seed uniquely

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsSeed.eqOn_ampl.text: Every amplitude satisfying the paper's seed conditions agrees on $[t_0,T] \times \mathbb R^3$ with the amplitude of any library seed over the parent coefficients, with no regularity assumption on the library amplitude (linear ODE uniqueness at each label uses only the equation and the initial data). In the proof of Lemma 5.3 this identifies the seed with the library seed obtained from the coframe bounds, which records no smoothness. The seed is the solution of the projected initial-value problem on the active interval. Near-origin quantitative comparison bounds are separate data and are proved later from smallness of the envelope; they are not part of the paper's seed conditions themselves.
TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsSeed.eqOn_ampl.summary: Identify seed amplitudes using their equation and initial data

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsSeed.eqOn_seed.text: Every amplitude satisfying the paper's seed conditions agrees on $[t_0,T] \times \mathbb R^3$ with the amplitude of any library seed over the parent coefficients whose amplitude is smooth. The seed is the solution of the projected initial-value problem on the active interval. Near-origin quantitative comparison bounds are separate data and are proved later from smallness of the envelope; they are not part of the paper's seed conditions themselves.
TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsSeed.eqOn_seed.summary: Identify a paper seed with a smooth library seed

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsTruncation.pre.text: Under the explicitly supplied periodic Poisson-pressure uniqueness assertion, two pressure representatives for the same truncation velocity agree on the slab. The gradient equation alone would leave a time-dependent constant; zero cell mean removes it. The ledger classifies the uniqueness helper as glue, so this note does not repeat the source comment's exclusive attribution to Proposition 5.11.
TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsTruncation.pre.summary: Pressure uniqueness needs the normalized Poisson problem

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsTruncation.pre.text: Under the supplied pressure-uniqueness hypothesis, the pressure of a paper truncation equals that of the corresponding child stage on the time slab. This is a normalization-sensitive comparison, rather than a new pressure estimate or a consequence of velocity equality alone.
TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsTruncation.pre.summary: Identify the normalized pressure of a child stage

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsTruncation.vel.text: The velocity of a truncation is the velocity of any child stage of the same field on $[0,T]$. The statement compares the paper truncation predicate with an existing child-stage construction on the same closed time interval. Pressure equality additionally uses the supplied uniqueness assertion and the chosen zero-mean normalization.
TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsTruncation.vel.summary: Identify a truncation with the constructed velocity

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsTruncation.vel.text: Two truncations of the same field have the same velocity on $[0,T]$, provided the field has a continuous torus lift at each time (every child stage provides one). The statement compares the paper truncation predicate with an existing child-stage construction on the same closed time interval. Pressure equality additionally uses the supplied uniqueness assertion and the chosen zero-mean normalization.
TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.IsTruncation.vel.summary: A Fourier truncation determines its velocity uniquely

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.Launch.active_su.text: The active interval lies inside the full interval. The parent is smooth, periodic, odd and divergence free on the closed time interval, with the deformation and velocity-gradient bounds of Section 5. The bridge extracts only the stated consequence of those hypotheses.
TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.Launch.active_su.summary: The active interval lies inside the full interval

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.Launch.carrier_e.text: The launch covector recovered from the central covector at $t_0$, $(D_aX(t_0,0))^T \kappa(t_0,0)$, is $k_*$ (as in the library seed constructions). The parent is smooth, periodic, odd and divergence free on the closed time interval, with the deformation and velocity-gradient bounds of Section 5. The bridge extracts only the stated consequence of those hypotheses.
TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.Launch.carrier_e.summary: The launch covector recovers the constant carrier

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.Launch.end_pos.text: The final time is strictly positive. The parent is smooth, periodic, odd and divergence free on the closed time interval, with the deformation and velocity-gradient bounds of Section 5. The bridge extracts only the stated consequence of those hypotheses.

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.MeanSolvable.text:
Every phase-independent source admits a smooth mean velocity and pressure solving the two-endpoint mean equation, with the pressure normalized to zero cell mean. This is an input hypothesis for the finite recursion; a separate theorem proves it from the cited Theorem 4.2. The comment in the formalization saying that the endpoint bridge is not yet written is out of date.

Default values: This is an existence statement over every phase-independent source. It includes pressure normalization rather than relying on a default representative. It has no fallback zero solution, and the actual existence proof is supplied by the separate theorem from Theorem 4.2.
TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.MeanSolvable.summary: Existence of normalized solutions of the mean equation

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.MeanUnique.text:
Two mean solutions for the same source agree as velocity-pressure pairs when both pressures have zero cell mean. The endpoint condition fixes the velocity and the normalization fixes the pressure constant. A separate theorem now proves this from Theorem 4.2, contrary to the out-of-date comment in the formalization saying the bridge is unfinished.

Default values: The statement compares two pairs only when both satisfy the mean equation and zero cell pressure mean. Dropping normalization would allow a time-dependent pressure constant, so the stored hypotheses are material. It is a conditional uniqueness statement rather than an asserted instance.
TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.MeanUnique.summary: Uniqueness of normalized solutions of the mean equation

TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.Origin.centerWav.text: The central-seed assumptions of Section 5.1 in the form used by the library seed lemmas: the central wave conditions at the parent gradient $\nabla U(t,0)$. TorusEuler.Paper.Bridge.Origin.weight_le.summary: The chosen amplitude normalization bounds the weight by one
