TorusEuler.inner_firstWaveTransportedCov.text: The explicit first-wave seed is perpendicular to its transported covector at every time and label. Substituting their first two components makes the pairing cancel exactly. The identity also holds for zero frequency or zero scale, although separate nonvanishing hypotheses are required when the pair is used to form a frame.
TorusEuler.inner_firstWaveTransportedCov.summary: The explicit seed stays perpendicular to the covector

TorusEuler.inner_fixedTransverse_lift_eq.text: The identities $RJ=I$ and $JR=P_k$ force every lifted coordinate vector $Jz$ to equal its transverse projection. For a nonzero covector $k$, its inner product with $Jz$ therefore vanishes. This proves that the solution constructed in a fixed coordinate space represents a physical seed in the moving transverse plane.
TorusEuler.inner_fixedTransverse_lift_eq.summary: Lifted coordinates lie in the transverse plane

TorusEuler.inner_frozenSymbol_eq.text: For a symmetric projection $r$, the quadratic form of the frozen operator equals $\langle B(rv),rv\rangle+\|v-rv\|^2$. The formula separates the coefficient acting on the range from the identity acting on the orthogonal complement. It does not require $B$ to be symmetric or positive.

TorusEuler.inner_kineticForm_self.text: For any bounded operator $F$, pairing $F^*Fv$ with $v$ gives $\|Fv\|^2$. No invertibility assumption is needed for this identity. With $F$ the deformation of the parent flow, it identifies the kinetic coefficient with a nonnegative form; a positive lower bound requires the additional inverse-deformation estimate.
TorusEuler.inner_kineticForm_self.summary: The kinetic quadratic form is a squared deformation norm

TorusEuler.inner_lerayModeProjection_lef.text: The inner product of the projected first coefficient with a second coefficient equals the inner product with projection applied to the second. This self-adjointness holds at every frequency. It permits projection to be moved onto a transverse test field in the coercivity calculation.

TorusEuler.inner_normalize_cross3_ge_of_.text: Converts a lower bound $c$ for the component of the scaled new wave vector $k'/\lambda$ along a preceding frame axis $e$, and an upper bound $L$ for its scaled norm, into the signed projection bound $\sigma c/L\le\langle k'/|k'|,k\times a\rangle$ for the preceding curl. It needs $k'\ne0$, positive carrier $\lambda$, nonnegative strength $\sigma$ and component $c$, and the exact frame identity $k\times a=\sigma e$. Positivity of the denominator follows from the nonzero scaled wave vector and its length bound.
TorusEuler.inner_normalize_cross3_ge_of_.summary: The preceding curl has a positive projected component

TorusEuler.inner_normalize_cross3_left.text: For $\kappa,\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^3$, the scalar product of the normalized covector with $\kappa\times\mathbf a$ is zero. For a nonzero covector this reads $(\kappa/|\kappa|)\cdot(\kappa\times\mathbf a)=0$. The formal formula also permits $\kappa=0$, with normalization defined as zero there; it makes no unit-vector assertion in that case. Applied to the gradient contribution $\widetilde\chi_j\mathbf a_j\otimes\kappa_j$, the identity removes the newest wave from the projection used in Proposition 8.2, for any real cutoff value. It does not give a lower bound for the projection of the preceding wave; that requires the separate angle and strength estimates.
TorusEuler.inner_normalize_cross3_left.summary: Projection along a covector removes its own rank-one curl contribution

TorusEuler.inner_normalize_twoLayerCurl.text: Expands the projection of a background curl plus two wave curls along the normalized newest wave vector. The newest term vanishes for every real cutoff value, so the identity is independent of its activation level. This remains an algebraic identity when the newest wave vector is zero; positivity and unit length are needed only in later norm bounds.
TorusEuler.inner_normalize_twoLayerCurl.summary: The newest wave drops out of the projection

TorusEuler.inner_oscillatoryTransversePr.text: For κ ≠ 0, the transverse projection of any forcing vector has zero inner product with κ. The nonvanishing hypothesis is essential to the usual projection interpretation.
TorusEuler.inner_oscillatoryTransversePr.summary: The projected forcing is perpendicular to the covector

TorusEuler.inner_periodicComplexLeray_le.text: The complex spatial $L^2$ pairing is unchanged when the Leray projection is moved from its first argument to its second. This self-adjointness is inherited from orthogonal projection. It is the all-field version of the finite-frequency identity used when testing a projected equation against a solenoidal solution.
TorusEuler.inner_periodicComplexLeray_le.summary: The full Leray projection is self adjoint

TorusEuler.inner_projectedHilbertOperato.text: Let $E$ be a real Hilbert space, $H\subseteq E$ a closed subspace and $A$ a bounded linear operator on $E$. Let $\Pi_H$ be the orthogonal projection onto $H$. For all $u,w\in H$, $\langle\Pi_HAu,w\rangle=\langle Au,w\rangle$. The projection changes only a component orthogonal to $H$.
TorusEuler.inner_projectedHilbertOperato.summary: Testing inside the subspace removes the projection

TorusEuler.instAddCommGroupHierarchyTwis.text: The twisted profile submodule inherits an additive commutative group from its periodic and smooth ambient spaces. Addition and subtraction are pointwise on representatives and preserve the stored periodicity constraints. The instance supplies algebraic operations for the finite hierarchy; it introduces no new functions or analytic hypotheses.
TorusEuler.instAddCommGroupHierarchyTwis.summary: Add and subtract profiles with the same twist

TorusEuler.instModuleHierarchyTwistedPro.text: The twisted submodule is a real vector space, with scalar multiplication inherited from periodic profiles. Multiplying a representative by a real scalar preserves both the unit phase period and its carrier-dependent lattice translation law. This instance enables linear and bilinear hierarchy operators on the same profile space.
TorusEuler.instModuleHierarchyTwistedPro.summary: Scale profiles without changing their carrier twist

TorusEuler.integrable_liftConvolution.text: An integrable scalar kernel times a translated continuous field with a uniform norm bound is integrable at every output point. The hypotheses are integrability of the kernel $K$, continuity of the field $f$ (giving measurability), and the dominating bound $\|f\|\le M$. This makes the defined convolution an ordinary vector-valued integral.
TorusEuler.integrable_liftConvolution.summary: An integrable kernel acts on bounded continuous fields

TorusEuler.integrable_operatorLiftConvol.text: An integrable operator-valued kernel applied to translates of a continuous uniformly bounded field gives an integrable function of the integration variable. The operator norm times the input bound supplies domination. This theorem establishes that the defined operator convolution is a genuine Bochner integral at every output point.
TorusEuler.integrable_operatorLiftConvol.summary: Integrable operator kernels act on bounded continuous fields

TorusEuler.integrable_scaledLiftKernel.text: If a kernel is integrable and the dilation parameter $\Lambda$ is positive, its dimensionally normalized dilation remains integrable. The factor $\Lambda^3$ compensates for three-dimensional volume scaling. Strict positivity excludes the collapsed zero-scale map and fixes the sign used in the change-of-variables formula.

TorusEuler.integrable_scaledMultiplierKe.text: For a positive scaling parameter, the normalized dilation of an integrable Banach-valued kernel is integrable. The theorem explicitly assumes integrability of the original kernel, so it supplies the convergence guard for later convolution identities. The zero-scale case is excluded even though the defining kernel expression still has a value there.
TorusEuler.integrable_scaledMultiplierKe.summary: Integrable multiplier kernels remain integrable after dilation

TorusEuler.integrable_sqrtNorm_mul_norm_.text: Every positive dilation of a Schwartz kernel has integrable norm times the square root of distance. The theorem combines the original kernel's weighted integrability with the scale change. It validates the moment appearing in the quantitative half-Hölder convolution bound for each frequency-localized kernel.
TorusEuler.integrable_sqrtNorm_mul_norm_.summary: The dilated Schwartz kernel retains a finite half-order moment

TorusEuler.integral_divergence_centeredC.text: A continuously differentiable, spatially periodic vector field has zero divergence integral over the centered fundamental cell. After transferring to coordinate functions, the divergence theorem gives opposite-face terms that cancel by periodicity. This is a classical statement on the Euclidean lift, without requiring the field itself to have zero divergence.
TorusEuler.integral_divergence_centeredC.summary: Periodic divergence integrates to zero over one cell

TorusEuler.integral_endpointEvenPart_cen.text: For a continuous scalar field, proves that its even part has the same integral over the centered torus cell. Continuity yields integrability on the compact cell, permitting linearity of the integral. Consequently an already normalized zero-mean pressure remains normalized after the symmetry selection.
TorusEuler.integral_endpointEvenPart_cen.summary: The even pressure retains its spatial mean

TorusEuler.integral_endpointFiniteFourie.text: Every finite pressure constructed from the pressure-correction modes has integral zero over the centered cell. The nonzero characters have zero average, and the pressure correction assigns zero to the constant mode. This fixes the additive constant without requiring any gradient compatibility for the supplied vector coefficients.

TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelEnergy_.text: On $[0,T]$, $T\ge0$, assume $F_t=MF$, $M_t$ is continuous, $z_t=v$ with continuous $v$, and $z(0)=z(T)=0$. Put $\xi=Fz$, $K=F^TF$, $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$, and $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$. Then $\int_0^T(Kv\cdot v+\Omega v\cdot z)\,dt=\int_0^T(|\xi_t|^2-H^\#\xi\cdot\xi)\,dt$. This is (4.7) for continuously differentiable paths in a real Hilbert space. The extension to all $H^1_0$ displacements is not part of this statement and is needed separately for Lemma 4.1.
TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelEnergy_.summary: Cancel the boundary contribution for a differentiable displacement

TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelVelocit.text: Let $0\le T\le1$, $F_t=MF$, $z_t=v$ with continuous $M,v$, and $z(T)=0$. Suppose $GF=I$, $\|G\|\le D$, $\|M\|\le L$, where $D,L\ge0$. Then, for $\xi=Fz$, $\int_0^T|v|^2\,dt\le D^2(1+L)^2\int_0^T|\xi_t|^2\,dt$. This gives the exact factor in (4.6) for continuously differentiable paths. It does not require $z(0)=0$, but it does require continuous $v$; the paper's complete $H^1_0$ assertion uses the separate square-integrable-velocity result.
TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelVelocit.summary: Compare label velocity and displacement derivatives before taking limits

TorusEuler.integral_endpointVelocity_nor.text: Assume $0\le T\le1$, terminal vanishing of $\xi$, continuous derivative and velocity, and $v=G(\xi_t-M\xi)$ on the slab. The bounds $\|G\|\le\mathsf D$ and $\|M\|\le L$ give $\int\|v\|^2\le\mathsf D^2(1+L)^2\int\|\xi_t\|^2$. The theorem needs no assertion that $G$ is an inverse; the displayed velocity relation carries the required algebra.
TorusEuler.integral_endpointVelocity_nor.summary: Displacement energy controls the label velocity

TorusEuler.integral_fourier_pair.text: The integral of the mode at $-k$ times the mode at $j$ is one when $k=j$ and zero otherwise. The product Haar measure has total mass one. This orthogonality fixes the normalization used to recover coefficients exactly from a finite Fourier synthesis.

TorusEuler.integral_gradient_pair_center.text: For continuously differentiable periodic $p$ and $v$, the cell integral of $\langle\nabla p,v\rangle$ equals minus the integral of $p\,\mathrm{div}\,v$. The proof applies zero integral of divergence to the product field. Both periodicity assumptions matter because they make opposite boundary faces cancel.
TorusEuler.integral_gradient_pair_center.summary: Periodic integration by parts removes the boundary

TorusEuler.integral_innerProduct_moment_.text: If the Fourier transform of a Schwartz kernel is constant in a neighborhood of zero, every directional signed moment of positive degree vanishes. The hypothesis $j>0$ excludes the mass term. The proof differentiates the locally constant transform and cancels the explicitly nonzero factor $(-2\pi i)^j$.
TorusEuler.integral_innerProduct_moment_.summary: A flat Fourier symbol forces every positive moment to vanish

TorusEuler.integral_inner_advection_cent.text: For periodic $C^1$ fields $w$ and $v$, assume only the advecting field $v$ is divergence free. Then the cell integral of $\langle w,Dw\,v\rangle$ vanishes. The proof differentiates $|w|^2$ and uses periodic integration by parts, providing the advection cancellation in the classical uniqueness argument for Proposition 8.1.

TorusEuler.integral_inner_endpointSpatia.text: For nonnegative duration, integrating the inner product of a joint field's spatial slice with a fixed spatial L2 field equals pairing that field with the joint time integral. The identity is independent of pointwise slice conventions on exceptional times.
TorusEuler.integral_inner_endpointSpatia.summary: Pairing commutes with time integration of spatial slices

TorusEuler.integral_inner_finiteFourierS.text: The spatial integral pairing of two Fourier polynomials over the same finite frequency set equals the sum of their coefficient inner products. The coefficients may lie in any complex Hilbert space. Finiteness justifies distributing both sums through the integral, and distinct frequencies contribute zero.
TorusEuler.integral_inner_finiteFourierS.summary: Finite Parseval preserves coefficient inner products

TorusEuler.integral_inner_gradient_cente.text: Let $w:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ and invariant under integer translations, and suppose $\operatorname{div}w=0$ everywhere. The formal theorem proves $\int_{[-1/2,1/2]^3}w\cdot\nabla q\,dx=0$. Opposite faces cancel in integration by parts. No mean-zero assumption on $q$ is needed for this cancellation. The result supplies the spatial pressure cancellation used in the endpoint energy argument, after the displacement constraint and the volume-preserving change of variables have been established. It does not itself prove that change of variables, the Jacobi equation, or the space-time identity (1.8).
TorusEuler.integral_inner_gradient_cente.summary: Periodic divergence-free fields are orthogonal to pressure gradients

TorusEuler.integral_inner_leray_finiteFo.text: If every test coefficient lies in the transverse mode space of its frequency, projecting the first Fourier polynomial leaves its integral inner product with the test polynomial unchanged. The proof moves projection across the coefficient inner product and fixes the transverse test coefficient. This is the finite version of the projected coercivity pairing.
TorusEuler.integral_inner_leray_finiteFo.summary: Transverse test fields do not see the Leray projection

TorusEuler.integral_lift_finiteFourierSu.text: The centered-cell integral of a finite Fourier synthesis is its zero-frequency coefficient when that frequency is present, and zero otherwise. The target complex normed space is complete. This is coefficient recovery at frequency zero, with the cell volume normalized to one.
TorusEuler.integral_lift_finiteFourierSu.summary: The spatial mean is the zero Fourier coefficient

TorusEuler.integral_lift_inverseLaplacia.text: The centered-cell integral of any finite synthesis weighted by the inverse Laplacian symbol is zero. This follows because its zero-frequency coefficient vanishes by definition. The theorem fixes the additive pressure constant and does not require the original source itself to have zero spatial mean.
TorusEuler.integral_lift_inverseLaplacia.summary: The finite Poisson solution has zero mean

TorusEuler.integral_lift_lerayMode.text: The centered-cell integral of the finite projected field equals that of the original Fourier polynomial. The proof reduces both integrals to their zero coefficients and uses the identity action of the zero-frequency Leray symbol. This preservation matters for the time-independent solenoidal field in the endpoint problem.
TorusEuler.integral_lift_lerayMode.summary: The Leray projection preserves the spatial mean

TorusEuler.integral_lift_pressureCorrect.text: The finite pressure correction synthesized from arbitrary vector coefficients has zero centered-cell integral. Its coefficients use the zero-mode-free inverse Laplacian, so the pressure constant is fixed. This normalization is compatible with subtracting its gradient in the finite Leray decomposition.
TorusEuler.integral_lift_pressureCorrect.summary: The Leray pressure correction has zero spatial mean

TorusEuler.integral_norm_iteratedFDeriv_.text: Let $K$ be a complex-valued Schwartz function on $\mathbb R^3$, let $\Lambda>0$, and set $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$. For any $m\ge0$ and any fixed vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_m$, the formal statement proves $\int|D^mK_\Lambda(y)[v_1,\ldots,v_m]|\,dy=\Lambda^m\int|D^mK(y)[v_1,\ldots,v_m]|\,dy$. Taking coordinate directions and replacing $\Lambda$ by $4\Lambda$ gives the kernel identity used for (B.1). The scaling factor accounts for both differentiation and the three-dimensional change of variables. No cutoff symbol is assumed; rapid decay makes the integrals finite.
TorusEuler.integral_norm_iteratedFDeriv_.summary: Scales the integral norm of any fixed directional derivative

TorusEuler.integral_norm_pow_iteratedFDe.text: For positive $\Lambda$, the $N$th weighted absolute moment of an $m$th directional derivative of the scaled kernel equals $\Lambda^m\Lambda^{-N}$ times the original moment. The derivative directions remain fixed on both sides. This records precisely how derivative loss and positive distance from support trade against the cutoff scale.
TorusEuler.integral_norm_pow_iteratedFDe.summary: Weighted kernel derivatives have the expected scaling

TorusEuler.integral_norm_pow_scaledLiftK.text: Let $\Lambda>0$, $m\ge0$, and $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$ for $K:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C$. The formal identity is $\int|y|^m|K_\Lambda(y)|\,dy=\Lambda^{-m}\int|y|^m|K(y)|\,dy$. It is stated for an arbitrary function $K$, with no integrability hypothesis, so its existence as an equality does not certify finite moments. For the Schwartz kernel $K=\check\psi$ in Appendix B, all these moments are finite and the identity has its usual integral meaning. It provides the factor $\Lambda^{s-M}$ after taking $m=M-s$ in the Taylor remainder estimate.
TorusEuler.integral_norm_pow_scaledLiftK.summary: Scales a weighted integral of the absolute kernel

TorusEuler.integral_norm_scaledLiftKerne.text: For positive frequency scale, the normalized dilation of a complex kernel has the same integral of its norm as the original kernel. The equality gives scale-independent convolution bounds once the kernel is integrable. The theorem states equality of the integral expressions without asserting their integrability separately.
TorusEuler.integral_norm_scaledLiftKerne.summary: Kernel dilation preserves its integral norm

TorusEuler.integral_norm_scaledMultiplie.text: At every positive scale, the integral of the norm of the normalized multiplier kernel equals that of the original kernel. This makes the basic convolution bound independent of the chosen dyadic frequency. Integrability is a separate property, supplied by the adjacent theorem when a classical kernel estimate is needed.
TorusEuler.integral_norm_scaledMultiplie.summary: Multiplier dilation leaves the integral norm unchanged

TorusEuler.integral_norm_sq_finiteFourie.text: The integral of the squared norm of a finite Fourier polynomial equals the sum of the squared coefficient norms. The measure is normalized product Haar measure on the torus. The result is derived from the inner-product Parseval identity and applies to arbitrary complex Hilbert-space coefficients.
TorusEuler.integral_norm_sq_finiteFourie.summary: Finite Parseval identifies spatial energy with coefficient energy

TorusEuler.integral_norm_sq_leray_finite.text: Projecting every coefficient of a finite vector Fourier polynomial by the Leray symbol cannot increase its spatial squared $L^2$ norm. Parseval reduces the claim to the contraction of each Euclidean coefficient projection. This is the finite-polynomial precursor of boundedness on the completed $L^2$ space.
TorusEuler.integral_norm_sq_leray_finite.summary: Finite Leray projection decreases spatial energy

TorusEuler.integral_scaledCompactMultipl.text: For a smooth compactly supported symbol $m$ and positive dilation, the integral of the dilated kernel is exactly $m(0)$. Thus it is zero when the symbol vanishes at the origin. The authors' comment highlights that application, but the formal statement proves the more general identity and does not assume zero mean.
TorusEuler.integral_scaledCompactMultipl.summary: The kernel integral equals the symbol at zero

TorusEuler.integral_scaledCutoffSchwartz.text: Suppose $\psi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ is smooth and vanishes outside the ball of radius two, let $K=\check\psi$, and let $\Lambda>0$. The formal statement proves $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)\,dy=\psi(0)$, with the right side viewed as a complex number. The kernel is Schwartz, so the integral is finite. Appendix B also assumes $\psi=1$ on the unit ball, which changes this right side to one. That plateau condition is not a hypothesis of this declaration; it must be supplied when reading the link as the paper's assertion of unit mass.
TorusEuler.integral_scaledCutoffSchwartz.summary: Computes the integral as the symbol value at zero

TorusEuler.integral_scaledCutoffSchwartz.text: Let $\psi$ be smooth on $\mathbb R^3$, zero outside the radius-two ball and identically one on the unit ball. For $\Lambda>0$, set $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3\check\psi(\Lambda y)$. The formal statement proves $\int y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_m}K_\Lambda(y)\,dy=0$ for every positive integer $m$ and every choice of coordinate indices, including repetitions. Thus it covers every positive-order multi-index moment used in Appendix B. The moment is the integral of the signed or complex kernel, not of its absolute value. No radiality or evenness is required for this cancellation.
TorusEuler.integral_scaledCutoffSchwartz.summary: An exact plateau makes every positive coordinate moment vanish

TorusEuler.integral_scaledCutoffSchwartz.text: For a smooth cutoff equal to one on the unit ball and zero outside radius two, every positive directional moment of its dilated inverse-Fourier kernel vanishes. The assumption $\Lambda>0$ ensures the scaled symbol is one near zero. This applies the general moment theorem to the actual kernel used in the cutoff.
TorusEuler.integral_scaledCutoffSchwartz.summary: The actual dilated cutoff kernel has vanishing positive moments

TorusEuler.integral_scaledCutoffSchwartz.text: For positive degree $j$, the dilated cutoff kernel integrates to zero against any continuous real multilinear diagonal term valued in a complete complex normed space. Coordinate expansion reduces the assertion to vanishing coordinate moments. Smoothness and unit-neighborhood assumptions belong to the cutoff; the multilinear map itself is arbitrary.
TorusEuler.integral_scaledCutoffSchwartz.summary: The cutoff kernel cancels positive homogeneous Taylor terms

TorusEuler.integral_sqrtNorm_scaledMulti.text: Positive dilation multiplies the integral of kernel norm times $\sqrt{\|y\|}$ by $\sqrt{\Lambda^{-1}}$. This scaling is responsible for the half-order gain in each dyadic block. The theorem is an equality of total integrals; the subsequent Schwartz lemmas supply finiteness of the weighted moment.
TorusEuler.integral_sqrtNorm_scaledMulti.summary: The half-order kernel moment gains an inverse square root

TorusEuler.integral_truncatedParentSlice.text: Proves that the integral of the slice pressure over the centered fundamental cell is zero. This fixes the additive constant in the pressure without imposing any condition on the average of the input vector field. The finite smooth potential is integrable on that bounded cell; the equality is not a fallback for a nonintegrable function.

TorusEuler.integratedLimit_of_uniformCon.text: Assume uniform convergence of approximate states and drift terms, uniform decay of residuals, continuous drift and residual curves, and their exact integrated relation. The limit satisfies $u(t)=u(0)-\int_0^t d(s)\,ds$ and has within-interval derivative $-d(t)$. The result works for $T\ge0$ in a Banach space; it does not establish smoothness or Euler structure by itself.
TorusEuler.integratedLimit_of_uniformCon.summary: A vanishing residual leaves the limiting evolution equation

TorusEuler.integrated_spatialJets_of_zer.text: Assume two compatible spatial jet towers $J$ and $U$, with $U$ continuous in time. An integrated identity for their zeroth entries then differentiates to the same identity at every finite order. The proof uses uniqueness of spatial derivatives at each induction step. The interval may have length zero; no evolution is inferred beyond the given identity.
TorusEuler.integrated_spatialJets_of_zer.summary: One integrated identity determines every spatial jet identity

TorusEuler.intervalIntegrable_sq_velocit.text: If a velocity is in $L^2$ for the restricted measure on an ordered interval, its squared norm is interval-integrable there. This is the integrability condition needed for Cauchy–Schwarz and energy bounds. The theorem concerns a representative together with the hypothesis that it is square-integrable, not an arbitrary function with a formal squared-integral expression.
TorusEuler.intervalIntegrable_sq_velocit.summary: The squared velocity norm is time-integrable

TorusEuler.intervalIntegrable_velocity_o.text: On an ordered finite interval, an $L^2$ representative is interval-integrable. The proof uses the finiteness of the restricted time measure to pass from exponent two to exponent one. The order hypothesis $a\le b$ identifies the oriented interval integral with the intended restriction to $(a,b]$.

TorusEuler.intervalIntegral_endpointSpat.text: A spatial $L^2$-valued path continuous on $[0,T]$ and equal almost everywhere to the spatial slices of a joint field has the same total time integral as that field. Nonnegative duration aligns the interval and restricted-measure integrals. Testing against arbitrary spatial $L^2$ vectors reduces the identity to scalar Fubini compatibility.
TorusEuler.intervalIntegral_endpointSpat.summary: The recovered spatial path has the original time integral

TorusEuler.inv_sq_norm_inv_smul.text: The reciprocal squared norm of the normalized vector is the coefficient of Proposition 5.1.
TorusEuler.inv_sq_norm_inv_smul.summary: The reciprocal covector norm after frequency normalization

TorusEuler.inverseAdjoint_activationWave.text: Let $F:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be any invertible linear map, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ and $E_3\in\mathbb R^3$. The formal statement proves $F^{-T}(\lambda F^TE_3)=\lambda E_3$. In §6.2, take $F=D_aX(t_0,0)$ and choose $k_*=\lambda F^TE_3(t_0)$; then the transported covector at activation is exactly $\lambda E_3(t_0)$. The theorem is linear algebra and does not itself assert that $F$ is a flow derivative or that $E_3$ is a unit vector. It does not require integer components of $k_*$; periodicity of the localized field is a separate issue.
TorusEuler.inverseAdjoint_activationWave.summary: The transpose choice yields the prescribed transported direction

TorusEuler.inverseLabel_materialDerivati.text: Assume that $A(r,X(r,a))=a$ for all times $r$ of the interval near $t$, so the inverse label identity holds locally along the trajectory. Suppose also that $A$ has derivative $(A_t,A_x)$ within the interval at $(t,X(t,a))$, that the trajectory $r\mapsto X(r,a)$ has derivative $u$ within the interval at $t$, that $t$ lies in the interval, and that derivatives within the interval at $t$ are unique. Then $A_t+A_xu=0$. The local identity is enough; a globally specified inverse flow is unnecessary.
TorusEuler.inverseLabel_materialDerivati.summary: Differentiating the inverse label identity gives transport

TorusEuler.inverseLabel_spatialDerivativ.text: At corresponding label and spatial points, assume that $A(t,\cdot)$ has derivative $A_x$ at $X(t,a)$, that $X(t,\cdot)$ has derivative $F$ at $a$, and that $A(t,X(t,b))=b$ for $b$ near $a$. The flow derivative is already given as an invertible continuous linear map $F$, so the inverse label derivative equals $F^{-1}$. This uses genuine invertibility data, rather than a formula for the inverse that would also be assigned a value at a singular matrix.
TorusEuler.inverseLabel_spatialDerivativ.summary: The inverse label derivative is the inverse deformation

TorusEuler.inverseLaplacianMode.text: This scalar is the reciprocal of the Laplacian symbol. At nonzero frequency it inverts $-(2\pi)^2|k|^2$; at zero frequency Lean assigns zero to the reciprocal of zero. Thus the definition selects a zero-mean pressure rather than attempting to solve for an arbitrary constant source.
TorusEuler.inverseLaplacianMode.summary: The pressure inverse sets the constant mode to zero

TorusEuler.inverseLaplacianMode_zero.text: The inverse Laplacian symbol at zero frequency is zero. This theorem records the normalization chosen through totalized scalar inversion. It does not state that the Laplacian is invertible on all periodic fields; the constant mode must be removed from the source.
TorusEuler.inverseLaplacianMode_zero.summary: The pressure inverse has zero constant coefficient

TorusEuler.inverseMultiplierKernel_decay.text: A Banach-valued Schwartz symbol has an inverse-transform kernel whose value and first derivative decay with weight $(1+\|y\|)^5$. The quantitative bound is thirty-two times the preceding derivative-mass constant. This supplies sufficient decay in three dimensions for the kernel's integral norm and its half-order moment.
TorusEuler.inverseMultiplierKernel_decay.summary: The kernel and its gradient decay to fifth order

TorusEuler.inverseMultiplierKernel_decay.text: For a Schwartz symbol, $(1+\|y\|)^p$ times the order $d$ inverse Fourier kernel derivative norm is bounded by the explicit decay coefficient $2^p(2\pi)^d(2d+2)^p$ times the weighted symbol derivative mass of orders $d$ and $p$. The proof treats points inside and outside the unit ball separately, using moment orders zero and $p$. Both the derivative order and decay order are arbitrary naturals.
TorusEuler.inverseMultiplierKernel_decay.summary: Every kernel derivative has arbitrary polynomial decay

TorusEuler.inverse_secondCoupling_le.text: Assuming the first coupling $\nu$ is at least $\pi$, the reciprocal of $\nu\,\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon=1/L^2$ is at most $L^2/\pi$. The theorem permits arbitrary real $L$; at zero gain the convention $1/0=0$ makes the inequality degenerate to zero. Applications to the induction use a positive prescribed gain.
TorusEuler.inverse_secondCoupling_le.summary: The first coupling bounds the reciprocal second coupling

TorusEuler.isClosed_endpointHalfHolderSo.text: The half-Hölder solenoidal submodule is closed as the inverse image of the closed Hilbert solenoidal subspace under the continuous embedding. This transfers the weak divergence constraint without differentiating Hölder fields. It ensures the fixed-time inverse is formulated on a complete constrained function space.

TorusEuler.isClosed_endpointJointSpatial.text: The weakly solenoidal submodule is closed for every real T. Each defining divergence test is a continuous linear functional, so its kernel is closed, and the intersection over the time tests and scalar potentials remains closed. This supplies the completeness needed to form the spatial orthogonal projection in the joint Hilbert space.

TorusEuler.isClosed_endpointSpatialSolen.text: The spatial weak divergence-free submodule is closed because every testing functional is continuous and has a closed kernel. An arbitrary intersection preserves closedness. This supplies the Hilbert-space foundation needed for orthogonal projection and coercive inverse constructions on the fixed-time solenoidal space.
TorusEuler.isClosed_endpointSpatialSolen.summary: The weak solenoidal Hilbert subspace is closed

TorusEuler.isClosed_endpointTorusSpace.text: The intersection defining the joint endpoint constraint space is closed because every test functional is continuous and has a closed kernel. This permits the orthogonal projection used by the mixed solve.
TorusEuler.isClosed_endpointTorusSpace.summary: The joint endpoint constraint space is closed

TorusEuler.isClosed_freezingFixedSpace.text: For any continuous linear operator $P$, the set of vectors satisfying $Pv=v$ is closed. Idempotence of $P$ is unnecessary for this topological fact. In the freezing argument it makes the projected space complete, allowing bounded inverse and continuation results to be applied on that subspace.

TorusEuler.isClosed_range_latticeVector.text: The set of embedded integer lattice vectors is closed in three-dimensional Euclidean space. It is the intersection of the inverse images of the closed integer subset under coordinate evaluation. This supplies the topology of the lifted torus origin, which consists of every lattice translate of zero.
TorusEuler.isClosed_range_latticeVector.summary: The integer lattice is closed in Euclidean labels

TorusEuler.isCompact_centeredCell.text: The centered fundamental cube is compact in three-dimensional Euclidean space. This makes spatial suprema and periodic boundedness arguments available on a fixed compact representative set.

TorusEuler.isCompact_closure_multiplierK.text: The closure of the half open fundamental cell is compact because it is a closed subset of the basis parallelepiped. This allows all differences between a fixed observation region and cell source points to be bounded uniformly. The theorem carefully concerns the closure, not compactness of the half open cell itself.
TorusEuler.isCompact_closure_multiplierK.summary: The periodization cell has compact closure

TorusEuler.isCompact_farPressureSourceSe.text: The far source set is compact because it is a closed support intersected with the compact closure of the kernel fundamental cell. No continuity of the cutoff is required: topological support is closed by definition. This compactness provides finite source measure and allows uniform kernel bounds after separation is proved.
TorusEuler.isCompact_farPressureSourceSe.summary: The support enclosure is compact for any cutoff

TorusEuler.isEulerSolution_of_prefix_lim.text: Joint smoothness of the candidate velocity and normalized periodic pressure is supplied, along with approximation symmetries, zero divergence, uniform velocity and derivative convergence on each prefix, and the limiting dynamics. The theorem then concludes that $(u,p)$ is a classical Euler solution on $[0,T)$ and that the velocity is odd. It does not independently prove the assumed smoothness or convergence.
TorusEuler.isEulerSolution_of_prefix_lim.summary: Assemble an Euler solution from the prefix limits

TorusEuler.isEulerSolution_stationaryShe.text: For any real $\rho$ and any $T>0$, the formal theorem proves that $u(t,x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$ with $p(t,x)=0$ is a smooth periodic Euler solution on $[0,T)$. The velocity varies only in $x_2$ and has zero second component, so both divergence and self-advection vanish. Pressure is automatically mean zero. This verifies the starting flow described in §1.1 and (6.1), under weaker assumptions on $\rho$: positivity and smallness are unnecessary for the stationary Euler identity. They are imposed later to obtain the positive couplings and separation used for amplification.
TorusEuler.isEulerSolution_stationaryShe.summary: Every real tilt gives a smooth periodic stationary solution

TorusEuler.isEulerSolution_zero.text: For every real $T>0$, the velocity $u(t,x)=0$ and pressure $p(t,x)=0$ form a classical Euler solution on $[0,T)$ (smooth, periodic, with mean-zero pressure, satisfying momentum and incompressibility). All regularity, periodicity, gauge and equation conditions are supplied explicitly. This is a useful check that the basic solution conditions can be met. It does not satisfy the conclusions of Theorem 1.1: it extends to longer intervals and its vorticity and both time integrals remain zero.

TorusEuler.isOpenQuotientMap_toUnitTorus.text: The map from real Euclidean coordinates to the unit three-torus is an open quotient map. The proof combines coordinate quotient maps with the Euclidean product homeomorphism. This topological property permits continuity of a torus field to be inferred from continuity of its periodic Euclidean lift.
TorusEuler.isOpenQuotientMap_toUnitTorus.summary: The Euclidean quotient map is open and surjective

TorusEuler.isOpen_offOrigin.text: The set $\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Z^3$ is open because it is the complement of the closed integer lattice. On the Euclidean lift, removing the torus origin removes every lattice representative, not only the vector zero. This permits local smoothness arguments on neighborhoods away from the singular torus point.

TorusEuler.isSelfAdjoint_kineticForm.text: The kinetic operator F-adjoint F is self-adjoint for every bounded operator F. Invertibility is unnecessary for this symmetry statement.

TorusEuler.iteratedDerivWithin_bilinear.text: For a continuous bilinear map $B$, smooth functions $f,g$ on a set $S$ on which derivatives within $S$ are unique, the $q$th derivative within $S$ of $B(f,g)$ is the usual binomial sum $\sum_j\binom qjB(f^{(j)},g^{(q-j)})$ at $t\in S$. This formulation includes nondegenerate closed intervals. The uniqueness condition prevents arbitrary choices of within-derivatives from entering the product identity.
TorusEuler.iteratedDerivWithin_bilinear.summary: The time Leibniz formula on a differentiable domain

TorusEuler.iteratedDerivWithin_timeSlice.text: Let $f$ be smooth on $I\times O$, with unique differentiation on both factors $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $O$. For $t\in I$, $x\in O$ and every order $n$, the one-variable within-time derivative of order $n$ of $r\mapsto f(r,x)$ at $t$ equals the full product derivative of $f$ within $I\times O$ at $(t,x)$ evaluated repeatedly on $(1,0)$. This converts normal multilinear jets into ordinary time derivatives.
TorusEuler.iteratedDerivWithin_timeSlice.summary: Time derivatives are full derivatives in the time direction

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_phaseMean_const.text: View the phase mean of a smooth one-periodic profile as a constant function of phase. Its derivative of order $j$ equals the mean of the corresponding derivative of the original profile. At order zero this preserves the mean; at positive orders both sides vanish by periodicity.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_phaseMean_const.summary: Phase differentiation commutes with a constant mean field

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_phaseOscillatio.text: For a smooth one-periodic function, taking any iterated phase derivative commutes with removing the phase mean. At positive orders the derivative of the subtracted constant is zero and the derivative itself has zero mean. This equality therefore works uniformly at order zero and at every higher order.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_phaseOscillatio.summary: Phase derivatives commute with subtracting the mean

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_phasePrimitive_.text: A smooth one-periodic profile with $\int_0^1f(s)\,ds=0$ has a normalized primitive that commutes with every phase derivative. The zero-mean assumption is essential to the periodic primitive identity and is explicitly carried by this theorem. The conclusion is equality of functions of phase, for each derivative order $j$.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_phasePrimitive_.summary: Phase derivatives commute with the periodic primitive

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_terminalBorelAt.text: Let $\beta_{n,\varepsilon}(t)=\varepsilon^n\phi_n(t/\varepsilon)$, where $\phi_n(t)=(t^n/n!)\chi(t)$ and $\chi$ is a fixed smooth bump equal to one for $|t|\le1$ and vanishing for $|t|\ge2$. For every $\varepsilon>0$ and all orders $n,k$, the $k$-th derivative of $\beta_{n,\varepsilon}$ at $t=0$ equals $1$ if $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Near zero the atom coincides with $t^n/n!$.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_terminalBorelAt.summary: Exactly one prescribed derivative at zero

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_waveSwitch.text: For every natural order $q$ and arbitrary real $t_0,r,t$, differentiating the affine-clock switch $q$ times gives $r^q$ times the $q$th derivative of the smooth transition function at $r(t-t_0)$. No positivity assumption on $r$ is needed for this chain-rule identity. Positive rate is required later when the physical switching interval is identified.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_waveSwitch.summary: Each switch derivative contributes one physical rate factor

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_waveSwitch_zero.text: If $q>0$, $r>0$, and $t$ lies outside $[t_0,t_0+1/r]$, the $q$th derivative of the physical switch vanishes at $t$. The affine clock maps such a point outside $[0,1]$, where the smooth transition is locally constant. The restriction to positive order matters because the switch itself remains one after activation.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_waveSwitch_zero.summary: Switch derivatives vanish beyond the closed switching interval

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_waveSwitch_zero.text: For $q>0$ and $r>0$, the $q$th switch derivative vanishes outside the open interval $(t_0,t_0+1/r)$, including both endpoints. The proof extends vanishing from the complementary open half-lines to their closures using continuity of the differentiated smooth switch. This is a stronger endpoint statement than support in the closed interval alone.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_waveSwitch_zero.summary: Switch derivatives are flat at both endpoints

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_angularLeray_p.text: For $c>0$ and $\xi\ne0$, the $n$th derivative of the angular Leray symbol at $\xi$ equals $c^n$ times its derivative at $c\xi$. Thus the derivative has degree $-n$. The proof differentiates the degree-zero symbol identity through a scalar linear map on the punctured space.

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_comp_sub_linea.text: Assume $n>0$, $f$ is $n$ times continuously differentiable at $g(x)$ and $g$ is $n$ times continuously differentiable at $x$. Derivatives are multilinear maps. The derivative of a composition, after subtracting the outer derivative applied to the highest inner derivative, is a sum indexed by partitions with at least two parts. Each term therefore involves lower-order inner derivatives. In Proposition 5.1, taking the composition $U\circ X$ produces the forcing $N_\beta$ in the higher variational equation.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_comp_sub_linea.summary: Removing the highest-order linear term leaves lower-order products

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_endpointParity.text: For a field smooth through order $m$, gives the iterated derivative of order $m$ of the reflection average. The reflected term is multiplied by $\varepsilon(-1)^m$. This parity alternation is what permits uniform treatment of every derivative order in the finite half-Hölder norms, rather than checking just the velocity itself.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_endpointParity.summary: Each spatial derivative contributes one reflection sign

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_fourier_schwar.text: For a Schwartz kernel, the order-$j$ Fourier derivative at zero in directions $v_1,\dots,v_j$ equals $(-2\pi i)^j$ times the integral of the kernel multiplied by the corresponding product of inner products. The statement also allows $j=0$, although the formalization's accompanying description speaks of positive degree. Schwartz decay ensures all moments used are integrable.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_fourier_schwar.summary: Fourier derivatives at zero encode signed moments

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_id_eq_zero_of_.text: At every point, the identity map has zero iterated Fréchet derivative of order at least two. The order condition $n\ge2$ excludes its nonzero first derivative. Applied to a flow initially equal to the identity, this supplies zero initial data for every higher variational equation.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_id_eq_zero_of_.summary: Higher derivatives of the initial identity vanish

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_liftConvolutio.text: For any continuous torus field, every derivative of its smooth spectral cutoff is convolution of the input lift with the corresponding derivative of the dilated kernel. Smoothness of the input is not assumed: the cutoff has finite Fourier support. Positive scale and smooth compact support of the symbol supply the kernel realization.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_liftConvolutio.summary: Differentiate the cutoff by differentiating its convolution kernel

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_liftConvolutio.text: For a complete complex normed target, an integrable kernel, and a $C^j$ function $f$, convolution commutes with the order-$j$ Fréchet derivative. The family of bounds controls every derivative from order zero through $j$, not only the top derivative. Induction repeatedly applies differentiation under an integrable majorant.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_liftConvolutio.summary: All bounded derivatives through the chosen order pass through convolution

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_liftConvolutio.text: For a Schwartz kernel and a finite Fourier input, every iterated derivative of the convolution equals convolution with the corresponding iterated kernel derivative. The proof compares the two finite Fourier formulas. Completeness of the complex target supports the Bochner integrals; finiteness of the Fourier sum avoids any series-limit issue.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_liftConvolutio.summary: Derivatives of polynomial convolutions move to the kernel

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_lift_finiteFou.text: For arbitrary finite Fourier synthesis and a list of derivative directions, the iterated derivative multiplies each amplitude by the product of the corresponding directional frequency factors. The target is any complex normed space. Smoothness is automatic for the finite synthesis, so no separate input regularity hypothesis is needed.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_lift_finiteFou.summary: Repeated derivatives act by products of frequency factors

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_phaseMean.text: Every parameter derivative of the phase mean equals the phase mean of the corresponding parameter derivative, provided the original profile is jointly smooth. The order $k$ is arbitrary and phase is integrated over one unit interval. This statement does not require periodicity because it is an identity for a fixed interval integral.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_phaseMean.summary: Parameter differentiation commutes with phase averaging

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_phaseOscillati.text: For a jointly smooth parameterized profile, subtracting the phase average commutes with every iterated parameter derivative. Both sides are evaluated at the same parameter $x$ and phase $s$. The result transfers derivative estimates to the oscillatory part without assuming that the original profile already has zero phase mean.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_phaseOscillati.summary: Parameter derivatives commute with removing the mean

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_phasePrimitive.text: For a jointly smooth parameterized profile, taking its normalized phase primitive commutes with all parameter derivatives. The identity includes the constant removed to normalize the primitive's phase mean. It is an algebraic-integral commutation statement; periodic primitive properties require the additional periodicity and mean conditions used elsewhere.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_phasePrimitive.summary: Parameter derivatives commute with the normalized primitive

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_scaledPhasePro.text: For a smooth profile, an iterated derivative of its rescaled version evaluated on coordinate directions equals the unscaled derivative at the scaled point, multiplied by the product of coordinate weights. Each label slot contributes $\ell$ and each phase slot contributes $h$. No nonzero assumption is needed for this forward scaling identity.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_scaledPhasePro.summary: Mixed derivatives acquire the product of their scales

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_slabPath_unifo.text: On a compact parameter set, every parameter derivative of order $m\le n$ of a $C^n$ path-valued map is uniformly bounded at all slab times. The bound is on the operator norm of the full multilinear derivative. Compactness bounds the path-space derivative and the evaluation operator costs at most one.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_slabPath_unifo.summary: Compact parameter sets give uniform jet bounds in time

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_terminalBorelA.text: Let $\beta_{n,\varepsilon}(t)=\varepsilon^n\phi_n(t/\varepsilon)$, where $\phi_n(t)=(t^n/n!)\chi(t)$ and $\chi$ is a fixed smooth bump equal to one for $|t|\le1$ and vanishing for $|t|\ge2$. For $\varepsilon>0$, orders $n,k$ and real directions $v_1,\dots,v_k$, the $k$-th derivative of $\beta_{n,\varepsilon}$ at zero, as a $k$-linear form, takes the value $v_1v_2\cdots v_k$ if $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_terminalBorelA.summary: The full derivative of a scalar atom at zero

TorusEuler.kineticForm.text: For a bounded linear operator $F$ on a real Hilbert space, define $K=F^*F$. Thus $\langle Kv,v\rangle=\|Fv\|^2$, so $K$ is nonnegative. For Euclidean particle labels the adjoint is the matrix transpose, and $F=D_aX$ gives $K=(D_aX)^TD_aX$ in (4.1). The definition imposes no invertibility or flow equation on $F$. A positive lower bound for $K$ requires a separate estimate on a left inverse of $F$.
TorusEuler.kineticForm.summary: Form the metric induced by a linear deformation

TorusEuler.kineticForm_elliptic.text: Let $F,G$ be bounded operators on a real Hilbert space, with $GF=I$ and $\|G\|\le D$, where $D>0$. Then $\langle F^*Fv,v\rangle\ge D^{-2}\|v\|^2$ for every vector $v$. For $F=D_aX$ this is the ellipticity $K\ge D_-^{-2}I$ used in Theorem 4.2. Only a left inverse is needed. No bound on $F$ itself, symmetry of the velocity gradient, incompressibility or particle-flow equation is required for this linear-algebraic conclusion.
TorusEuler.kineticForm_elliptic.summary: Convert an inverse norm bound into a quadratic lower bound

TorusEuler.kineticForm_identity.text: The identity deformation has identity kinetic coefficient. In the flow application this identifies K at initial time and helps recover the initial correction from the constant field.
TorusEuler.kineticForm_identity.summary: The kinetic coefficient of the identity deformation

TorusEuler.kineticForm_inverse.text: If $G$ is a two-sided inverse of $F$, assumed as both $GF=I$ and $FG=I$, then $GG^*$ is a two-sided inverse of the kinetic form $F^*F$. The conclusion explicitly gives both compositions as the identity. This statement uses a supplied inverse rather than relying on an inverse defined for every operator.
TorusEuler.kineticForm_inverse.summary: The inverse deformation gives a two sided kinetic inverse

TorusEuler.kineticForm_quadratic_upper.text: The kinetic pairing of $v$ is at most $\|F\|^2\|v\|^2$. This follows by identifying it with $\|Fv\|^2$ and applying the operator norm bound. The result is an upper estimate for any bounded deformation operator; ellipticity and a lower estimate require distinct assumptions.
TorusEuler.kineticForm_quadratic_upper.summary: The deformation norm bounds the kinetic quadratic form

TorusEuler.labelFlow_firstVariation.text: On $[l,r]$, suppose flows exist for every velocity $u+\varepsilon b$ with the same starting position $a$. Assume $u$ is spatially differentiable and uniformly Lipschitz, its spatial derivative is uniformly Lipschitz, and $b$ is jointly continuous, uniformly bounded and uniformly Lipschitz in space. Also require continuity of $D_xu$ along the unperturbed trajectory. Then the derivative of the perturbed flow at $\varepsilon=0$ exists at every time and is a path $\xi$ satisfying $\xi(l)=0$ and $\xi_t=D_xu(t,X(t,a))\xi+b(t,X(t,a))$. This establishes the actual first variation used in §4.1, not merely existence of a solution to its linear equation.
TorusEuler.labelFlow_firstVariation.summary: Identify the actual perturbation derivative of the flow

TorusEuler.labelPhaseScale.text:
Scaling the label by the envelope radius and the phase by the profile width makes the weighted coordinate derivatives into the ordinary derivatives of a rescaled profile.

If either scale is zero the linear map collapses the corresponding coordinates. Results recovering unscaled derivatives assume the positive scales used by the construction.

TorusEuler.labelPhaseScale_apply.text: The rescaling map sends (a,s) to (ℓa,hs). The label radius and phase width are independent scalar factors; positivity or invertibility is needed only when later results undo the scaling.

TorusEuler.labelPhaseScale_phaseCoordina.text: Applying the label-phase scaling map to a coordinate direction multiplies that direction by its assigned weight. The equality holds for arbitrary real scales, including zero. It is the linear algebra input that attaches one envelope factor or one phase-width factor to each slot of a mixed derivative.
TorusEuler.labelPhaseScale_phaseCoordina.summary: Scaling acts diagonally on the four directions

TorusEuler.labelPhaseSlope.text: Map a label increment $v$ to its scaled label component and the corresponding scaled phase increment: $(\ell^{-1}v,h^{-1}\langle k,v\rangle)$. This continuous linear map records both derivative costs in evaluating a phase profile along a graph. The definition allows arbitrary real scales; inverse identities later require them nonzero.
TorusEuler.labelPhaseSlope.summary: Label increments on the scaled phase graph

TorusEuler.labelPhaseSlope_apply.text: Evaluating the label-phase slope at $v$ gives the explicit pair $(\ell^{-1}v,h^{-1}\langle k,v\rangle)$ of scaled label and phase components. The equality is definitional for every real scale and vector. In applications, the first component costs the reciprocal envelope radius and the second costs the wave-vector magnitude divided by the phase width.

TorusEuler.labelWaveVector.text: For a particle at $a$ at time $s$, the formal definition is $\kappa(t)=(D_xX(t,s)|_{X(s,t,a)})^Tk_*$. It differentiates the reverse map at the current particle position. When $X$ is the smooth parent flow, this equals $(D_aX(s,t,a))^{-T}k_*$; the paper uses $s=0$. The transpose is with respect to the Euclidean inner product. The formula accepts arbitrary maps and initial covectors, so nonvanishing and inverse identities are not automatic. Derivatives are assigned zero where they do not exist; the smooth-flow hypotheses and $k_*\ne0$ give the intended nondegenerate covector.
TorusEuler.labelWaveVector.summary: The reverse-flow derivative transports the initial covector

TorusEuler.labelWaveVector_smul.text: Multiplying the launch covector $k$ by a real scalar $c$ multiplies its transported wave vector by the same scalar. This is linearity of the inverse deformation transpose in the covector argument. No flow equation or invertibility assumption is imposed here; those hypotheses are needed when interpreting this algebraic expression as transport.
TorusEuler.labelWaveVector_smul.summary: Transport preserves the launch covector scale

TorusEuler.laplacianMode.text: The Laplacian symbol is $-(2\pi)^2|k|^2$, regarded as a complex scalar. It corresponds to the sum of second derivatives for the unit-torus Fourier normalization. The negative sign is the usual Laplacian convention, which determines the sign of the pressure inverse used below.
TorusEuler.laplacianMode.summary: The Laplacian multiplier has negative frequency square

TorusEuler.laplacianMode_mul_inverseLapl.text: Multiplying the Laplacian symbol by its inverse gives zero at zero frequency and one at every other frequency. This explicit case distinction prevents treating the pressure inverse as an unrestricted inverse. It is the coefficient-level statement that a periodic Poisson solution recovers the source minus its mean.
TorusEuler.laplacianMode_mul_inverseLapl.summary: The pressure inverse recovers every nonconstant mode

TorusEuler.laplacianMode_ne_zero.text: If the integer frequency satisfies $k\ne0$, its Laplacian symbol $-(2\pi)^2|k|^2$ is nonzero. Positivity of the squared frequency length and the nonvanishing of $2\pi$ justify this statement. The lemma provides the scalar cancellation guard for the inverse Laplacian at nonzero modes.
TorusEuler.laplacianMode_ne_zero.summary: The Laplacian symbol is invertible away from zero frequency

TorusEuler.laplacianMode_zero.text: The Laplacian symbol at zero frequency is zero. This follows directly from the sum of squared frequency coordinates. It records the constant-mode obstruction to inverting the periodic Laplacian and supplies the base case for the deliberately zero-mean pressure inverse.
TorusEuler.laplacianMode_zero.summary: The Laplacian annihilates the constant frequency

TorusEuler.laterPhysicalWindow_fits_pare.text: The scheduled half-length shrinkage and a crossing in the old first half imply strict separation of the new endpoint from the old endpoint, together with containment of the whole new slab. The hypotheses refer to adjacent induction half lengths. The statement does not itself prove the shrinkage or locate the crossing.
TorusEuler.laterPhysicalWindow_fits_pare.summary: The scheduled next interval stays strictly inside its parent

TorusEuler.latticeVector.text: For an integer triple $n=(n_1,n_2,n_3)\in\mathbb Z^3$, this is the vector of $\mathbb R^3$ with real coordinates $n_1,n_2,n_3$. These are exactly the translations under which periodic fields are required to be invariant; the map is not a rounding or a choice of representative.

TorusEuler.le_exp_integral_of_volterra.text: If continuous $u$ and nonnegative continuous $k$ satisfy $u(t)\le c+\int_a^t k(r)u(r)\,dr$, then $u(t)\le c\exp(\int_a^t k)$. The proof differentiates an integrating factor and shows it decreases. Neither $u\ge0$ nor $c\ge0$ is assumed; their usual nonnegativity in the norm application is not needed for this abstract inequality.
TorusEuler.le_exp_integral_of_volterra.summary: An exponential bound from the integral inequality

TorusEuler.lemma31_waveProfile.text: The formal theorem proves the full conclusion of Lemma 3.1 for the specified families $F_h,P_h$. For $0<h\le1$, both are smooth and period one, $F_h$ is odd, $P_h'=F_h$, and $P_h$ has zero average over one phase period. One positive $C$ gives $F_h'(0)=1$, $-Ch\le F_h'\le1$ and $|F_h|\le Ch$ for all widths and phases. Each integer $j\ge2$ has its own positive width-independent $C_j$ with $|\partial_s^jF_h|\le C_jh^{1-j}$. The exponent is integral, preserving negative powers. The conclusion gives particular witnesses for the paper's existence claim; no properties are asserted for widths outside $(0,1]$.
TorusEuler.lemma31_waveProfile.summary: One constructed family satisfies every estimate of Lemma 3.1

TorusEuler.length_hierarchyLeibnizSplits.text: The ordered Leibniz list for a word of length $m$ contains exactly $2^m$ entries. Each derivative is assigned to either the first or second factor. Repeated coordinate letters retain their multiplicities, so this counts product-rule terms rather than distinct pairs of resulting words.
TorusEuler.length_hierarchyLeibnizSplits.summary: There are two choices for each derivative

TorusEuler.lerayMode.text: The coefficient $a$ is sent to $a-(k\cdot a)|k|^{-2}k$, using complex coordinate arithmetic. For nonzero frequency this removes the component parallel to $k$. At zero frequency, totalized division makes the correction vanish and preserves the constant vector mode, as required for the periodic Leray projection.

TorusEuler.lerayModeProjection.text: This continuous complex-linear map is the orthogonal projection onto the transverse mode space $\{a\in\mathbb C^3:\ a\perp k\}$. It is a Hilbert-space realization of the earlier coordinate Leray formula. Subsequent lemmas identify the two realizations and obtain the operator norm bound needed to extend the projection to square-integrable fields.
TorusEuler.lerayModeProjection.summary: The bounded orthogonal projection onto transverse coefficients

TorusEuler.lerayModeProjection_toLp.text: Applying the bounded orthogonal projection to a coefficient vector gives the explicit Leray coefficient $a-\frac{k\cdot a}{|k|^2}k$. The proof expands the projection onto a one-dimensional span and matches the inner product and squared norm. This identity includes the intentional identity action at frequency zero.
TorusEuler.lerayModeProjection_toLp.summary: The orthogonal projection equals the explicit Leray formula

TorusEuler.lerayModeProjection_zero.text: At zero frequency, the continuous linear Leray projection equals the identity operator. This is operator equality, extending the earlier coefficientwise identity. It ensures that the Hilbert-space construction retains constant vector fields rather than projecting onto a mean-zero spatial subspace.
TorusEuler.lerayModeProjection_zero.summary: The bounded zero frequency projection is the identity

TorusEuler.lerayMode_eq_angularLeray_com.text: For an arbitrary complex coefficient, the Leray output is reconstructed from the angular projection of its real coordinate vector and that of its imaginary coordinate vector. The formula uses the same real frequency for both. This permits real Hilbert-space coercivity estimates to be applied to complex Fourier coefficients.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_eq_angularLeray_com.summary: Leray acts separately on real and imaginary parts

TorusEuler.lerayMode_eq_sub_gradient.text: The Leray-projected coefficient equals the original coefficient $a$ minus the gradient symbol $2\pi ik$ applied to the pressure correction, the inverse Laplacian symbol times the divergence symbol of $a$. This identity holds at zero and nonzero frequencies, using the chosen inverse Laplacian that assigns zero to the zero mode. It ties the geometric transverse projection to the pressure formulation needed in the endpoint equation.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_eq_sub_gradient.summary: The Leray correction is a pressure gradient

TorusEuler.lerayMode_idempotent.text: The Leray symbol is idempotent at every frequency. Its first application produces a transverse coefficient, and the preceding fixed-point lemma shows that the second application preserves it. The identity includes the zero mode, where the symbol is already the identity.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_idempotent.summary: Applying the Leray symbol twice changes nothing

TorusEuler.lerayMode_ofRealVector.text: Applying the coordinate Leray symbol to a real vector cast into complex coordinates is the same as applying the angular Leray operator at the real frequency and then casting its result. This holds for all integer modes, including zero. It verifies compatibility of the real and complex formalizations.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_ofRealVector.summary: The complex Leray formula agrees with the real symbol

TorusEuler.lerayMode_of_transverse.text: If the frequency contraction $\sum_ik_ia_i$ of $a$ is zero, the Leray symbol fixes $a$. This hypothesis expresses transversality; it automatically holds at zero frequency. The result requires no norm estimate and directly identifies vectors in the symbol range as fixed points.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_of_transverse.summary: Transverse coefficients are unchanged by Leray projection

TorusEuler.lerayMode_tensorDivergenceMod.text: At every Fourier mode, Leray-projected tensor divergence equals the original tensor divergence plus the gradient mode of the normalized pressure symbol. The formula includes the zero mode consistently. It identifies the nonlocal pressure contribution used when the source is separated from the observation region.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_tensorDivergenceMod.summary: Projected tensor divergence splits into local and pressure parts

TorusEuler.lerayMode_zero.text: The zero-frequency Leray symbol is the identity on every coefficient vector. This is proved from the actual totalized formula, not assumed as a separate branch. Preserving the constant mode is necessary for the spatial projection to retain divergence-free mean fields used in the endpoint problem.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_zero.summary: The Leray projection preserves the constant mode

TorusEuler.liftConvolution.text: Define the convolution at $x$ by integrating the scalar kernel value times the field at $x-y$ over Euclidean three-space. The field can be a periodic lift, but periodicity is not built into the definition. Analytic integrability conditions are supplied by the subsequent bounded-field lemmas.
TorusEuler.liftConvolution.summary: Convolving the periodic lift with a scalar kernel

TorusEuler.liftConvolution_cutoffSchwart.text: Let $g$ be continuous on $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$ with values in a complex Banach space. Assume $\psi$ is smooth and zero outside the radius-two ball, and let $\Lambda>0$. For the periodic lift $f$ and $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3\check\psi(\Lambda y)$, the formal statement proves $(S_\Lambda g)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}K_\Lambda(y)f(x-y)\,dy$. The field is bounded by compactness and the kernel is integrable. This is the representation used in Appendix B. No plateau, radiality or evenness is needed, but this particular result assumes a continuous complex-valued or complex Banach-valued field, not an arbitrary measurable real velocity.
TorusEuler.liftConvolution_cutoffSchwart.summary: Identifies periodic Fourier synthesis with Euclidean convolution

TorusEuler.liftConvolution_cutoffSchwart.text: For a smooth compactly supported cutoff symbol and positive frequency scale, convolution of any finite torus Fourier sum with the dilated constructed Schwartz kernel equals the prescribed cutoff. This combines Fourier inversion with the preceding polynomial identity. Extending the conclusion to larger function spaces requires the later boundedness and density arguments.
TorusEuler.liftConvolution_cutoffSchwart.summary: The constructed Schwartz kernel realizes the cutoff

TorusEuler.liftConvolution_fourierMode.text: Convolving a scalar lifted Fourier character by $K$ multiplies that character by the Fourier transform of $K$ at the lattice frequency. This is the scalar specialization of the vector-valued mode identity. It fixes the torus multiplier convention before finite Fourier sums are treated term by term.

TorusEuler.liftConvolution_fourierMode_s.text: For a complex Banach-valued coefficient $a$, convolution of its Fourier mode by $K$ multiplies it by the whole-space Fourier transform of $K$ at the corresponding lattice vector. The declaration has no explicit integrability hypothesis: it is an identity of integral expressions, which take the value zero for nonintegrable integrands. Concrete kernel applications later establish integrability and continuity.
TorusEuler.liftConvolution_fourierMode_s.summary: Each Fourier mode is a convolution eigenfunction

TorusEuler.liftConvolution_lift_finiteFo.text: For an integrable kernel, convolving a finite torus Fourier sum on its Euclidean lift multiplies each coefficient by the kernel's Fourier transform at that lattice frequency. The finite sum can be interchanged with integration directly. This establishes the convolution representation first on trigonometric polynomials, before any density argument.
TorusEuler.liftConvolution_lift_finiteFo.summary: Convolution acts mode by mode on a finite Fourier sum

TorusEuler.liftConvolution_scaledLiftKer.text: An integrable Euclidean kernel whose Fourier transform is the prescribed compactly supported real symbol realizes the torus cutoff after positive dilation. The equality is proved for arbitrary finite Fourier sums. The identity between the kernel's Fourier transform and the symbol is an explicit input, so this theorem does not itself construct the kernel.
TorusEuler.liftConvolution_scaledLiftKer.summary: The dilated kernel realizes the periodic cutoff on polynomials

TorusEuler.lift_lerayMode_eq_sub_gradien.text: The synthesized Leray field equals the original vector polynomial minus the gradient of its synthesized pressure correction. This is a pointwise identity on the Euclidean lift. It combines the modewise algebraic decomposition with the exact gradient formula for finite Fourier sums.
TorusEuler.lift_lerayMode_eq_sub_gradien.summary: Finite Leray projection subtracts the pressure gradient

TorusEuler.linearFundamental_parameterDe.text: A parameter-dependent fundamental solution with uniformly bounded norm has a parameter derivative satisfying the inhomogeneous variational equation. The inputs include a global parameter Lipschitz bound on the coefficient $A$, its derivative at the selected parameter, continuity of that derivative in time, and parameter continuity of the fundamental solution $F$. Differentiation under a dominated integral proves the derivative instead of assuming it.
TorusEuler.linearFundamental_parameterDe.summary: Differentiate the fundamental solution through its coefficient

TorusEuler.linearODEWordFactor.text: Defines the recurrence $F(0)=1$ and $F(n+1)=1+2^{n+1}qF(n)$. In applications, $q$ is the product of homogeneous stability, time length, and the positive-order coefficient bound. The recurrence records dependence on differentiation order explicitly, without claiming that this factor is uniform in order.
TorusEuler.linearODEWordFactor.summary: Order-dependent factor for the coefficient commutator

TorusEuler.linearODEWordFactor_mono.text: If $0\le q\le r$, then the recurrence factor at every fixed order is no larger at $q$ than at $r$. The proof combines induction with nonnegativity of the earlier factor. This allows a uniform cap on stability times duration times coefficient size to replace the actual product.
TorusEuler.linearODEWordFactor_mono.summary: Increasing the coefficient cost increases the order factor

TorusEuler.linearODEWordFactor_nonneg.text: For $q \ge  0$, every value of the order recurrence is nonnegative. Induction uses its constant one and the nonnegative product in the successor step. This sign control is needed when the factor multiplies initial-data and forcing budgets or is replaced by a larger commutator cap.
TorusEuler.linearODEWordFactor_nonneg.summary: Nonnegative commutator cost gives a nonnegative factor

TorusEuler.linearODE_exists_Icc.text: For $a\le b$, continuous bounded-linear-operator coefficients on $[a,b]$, and arbitrary initial data, constructs a path satisfying $x\prime=A(t)x$ there and $x(a)=x_0$. The ambient real normed space must be complete. Derivatives are taken within the closed interval, allowing endpoint data; the function is defined on all real times but the ODE is asserted only on this interval.
TorusEuler.linearODE_exists_Icc.summary: Solve a linear equation from the left endpoint

TorusEuler.linearODE_exists_Icc_of_mem.text: A continuous homogeneous linear ODE has a solution on the full closed interval, with initial data at any point of the interval.
TorusEuler.linearODE_exists_Icc_of_mem.summary: Solving a linear equation from any slab time

TorusEuler.linearODE_forced_norm_le.text: Let $E$ be a real Banach space, $A(r)$ a continuous family of bounded operators on $E$ and $f$ continuous on $[a,b]$. Suppose every solution of $x'=A(r)x$ on $[a,b]$ (derivatives within $[a,b]$) satisfies $\|x(t)\|\le M\|x(r)\|$ whenever $a\le r\le t\le b$. If $z'=A(r)z+f(r)$ on $[a,b]$, then for every $t\in[a,b]$, $\|z(t)\|\le M\|z(a)\|+\int_a^tM\|f(r)\|\,dr$. The stability bound is a hypothesis, and the proof uses variation of constants.
TorusEuler.linearODE_forced_norm_le.summary: A uniform bound on the homogeneous flow controls the forced solution

TorusEuler.linearODE_fundamental_comp_in.text: Proves the reverse composition $\Phi(t)\Psi(t)=I$ from the normalized fundamental and inverse equations. This direction additionally assumes that the coefficient $A$ is continuous on $J$. The product solves the commutator equation $X\prime=AX-XA$, and uniqueness identifies it with the identity. The result applies to normed real spaces without a finite-dimensional or completeness hypothesis.

TorusEuler.linearODE_inhom_exists_Icc.text: Constructs a solution of $x\prime=A(t)x+g(t)$ for continuous $A$ and $g$ on a closed interval, with data prescribed at any member $t_0$. Completeness of the ambient space is required. The proof adjoins a scalar coordinate equal to one and solves a homogeneous equation on the product space; it asserts no uniqueness or bounds beyond existence.
TorusEuler.linearODE_inhom_exists_Icc.summary: Solve a forced linear equation on a closed interval

TorusEuler.linearODE_inv_comp_fundamenta.text: If operator paths $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ solve $\Phi\prime=A\Phi$ and $\Psi\prime=-\Psi A$ within an order-connected set, and both equal the identity at a point of that set, then $\Psi(t)\Phi(t)=I$ throughout it. Product differentiation gives zero derivative. No continuity assumption on $A$ is needed for this order of composition, because the resulting equation is constant.
TorusEuler.linearODE_inv_comp_fundamenta.summary: The inverse flow cancels the fundamental flow

TorusEuler.linearODE_ne_zero_of_mem.text: Let $J$ be an interval, let $A(t)$ be continuous in operator norm on $J$, and let $x$ solve $x'=A(t)x$ there, with derivatives relative to $J$. The formal statement proves that $x(t_0)\ne0$ at one $t_0\in J$ implies $x(t)\ne0$ for every $t\in J$, both before and after $t_0$. It holds in any real normed vector space for bounded linear coefficients; no existence of a solution is asserted. In Lemma 2.1 it is applied separately to the wave-vector and amplitude equations, after verifying continuity of their coefficients.
TorusEuler.linearODE_ne_zero_of_mem.summary: A nonzero solution cannot reach zero within the same time interval

TorusEuler.linearODE_parameters_joint_co.text: A supplied family of solutions is jointly continuous in time and a pseudometric parameter if coefficients, forcing, and initial data have the stated uniform Lipschitz bounds. The size assumption $\|x(t,p)\|\le C$ controls the solution itself, with $C\ge0$. The conclusion also produces one parameter Lipschitz constant for the whole slab; no existence assertion is hidden here.
TorusEuler.linearODE_parameters_joint_co.summary: Uniform coefficient bounds give continuous parameter dependence

TorusEuler.linearODE_perturbation_bounds.text: Assume the unperturbed Banach-space flow has forward bound $M\ge0$, the continuous matrix error has norm at most continuous $\rho$, and $x,y$ solve the perturbed and unperturbed equations. With $D=\int_a^t\rho$, the theorem bounds growth by $M\|x(a)\|e^{MD}$ and the comparison error by $M\|x(a)-y(a)\|+M^2\|x(a)\|e^{MD}D$. No smallness condition is imposed; later estimates make the exponential harmless.
TorusEuler.linearODE_perturbation_bounds.summary: Growth and error under an integrated matrix perturbation

TorusEuler.linearODE_unique_of_mem.text: Two solutions of a continuous linear ODE on an interval agree everywhere if they agree at any time in the interval.
TorusEuler.linearODE_unique_of_mem.summary: A continuous linear equation has unique trajectories

TorusEuler.linearODE_variation_of_consta.text: In a real Banach space, let $A$ and $f$ be continuous on $[a,b]$. Suppose bounded linear maps $\Phi,\Psi$ satisfy $\Phi(a)=\Psi(a)=I$, $\Phi\prime=A\Phi$ and $\Psi\prime=-\Psi A$, and let $z\prime=Az+f$ on the interval. Then $z(t)=\Phi(t)z(a)+\int_a^t\Phi(t)\Psi(r)f(r)\,dr$ for every $t\in[a,b]$. Derivatives at the endpoints are taken within the interval. The paper applies this general identity with the unperturbed triangular flow and forcing equal to the coefficient error applied to the perturbed solution. The statement assumes the two fundamental evolutions; it supplies neither their existence nor a propagator bound.
TorusEuler.linearODE_variation_of_consta.summary: A fundamental solution and its inverse give the integral identity

TorusEuler.linearODE_weightedHierarchyWo.text: Specializes the localized weighted word estimate to $x(l)=0$. Under the same closed-support, smoothness, positive-weight, stability, and commutator-cap assumptions, the resulting constant is the order factor times $K\cdot (r-l)\cdot H$. The proof verifies a zero initial word bound and invokes the general theorem, so support propagation remains part of the argument.
TorusEuler.linearODE_weightedHierarchyWo.summary: Zero initial data removes the initial-value contribution

TorusEuler.linearODE_weightedHierarchyWo.text: On $[l,r]$, initial data and forcing vanish outside a closed set $S$, while weighted homogeneous stability and positive-order coefficient estimates are required only on $S$. Smoothness, a strictly positive time weight, and a cap on $K\cdot (r-l)\cdot C$ yield a global finite-word bound for the weighted solution. Outside $S$, uniqueness gives zero solution and closedness gives zero derivatives.
TorusEuler.linearODE_weightedHierarchyWo.summary: Localized initial data and forcing give a global word bound

TorusEuler.linearODE_wordBounds.text: On a positive slab $[0,T]$, assumes smooth coefficients, forcing, and solution, a strictly positive differentiable weight, weighted homogeneous stability on $S$, and initial, forcing, and positive-order coefficient bounds through order $N$. Every solution word through that order is bounded by $F_N(KTC)\,K(B+TH)$, where $F_N(q)$ is the order factor given by $F_0=1$ and $F_{n+1}=1+2^{n+1}qF_n$. Independence from other parameters requires a separate uniform bound on $K\cdot T\cdot C$.
TorusEuler.linearODE_wordBounds.summary: Control all parameter words through a prescribed order

TorusEuler.linearODE_wordBounds_Icc.text: For $l<r$, gives the same all-word estimate on $[l,r]$, replacing time length $T$ by $r-l$ and initial data at zero by data at $l$. All smoothness, positive-weight, homogeneous-stability, and coefficient hypotheses are stated on that interval. The proof translates the problem to a zero-start slab and translates solutions back.
TorusEuler.linearODE_wordBounds_Icc.summary: The weighted word estimate allows any launch time

TorusEuler.lipschitzOnWith_halfHolder_of.text: If every label evaluation has the stated within-interval time derivative and the derivative fields have half-Hölder norm at most $B\ge0$, the entire field curve is Lipschitz with constant $B$ in the half-Hölder norm. The proof controls values and spatial increments separately. A pointwise value bound on derivatives alone would not establish this norm-level conclusion.
TorusEuler.lipschitzOnWith_halfHolder_of.summary: Uniform derivative control gives a Lipschitz Hölder-space curve

TorusEuler.lipschitzWith_toUnitTorus.text: The map from Euclidean space to the unit torus is Lipschitz with constant one. It packages the preceding distance comparison as a Lipschitz statement, supplying continuity and quantitative control for translated curves. This concerns the quotient map, not a discontinuous choice of real representatives of torus points.
TorusEuler.lipschitzWith_toUnitTorus.summary: The quotient map to the torus is 1-Lipschitz

TorusEuler.localizedCoefficient_holderHa.text: Suppose $r>0$, $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi$ vanishes beyond distance $2r$ from $a_0$, and $|\chi(a)-\chi(b)|\le(C/r)d(a,b)$ with $C\ge0$.
