This pointwise identity identifies the bounded map with the usual real-part operation, despite the different representations of Euclidean space used for the real and complex vectors.

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartVector_comple.text: Complexification followed by real projection recovers the original vector.

TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJets.text: This function is the canonical completed jet tuple of a smooth periodic velocity. It is the evaluation of the corresponding linear embedding of smooth periodic velocities into the completed jet space, so all components still equal actual derivatives of the same field. The completed space is needed for integration and time regularity arguments, while these particular inputs remain smooth.
TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJets.summary: A smooth velocity enters the completed jet space

TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJets_apply.text: For a smooth periodic input, evaluating any component of its completed jet tuple gives the corresponding actual iterated Fréchet derivative. The index $i\in\{0,\dots,m\}$ limits the order to the stored range. Completion has changed the ambient space, not the value of an embedded smooth tuple.
TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJets_apply.summary: Completed smooth tuples still evaluate to actual derivatives

TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump.text: The scaled bump is evaluated after subtracting the nearest integer, implemented by $\lfloor s+1/2\rfloor$. The formula is one-periodic for all scales. Smoothness and evenness across the cell seams are proved under $0<h\le1$, where the bump vanishes well before those seams.
TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump.summary: Repeating the scaled bump in each unit phase cell

TorusEuler.periodic_iteratedDeriv_phase.text: If a function is periodic with period $\tau$, every iterated derivative has the same period. No smoothness hypothesis is present because the derivative in the formalization is defined at every point, with a default value where it does not exist, and translation preserves its definition. In applications to smooth profiles, these derivatives agree with the ordinary analytic derivatives.

TorusEuler.periodic_odd_of_pointwise_lim.text: If each vector field is spatially periodic and odd and the sequence converges pointwise, its limit has both symmetries. The proof compares limits at translated points and at $x$ and $-x$. No smoothness or uniform convergence is assumed here; these are purely closed symmetry identities in a normed target.
TorusEuler.periodic_odd_of_pointwise_lim.summary: Periodicity and oddness survive pointwise convergence

TorusEuler.periodic_periodicWaveBump.text: Adding one to the phase leaves the periodic bump unchanged because the nearest-integer floor also increases by one. The theorem holds for every real scale, even degenerate scales. It is an algebraic periodicity statement; smoothness at the wrapping points requires the separate admissible-scale hypotheses.

TorusEuler.periodic_phaseOscillation.text: If a profile is one-periodic, subtracting its phase mean gives another one-periodic profile. This proof only uses that the subtracted mean is constant in the phase; continuity and integrability are not hypotheses. It does not assert that the resulting profile has zero mean, which is proved separately under the appropriate integration assumptions.
TorusEuler.periodic_phaseOscillation.summary: Subtracting the mean preserves the phase period

TorusEuler.periodic_phasePrimitive.text: Let $f:\mathbb R\to E$ be continuous and period-one, with $E$ a real normed space and $\int_0^1f(s)\,ds=0$. Put $J(s)=\int_0^sf(r)\,dr$ and $F(s)=J(s)-\int_0^1J(r)\,dr$. The formal statement proves $F(s+1)=F(s)$ for every real $s$. It has no completeness hypothesis. For the Banach targets of the paper these are ordinary integrals, and zero input mean removes the drift of $J$ between periods. Subtracting a constant alone would not remove such drift. This declaration proves periodicity only: zero mean of $F$ and the identity $F'=f$ are separate results whose hypotheses include completeness.
TorusEuler.periodic_phasePrimitive.summary: Zero mean prevents a primitive from drifting between periods

TorusEuler.periodic_wavePotential.text: For continuous one-periodic $V$ with zero phase mean, proves one-periodicity of the wave potential, the normalized phase primitive of $s\mapsto-|\kappa|^{-2}\kappa\times V(s)$. The proof transfers the mean through the fixed cross-product operator and uses the periodic primitive theorem. It does not require $\kappa\ne0$ or transversality; these conditions enter the separate fast-curl recovery theorem.
TorusEuler.periodic_wavePotential.summary: The wave potential has the prescribed phase period

TorusEuler.periodic_wavePressurePrimitiv.text: For every $0<h\le1$, the formal statement proves $P_h(s+1)=P_h(s)$ for all real $s$. The chosen $P_h$ is the integral of the constructed $F_h$ with the integral's phase mean subtracted. Continuity, period one and zero phase mean of $F_h$ make that primitive periodic. This is the pressure-profile periodicity required in Lemma 3.1 and (3.3). The theorem concerns the phase variable alone; it does not assert spatial periodicity of a pressure evaluated at an arbitrary real plane phase. That requires the lattice condition or localization and periodic extension.
TorusEuler.periodic_wavePressurePrimitiv.summary: The normalized primitive repeats after one phase cycle

TorusEuler.periodic_waveProfile.text: For each $0<h\le1$, the constructed profile satisfies $F_h(s+1)=F_h(s)$ at every real phase. Its definition integrates the normalized periodized bump slope from zero, and the zero integral of that slope over one period eliminates any additive drift. This is the periodicity asserted in Lemma 3.1. The theorem does not use a lattice condition on a spatial wave vector: it concerns only the one-dimensional phase function. Oddness, derivative bounds and the normalized pressure primitive are separate properties of the same family.
TorusEuler.periodic_waveProfile.summary: The mean-free slope integrates to a period-one function

TorusEuler.periodizeCentered.text:
Extend a label profile periodically using its values on the centered cell.

Periodicity is automatic, but continuity across cell faces is not. The construction uses profiles vanishing near the boundary before claiming smooth periodic extension.
TorusEuler.periodizeCentered.summary: Periodic extension from the centered cell

TorusEuler.periodizeCentered_eq_on_cente.text: The periodic extension agrees on the whole closed cell when the profile vanishes near its boundary.
TorusEuler.periodizeCentered_eq_on_cente.summary: The periodic extension agrees on the closed cell

TorusEuler.periodizeCentered_neg_equivar.text: If a profile transforms under reflection by a map $L$ fixing zero and vanishes on the negative cell walls, its centered periodic extension obeys the same reflection law. No continuity is assumed. The wall hypothesis handles points where negation does not commute with the half-open centered representative; away from those walls the representatives are exact negatives.
TorusEuler.periodizeCentered_neg_equivar.summary: Periodic extension preserves reflection when cell walls vanish

TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateDirection.text:
The label coordinate directions and the separate phase direction.

The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateDirection.summary: Three label directions and one phase direction

TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateWeight.text: Assign the envelope scale $\ell$ to each label-coordinate direction and the profile width $h$ to the phase direction. Products of these weights encode the mixed derivative factors in the finite profile norm. The definition records scaling alone; positivity and smallness are separate assumptions in estimates.
TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateWeight.summary: Each derivative receives its own geometric scale

TorusEuler.phaseDirectionalDerivative.text:
A coordinate derivative, with a direction field allowed to vary with the base point.

A raw fderiv value is zero at nondifferentiability points. Smoothness is supplied separately in the word-calculus theorems; a numerical bound for this expression alone is not a differentiability theorem.
TorusEuler.phaseDirectionalDerivative.summary: Differentiation along a possibly varying direction field

TorusEuler.phaseDirectionalDerivative_je.text: For smooth coefficient field $D$ and profile $f$, bounds through orders $n$ and $n+1$ give a bound $2^nCM$ through order $n$ for the derivative of $f$ in direction $D$. The nonnegative constants are explicit. Time weights can stay inside $M$ because every derivative here acts only on the profile domain.
TorusEuler.phaseDirectionalDerivative_je.summary: One directional derivative obeys the weighted product bound

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_bilinear_produc.text: Let $L$ be a continuous bilinear map with operator norm at most one, and let $f,g$ be smooth with $A,B\ge0$. If every derivative of $f$ of order at most $N$ is bounded everywhere by $A$, and every derivative of $g$ of order at most $N$ by $B$, then every derivative of $a\mapsto L(f(a),g(a))$ of order at most $N$ is bounded everywhere by $2^N AB$.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_bilinear_produc.summary: A bilinear product has a finite Leibniz bound

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_comp_left_contr.text: Postcomposing a smooth function with a continuous linear map of norm at most one preserves its finite Fréchet-jet bound. The order and the numerical bound are unchanged.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_comp_left_contr.summary: A linear contraction preserves a finite derivative bound

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_normalizedPress.text: For a positive frequency and a smooth nonvanishing covector, assumes finite jet bounds for the normalized covector, strain, and normalized reciprocal squared norm. Their product gives smoothness and an explicit bound $2\cdot 2^N\cdot \mathrm{BQ}\cdot 2^N\cdot \mathrm{BK}\cdot \mathrm{BM}$ for the normalized pressure-amplitude coefficient. All three budgets are nonnegative; no frequency-independent estimate follows until their sizes are supplied.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_normalizedPress.summary: Normalized pressure coefficients inherit three product budgets

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_normalizedPress.text: Assumes a positive frequency and radius, $D \ge  1$, radius smallness $\ell\cdot D^{16} \le  1$, and prescribed raw jets of strain, normalized covector, and reciprocal squared norm. The normalized pressure-amplitude coefficient after label scaling is smooth and has finite jet budget $2\cdot 2^{2\cdot N}\cdot C^3\cdot D^7$. The exponent seven is independent of the derivative order; the prefactor is not.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_normalizedPress.summary: Scaled pressure coefficients cost seven parent powers

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaledPhasePote.text: For positive frequency $\lambda$, nonnegative radius $\ell$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, and $\ell\,\mathsf D^{16}\le1$, assumes raw jet bounds for the normalized covector and its reciprocal squared norm through order $N$. The scaled potential coefficient is smooth and has jet bound $2^N C^2\mathsf D^6/\lambda$. The covector must be smooth and nonvanishing; the bound isolates an inverse frequency before the later slow curl costs a label derivative.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaledPhasePote.summary: Scaled potential jets retain an inverse frequency factor

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_labelDiv.text: For a smooth profile and positive envelope radius, a second-order bound on the rescaled profile gives a first-order bound $3\ell^{-1}M$ on its label divergence. One derivative is spent to form divergence and three coordinates contribute the constant. The result tracks the envelope cost separately from phase differentiation.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_labelDiv.summary: Label divergence costs one envelope reciprocal

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_longitud.text: The combined divergence identity replaces the large phase derivative of $\langle k,c\rangle$ by label divergence. With positive scales, smooth one-periodic data, a second-order oscillation bound, and a first-order mean bound, the longitudinal first-order bound is $(2+h)3\ell^{-1}M_{\rm osc}+\|k\|M_{\rm mean}$. The full wave-number factor applies only to the mean.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_longitud.summary: Divergence cancellation controls the longitudinal phase velocity

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_periodic.text: For a smooth, one-periodic, zero-mean profile and nonzero phase scale, a scaled jet bound $B$ through order $n$ gives the bound $2B$ for its normalized phase primitive through the same order. Derivatives may involve both label and evaluation phase. The proof translates the integrand and applies a mixed-jet integral estimate; the nonzero phase scale permits division in that translation.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_periodic.summary: A normalized periodic primitive preserves the jet order

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_phasePri.text: For a smooth one-periodic profile of zero mean at every label, an order-one bound $M$ on its rescaled profile gives an order-one bound $(2+h)M$ for the rescaled normalized primitive. The phase width is positive and differentiability of the primitive is a hypothesis. Label integration costs at most two, while phase differentiation recovers the input with a factor $h$.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_phasePri.summary: The phase primitive gains one phase-width factor

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_slowCurl.text: For a positive label radius $\ell$ and smooth potential and inverse coframe, assumes scaled potential jets bounded by $B_P$ through order $n+1$ and radius-weighted coframe jets bounded by $B_G$ through order $n$. The scaled slow curl is smooth and has budget $\|\mathrm{curl}\|\,\ell^{-1}\,2^n B_PB_G$, where $\|\mathrm{curl}\|$ is the operator norm of the linear map sending a $3\times3$ derivative matrix to its curl. The extra derivative and inverse radius are explicit, so a two-jet activation estimate requires three potential jets.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_slowCurl.summary: A slow curl uses one extra potential derivative

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_wavePote.text: For a smooth periodic zero-mean profile, smooth potential coefficients, and nonzero phase scale, bounds the exact wave potential from a profile budget $B_V$ and a coefficient budget $B_K$ through the same order $n$. The resulting budget is $2\cdot2^nB_KB_V$, and joint smoothness is also proved. One finite Leibniz factor comes from applying the coefficient; the factor two comes from the normalized primitive.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_wavePote.summary: The actual wave potential inherits a product jet bound

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_sum_of_level_bo.text: For every level from two through $P$, assume the profile is differentiable to order $n$ and satisfies the stated jet bound. The finite sum then has the sum of those constants as a jet bound. An empty higher-level range gives the zero profile, so the lemma also covers shallow truncations.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_sum_of_level_bo.summary: Sum the higher pressure profiles at fixed derivative order

TorusEuler.phaseMean.text: For a real normed-space-valued phase function, the formal definition is $\langle f\rangle_s=\int_0^1 f(s)\,ds$. Because the phase period is one, no further normalizing factor appears. Time and particle label are held fixed, so this is distinct from a spatial average over $\mathbb T^3$. For the smooth periodic profiles used in §1.3, it is the ordinary phase mean separating mean and oscillatory forcing. The formal integral is assigned zero when its integrability conditions fail; such a value does not certify a mathematical average. Continuity on the period ensures the intended integral in the applications.
TorusEuler.phaseMean.summary: The average holds time and particle label fixed

TorusEuler.phaseMean_add.text: The phase mean of the sum of two continuous profiles is the sum of their phase means. Continuity supplies the integrability required by the interval integral.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_const.text: The average of a constant over a phase interval of length one is the same constant. This fixes the normalization of the phase average.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_const.summary: A constant profile equals its phase average

TorusEuler.phaseMean_const_smul.text: A real scalar factor may be moved outside the unit-period phase mean. The scalar is constant in the phase variable.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_const_smul.summary: A constant scalar passes through the phase average

TorusEuler.phaseMean_deriv.text: If f has a continuous derivative df everywhere and period one, the phase mean of df vanishes. The proof is the fundamental theorem of calculus with matching endpoints.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_deriv.summary: A periodic derivative has zero phase mean

TorusEuler.phaseMean_fastSource.text: Assume periodic completion and profile, a continuous phase derivative of the profile, and the slaving identity $C\cdot\kappa=-\Pi(\mathrm{div}V)$, where $\Pi$ is the zero-mean phase primitive of the continuous scalar $\mathrm{div}V$. Phase integration by parts converts the mean of $(C\cdot\kappa)Y_s$ into the mean of $\mathrm{div}V\,Y$. Periodicity cancels the boundary term; the slaving identity supplies the sign.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_fastSource.summary: Integration by parts removes the fast derivative

TorusEuler.phaseMean_iteratedDeriv_succ.text: For a smooth one-periodic profile, the phase average of every positive-order derivative is zero. The fundamental theorem of calculus reduces that average to equal endpoint values of a periodic lower derivative. The theorem supplies the mean-zero condition needed when the normalized primitive is applied after phase differentiation.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_iteratedDeriv_succ.summary: Positive phase derivatives have zero mean

TorusEuler.phaseMean_meanFastSource.text: The phase average of $(B\cdot\kappa)Y_s$ vanishes when $Y$ is periodic with continuous derivative. Here $B$ and $\kappa$ do not depend on the phase variable. The statement uses the integral of a derivative over one period, and does not require either constant vector to vanish or be transverse.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_meanFastSource.summary: A constant phase coefficient has zero derivative mean

TorusEuler.phaseMean_phaseOscillation.text: For a continuous profile in a complete real normed space, the average of $f-\operatorname{phaseMean}(f)$ over the unit period is zero. Linearity of the integral and the unit interval length give the cancellation. Periodicity is not required for this identity, because only values on the integration interval enter the mean.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_phasePrimitive.text: For continuous $f:\mathbb R\to E$ in a real Banach space, define $F(s)=\int_0^s f(\sigma)\,d\sigma-\int_0^1\int_0^r f(\sigma)\,d\sigma\,dr$. The formal statement proves $\int_0^1F(s)\,ds=0$. The averaging interval has length one, so subtracting that constant removes the mean exactly. For the Banach and finite-dimensional targets used in Appendix D this is the usual integral normalization. The declaration does not require the input to be periodic or to have zero average; those assumptions enter the separate result that makes $F$ periodic. Recovery of $f$ by differentiation is also a separate assertion.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_phasePrimitive.summary: Subtracting the mean makes the phase primitive have zero average

TorusEuler.phaseMean_reflect_periodic.text: Shows that averaging a one-periodic phase function after replacing phase by its negative gives the original mean. Orientation reversal and periodicity move the integral back to one period. This preserves the normalization used to identify reflected pressure primitives; integrability is supplied in the smooth applications, rather than asserted by this theorem.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_reflect_periodic.summary: Reflection leaves a periodic phase average unchanged

TorusEuler.phaseMean_smul_deriv.text: For a scalar one-periodic weight $u$ and a vector one-periodic profile $v$, both differentiable with continuous displayed derivatives, proves $\langle u v\prime\rangle=-\langle u\prime v\rangle$. The two periodicity hypotheses cancel the boundary term over $[0,1]$. Completeness is required for the vector-valued integral; no spatial derivative or zero-mean hypothesis is included.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_smul_deriv.summary: Move a phase derivative by integration by parts

TorusEuler.phaseMean_sub.text: The phase mean of the difference of two continuous profiles is the difference of their phase means. This is used when separating the mean from the oscillation.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_translate_periodic.text: For a one-periodic phase function, translating its phase argument by any real number leaves the phase mean unchanged. The proof changes variables in the interval integral and uses periodicity. No separate integrability hypothesis appears in this algebraic identity; analytic uses have smooth phase slices so that the integral has its usual meaning.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_translate_periodic.summary: A periodic phase average is invariant under translation

TorusEuler.phaseMean_wavePotential.text: For continuous $V$, the potential defined by taking the mean-adjusted primitive of the cross-product integrand has zero phase mean. This property holds for every fixed $\kappa$, with no transverse, periodic, or zero-mean assumption on $V$. Those stronger assumptions are needed for its intended periodic inverse-curl interpretation, not for the normalization itself.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_wavePressurePrimiti.text: For the constructed family and $0<h\le1$, the formal statement proves $\int_0^1P_h(s)\,ds=0$. The primitive is defined by integrating $F_h$ and subtracting the resulting phase mean, which chooses one function from the primitives differing by constants. This is the normalization used in Lemma 3.1 and the pressure formula (3.3). It is an average in the independent phase coordinate. Multiplying by a label-dependent coefficient and evaluating at a transported phase does not preserve a spatial mean-zero condition automatically; no such assertion about the full Eulerian pressure is made here.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_wavePressurePrimiti.summary: The phase normalization fixes the additive constant of the primitive

TorusEuler.phaseMean_waveProfile.text: For an admissible positive width h ≤ 1, the selected wave profile has zero average over one phase period. This normalization makes the oscillatory profile compatible with the hierarchy.

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord.text:
The first letter of an ordered word is the outermost derivative.

The empty word is the identity on functions. Nonempty words use totalized Fréchet derivatives; analytic word identities require the stated smoothness of fields and directions.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord.summary: Ordered directional derivatives of a profile

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear.text: Exact ordered Leibniz formula for a real continuous bilinear operator, including application of an operator-valued coefficient to a vector field.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear.summary: The exact ordered Leibniz formula for bilinear products

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear_bo.text: Finite-order sup and difference bounds for a product. The hypotheses need only hold for subwords of the specified derivative.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear_bo.summary: Finite sup and difference bounds for differentiated products

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear_co.text: Subtracting $B(f,D_wg)$ from the full derivative $D_w(B(f,g))$ leaves precisely those Leibniz terms with a derivative on $f$. Smoothness of the direction fields and both factors is explicit. Each remaining second word is shorter than $w$, providing the lower-order terms in the derivative-lifting argument.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear_co.summary: Remove the highest derivative of the solution

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_const_smul.text: A time weight may be applied to the field before taking any label or phase derivative at fixed time.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_const_smul.summary: A fixed time weight commutes with spatial differentiation

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constantDir.text: Smooth directional derivatives in constant real directions are unchanged by a permutation of the ordered coordinate word.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constantDir.summary: Constant directional derivatives are invariant under permutation

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constant_eq.text: For a smooth function, an ordered word of constant directional derivatives is its iterated Fréchet derivative evaluated on the same ordered directions. This identifies the word calculus with the usual finite derivative norms.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constant_eq.summary: Constant derivative words equal evaluated Fréchet derivatives

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_eq_jet.text: For a smooth function, successive derivatives in constant directions equal evaluation of the iterated Fréchet derivative on that ordered list. This is the word-to-tensor identification used by the differentiated ODE estimates.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_eq_jet.summary: Constant words evaluate the Fréchet derivative tensor

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_hierarchyLa.text: Each weighted label derivative introduces one factor of the label radius.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_hierarchyLa.summary: Each weighted label derivative contributes the radius

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_jetBound.text: A list $w$ of smooth directional operators maps an order-$N$ profile bound to an order-$n$ bound when $n+|w|\le N$. Each step contributes at most $2^NC$. The resulting constant is $(2^NC)^{|w|}M$, and the order of the operators is preserved by the list.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_jetBound.summary: A word of derivatives consumes its length in regularity

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_linearODE_t.text: Parameter word derivatives of a linear solve satisfy the time derivative of the differentiated right-hand side, including at both slab endpoints.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_linearODE_t.summary: Spatial derivative words satisfy the differentiated time equation

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_scaled_dire.text: Replacing each smooth direction field $D_i$ by the constant scalar multiple $r_iD_i$ multiplies the word derivative by the product of its letter weights. The weights depend on the index, not on position. For coordinate directions this accounts for the factors $\ell^m h^j$ in the finite norm.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_scaled_dire.summary: Coordinate weights multiply along the derivative word

TorusEuler.phaseOscillation.text: The formal definition gives $f^\circ(s)=f(s)-\int_0^1f(r)\,dr$. This is the decomposition used for $H_2-\langle H_2\rangle_s$ in (1.12); it subtracts a vector independent of phase at each fixed time and label. For an integrable period-one profile, the result has zero phase average and remains periodic. Those conditions are not required merely to write the formula: if the integral is not defined in the usual sense, the formal integral has a default value. The paper's smooth profiles are integrable, so the intended mean and oscillatory split applies.
TorusEuler.phaseOscillation.summary: Subtract the phase mean at each fixed time and label

TorusEuler.phaseOscillation_longitudinal.text: Let $c(a,s)\in\mathbb R^3$ be smooth and one-periodic in $s$. At the label considered, assume $\operatorname{div}_a c+k_*\cdot\partial_s c=0$ for every phase. Write $\bar c=\int_0^1c\,ds$ and $c_{\rm osc}=c-\bar c$. Then $\operatorname{div}_a\bar c=0$ and $k_*\cdot c_{\rm osc}=-\partial_s^{-1}\operatorname{div}_a c_{\rm osc}$, where $\partial_s^{-1}$ is the periodic primitive with zero phase mean. This is the identity used in Lemma 5.10 to estimate the longitudinal oscillation through label derivatives. The statement is spatial at one label and does not assume a time evolution, a small norm, or nonzero $k_*$.
TorusEuler.phaseOscillation_longitudinal.summary: Recover the oscillatory longitudinal component by a zero mean primitive

TorusEuler.phasePrimitive.text: For $f:\mathbb R\to E$ in a real normed space, put $J(s)=\int_0^sf(r)\,dr$. The formal definition is $F(s)=J(s)-\int_0^1J(r)\,dr$. For a real Banach target and continuous input, $F'=f$ and $F$ has zero mean on $[0,1]$; if $f$ is also period-one with zero mean, $F$ is periodic. These properties are separate theorems, not part of the formula. The normalization fixes the mean, not the value at phase zero. Nonzero input mean produces drift. The formal integrals also have assigned values outside the usual integrable, complete-target setting, so the formula alone does not justify calling its output a primitive there.
TorusEuler.phasePrimitive.summary: Integrate from zero and subtract the mean of that integral

TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_deriv.text: Assuming $df$ is the derivative of $f$ at every phase and is continuous, proves that the zero-mean primitive of $df$ equals $f-\int_0^1f$. The primitive starts at zero and then has its own mean over $[0,1]$ removed. The identity does not require periodicity; periodicity is an additional condition when interpreting this operation as the inverse phase derivative.
TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_deriv.summary: A primitive recovers the profile without its mean

TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_wavePotentialT.text: The primitive of the potential time source for the covector $\lambda k$ is exactly $\lambda^{-1}$ times the primitive for $k$, with positive frequency $\lambda$. The statement is an equality of normalized phase integrals, not a derivative assertion. It combines the source’s algebraic homogeneity with linearity of the primitive.
TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_wavePotentialT.summary: Phase integration preserves the inverse-frequency factor

TorusEuler.phaseProfile_eq_of_hasDerivAt.text: Phase normalization determines the additive constant of a primitive.
TorusEuler.phaseProfile_eq_of_hasDerivAt.summary: The phase mean fixes the primitive constant

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text:
Extend a profile by shifting its phase with its lattice translation.

The centered representative jumps across cell walls. This raw extension is periodic with the matching phase shift but need not be smooth; compact support away from the walls is used by the smooth-extension theorem.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: Periodic extension with the matching phase shift

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: The extension agrees with the profile on the entire closed cell.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The twisted extension agrees on the closed cell

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: If simultaneous label and phase reflection transforms a profile by a zero-preserving map $L$, and the profile vanishes on every negative cell wall, its twisted extension has the same reflection law. The wall condition handles the centered representative’s half-open boundary convention. The map $L$ need not be linear for this algebraic result, only satisfy $L(0)=0$.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: Wall vanishing preserves reflection through the twisted extension

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: Evaluating the phase-twisted extension at label $A(t,x)$ and phase $\langle k,A(t,x)\rangle$ gives exactly the localized transported profile. The phase shift cancels the uncentered label contribution, leaving the graph phase at the centered representative. This is an identity for arbitrary maps, profiles and real covectors; it does not require smoothness, periodicity or an integer frequency.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The twisted profile agrees with its transported phase evaluation

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: If each original label slice has a specified phase period, the twisted periodized profile has that same phase period. The period need not equal one in this general statement.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: Twisted periodization preserves a supplied phase period

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: When the positive envelope radius leaves a strict collar before the cell walls, the twisted extension equals the original enveloped profile at every point of the closed centered cell and every phase. This includes boundary points that have different centered representatives, since the envelope vanishes there. The equality does not require smoothness of the underlying profile.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The twisted extension agrees throughout the closed cell

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: The envelope confines the extension to the translates of its original support ball.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The periodized envelope stays near lattice points

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: For a positive envelope radius with $2\ell\le1/2$, multiplying a profile by the radial envelope preserves any simultaneous label-phase reflection represented by a continuous linear map $L$. The twisted extension inherits that same law. The weak radius inequality suffices because only zero values at the cell walls are needed; smooth gluing elsewhere uses a strict inequality.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The radial envelope preserves a linear reflection law

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: The twisted periodization is invariant when labels and phase are shifted together by the lattice vector and its pairing with k. The identity is valid for the raw extension; smoothness across cell walls is a separate result.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The extension respects simultaneous lattice and phase shifts

TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_graph_cost.text: Assume $\mathsf D,\lambda\ge1$, a nonnegative integer $a$, $\ell_*^{-1}\le\mathsf D^a$, $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$ and $|k_*|\le\mathsf D\lambda$. Then $\ell_*^{-1}+h^{-1}|k_*|\le2\mathsf D^{\max(a,1)}\lambda^{3/2}$. This is the scalar estimate behind the derivative cost in Lemma 5.7: a label derivative contributes $\ell_*^{-1}$ and a phase derivative contributes $h^{-1}|k_*|$. The derivative of the inverse flow contributes another factor separately. The formal inequality contains no profile, function norm or chain rule, so those analytic identifications must be supplied before applying it to a physical field.
TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_graph_cost.summary: Combine the label scale and the carrier divided by phase width

TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_residual_ho.text: Let $\lambda\ge1$, $C_{\rm tail},C_{\rm prim},\gamma\ge0$, $6C_{\rm tail}\le C$, $6C_{\rm prim}\le C$ and $|\chi'|\gamma\le S$. Suppose the residual is $R=T+\chi' F$ for smooth fields $T,F$, where all derivatives of $T$ of order at most two are bounded by $C_{\rm tail}\lambda^{7/4}\lambda^{-2P/3}$ and those of $F$ by $C_{\rm prim}\lambda^{7/4}\gamma$ (real powers, $P$ a nonnegative integer). Then $R$ has bounded derivatives and half-Hölder quotients through order one, and its spatial $C^{1,1/2}$ norm is at most $C\lambda^2(\lambda^{-2P/3}+S)$. The power $\lambda^{7/4}$ is enlarged to $\lambda^2$ using $\lambda\ge1$.
TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_residual_ho.summary: Depth tail and switch remainder together give the residual bound $C\lambda^2(\lambda^{-2P/3}+S)$

TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_velocity_ho.text: Let $\lambda\ge1$, $\mathsf D\ge0$, $C_{\rm osc},C_{\rm mean}\ge0$, $0\le\gamma\le1$, and nonnegative integers $b,m$. Let the oscillation and the mean be smooth fields on $\mathbb R^3$ whose derivatives of order at most $m+1$ are bounded by $C_{\rm osc}\mathsf D^{b(m+2)}\lambda^{3(m+1)/2}\gamma\lambda^{-5/4}$ and by $C_{\rm mean}\mathsf D^{b(m+2)}\lambda^{-5/2}$ respectively. Then both have bounded derivatives and half-Hölder quotients through order $m$, the oscillation has spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm at most $3(m+1)C_{\rm osc}\mathsf D^{b(m+2)}\lambda^{3(m+1)/2-5/4}$, and the mean has norm at most $3(m+1)C_{\rm mean}\mathsf D^{b(m+2)}\lambda^{-5/2}$. The factor $\gamma\le1$ is dropped.
TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_velocity_ho.summary: Oscillation and mean keep their separate Hölder frequency rates

TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection.text: Let $w(y)=F(k\cdot y)\mathbf a$ in Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$. If $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$ and $F$ is differentiable at $k\cdot x$, the formal statement proves $(w\cdot\nabla)w(x)=0$. This is the self-advection cancellation used in §1.1 and Lemma 2.1. It is a spatial identity at a fixed point; no time equation, nonzero vector assumption or global profile regularity is needed. The statement gives the zero conclusion directly, while the paper also displays the intermediate expression $(k\cdot\mathbf a)FF'\mathbf a$.
TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection.summary: A transverse plane wave has no self-advection at a differentiable phase

TorusEuler.preceding_curl_projection_of_.text: If the newest covector is nonzero, its scale is positive, and its third scaled coordinate in the preceding frame is at least one half, a bound on its scaled length gives a lower bound for its normalized projection against the preceding curl. The formula uses the actual cross product, with its sign retained.
TorusEuler.preceding_curl_projection_of_.summary: The newest direction detects a positive preceding curl component

TorusEuler.preceding_curl_projection_of_.text: Combining coordinate bounds, window length at most $CL^4$, logarithmic loss $L^8\le\mu^{1/8}$, and preceding strength at least $c\mu^{1/4}$ gives a signed curl projection of at least $c\mu^{1/8}/(6C^2)$. Nonzero perpendicular preceding data and positive frequency scales are explicit. The conclusion retains the constant $c$ as supplied; its positivity is not assumed here.
TorusEuler.preceding_curl_projection_of_.summary: The projected preceding curl grows as a positive frequency power

TorusEuler.preceding_strength_retained_o.text: Let $\mu\ge1$ and $r-l\le\mu^{-1/16}$. On $[l,r]$, assume nonzero transverse $\kappa,\mathbf a$ solve $\dot\kappa=-B^T\kappa$ and $\dot{\mathbf a}=-B\mathbf a+2\langle\kappa,B\mathbf a\rangle\kappa/|\kappa|^2$, with trace-free $B$ and $\|B\|\le\mu^{1/32}$. Then for every $t\in[l,r]$, $|\kappa(t)||\mathbf a(t)|\ge e^{-1}|\kappa(l)||\mathbf a(l)|$. Derivatives at the endpoints are taken within the closed interval. Nonvanishing makes the denominator and the logarithm of the strength legitimate. The formal statement makes the fixed loss explicit; it gives a lower bound, not conservation of strength. In Proposition 8.2 one takes $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$ and $[l,r]=[t_j,t_{j+1}]$.
TorusEuler.preceding_strength_retained_o.summary: A short interval limits the multiplicative loss of wave strength

TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode.text: For an integer frequency $k$ and a complex vector coefficient $a\in\mathbb C^3$, the formal definition multiplies the divergence coefficient $2\pi i\,k\cdot a$ by the inverse Laplacian coefficient $-1/(4\pi^2|k|^2)$. At nonzero $k$, this gives the scalar coefficient of $\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}v$ in the paper’s Leray formula. At $k=0$, inversion of zero is defined to be zero, so the scalar correction vanishes and its mean is fixed. The contraction $k\cdot a$ is complex-linear in $a$, with no complex conjugation. The definition alone does not construct a spatial pressure or establish convergence of a Fourier series.
TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode.summary: The inverse Laplacian fixes the scalar zero mode

TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode_zero.text: For every complex vector coefficient $a\in\mathbb C^3$, the formal theorem states that the scalar pressure correction at frequency $k=0$ is zero. This follows from the Fourier definition of $\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$, which assigns the inverse Laplacian the value zero on the constant mode. It is the normalization used for the scalar potential in $\mathbb P=I-\nabla\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$. It does not set the velocity’s constant coefficient to zero: the Leray projection preserves constant divergence-free velocities. Nor does this single coefficient identity assert the full spatial projection formula or establish a solution of the Euler equations.
TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode_zero.summary: The Fourier coefficient at zero is exactly zero

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular.text: Defines the real angular operator $I-\mathbb P(\xi)$, which projects onto the frequency direction for nonzero $\xi$. Its value at zero is zero because the Leray symbol there is the identity. This is the angular part of $D^2\Delta^{-1}$; the definition alone does not identify any field as an actual pressure Hessian.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular.summary: The pressure projection onto the frequency direction

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_apply.text: Applying the angular pressure operator to $v$ gives $(\langle\xi,v\rangle/\|\xi\|^2)\xi$. The formula is valid also at zero under Lean’s total division convention, where both sides vanish. To interpret it as projection onto a one-dimensional direction one must additionally have $\xi\ne0$.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_apply.summary: The pressure projection is the longitudinal component

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_neg.text: The angular pressure operator is even in its frequency argument: replacing $\xi$ by $-\xi$ leaves it unchanged. This includes zero. The identity is used to pair positive and negative Fourier modes when proving the real cosine and sine moment formula; it is not a regularity statement about the symbol.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_neg.summary: Opposite frequencies have the same pressure projection

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_pos_sm.text: For $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$ let $P(\xi)=I-(I-\hat\xi\otimes\hat\xi)$, the orthogonal projection onto the line of $\xi$, where $\hat\xi=\xi/|\xi|$ and $\hat0=0$, so that $P(0)=0$. For every real $c>0$ and every $\xi$ (including $\xi=0$), $P(c\xi)=P(\xi)$.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_pos_sm.summary: The projection onto the frequency direction is unchanged by positive rescaling

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_zero.text: The angular pressure operator is zero at frequency zero. This is the intended Fourier convention for a Hessian, which cannot contain a nonzero constant Fourier mode when obtained by differentiating a periodic potential. The declaration is a symbol identity; the later Poisson comparison proves that the constructed multiplier has the corresponding physical meaning.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_zero.summary: The pressure Hessian has zero constant mode

TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier.text: This is the continuous linear operator $D^2\Delta^{-1}:C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3)\to C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^{3\times3})$. At a nonzero frequency $\xi\in\mathbb Z^3$ it multiplies the scalar Fourier coefficient by $\xi\otimes\xi/|\xi|^2$; its zero-frequency value is zero. Thus constants are discarded, as required when the inverse Laplacian is normalized on the torus. Both function spaces use finite half-Hölder norms. The declaration supplies boundedness and the chosen multiplier, not a Poisson equation for a particular pressure. To identify its output with $D^2q$, Lemma 5.9 uses the equation satisfied by the summed mean pressure.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier.summary: Define the bounded multiplier and remove its zero Fourier mode

TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier_eq_.text: Let $f$ be a scalar bounded half-Hölder field on the unit torus, normed by $\max\{\sup|f|,[f]_{1/2}\}$ with the product metric and $H$ a matrix-valued one. Let $\pi$ be $C^2$ and $\mathbb Z^3$-periodic, represented by a continuous function on the torus, with $H=D(\nabla\pi)$ and $f=\Delta\pi$ at every point. Then the pressure Hessian multiplier $\mathcal H$, the bounded operator from scalar to matrix-valued bounded half-Hölder fields on the unit torus, normed by $\max\{\sup|f|,[f]_{1/2}\}$ with the product metric, with Fourier symbol $k\otimes k/|k|^2$ at $k\ne0$ and zero at $k=0$, that is, $D^2\Delta^{-1}$ with the constant mode removed, applied to $f$, equals $H$. The proof compares Fourier coefficients entry by entry.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier_eq_.summary: The pressure multiplier reproduces the actual Hessian of a periodic solution

TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier_rea.text: Let $f$ be a scalar bounded half-Hölder field on the unit torus, normed by $\max\{\sup|f|,[f]_{1/2}\}$ with the product metric, $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ and $c\in\mathbb C$, and let the pressure Hessian multiplier $\mathcal H$, the bounded operator from scalar to matrix-valued bounded half-Hölder fields on the unit torus, normed by $\max\{\sup|f|,[f]_{1/2}\}$ with the product metric, with Fourier symbol $k\otimes k/|k|^2$ at $k\ne0$ and zero at $k=0$, that is, $D^2\Delta^{-1}$ with the constant mode removed. Then $\int\operatorname{Re}\bigl(c\,e^{2\pi ik\cdot a}\bigr)\,(\mathcal Hf)(a)\,da=\Bigl(\int\operatorname{Re}\bigl(c\,e^{2\pi ik\cdot a}\bigr)f(a)\,da\Bigr)\,\frac{k\otimes k}{|k|^2}$, integrals over the unit torus, with the matrix replaced by zero at $k=0$. Varying $c$ covers both cosine and sine moments.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier_rea.summary: The real pressure multiplier acts on each cosine and sine moment

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol.text: At each real frequency, constructs a complex-linear map taking a scalar Fourier coefficient to that coefficient times the complexified angular pressure operator. The result is operator-valued, so its coordinate entries represent the Hessian entries. Boundedness of the resulting periodic operator and agreement with a Poisson solution are later theorems.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol.summary: The complex symbol converts a scalar to a Hessian

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_apply.text: Unfolds the complex symbol as scalar multiplication of the complexified angular projection. This identity is valid for every frequency and complex scalar. It exposes the exact action used in the Fourier coefficient calculations, without requiring the scalar to be real or the frequency to be nonzero.

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_lattice.text: At each lattice frequency $k\in\mathbb Z^3$, every matrix entry of the pressure symbol, applied to a scalar input $s\in\mathbb C$ and then to $e_j$ with component $i$ read off, equals the two Fourier derivative factors times the inverse Laplacian eigenvalue and the scalar input: $(2\pi ik_i)(2\pi ik_j)\,m(k)\,s$, where $m(k)=-1/(4\pi^2|k|^2)$ for $k\ne0$ and $m(0)=0$. The zero frequency is handled separately before cancelling the nonzero Laplacian eigenvalue. This fixes the sign and the $2\pi$ normalization of $\partial_i\partial_j\Delta^{-1}$ at every frequency.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_lattice.summary: Each entry of the pressure symbol is two derivative factors over the Laplacian

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_neg.text: The scalar-to-operator symbol is unchanged when the real frequency is negated. This follows from evenness of the underlying real angular projection and is valid including at zero. It supports the comparison of conjugate Fourier modes needed to recover a real operator from real source data.

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_pos_smu.text: The complex pressure symbol sends $s\in\mathbb C$ to $s$ times the complexified projection $\hat\xi\otimes\hat\xi$ onto the line of $\xi$ (zero at $\xi=0$). For every real $c>0$ and every $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$, the symbol at $c\xi$ equals the symbol at $\xi$.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_pos_smu.summary: The complex pressure symbol is homogeneous of degree zero

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_zero.text: At the zero frequency, the complex scalar-to-operator symbol is the zero continuous linear map. This eliminates the constant mode before any Fourier reconstruction. It records a deliberate normalization for the Hessian multiplier rather than a statement that arbitrary sources have zero mean.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_zero.summary: The complex pressure symbol vanishes at zero

TorusEuler.pressureHessian_quadratic_upp.text: Let the Hessian operator split into leading, geometric, higher and mean pieces. A signed leading upper bound at scale $\mathrm{freq}^{-1/4}$ and nonnegative norm bounds for the other three pieces at faster decays give a common signed upper bound with summed constants. The theorem never deduces a norm bound for the leading piece or the total Hessian.
TorusEuler.pressureHessian_quadratic_upp.summary: Combine one signed contribution with three norm bounds

TorusEuler.pressureTensorAnnularSymbol.text: The fixed dyadic cutoff localizes the pressure symbol into a compactly supported smooth operator-valued symbol, packaged as a Schwartz map. The cutoff removes the singular frequency origin before the Schwartz construction. Its inverse Fourier transform is the building block for the actual periodic far pressure kernel.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorAnnularSymbol.summary: The pressure symbol is localized to one smooth frequency annulus

TorusEuler.pressureTensorDoubleDivergenc.text: The double divergence of a complex tensor field is $\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j a_{ij}$, expressed using the coordinate Hessian entries. It is the source with a minus sign in the normalized pressure Poisson equation. The definition fixes the coordinate order used in the Fourier symbol and in the real Euler comparison.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorDoubleDivergenc.summary: Contract both spatial derivatives of the tensor source

TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift.text: The real pressure lift is the real part of the complex dyadic pressure sum. For smooth periodic tensor fields it is smooth and agrees with the actual half Hölder pressure multiplier. Its identification with a prescribed pressure additionally requires the periodic Poisson equation and zero spatial mean.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift.summary: Take the real pressure produced by the dyadic series

TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_eq_l.text: If a half Hölder torus tensor $q$ pulls back pointwise to a smooth periodic lift $f$, their real pressures agree pointwise after lifting. Finite dyadic convolutions converge both to the block sum and to the bounded multiplier output. The hypothesis that $f$ represents $q$ pointwise is explicit; the theorem does not select an arbitrary torus representative.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_eq_l.summary: The smooth dyadic construction equals the bounded torus multiplier

TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_eq_r.text: For a smooth periodic tensor and a $C^2$ periodic complex pressure solving its Poisson equation with zero mean, the real dyadic lift is exactly the real part of that pressure. Smoothness provides the tensor’s half Hölder torus representative, continuity provides the pressure representative, and Fourier uniqueness identifies them. The equation alone would leave an additive constant.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_eq_r.summary: The dyadic pressure equals the normalized Poisson solution

TorusEuler.pressureTensorMultiplier.text: This bounded real operator composes the complex pressure tensor multiplier with pointwise real part. It accepts complex tensor fields but returns a real half Hölder field. For tensors built from real velocities, later Fourier Poisson uniqueness identifies this output with the actual normalized Euler pressure.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorMultiplier.summary: The real pressure is the real part of the complex multiplier

TorusEuler.pressureTensorRealOutput.text: This real continuous linear map converts a complex-linear tensor-to-scalar operator into a real-linear one by taking the real part of its output. The input tensor remains complex. This lets the periodized complex Fourier kernel produce real pressure values without changing the source coordinate convention.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorRealOutput.summary: Take the real scalar output of a complex tensor operator

TorusEuler.pressureTensorRealOutput_appl.text: Applying the converted tensor operator to a complex tensor returns the real part of the original complex result. This definitional identity is used to commute the real-output map with integrals and to compare real pressure with its complex Fourier representation. It asserts no symmetry of the input tensor.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorRealOutput_appl.summary: The real output map is pointwise real part

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol.text: The scalar operator sends a tensor to $-\sum_{i,j}\xi_i\xi_j A_{ij}/\|\xi\|^2$. It is the symbol of $-\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}\operatorname{div}$ with zero constant mode. The negative sign is essential for the pressure Poisson equation, and the finite tensor coordinate functionals make the operator continuous.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol.summary: The normalized pressure symbol contracts the tensor twice

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_apply.text: Applying the pressure symbol equals the negative finite double sum of weighted tensor entries. This expands the bundled continuous linear operator into coordinates. The formula is valid at zero as well, where all weights vanish; nonzero-frequency inversion is justified in later Fourier-mode identities.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_apply.summary: The symbol has the explicit double contraction formula

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_lattice_.text: At a lattice frequency, applying the scalar pressure symbol equals negative inverse Laplacian mode times the double-divergence Fourier contraction. The formula holds at zero with the prescribed normalization. This gives the exact modal interpretation of the abstract angular symbol used to build the bounded multiplier.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_lattice_.summary: The pressure symbol solves the Fourier Poisson equation

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_lattice_.text: The pressure symbol applied to a tensor equals the negative scalar pressure-correction mode of its single divergence. This aligns the tensor convention with the existing Leray decomposition. The sign means the projected tensor divergence is the unprojected divergence plus the gradient of this normalized pressure.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_lattice_.summary: The pressure scalar has the opposite complement sign

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_neg.text: Changing the frequency vector to its negative leaves the pressure operator unchanged. Each weight contains two coordinate factors and a squared norm. This parity matches the real pressure operator and is distinct from a parity assumption on the tensor field to which the multiplier is applied.

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_pos_smul.text: Positive scaling of the frequency vector leaves the pressure symbol unchanged. The proof transfers the homogeneity of each angular weight through the finite sum of coordinate operators. This is the degree-zero homogeneity premise needed to identify the dyadically constructed multiplier with its claimed Fourier coefficients.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_pos_smul.summary: The pressure multiplier depends only on frequency direction

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_zero.text: The pressure symbol at frequency zero is the zero operator. This follows from the chosen coordinate quotient convention and is used to normalize pressure and remove any constant-mode term from the far-kernel formula. It does not invert the Laplacian at zero; it prescribes the missing mode.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_zero.summary: The pressure symbol removes the constant mode

TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.text: For two matrix-valued bounded half-Hölder fields $U,V$ on a metric space, this is the scalar half-Hölder field $x\mapsto\operatorname{tr}\bigl(U(x)^2\bigr)-\operatorname{tr}\bigl(V(x)^2\bigr)$, with products taken as compositions of linear maps. It becomes the quadratic part of the pressure source when $U,V$ are the two velocity gradients.
TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.summary: The trace difference of the two gradient squares

TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.text: For matrix-valued bounded half-Hölder fields $U,V,D$ on a metric space with $D=U-V$, the field $\operatorname{tr}(U^2)-\operatorname{tr}(V^2)$ equals the trace of the field $DV+UD$. The identity holds for noncommuting matrices, and the difference $D$ appears once in each term.
TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.summary: The trace-square difference factors through $D=U-V$ without commuting

TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.text: At each label, the scalar field evaluates to the difference of the traces of the two operator squares. This exposes the definition’s actual order of composition and trace convention. No assumption that either input is a derivative is used, so the identity remains an algebraic one until the physical representations are supplied.
TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.summary: Evaluate the traces of the operator squares

TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.text: At a fixed label $x$, with $D=U-V$ for matrix-valued bounded half-Hölder fields $U,V,D$ on a metric space, the trace-square difference $\operatorname{tr}(U(x)^2)-\operatorname{tr}(V(x)^2)$ equals $\operatorname{tr}\bigl(D(x)V(x)\bigr)+\operatorname{tr}\bigl(U(x)D(x)\bigr)$. This is the pointwise form of the field factorization. It neither commutes the operator factors nor identifies $D$ as a derivative of the cutoff velocity.
TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.summary: Pointwise form of the trace-square factorization

TorusEuler.pressureVelocityTensor.text: The tensor field at $x$ has complex coordinates $v_i(x)v_j(x)$, using the bounded bilinear velocity tensor map on the diagonal. It is the source of the pressure double divergence. Reality and symmetry follow from the diagonal real input, while smoothness and periodicity are established separately from properties of $v$.
TorusEuler.pressureVelocityTensor.summary: Form the quadratic velocity source for pressure

TorusEuler.pressure_sub_at_zero_eq_lineI.text: If $g$ is the actual continuous gradient of a scalar field $p$, then $p(x)-p(0)$ equals the integral of $\langle g(sx),x\rangle$ from zero to one. This is the fundamental theorem of calculus along the radial segment. Periodicity and mean normalization are unnecessary for this difference identity.
TorusEuler.pressure_sub_at_zero_eq_lineI.summary: Recover pressure differences along radial lines

TorusEuler.profileFlowCoframeCost.text: The order-$m$ cost multiplies $4^m$, the product constant for four label-and-phase directions at order $m$, and the parent’s finite coefficient-order constant. The factors account respectively for conversion to scaled Fréchet jets, the product estimate, and the inverse-coframe norm. The following lemmas use this fixed-order coefficient when turning a profile seminorm into a pullback derivative bound.
TorusEuler.profileFlowCoframeCost.summary: The finite cost of applying the inverse coframe

TorusEuler.profileFlowJetConstant.text: The common coefficient adds the oscillatory and mean costs and a further $1+C(1)$ allowance for the cutoff tail after applying the inverse coframe. It packages the three contributions without taking another maximum. Under nonnegative coefficient and level costs it is at least one, as the next theorem proves.
TorusEuler.profileFlowJetConstant.summary: One coefficient pays for both profiles and the added tail

TorusEuler.profileFlowJetPower.text: The chosen exponent is six times the hierarchy loss exponent plus eight. It dominates the oscillatory exponent $2r+1$, the mean exponent $6r+1$, and the cutoff-coframe exponent eight. This permits one parent power in the final pullback-jet record while retaining different frequency decay rates for the oscillation and mean.
TorusEuler.profileFlowJetPower.summary: One parent exponent covers both profiles and the cutoff tail

TorusEuler.profileFlowMeanCost.text: The mean coefficient uses the first-order coframe cost, the number of retained levels, and the common level constant. Only one mean term is counted per level, unlike the two oscillatory contributions. Its first-order choice matches the mean field required by the corrected pullback-jet interface used in the deformation argument.
TorusEuler.profileFlowMeanCost.summary: The finite level sum determines the mean cost

TorusEuler.profileFlowOscillationCost.text: The oscillatory coefficient is the second-order coframe cost times twice the number of retained levels and the common level constant. The factor two comes from summing both transverse oscillations and their completion corrections. The count is exactly the cardinality of the natural interval from one through the chosen depth.
TorusEuler.profileFlowOscillationCost.summary: The finite level sum determines the oscillatory cost

TorusEuler.profileWidth_and_seedScale.text: The profile width lies in the range of Lemma 3.1. Its product with the normalized seed scale is the leading velocity scale in §5.
TorusEuler.profileWidth_and_seedScale.summary: The profile width gives the required velocity scale

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertEquiv.text: For a closed Hilbert subspace and a bounded ambient operator coercive there with strictly positive constant, Lax–Milgram gives a continuous linear equivalence of the subspace. Its forward map is later identified with the compressed operator. This construction supplies an actual inverse on the constrained space, not an extension to arbitrary ambient vectors.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertEquiv.summary: Positive coercivity makes the compressed operator invertible

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertEquiv_apply.text: Let $H$ be a closed subspace of a real Hilbert space $E$ and $A$ a bounded operator on $E$ satisfying the positive coercivity hypothesis $c\|u\|^2\le\langle Au,u\rangle$ for $u\in H$, with $c>0$. Then the continuous linear equivalence of $H$ produced by Lax–Milgram from the form $(u,w)\mapsto\langle\Pi_HAu,w\rangle$ agrees on every subspace vector $u$ with the compressed operator $\Pi_HAu$, where $\Pi_H$ is orthogonal projection onto $H$. Its inverse therefore solves the projected equation on $H$.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertEquiv_apply.summary: The Lax–Milgram equivalence acts as the compressed operator

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertOperator.text: Let $E$ be a real Hilbert space, $H\subseteq E$ a closed subspace and $A$ a bounded linear operator on $E$. The compressed operator is the bounded linear map $H\to H$, $u\mapsto\Pi_HAu$, where $\Pi_H$ is the orthogonal projection of $E$ onto $H$. Closedness of $H$ makes it complete, so the projection exists. No coercivity is assumed here.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertOperator.summary: An operator compressed to a closed subspace

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertOperator_eq_p.text: Let $H$ be a closed subspace of a real Hilbert space $E$, $A$ a bounded operator on $E$, $u\in H$ and $f\in E$, and let $\Pi_H$ be orthogonal projection onto $H$. Solving the compressed equation $\Pi_HAu=\Pi_Hf$, whose right-hand side is the projection of $f$, is equivalent to the ambient inner-product identity $\langle Au,w\rangle=\langle f,w\rangle$ against every test vector $w\in H$. Closedness provides the orthogonal projection, and no coercivity is needed.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertOperator_eq_p.summary: The projected equation is equivalent to testing against the subspace

TorusEuler.projectedMomentum_realFourier.text: The supplied projection converts the unprojected truncated momentum identity into the projected residual formula, provided it removes the cutoff pressure term from this particular momentum expression. The projection is otherwise an arbitrary map; no general linearity or gradient-annihilation theorem is assumed implicitly. The hypotheses retain the exact momentum representatives and incompressibility required by the preceding algebraic identity.
TorusEuler.projectedMomentum_realFourier.summary: Apply a compatible projection to truncated momentum

TorusEuler.projected_residual_of_cutoff.text: Let a linear cutoff commute with the linear divergence operator, and let a linear projection annihilate the cutoff pressure gradient. Suppose $u_t=S_\Lambda V_t$, $V_t+\operatorname{div}(V\otimes V)+\nabla\Pi=R_V$, and $R_u=\mathbb P[u_t+\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)]$. Then $R_u=\mathbb P[S_\Lambda R_V+\operatorname{div}((u-V)\otimes u+V\otimes(u-V)+(I-S_\Lambda)(V\otimes V))]$. The formal identity works with any real vector spaces, bilinear product and linear operators satisfying these algebraic premises. It does not itself assert $u=S_\Lambda V$, boundedness of a multiplier, or a pressure Poisson equation. In §5.7 those facts identify the objects with the physical cutoff and turn this identity into (5.58).
TorusEuler.projected_residual_of_cutoff.summary: Derive the three cutoff tensors by bilinear algebra

TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_eq_coordinate_.text: For continuous linear maps $J$ and $G$, the curl associated with the composite $JG$ is the sum of cross products between the transformed coordinate directions and $J$ applied to those directions. This is a purely algebraic derivative-map identity. No claim that $J$ or $G$ comes from a genuine flow is required.
TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_eq_coordinate_.summary: The pulled-back curl splits into three coordinate cross products

TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_eq_weightedCoo.text: When the label scale $\ell$ is nonzero, the pulled-back curl equals the sum of three weighted label derivatives multiplied by the inverse-scale curl rows. This is an algebraic identity involving the Fréchet derivative expression, which is zero wherever the function is not differentiable. No smoothness hypothesis is needed for this rewrite; analytic bounds later supply genuine differentiability and coefficient control.
TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_eq_weightedCoo.summary: Weighted coordinate derivatives reproduce the pulled-back curl

TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_material_eq.text: Let $J,G$ be curves of linear maps on $\mathbb R^3$. At $t$ in a time set where the derivative is uniquely determined, assume $J'=J_t$ and $G'=-GM$. For a matrix $B$, write $\operatorname{curl}B$ for its antisymmetric contraction, the vector that equals $\nabla\times q$ when $B=Dq$. The formal identity is $\frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{curl}(JG)+M\operatorname{curl}(JG)=\operatorname{curl}(J_tG)-\operatorname{curl}(JGM)+M\operatorname{curl}(JG)$. It is a matrix product rule. Taking $J=D_aQ[V]$, $G=(D_aX)^{-1}$ gives the paper's curl commutator only after justifying $J_t=D_a\partial_tQ[V]$. Neither existence of those spatial derivatives nor interchange of time and label differentiation follows from this identity itself.
TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_material_eq.summary: Separate the differentiated potential and the coframe commutator

TorusEuler.pulledBackGradient_eq_weighte.text: For nonzero label scale, applying the inverse coframe’s adjoint to the label gradient equals a sum of weighted label derivatives multiplied by the corresponding pressure rows. The scalar derivative is converted to a vector through the inner-product duality map. This is an identity for arbitrary input functions and linear maps, before regularity assumptions are applied.
TorusEuler.pulledBackGradient_eq_weighte.summary: The pressure gradient splits into weighted label coordinates

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope.text: The formal envelope is $g(a)=\chi(|a|/\ell_*)$, where one particular smooth function $\chi$ equals one for arguments at most one and zero for arguments at least two, with values in $[0,1]$. For $\ell_*>0$, the resulting field is even, equals one on $|a|\le\ell_*$ and vanishes for $|a|\ge2\ell_*$. These are the properties prescribed in §5.1; the formalization fixes this cutoff rather than quantifying over every possible choice. The formula is also defined at $\ell_*=0$: division by zero is zero, giving $g\equiv1$. Hence positivity of the radius is essential for the stated localization.
TorusEuler.radialEnvelope.summary: Fix a smooth radial cutoff at the chosen label scale

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_one.text: For the fixed radial cutoff $g(a)=\chi(|a|/\ell_*)$, assume $\ell_*>0$ and $|a|\le\ell_*$. Then $g(a)=1$. The positivity assumption makes $|a|/\ell_*\le1$, where the chosen smooth cutoff is exactly one. This is the plateau property required in §5.1 and used when computing the central gradient. The assertion is only about the spatial envelope in parent labels; it does not assert that the time cutoff is one, or by itself prove that the physical leading wave is active. Other admissible radial cutoffs are not quantified over.
TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_one.summary: The chosen positive radius gives an exact unit plateau

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_unit_scaled.text: For $\ell>0$, the radial envelope of radius $\ell$ satisfies $g_\ell(a)=g_1(\ell^{-1}a)$ for every label $a$, where $g_1$ is the unit-radius envelope. Thus all dependence on the radius is a linear rescaling of the label, and derivative constants can be taken from the fixed unit envelope.
TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_unit_scaled.summary: Every positive-radius envelope rescales the unit envelope

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_zero.text: For positive radius, the chosen radial envelope is zero at every point whose norm is at least twice that radius. This is the outer support condition of the localized wave; smoothness is proved separately.
TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_zero.summary: The envelope vanishes outside its outer ball

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_mem_Icc.text: The chosen radial envelope takes values in the closed unit interval for every real radius and every point. This unrestricted range bound does not supply the intended support geometry when the radius is nonpositive.

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_neg.text: The radial envelope has the same value at a point and its negative, since the norm is even. No positivity or smoothness assumption is needed for this identity.

TorusEuler.radius_power_small.text: The first-order envelope threshold bounds every smaller radius power.
TorusEuler.radius_power_small.summary: The envelope threshold controls smaller radius powers

TorusEuler.range_endpointJointConstraint.text: The range of the ambient orthogonal projection onto the endpoint constraints is precisely the weak endpoint space on $(0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$. That space combines zero time mean at almost every label with the weak spatial divergence condition. The statement identifies the projection range; it does not separately reconstruct the displacement or its pointwise endpoint values.
TorusEuler.range_endpointJointConstraint.summary: The joint projection range is the endpoint constraint space

TorusEuler.range_endpointJointSubtractMe.text: For $T>0$, the range of time-mean removal equals the kernel of time integration. One inclusion is the zero-integral theorem. For the other, a field with zero integral is fixed by $Q$ and supplies its own preimage. The equality concerns submodules of joint $L^2$, before imposing any spatial divergence constraint.

TorusEuler.range_periodicComplexLeray.text: The range of the bounded complex Leray operator equals the Fourier solenoidal submodule. This equality establishes both that every projected field is solenoidal and that every field in that submodule is attained. It concerns Hilbert-space elements, with no additional pointwise regularity claim.
TorusEuler.range_periodicComplexLeray.summary: The full Leray range is precisely the solenoidal subspace

TorusEuler.range_periodicRealLeray.text: The range of the ambient real Leray operator is precisely the weak solenoidal subspace: the $L^2$ fields annihilated by every weak divergence test against a smooth periodic potential. Thus every output passes the weak gradient tests, and every field passing them is attained by the projection. This identifies the subspace intrinsically before later arguments recognize it through transverse Fourier coefficients.
TorusEuler.range_periodicRealLeray.summary: The projection range is exactly the weak solenoidal space

TorusEuler.rankOne_directionProjection_s.text: The longitudinal rank-one projection is invariant under nonzero real rescaling of its direction.
TorusEuler.rankOne_directionProjection_s.summary: Longitudinal projection is unchanged by nonzero rescaling

TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff.text: Defines the real-valued convolution operator by integrating the real part of the finite spectral kernel against a field with values in a real normed space. The Fourier multiplier identification for an even symbol is proved separately by scalar testing. The definition itself accepts arbitrary representatives and does not assert their integrability.

TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_congr.text: Almost-everywhere equality of two real normed-space-valued representatives gives pointwise equality of their real convolution cutoffs. The integrands agree almost everywhere at each fixed output point, so integral congruence applies. The declaration explicitly omits the surrounding completeness assumption; it is only a congruence statement for the integral expression.
TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_congr.summary: Real convolution respects almost everywhere equality

TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_scala.text: With an even symbol, an integrable field $g$ in a real Banach space, and a continuous real linear functional $l$, scalarization of the real cutoff equals the complex scalar Fourier cutoff of $l\circ g$. Evenness makes that scalar cutoff real. This identifies the operator’s Fourier meaning, beyond its real-kernel definition.
TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_scala.summary: Testing the real cutoff by a scalar functional

TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_vec_e.text: For an integrable field with values in $\mathbb R^3$, the real-kernel convolution equals complexification followed by the complex Fourier cutoff and real projection. The proof commutes the real-part map with an integrable vector-valued integral and checks the scalar multiplication coordinatewise. Integrability is essential to this identification as stated.
TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_vec_e.summary: The real convolution agrees with the velocity cutoff

TorusEuler.realFourierFrequency.text: This definition casts the three integer frequency components to real numbers and places them in the Euclidean vector wrapper. It supplies the real frequency at which the angular Leray symbol is sampled. The associated norm and inner-product lemmas connect this representation to the earlier complex coefficient formulas.
TorusEuler.realFourierFrequency.summary: Integer modes embedded as real Euclidean frequencies

TorusEuler.realFourierScalarization.text:
A real linear measurement viewed as a complex-valued torus function.

The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.realFourierScalarization.summary: Testing a real Fourier field by a linear functional

TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.text: For a complex operator symbol smooth away from the origin, constructs the fixed-cutoff dyadic operator on half-Hölder fields and restricts it to real fields through the chosen complexification, embedding real inputs and taking real parts of outputs. The value of the symbol at zero supplies the mean action in the underlying construction. Positive homogeneity is not assumed by this definition; it enters separately when identifying every nonzero Fourier coefficient with the requested symbol.
TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.summary: Construct the real multiplier using a fixed cutoff

TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.text: For a smooth, even, degree-zero homogeneous symbol $P$, the real half-Hölder multiplier acts on every real-character moment by $P$ at the lattice vector. Evenness and homogeneity are explicit hypotheses, and the conclusion includes the zero Fourier mode. This identifies the constructed real operator with the desired projection symbol.
TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.summary: The real multiplier has the prescribed Fourier moments

TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3.text: For an arbitrary measure $\mu$, lift the coordinatewise real-part map to complex vector-valued $L^2$ functions. The result is a real continuous linear map into real vector $L^2$. It is one of the projection maps used to build the complexification of the entire time-path Hilbert space.
TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3.summary: Take real parts of vector valued L² paths

TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_I_smul.text: The real part of $iv$ is minus the imaginary part of $v$ as an $L^2$ equality. Representative compatibility reduces the assertion to the corresponding scalar complex identity in each coordinate. It records the sign convention needed to prove that componentwise real-operator extension is complex-linear.
TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_I_smul.summary: Multiplication by i turns imaginary paths into negative real parts

TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_apply_ae.text: Taking the $L^2$ real-part map has the same representative as applying the coordinatewise real part $v\mapsto(\operatorname{Re}v_i)_i$ pointwise, almost everywhere. The measure is arbitrary and no time-interval assumption is involved. This equality permits integrals and norm identities to use the familiar finite-dimensional real-part formula.
TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_apply_ae.summary: Path real parts agree with pointwise real projection

TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_complexify.text: A real L² path is unchanged by first complexifying it and then taking its real part. This equality holds in the quotient space and is proved by representative comparison. It provides the left-inverse axiom of the concrete L² complexification, ensuring that real data retain their identity under embedding.
TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_complexify.summary: Real projection recovers the original real path

TorusEuler.realPart_fourierCoeff_pair.text: For a continuous field $f$ with values in a complex space, a real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$, frequency $k$, and complex scalar $c$, the real-character moment of $\operatorname{Re}f$ is half of $\operatorname{Re}$ applied to the combination of coefficients at $-k$ and $k$. The input need not be real-valued. Both opposite modes are required by the real part of the character.
TorusEuler.realPart_fourierCoeff_pair.summary: Real character moments use both opposite Fourier coefficients

TorusEuler.realPart_fourierCoeff_pair_tr.text: Assume a complex operator is compatible with a real operator under the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$, and the same complex multiplier relation between $f$ and $g$ holds at both opposite frequencies $-k$ and $k$. Then the corresponding real-character moment of $g$ is the real operator applied to that of $f$. A single-frequency identity would not suffice for this conclusion.
TorusEuler.realPart_fourierCoeff_pair_tr.summary: Paired Fourier identities transfer a real multiplier action

TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff.text: Defines the scalar cutoff by complexifying a continuous real torus function, taking the finite Fourier sum with symbol $\psi$ and scale $\Lambda$, and extracting its real part. It is defined even for scales and symbols outside the analytic cutoff regime. Approximation estimates and the intended symmetric multiplier interpretation require their own hypotheses.
TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff.summary: Take the real scalar Fourier cutoff

TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff_diver.text: For a continuously differentiable lifted vector field with a continuous scalar divergence representative, cutting off that representative equals taking the divergence of the vector cutoff.
