The proof combines the coordinate derivative identities with scalar finite-sum linearity. The statement is valid for arbitrary symbol and scale and does not itself supply norm bounds.
TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff_diver.summary: The real cutoff commutes with vector divergence

TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart.text: Turns a complex-linear operator into a real-linear operator by complexifying a real input and taking the real part of the output. The construction is itself a continuous real-linear map on operators. It is used after Fourier reconstruction to obtain a real pressure Hessian from real scalar source data.
TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart.summary: Restrict a complex operator to real vectors

TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart_apply.text: For a complex-linear operator $A$ on $\mathbb C^3$ and a real vector $v\in\mathbb R^3$, the real part of $A$ applied to $v$ is $\operatorname{Re}\bigl(A(v)\bigr)$, where $v$ is first regarded as a complex vector and the real part is taken coordinatewise. The identity holds by definition for every complex operator.
TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart_apply.summary: Evaluation rule for the real part of a complex operator

TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart_press.text: Taking the real operator part of the pressure symbol applied to a complex scalar gives the scalar’s real part times the real angular projection. The identity holds for every frequency. It is the algebraic step that converts paired complex Fourier coefficients into the real cosine and sine moment formula.
TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart_press.summary: Recover the real scalar pressure projection

TorusEuler.realTensorFourierCutoff.text:
The real Fourier cutoff on a tensor field represented in a complex normed space.

The maps J and R are arbitrary continuous linear maps in the definition. Recovering the original real tensor requires the retraction property R∘J=id, and approximation bounds also require a positive cutoff scale.

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff.text:
The Fourier cutoff on real Euclidean vector fields, obtained by complex Fourier synthesis followed by the coordinatewise real projection.

The cutoff delegates to finite Fourier synthesis and uses an arbitrary real scale in the raw definition. Positive scale, symbol support and regularity are supplied by the cutoff estimates.

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.text: Complexifies a possibly noncontinuous real velocity field, applies the complex Fourier cutoff, then takes its real part. The definition accepts an arbitrary function on the torus. Subsequent results relate this representative-level construction to continuous fields and to almost-everywhere classes; meaningful analytic estimates use integrability or essential boundedness.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.summary: Applying the real vector cutoff to a representative

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.text: Almost-everywhere equal real velocity representatives give exactly equal cutoffs. The proof passes their equality through complexification, applies the complex cutoff congruence, and then takes real parts. The result is pointwise equality of output functions; it does not require the inputs themselves to have pointwise equal values.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.summary: Real velocity cutoffs ignore null-set changes

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.text: For a continuous real velocity field, the cutoff defined on arbitrary representatives agrees with the earlier real vector Fourier cutoff of continuous torus fields. This is an equality of the two operator definitions, not a proof that an arbitrary input is continuous. It allows estimates stated for continuous torus fields to be used with the representative-level formulation.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.summary: Agreement with the continuous velocity cutoff

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_T1_of.text: With smooth time-dependent Fourier coefficients in the retained band, smooth odd divergence-free input slices and an even symbol, the cutoff is jointly smooth on the specified time set. Every slice is periodic, odd, divergence free and has no frequencies beyond $2\Lambda$. These are the listed admissibility properties; no bound on the residual or deformation is asserted.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_T1_of.summary: Smooth coefficient paths produce an admissible next parent

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_add.text: Real vector cutoff preserves addition of continuous torus fields.

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_gradi.text: For a continuously differentiable scalar torus lift and a continuous vector field representing its gradient, the real vector cutoff of that field is the gradient of the real scalar cutoff. The proof differentiates the finite Fourier sum coordinatewise. This exact identity holds for arbitrary real symbol and scale, independently of the later analytic cutoff bounds.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_gradi.summary: The real cutoff preserves the form of a gradient

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_sum.text: The commutation with finite vector field sums, used in tensor divergence.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_sum.summary: Fourier truncation commutes with finite sums

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_tenso.text: For a continuous torus tensor whose lift is continuously differentiable, let $d$ be a continuous torus field whose lift equals the physical divergence of that tensor at every point. The real vector cutoff of $d$ equals the divergence of the real tensor cutoff. The proof uses each coordinate derivative and a finite sum; no smooth-symbol or positive-scale assumption is needed for this exact identity.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_tenso.summary: The real cutoff commutes with tensor divergence

TorusEuler.real_inner_angularLeray_eq_ze.text: For any real frequency vector $\xi$ and vector $z$, the angular Leray projection of $z$ is orthogonal to $\xi$. The proof splits off the case $\xi=0$ before cancellation of its squared norm. At zero frequency the orthogonality statement is automatic and is consistent with retaining every amplitude.
TorusEuler.real_inner_angularLeray_eq_ze.summary: The angular projection removes the frequency component

TorusEuler.realifyHalfHolderMultiplier.text: Given a bounded real-linear operator $L$ on half-Hölder fields valued in the complexification, embeds each real input pointwise into the complexification, applies $L$, and then takes the real part pointwise. This yields a bounded real-linear operator on real-valued fields. The construction works for arbitrary $L$ and does not require its outputs on real inputs to have zero imaginary part.
TorusEuler.realifyHalfHolderMultiplier.summary: Transport a multiplier to real Hölder fields

TorusEuler.realifyHalfHolderMultiplier_i.text: If the complex embedding of $v$ equals $F$ applied to the embedded $f$ plus $G$ applied to the embedded $s$, then $v$ equals the sum of the two corresponding realified outputs. Applying the real-part map proves the equality pointwise. The premise supplies the exact embedded identity, so preservation of the real subspace by each operator separately is unnecessary.
TorusEuler.realifyHalfHolderMultiplier_i.summary: Transport an embedded multiplier identity to real fields

TorusEuler.reciprocal_inductive_frequenc.text: Let $\lambda_n$ be real frequencies with $\lambda_0\ge2$ and $\lambda_{n+1}\ge\lambda_n^2$ for every nonnegative integer $n$. For every $j\ge0$, the series $\sum_{k\ge0}\lambda_{j+k}^{-1}$ converges and is at most $2\lambda_j^{-1}$. The hypotheses imply all frequencies are positive, so the reciprocals are ordinary reciprocals with no zero-denominator convention involved. This numerical result is independent of the Euler equations and does not itself bound velocity differences. Section 8 combines it with the increment estimates and, for higher derivatives, vanishing of the later oscillations. Taking the tail to start at $j=n+1$ gives the last bound in Proposition 8.1.
TorusEuler.reciprocal_inductive_frequenc.summary: Squaring growth gives summability and an explicit bound for every tail

TorusEuler.referenceCouplingNumerators.text: Let real numbers $\varepsilon,\tau,x,s,e,Y$ satisfy $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, $(1+x^2)s^2=1$ and $Y=s(1+e)-\varepsilon\tau xs^2/2$. The formal statement proves $x+\varepsilon+2\varepsilon\tau Y=x-\varepsilon+2\varepsilon s^2+2\varepsilon\tau s(1+e)$ and $-1+\varepsilon x+2(1+x^2)Y^2+2\varepsilon\tau xY=1+4e+2e^2+\varepsilon xs^2$. Multiplying by $s=\cos\varphi$ gives the simplified reference couplings in (2.22). The algebraic statement also permits the negative square-root choice of $s$, since it assumes only its square; the wave application selects $s>0$. Neither smallness of $e$ nor a differential equation is required for the cancellation.
TorusEuler.referenceCouplingNumerators.summary: Two polynomial identities remove the apparently large terms

TorusEuler.relayCrossMap.text: The map sends $v$ to the continuous linear operator $w\mapsto v\times w$. Its norm is controlled by one, so composing it with the normalized wave-vector profile preserves parent derivative bounds. This public construction supplies the same geometric operation needed in the potential and its time derivative.
TorusEuler.relayCrossMap.summary: The cross product as an operator-valued linear map

TorusEuler.relayCrossMap_apply.text: For any vector $v$, evaluation of the operator-valued cross-product map at $v$ returns the operator $w\mapsto v\times w$. The equality is definitional, exposing the concrete cross-product operator after it has been expressed as a continuous linear map. This allows the jet algebra to be identified with the normalized coefficient formulas used in the relay.

TorusEuler.relayCurlRowCLM.text: The map sends a coframe $G$ to $\ell^{-1}(G^*e_i)\times\cdot$, the coefficient paired with one scaled label derivative in the curl. It is linear in $G$, so every label derivative of the row is controlled by the corresponding derivative of $G$. The inverse width is kept explicit.
TorusEuler.relayCurlRowCLM.summary: The linear coefficient of a scaled curl row

TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile.text:
Apply the mean-zero oscillatory pressure construction to the fixed-label strain, covector, forcing and velocity profile. This is a scalar phase profile used by the slow pressure-gradient term.

This is a normalized phase primitive, not a pressure solution predicate. Smoothness, phase periodicity, nonzero covectors and the transverse momentum equation justify its use as pressure.
TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile.summary: The normalized phase pressure used in the relay

TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile_con.text: The normalized phase pressure is linear under simultaneous scalar multiplication of the velocity and forcing slices. Both terms in its pressure slope $(\kappa\cdot f-2\kappa\cdot MV)/|\kappa|^2$ scale, and so does their zero-mean phase primitive. The coefficients $M$ and $\kappa$ are held fixed; the theorem does not describe scaling the wave vector or strain.
TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile_con.summary: Velocity and forcing scale the phase pressure together

TorusEuler.relayPotentialProfile.text:
The actual primitive fields in the relay with the frequency removed from the covector. Each depends only on the indicated fixed-time coefficient and profile data.

This uses the raw wave potential; nonzero covectors and integrable phase profiles are needed for its physical primitive interpretation. The coefficients and profiles in the construction provide those hypotheses.
TorusEuler.relayPotentialProfile.summary: The normalized primitive profile for the relay

TorusEuler.relayPotentialProfile_const_s.text: Scaling the velocity slice by a constant multiplies its relay potential by that constant. The normalized wave-vector coefficient is a continuous linear map and the centered phase primitive commutes with scalar multiplication. The equality is pointwise in label and phase, so a time-dependent weight may be treated as constant on each fixed-time slice.
TorusEuler.relayPotentialProfile_const_s.summary: The potential is linear under simultaneous scaling

TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile.text:
At fixed label, take the normalized phase primitive of the potential-time source built from M, k, V and f. The definition prepares the primitive used in the linear relay; the solution equation is supplied separately.

The phase integral is a totalized integral. Smooth phase profiles, the nonzero covector and the time evolution identity must be supplied before identifying this primitive with an actual time derivative.
TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile.summary: The phase primitive of the potential-time source

TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile_con.text: If both the velocity and forcing slices are multiplied by a real number $r$, the potential-time profile is multiplied by $r$. Its integrand is linear in those two inputs through separate coefficient maps. This identity permits amplitude normalization after the physical time derivative has been evaluated, without introducing a derivative of the weight.
TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile_con.summary: Velocity and forcing scale the potential derivative together

TorusEuler.relayPressureRowCLM.text: This map sends $G$ to the scalar-to-vector operator $c\mapsto\ell^{-1}cG^*e_i$. It provides the $i$th pressure-gradient coefficient in label coordinates. Expressing the operation as a continuous linear map lets the same coframe derivative estimate control both the pressure row and the curl row.
TorusEuler.relayPressureRowCLM.summary: The linear coefficient of a scaled pressure gradient

TorusEuler.scalarODE_exists_Icc.text: A continuous scalar vector field $f(t,y)$, uniformly Lipschitz in its state variable on the strip $[lo,hi]$ (one constant for all times in $[a,b]$, $a\le b$), with the inward inequalities $f(t,lo)\ge0$ and $f(t,hi)\le0$ for $t\in[a,b]$, has a solution starting from any $y_0\in[lo,hi]$ that stays in that strip: $y(a)=y_0$, $y'(t)=f(t,y(t))$ within $[a,b]$ and $y(t)\in[lo,hi]$ for every $t\in[a,b]$. The proof projects the state onto the strip, solves the projected equation on the time window, and shows that the projection has no effect along the solution.
TorusEuler.scalarODE_exists_Icc.summary: A scalar equation with an invariant interval has a solution on a bounded time interval

TorusEuler.scalarODE_exists_Ici.text: Let $f(t,y)$ be jointly continuous and $y_0\in[lo,hi]$. Suppose that for every $b\ge a$ there is $K$ with $f(t,\cdot)$ $K$-Lipschitz on $[lo,hi]$ for all $t\in[a,b]$, and that $f(t,lo)\ge0$ and $f(t,hi)\le0$ for all $t\ge a$. Then there is $y$ with $y(a)=y_0$, $y'(t)=f(t,y(t))$ within $[a,\infty)$ for every $t\ge a$, and $y(t)\in[lo,hi]$ for every $t\ge a$. Values before $a$ are unconstrained.
TorusEuler.scalarODE_exists_Ici.summary: A scalar equation with an invariant interval has a solution on the whole forward ray

TorusEuler.scalar_le_of_derivWithinAt_no.text: Suppose $y$ has derivative $y'(t)$ within $[a,b]$ at every $t\in[a,b]$, $y(a)\le c$, and $y'(t)\le0$ at every $t\in[a,b)$ with $y(t)\ge c$. Then $y(t)\le c$ for every $t\in[a,b]$. The proof compares $y$ with the barriers $c+\delta(t-a)$ and lets $\delta\to0$.
TorusEuler.scalar_le_of_derivWithinAt_no.summary: A constant upper barrier for a scalar path

TorusEuler.scalar_le_of_derivWithinAt_no.text: The same constant upper barrier holds on the entire ray $[a,\infty)$ when the derivative and sign assumptions hold there. At a requested time the proof applies the compact-interval barrier on $[a,t]$. This theorem assumes a path already defined on the ray; it does not supply global existence.
TorusEuler.scalar_le_of_derivWithinAt_no.summary: A scalar upper barrier for all future times

TorusEuler.scalar_lt_of_derivWithinAt_ne.text: Suppose $y$ is differentiable within $[a,\infty)$, $a\le b$, and $y(b)\le c$. If its derivative is strictly negative whenever it equals $c$ at or after $b$, then $y(t)<c$ for every $t>b$. Only the derivative on the boundary is constrained. The theorem provides the strict sign needed after the reference rate crosses zero.
TorusEuler.scalar_lt_of_derivWithinAt_ne.summary: Strict descent after touching an upper barrier

TorusEuler.scaledCoframe_jet_bound.text: Let $B$ be a field of linear maps on $\mathbb R^3$ and assume $\ell\ge0$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, $L\ge0$ and $\ell\mathsf D^7\le1$. If $\|D^jB(a)\|\le L\mathsf D^{7j+1}$ for every $j\le n$ and every $a$, then $\ell^j\|D^jB(a)\|\le L\mathsf D$ for every $j\le n$ and every $a$. The remaining power of $\mathsf D$ does not depend on the derivative order.
TorusEuler.scaledCoframe_jet_bound.summary: The label radius absorbs the growth of the coframe derivatives

TorusEuler.scaledFlow_differentiable_tra.text: For a finite-dimensional state space, joint smoothness of the scaled field, uniform Lipschitz control, and the smallness bound give differentiability of every transition between allowed times. The two-time trajectory family is supplied by its initial-value and trajectory hypotheses. The conclusion also covers reversed transitions and does not assume their derivatives in advance.
TorusEuler.scaledFlow_differentiable_tra.summary: Smooth scaled flows have differentiable transitions

TorusEuler.scaledFlow_fderiv_and_displac.text: Let $\Phi_{s,t}$ solve $\partial_t\Phi_{s,t}(z)=F(t,\Phi_{s,t}(z))$ on $[l,r]$ with $\Phi_{s,s}=I$. Suppose each $F(t,\cdot)$ is differentiable, $\|D_zF\|\le K$, and $\|D_z(\pi F)\|\le M$ for a continuous linear map $\pi$. If $K(r-l)\le1/2$, then $\|D\Phi_{s,t}(z)\|\le2$ and $\|D_z[\pi\Phi_{s,t}(z)-\pi z]\|\le2M|t-s|$ for either ordering of $s,t$ in the interval. These are the transition and displacement estimates used in Lemma 5.10. The formal conclusion bounds derivative expressions; it does not itself include differentiability of the transition maps, which is supplied separately for the smooth lifted flow.
TorusEuler.scaledFlow_fderiv_and_displac.summary: A small derivative bound controls forward and reverse transitions

TorusEuler.scaledFlow_lipschitz_and_disp.text: For a two-time trajectory family, uniform Lipschitz bounds $K$ on the field and $M$ on its projection combine with $K(r-l)\le1/2$ on the slab $[l,r]$ to make each transition Lipschitz with constant two. The projected displacement has Lipschitz constant $2M|t-s|$. The initial and trajectory equations are hypotheses, and the bounds hold in either time direction.
TorusEuler.scaledFlow_lipschitz_and_disp.summary: Small scaled gradients bound transitions and projected displacement

TorusEuler.scaledFlow_restart.text: Any two-time trajectory family for a uniformly Lipschitz field, with the prescribed initial values, satisfies the restart identity $\Phi(t,u)\Phi(s,t)=\Phi(s,u)$ for times in the slab. ODE uniqueness gives the equality. Choosing the final time equal to the first then identifies reverse transitions as inverses.
TorusEuler.scaledFlow_restart.summary: Transitions compose across an intermediate time

TorusEuler.scaledHigherPressureGradient_.text: The coframe adjoint, strain and longitudinal projection have first-order scaled coefficient bounds, while pressure has a second-order bound and force and velocity have first-order bounds. Under the listed smoothness and nonnegativity assumptions, their reconstructed gradient has the explicit first-order bound in the conclusion. The transverse equation has not been assumed here; it is used separately to identify this expression.
TorusEuler.scaledHigherPressureGradient_.summary: Bound the reconstructed gradient before physical differentiation

TorusEuler.scaledLiftKernel.text: For a complex-valued function $K$ on $\mathbb R^3$, the formal object is $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$. The exponent three is the spatial dimension, so for positive $\Lambda$ it compensates for the change of variables in an integral. This definition matches the kernel dilation in Appendix B. It is given for every real scale without integrability or decay assumptions; at $\Lambda=0$ it is identically zero. The unit-mass, moment-scaling and convolution results therefore separately assume $\Lambda>0$ and the appropriate kernel hypotheses. The definition alone asserts none of those analytic properties.
TorusEuler.scaledLiftKernel.summary: Rescales a three-dimensional kernel at the chosen frequency

TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel.text: Dilate a Banach-valued Euclidean kernel $K$ to $y\mapsto\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$. The cubic factor is the dimension-three volume normalization. This definition works for every real scale, while the integral and Fourier scaling theorems explicitly restrict to positive $\Lambda$.
TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel.summary: A multiplier kernel at a new frequency scale

TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel_decay.text: Let $\sigma$ be a rapidly decreasing smooth symbol on $\mathbb R^3$ with values in a complex Banach space, and let $G$ be its inverse Fourier kernel. Define $M=\sum_{i=0}^1\sum_{j=0}^5\int|\xi|^i\|D^j\sigma(\xi)\|\,d\xi$. For $\Lambda>0$ and integer $d\in\{0,1\}$, the formal statement gives $(1+\Lambda|y|)^5\|D^dG_\Lambda(y)\|\le32(1+2\pi)4^5M\Lambda^{3+d}$, where $G_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3G(\Lambda y)$. Taking $\Lambda=2^j$ gives the decay form in Appendix A.1. To recover its constant $CC_0$, one must also bound $M$ using the annular support and frozen-symbol derivative estimates.
TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel_decay.summary: Control the kernel and its first spatial derivative

TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel_decay_.text: At positive frequency scale $\Lambda$, the weighted order $d$ derivative of the rescaled kernel is bounded by $\Lambda^{3+d}$ times the unscaled decay coefficient. Three powers come from volume scaling in dimension three, and each derivative contributes one more. Positivity of the scale is explicit in the chain-rule and norm calculation.
TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel_decay_.summary: Scaling records volume and derivative powers exactly

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseCoefficient.text: Evaluate the coefficient field $B$ at $\ell p_1$, ignoring the independent phase coordinate. This expresses a label-dependent inverse differential in the coordinates of the rescaled profile. The definition itself does not assert that $B$ is an inverse Jacobian; that identification is a hypothesis of the physical chain-rule theorems.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseCoefficient.summary: The inverse differential at the rescaled label

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseCoefficient_jetBou.text: If every label derivative through order $n$ obeys $\ell^j\|D^jB\|\le C$ and $B$ is smooth, then every Fréchet derivative of the rescaled coefficient of order at most $n$ is bounded by $C$ everywhere. One hypothesis is nonnegativity of the label scale, $\ell\ge0$. Phase directions add no derivatives because this coefficient does not depend on phase.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseCoefficient_jetBou.summary: Weighted label derivatives bound the rescaled coefficient

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseDirection.text: Apply the rescaled inverse-differential coefficient to a spatial basis vector, then send that label increment through the label-phase slope $v\mapsto(\ell^{-1}v,h^{-1}\langle k,v\rangle)$. The resulting vector field differentiates the enlarged profile in the direction induced by one physical spatial derivative. It includes both the envelope scale and the phase scale without differentiating time.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseDirection.summary: A spatial direction lifted to label and phase

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseDirection_jetBound.text: An order-$n$ bound $C$ for the rescaled coefficient gives the same derivative order for the lifted spatial direction, multiplied by $\ell^{-1}+h^{-1}\|k\|$. Smoothness of $B$ and nonnegative scales are explicit hypotheses. This supplies the coefficient bound used when iterating variable-direction derivatives of a profile.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseDirection_jetBound.summary: The lifted direction inherits the graph cost

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseGraph.text: Compose the label map $A(t)$ with the scaled label-phase slope to embed physical space into the enlarged profile space. Its components are the scaled label and the initial linear phase evaluated at that label. No assumption that $A$ is a flow inverse is part of this definition.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseGraph.summary: The transported phase graph in scaled coordinates

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile.text:
The label-phase profile in the coordinates with unit envelope and phase scales.

The composition is defined for arbitrary scales. At zero scales it loses spatial or phase dependence; invertible rescaling arguments use positive ℓ and h.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile.summary: The profile in unit label and phase coordinates

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_comp_graph.text: With nonzero label radius and phase width, evaluating the rescaled profile on the scaled phase graph gives precisely the transported physical profile. The equality holds for an arbitrary time-dependent profile $f$, without differentiability assumptions. It removes the coordinate rescaling before later spatial chain-rule estimates are interpreted physically.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_comp_graph.summary: Scaled graph evaluation recovers the transported profile

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.text: The normalized finite directional norm itself supplies the graph input. Its boundedness is explicit, since a real supremum requires it.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.summary: Weighted derivative norms control the rescaled profile

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.text: If every weighted mixed coordinate derivative through order $n$ is bounded by nonnegative $M$, the rescaled profile has full Fréchet derivative bound $4^nM$. The factor four counts the three label directions and one phase direction. The theorem requires joint smoothness but permits arbitrary real scaling parameters.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.summary: Weighted component bounds give a full profile bound

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.text: Assume $M\ge0$ and, for every time $t$, every point $(a,s)$ and every label multi-index $\beta$ and phase order $j$ with $|\beta|+j\le n$, $\ell^{|\beta|}h^j|\partial_a^\beta\partial_s^jf(t,a,s)|\le M$. Fix $t$ with $(a,s)\mapsto f(t,a,s)$ smooth. Then every Fréchet derivative of order at most $n$ of the rescaled profile $(a,s)\mapsto f(t,\ell a,hs)$ has operator norm at most $4^nM$. Smoothness lets every ordered coordinate derivative be rearranged into sorted multi-index form.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.summary: Mixed weighted derivative bounds control all Fréchet derivatives of the rescaled profile

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.text: Restoring the amplitude weight recovers the profile size. Assume the finite weighted mixed-derivative bound for the profiles divided by $\gamma$: $M\ge0$ and $\ell^{|\beta|}h^j|\partial_a^\beta\partial_s^j(\gamma(t)^{-1}f)(t,a,s)|\le M$ for all times $t$, labels and phases, and $|\beta|+j\le n$. At a selected time $t$ with $\gamma(t)>0$ and $(a,s)\mapsto f(t,a,s)$ smooth, every Fréchet derivative of order at most $n$ of the original scaled profile $(a,s)\mapsto f(t,\ell a,hs)$ is bounded by $\gamma(t)\,4^nM$. Positivity at the selected time cancels the inverse weight, and the weight depends only on time, so label and phase derivatives do not differentiate it.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.summary: Restoring the amplitude weight recovers the profile size

TorusEuler.scaledPressureLabelGradient_j.text: If $\ell>0$, the pressure is smooth and its scaled profile has a second-order jet bound $B$, then the scaled label gradient has a first-order jet bound $\ell^{-1}B$. This spells out the single lost label derivative and length factor used in the higher-pressure Hessian argument.
TorusEuler.scaledPressureLabelGradient_j.summary: Two pressure derivatives control one gradient derivative

TorusEuler.scaledSchwartzKernel.text: Assuming $\Lambda\ne0$, package $\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$ as a Schwartz function. Nonzero scale makes dilation an invertible linear map, so rapid decay is preserved. The definition allows negative scales and uses the signed cubic factor; the normalized convolution and moment estimates later impose $\Lambda>0$.
TorusEuler.scaledSchwartzKernel.summary: Dilate a Schwartz kernel with the cubic scale factor

TorusEuler.scaledSchwartzKernel_apply.text: Evaluating the scaled Schwartz function gives the already-defined raw dilated kernel $y\mapsto\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$. This is a definitional equality for any nonzero scale. It lets proofs use the Schwartz function for decay and integrability while keeping the explicit $\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$ function in convolution formulas.
TorusEuler.scaledSchwartzKernel_apply.summary: The bundled dilation has the expected kernel values

TorusEuler.scheduledCrossingRatio.text: The ratio at transition $i$ is $L^{-2}$ with gain $L=4\log\lambda_{i+3}$. Index zero represents the transition starting the second wave, so the gain looks three positions ahead in the zero-based frequency sequence. The definition alone imposes no growth or positivity assumption on that sequence.
TorusEuler.scheduledCrossingRatio.summary: The ratio prescribed for the next physical crossing

TorusEuler.seminorm_word_le_appendixExac.text: Under pairwise commutation of the derivative maps, the seminorm of a word is bounded by the sum over admissible words of exactly its length. Sorting provides a representative of that same length. This sharper version avoids introducing lower-order coefficient terms in the slow-coefficient bound of the lifting proof.

TorusEuler.slabAdvection.text: For velocity fields $v$ and $w$, this is $D_xv(t,x)[w(t,x)]$, so $w$ is the advecting direction and $v$ is the differentiated field. The argument order matters when the binomial rule splits time derivatives between two copies of the velocity. The definition itself asserts neither smoothness nor an Euler equation.
TorusEuler.slabAdvection.summary: Advection with the differentiated field first

TorusEuler.slabAdvection_periodic.text: If $v$ is differentiable and both spatial fields $v$ and $w$ are periodic, then $x\mapsto Dv(x)[w(x)]$ is periodic. The proof uses periodicity of the derivative of $v$ and then periodicity of $w$. There is no time variable or equation hypothesis here; this supplies the spatial periodicity needed to pass differentiated advection to torus norms.

TorusEuler.slabSpatialHolderHalfNorm.text:
The time-uniform spatial half-Hölder norm on the closed slab.

The slab supremum is a real supremum. Actual upper and lower norm bounds require boundedness of the spatial Hölder norms over a nonempty slab; smooth periodic closed-slab inputs supply it in the applications.
TorusEuler.slabSpatialHolderHalfNorm.summary: The uniform spatial Hölder norm on a time slab

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet.text: For a field $f(t,x)$, a nonnegative integer $q$ and a closed interval $[a,b]$, the formal object is the $q$th derivative of $t\mapsto f(t,x)$ taken within that interval while $x$ remains fixed. At order zero it is $f$ itself. When $a<b$ and the field is jointly smooth on the slab, these are the usual interior derivatives and their one-sided endpoint values. The formula is defined for arbitrary fields and intervals, but it does not assert differentiability or justify a classical interpretation without those hypotheses. The auxiliary stage estimates use $a=0$, $b=S_j>0$, and impose their conclusions only within the slab.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet.summary: Differentiate within the closed physical time interval

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_cutoffResidual_ra.text: Fix $\lambda\ge2$, an integer $K$, a real $\psi\ge0$, and $\lambda_+=\lambda^K$, with $K\ge16+2\psi$. Suppose $0\le C_R\le\lambda$, $C_T\le\lambda$, and $\|\partial_t^iR_V\|_{C^{1,1/2}}\le\lambda^\psi\lambda_+^{-4}$. Assume the actual residual has finite formal $C^{1,1/2}$ norm bounded by $C_R$ times this quantity plus $C_T(\lambda^5)^{2-6K}(\lambda^{2(6K+1)+\psi})^2$. The formal statement concludes $|\partial_t^iR_j(t,x)|\le\lambda_+^{-5/2}$ for every $x$. It is a numerical implication at the chosen time and derivative order; it does not establish the analytic cutoff-error bound, time continuity, or eventual validity of its premises.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_cutoffResidual_ra.summary: The next frequency absorbs the remaining cutoff losses

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_endpointTimeParit.text: Let $T>0$ and let $f$ be a jointly smooth velocity on the positive-length slab $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$. For every real parity coefficient $\sigma$, every order $q$, every time $t\in[0,T]$ and every point $x$, time differentiation at the fixed point commutes with taking the parity part: the $q$th time derivative within $[0,T]$ of $\tfrac12(f(t,x)+\sigma f(t,-x))$ is $\tfrac12(\partial_t^qf(t,x)+\sigma\partial_t^qf(t,-x))$. This is an exact equality, not a contraction estimate.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_endpointTimeParit.summary: Taking a parity part commutes with every time derivative

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_eq_of_subset.text: For a smooth field on $[a,b]$, its time derivatives agree with those computed on a contained interval $[c,d]$ whenever both intervals are nondegenerate and $t\in[c,d]$. The equality includes the smaller interval endpoints. The inclusion $[c,d]\subseteq[a,b]$ and the conditions $a<b$, $c<d$ are what allow finite-stage estimates on different time slabs to be compared without changing their time derivatives.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_eq_of_subset.summary: Restrict time jets to a smaller closed interval

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_normContinuity.text: If $f$ is jointly smooth on a closed slab $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$ with $T>0$ and spatially periodic at every slab time, each fixed time jet is continuous there in both the spatial supremum norm and every half-Hölder norm. The proof uses uniformly continuous spatial jets on the torus through one order above the requested Hölder order. It establishes continuity, not a quantitative size bound on the jet.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_normContinuity.summary: Smooth periodic time jets are continuous in spatial norms

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_periodic.text: If every time slice is spatially periodic on the chosen closed interval, each total within-time jet is periodic at times in that interval. Unlike the smoothness lemmas, this identity needs neither joint smoothness nor a nondegenerate interval. The proof differentiates equal periodic slices; interpreting the resulting jets as classical derivatives requires the separate regularity hypotheses.

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_periodicLerayHold.text: For a jointly smooth periodic velocity on $[0,T]$ with $T>0$, each fixed-position time derivative $\partial_t^j$ within $[0,T]$ commutes with the periodic Leray projection $\mathbb P$. The proof represents the time derivatives as smooth curves in the half-Hölder space on the torus and differentiates a continuous linear map there. This is the analytic justification for moving time derivatives through the projected residual.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_periodicLerayHold.summary: The periodic Leray projection commutes with time jets

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_realVectorFourier.text: Given a smooth field $V$ and torus representatives $g_j(t)$ of every time derivative $\partial_t^jV(t)$ for $t\in[0,T]$, the $j$th time derivative of its fixed Fourier cutoff $S_\Lambda V$ equals $S_\Lambda g_j(t)$. The multiplier and radius are independent of time. The statement holds on the closed slab assuming $T>0$; it does not cover cutoffs whose frequency radius moves with time.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_realVectorFourier.summary: Fixed Fourier cutoffs commute with time differentiation

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_slabAdvection.text: Assuming $T>0$ and that $v$ and $w$ are jointly smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, the $q$th fixed-position time derivative of $D_xv[w]$ is the binomial sum $\sum_{i\le q}\binom qi D_x(\partial_t^iv)[\partial_t^{q-i}w]$. The identity holds at every $t$ in the closed interval, including both endpoints. Commutation of spatial differentiation with differentiation within the time interval justifies differentiating the first factor.

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_slice_smooth.text: For a jointly smooth field on a nondegenerate closed slab $[a,b]\times\mathbb R^3$, the spatial field obtained from any time derivative at $t\in[a,b]$ is smooth on all of $\mathbb R^3$. The proof composes joint smoothness with the fixed-time inclusion. It gives spatial regularity at the endpoints as well as in the interval interior.

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_smooth.text: If $a<b$ and the field is jointly smooth on $[a,b]\times\mathbb R^3$, every time derivative within $[a,b]$ is jointly smooth on that same set. The proof inducts using the within-slab slice derivative theorem. The strict interval inequality is part of the mathematical content, ensuring the derivative behavior used at both endpoints is well determined.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_smooth.summary: Time jets remain jointly smooth on the closed slab

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_succ.text: The time derivative of order $q+1$ equals the derivative within $[a,b]$ of the order-$q$ time derivative at the fixed spatial point, using the same closed interval. This is an unconditional identity between derivative expressions. It does not assert that the field has a classical derivative; later lemmas supply joint smoothness and a nondegenerate interval.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_succ.summary: Differentiate the preceding time jet within the slab

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_succ'.text: The time derivative of order $q+1$ can also be written as the order-$q$ time derivative of the first derivative within the interval. This functional identity keeps the spatial coordinate fixed throughout. It reorganizes derivative induction and product recurrences; by itself it supplies no regularity or endpoint uniqueness beyond the meaning of the derivative expressions.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_succ'.summary: Iterate time jets after the first within-derivative

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_zero.text: At time order zero, the time derivative within $[a,b]$ is exactly the original field as a function of both time and space. The statement has no smoothness, interval-ordering, or membership hypothesis. It is a definitional starting case used when the time induction returns to already established spatial estimates for the unmodified construction.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_zero.summary: The zeroth time jet is the original field

TorusEuler.slowFastDivergence_curlComple.text: Assume the potential is twice differentiable, the completed field differentiable, and its fast curl and slow-curl decomposition are the supplied $V$ and $W$. For a twice differentiable label map and phase with gradient $\kappa$, the slow-plus-fast divergence of $W$ vanishes at any chosen phase. Shifting the physical phase graph makes it pass through that phase.
TorusEuler.slowFastDivergence_curlComple.summary: A curl completion has zero total divergence at every phase

TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff.text: For $g$ on $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$, the formal object is the finite sum over integer frequencies $|\xi|\le2\Lambda$ with coefficients $\psi(\xi/\Lambda)\widehat g(\xi)$ and modes $e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot x}$. For $\Lambda>0$ and a symbol zero outside the radius-two ball, this is the multiplier $S_\Lambda$ of Appendix B. The definition itself permits arbitrary symbols, fields and real scales; outside those hypotheses the explicit finite frequency restriction still applies. Division by zero is assigned zero, so the zero-scale formula does not describe the paper's positive-frequency cutoff. Fourier-integrability and norm estimates are supplied by separate hypotheses and results.
TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff.summary: Builds the cutoff from a finite set of torus modes

TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff_conj.text: For a real-valued even symbol $\psi$, applying the cutoff to the conjugated scalar field $\bar g$ equals conjugating its output. The proof pairs opposite frequencies in the finite band. The conclusion is purely algebraic and does not require input smoothness or a positive cutoff scale.
TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff_conj.summary: A real even cutoff commutes with conjugation

TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff_eq_integr.text: For an integrable torus function $g$, the finite Fourier cutoff at $x$ equals the integral of $K_{\psi,\Lambda}(x,z)\,g(z)$ in $z$, where $K_{\psi,\Lambda}$ is the cutoff kernel. The proof interchanges a finite sum with the integral and expands Fourier coefficients. It establishes this representation for arbitrary symbol and scale; the uniform analytic estimate comes later.
TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff_eq_integr.summary: The cutoff as an integral against its kernel

TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff_neg_arg.text: If the cutoff symbol $\psi$ is even and the input satisfies the real-scalar parity relation $g(-z)=c\,g(z)$, the output satisfies that same relation. The scale $\Lambda$ may be any real number. This algebraic assertion establishes parity preservation independently of the analytic cutoff estimates requiring positive scale.
TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff_neg_arg.summary: An even cutoff preserves spatial parity

TorusEuler.smoothPeriodicVelocity.text: This submodule consists of Euclidean vector fields that are smooth and spatially periodic. Closure under addition and real scalar multiplication is proved in the definition. It provides the common algebraic domain for the momentum construction. Neither divergence freedom nor odd parity is part of membership.
TorusEuler.smoothPeriodicVelocity.summary: Smooth periodic fields form the velocity domain

TorusEuler.smoothPeriodicVelocityJets.text: The map sends a smooth periodic field to all its bounded spatial derivatives through order $m$. It is linear because differentiation preserves sums and scalar multiplication on smooth inputs. Including the zeroth derivative makes the tuple remember the original velocity, which is used to prove injectivity.
TorusEuler.smoothPeriodicVelocityJets.summary: A smooth velocity determines its finite jet tuple

TorusEuler.smooth_slabAdvection.text: Given $T>0$ and jointly smooth $v$ and $w$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, their advective product $D_xv[w]$ is jointly smooth on the same closed slab. The proof first differentiates $v$ spatially within the slab calculus and then applies that field of linear maps to $w$. It preserves endpoint regularity needed by subsequent time derivatives.
TorusEuler.smooth_slabAdvection.summary: Advection is smooth on the closed slab

TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord.text:
The usual ordered coordinate partials of a field on the lift.

The word map is defined using totalized derivatives. Permuting words or identifying them with classical partial derivatives uses separate smoothness hypotheses.

TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_comp.text: The chain rule iterated along a coordinate word, for a graph with a supplied direction field over each of its Eulerian coordinate derivatives.
TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_comp.summary: The chain rule along a transported derivative word

TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_endpoin.text: For a smooth field and an ordered word $w$ of coordinate derivatives, identifies differentiation of the parity part with selecting the sign $\varepsilon(-1)^{|w|}$ after differentiating, where $|w|$ is the length of the word. The word order remains unchanged. This converts the abstract iterated Fréchet derivative formula into the coordinate-word notation used for hierarchy estimates.
TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_endpoin.summary: Coordinate derivatives alternate the selected parity

TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_eq_iter.text: A spatial derivative word agrees with evaluating the actual Fréchet derivative in the corresponding ordered coordinate directions.
TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_eq_iter.summary: Spatial words evaluate the actual derivative tensor

TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_transpo.text: Under nonzero scales, smooth profile and coefficient fields, and the hypothesis identifying $B$ with the label-map derivative, every ordered spatial derivative word of the physical profile is the corresponding lifted profile word evaluated on the graph. The list records order explicitly. No commutation of variable-coefficient derivatives is presumed.
TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_transpo.summary: Physical derivative words become profile derivative words

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm.text:
Sum the uniform norm and half-Hölder seminorm of all iterated Fréchet derivatives through the specified order $m$. It is used together with the spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ condition, which ensures that every supremum is finite and the derivatives have their intended meaning.

The formula is defined even when derivatives are not meaningful or their supremum ranges are unbounded, because iterated derivatives and real suprema are defined everywhere. The spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ condition ($m$ times differentiable, with bounded derivative values and bounded half-Hölder quotients through order $m$) is the intended validity condition. Order zero contains the value and increment terms.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm.summary: The higher spatial Holder norm on the lift

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffP.text:
Let $u,V,R,p,\Pi$ be smooth periodic fields, with $V$ divergence free, and suppose $W$ is differentiable and divergence free. Assume $\Delta p=-\operatorname{tr}((
abla u)^2)$ and $W+(V\cdot
abla)V+
abla\Pi=R$. Then $\|D^2(p-\Pi)\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le24\|D^2\Delta^{-1}\|[\|u-V\|_{C^{1,1/2}}(\|u\|_{C^{1,1/2}}+\|V\|_{C^{1,1/2}})+\|R\|_{C^{1,1/2}}]$. In §5.7, $W=V_t$ and $R=R_V$. This estimate is spatial at a fixed time and does not require $u$ to be a Fourier cutoff; that relation is used afterward to bound $u-V$. The residual contribution cannot be omitted merely because $p$ is a Poisson pressure.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffP.summary: Keep both the velocity difference and approximate momentum error

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffP.text: For a smooth symbol equal to one on the unit ball and zero beyond radius two, assumes cutoff scale at least one, depth $P\ge2$, and that the input lift $V$ has bounded derivatives and bounded half-Hölder quotients through order $P$. It bounds the order-one tail norm times the sum of the old and new order-one velocity norms by $C(2+C)$ times the truncation error. Evenness is not required here.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffP.summary: The quadratic pressure tail has the cutoff decay

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffT.text: For $s\le M$, proves that the periodic cutoff tail has order-$s$ half-Hölder regularity and norm at most $C_M\Lambda^{s-M}$ times the order-$M$ input norm. The exponent is an integer power, and positive $\Lambda$ justifies its reciprocal form. Unlike the paper’s setup $\Lambda\ge1$, this statement allows any positive cutoff scale.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffT.summary: The cutoff tail gains a power of the cutoff scale

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffV.text: Let $V$ be a continuous periodic vector field with finite $C^{P,1/2}$ norm. Let the smooth symbol $\psi$ equal one on $|\xi|\le1$ and vanish for $|\xi|>2$, and let $\Lambda>0$. For each integer $0\le m\le P$, the cutoff error satisfies $S_\Lambda V-V\in C^{m,1/2}$ and $\|S_\Lambda V-V\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le C_P\Lambda^{m-P}\|V\|_{C^{P,1/2}}$, with $C_P$ depending on the fixed cutoff and order. The exponent is an integer difference, so it is genuinely negative when $m<P$. This extends the range $m\le2$, $\Lambda\ge1$ used in §5.7. Oddness, incompressibility and a momentum equation are not hypotheses of the tail estimate.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffV.summary: Estimate every lower derivative order using the cutoff frequency

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_endpoin.text: For a $C^m$ field with bounded suprema and half-Hölder quotients of its derivatives through order $m$, proves the same regularity after reflection averaging and a nonincreasing full spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm when $|\varepsilon|\le1$. Derivative parity alternates with order, but each sign still has absolute value at most one. Both differentiability and bounded quotient sets are preserved.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_endpoin.summary: Selecting parity costs no half-Hölder norm constant

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_le_of_u.text: Let $g:\mathbb R^3\to E$ be smooth, where $E$ is a real normed space. If $B\ge0$ and every derivative of order $0\le j\le m+1$ has operator norm at most $B$ everywhere, then $g\in C^{m,1/2}$ and $\|g\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le3(m+1)B$. Order zero includes the value of the function itself. The estimate uses the derivative bound at short distances and the supremum bound at long distances. No periodicity or bounded spatial domain is assumed. Lemma 5.7 applies this result to obtain its Hölder estimate with one additional profile derivative.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_le_of_u.summary: Uniform bounds through the next order imply half Hölder regularity

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_one_eq.text: The order-one lift norm is exactly the order-zero norm of the field plus the order-zero norm of its Fréchet derivative. This follows by expanding the two derivative levels and using the isometric first-derivative encoding. The identity supports separate estimates for the projected field and its projected derivative columns.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_one_eq.summary: The first-order norm separates value and derivative

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_realTen.text: For real and complex tensor spaces linked by continuous real-linear maps $J$ and $R$ with $R(Jq)=q$ for every $q$, the real tensor cutoff tail obeys the usual $\Lambda^{s-M}$ estimate. The constant gains the factor $\|R\|\|J\|$. The retraction identity is essential: it makes the projected complex tail equal the original real tensor error.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_realTen.summary: The Hölder tail estimate extends to real tensors

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_realVec.text: Let $f$ be the periodic lift of a continuous real velocity on $\mathbb T^3$, with $f\in C^{M,1/2}$ and $0\le s\le M$. Suppose $\psi$ is smooth, one on the unit ball and zero outside the radius-two ball. For every $\Lambda>0$, the formal statement proves $(I-S_\Lambda)f\in C^{s,1/2}$ and $\|(I-S_\Lambda)f\|_{C^{s,1/2}}\le C_M\Lambda^{s-M}\|f\|_{C^{M,1/2}}$. The constant depends on the kernel and $M$, not on $s$, frequency or field. These norms sum uniform and half-Hölder bounds for the derivative tensors through the indicated order. The exponent is an integer difference, so $s<M$ gives an inverse power. This supplies (B.2) for the paper's velocity fields and extends its frequency range below one. The derivative tensors are the full iterated derivatives, measured in operator norm.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_realVec.summary: Proves the Hölder tail estimate for every positive frequency

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_succ_eq.text: The implemented order-$m+1$ norm is the order-zero norm of $f$ plus the order-$m$ norm of $Df$. This is an exact algebraic equality for the finite sum defining the norm. It holds without regularity hypotheses; interpreting each real supremum as a genuine bound still requires the separate $C^{m+1,1/2}$ membership hypothesis.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_succ_eq.summary: Split the higher Hölder norm at order zero

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_zero_eq.text: The lift norm at order zero equals the sum of the field’s real supremum norm and half-Hölder seminorm. This equality is definitional up to the isometric encoding of zero-argument multilinear maps. No boundedness hypothesis is present in the identity; interpreting either real supremum as a norm still requires the appropriate boundedness condition.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_zero_eq.summary: The order-zero norm is supremum plus seminorm

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfQuotient.text:
Define the norm of a field increment divided by the square root of the increment length. The quotient uses the lifted field on Euclidean labels and is formally zero at a zero increment by totalized division.

At zero increment both numerator and denominator are zero, and total division gives zero. This harmless convention adds an equal-point quotient without affecting a genuine seminorm; nonzero increments are needed for reciprocal manipulations.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfQuotient.summary: The half Holder quotient of a spatial increment

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfSeminorm.text: Take the real supremum of the increment quotients $|f(x+v)-f(x)|/|v|^{1/2}$ over all base points and increments. Boundedness of this range is a separate part of the spatial Hölder regularity condition. The quotient at zero increment is zero. The real supremum takes the default value zero when its range is unbounded, so boundedness must be supplied before treating it as a finite Hölder seminorm.

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_add.text: A spatial half-Hölder sum estimate for an arbitrary normed target.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_add.summary: Adding fields preserves finite spatial Hölder regularity

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_add_exact.text: If both vector fields have the specified finite half-Hölder regularity, their sum has it too and its norm is bounded by the sum of the two norms. The derivative order is unchanged.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_add_exact.summary: The half-Hölder norm obeys the triangle inequality

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_bilinear.text: Let $E,F,G$ be real normed spaces and $B:E\times F\to G$ a continuous bilinear map. If $f:\mathbb R^3\to E$ and $g:\mathbb R^3\to F$ belong to $C^{m,1/2}$ for an integer $m\ge0$, then $B(f,g)$ also belongs to that space and $\|B(f,g)\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le3(m+1)2^m\|B\|\|f\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\|g\|_{C^{m,1/2}}$. This is the precise estimate used to establish (5.59). The constant depends only on derivative order, while $\|B\|$ records the operation’s size. It applies to scalar multiplication, tensor products and contractions, without assuming periodicity or a fluid equation.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_bilinear.summary: A single operator norm accounts for the choice of product

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_comp_clm.text: Continuous linear maps preserve finite spatial half-Hölder regularity.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_comp_clm.summary: Linear maps preserve finite spatial Hölder regularity

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_contraction.text: Contracting a first spatial derivative, as for a tensor divergence, loses one Hölder order.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_contraction.summary: Tensor divergence costs one spatial Hölder derivative

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_halfHolderP.text: A bounded torus operator commuting with actual line derivatives preserves every finite lifted half-Hölder order. The norm factor remains $2\sqrt{2}\|P\|$, independent of the order $m$. The input must be periodic and of class $C^{m,1/2}$; induction uses the derivative operator’s norm bound and the exact splitting of the higher norm.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_halfHolderP.summary: Bound every Hölder order of the projected lift

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_of_bounded_.text: Uniform adjacent spatial jet bounds control the lift half-Hölder norm.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_of_bounded_.summary: Adjacent derivative bounds control the half-Hölder norm

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_of_contDiff.text: A smooth periodic lift has finite spatial half-Hölder norm at every order.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_of_contDiff.summary: A smooth periodic lift has finite Hölder regularity

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_one_halfHol.text: If $P$ preserves all torus line-derivative relations, its guarded lift maps periodic order-one half-Hölder fields to the same class. The norm bound is $2\sqrt2\|P\|$ times the input norm. The proof separately controls the field and reconstructed derivative columns; the periodicity and regularity hypotheses select the meaningful branch of the lifted definition.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_one_halfHol.summary: A derivative-preserving operator is bounded on first-order lifts

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_one_iff.text: A field has first-order half-Hölder regularity exactly when it is $C^1$ and both the field and its Fréchet derivative have order-zero half-Hölder regularity. The explicit $C^1$ condition prevents a totalized derivative value from being mistaken for genuine differentiability. This decomposition is used to establish the projected field’s regularity.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_one_iff.summary: First-order regularity is regularity of value and derivative

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_periodicLer.text: The actual periodic Leray projection preserves every spatial half-Hölder order.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_periodicLer.summary: The Leray projection preserves every spatial Hölder order

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_sub_le_of_u.text: If smooth fields differ by at most a nonnegative $\delta$ in every derivative through order $m+1$, their difference belongs to $C^{m,1/2}$ and its norm is at most $3(m+1)\delta$. The extra derivative controls the half Hölder quotient. The theorem supplies the regularity membership as well as the numerical norm bound.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_sub_le_of_u.summary: Uniform derivative errors control the full Hölder difference

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_succ_iff.text: Order $m+1$ half-Hölder regularity is equivalent to differentiability of $f$, order-zero regularity of $f$, and order-$m$ regularity of its Fréchet derivative. The order-zero clause retains control of the original function as well as its derivatives. This equivalence includes bounded derivative norms and Hölder quotients, not merely a formal derivative identity.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_succ_iff.summary: Separate the first derivative from higher regularity

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_iff.text: Order-zero half-Hölder regularity is equivalent to continuity of the field, boundedness of its norm range and boundedness of its increment-quotient range. The theorem makes the finiteness requirements explicit. It is the entry criterion for descending a periodic Euclidean field into the bundled quotient half-Hölder space.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_iff.summary: Order zero means continuity and two finite bounds

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_of_con.text: A continuously differentiable periodic lift belongs to the spatial half-Hölder domain.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_of_con.summary: A differentiable periodic field has zeroth Hölder regularity

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_of_hal.text: Pulling back a bundled half-Hölder torus field gives order-zero half-Hölder regularity on Euclidean space and lift norm at most twice the bundled norm. The factor two comes from adding the separate supremum and seminorm contributions. This is a norm comparison, not equality or an isometric identification of the two spaces.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_of_hal.summary: A quotient Hölder field has a controlled lift norm

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_of_uni.text: If $f$ is differentiable everywhere and its value and Fréchet derivative have uniform bounds $A$ and $B$, then $f$ has spatial half Hölder regularity and norm at most $3A+B$. Small displacements use the derivative estimate; large displacements use the value estimate. The hypotheses themselves imply $A,B\ge0$, and zero displacement is handled separately.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_of_uni.summary: Supremum and gradient bounds imply half Hölder control

TorusEuler.spatialSupNorm.text: Define the real supremum of the pointwise norm over all Euclidean labels. It acts as the intended uniform norm only when the range is bounded above; the definition itself imposes no boundedness. This is a real-valued supremum, not an extended-real one; unbounded norm ranges take the assigned default value zero. Only bounded-above ranges support the intended pointwise norm comparison.

TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift.text: This bounded real linear map takes a bounded operator on three-vectors to its pointwise action on $L^2$ time paths over $(0,T]$. The result is an operator on equivalence classes of paths. Its almost-everywhere evaluation lemma supplies the precise connection with the informal pointwise description.
TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift.summary: A spatial operator acts at every time along a path

TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift_apply_ae.text: The path obtained by applying the lifted operator agrees almost everywhere with $t\mapsto A(v(t))$. Equality is deliberately almost everywhere because $L^2$ paths are equivalence classes. This evaluation identity is used to prove symmetry, idempotence, and commutation with time integration.
TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift_apply_ae.summary: The lifted spatial action is pointwise almost everywhere

TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift_commutes_endp.text: Any fixed bounded spatial operator, lifted to time paths, commutes with the mean-subtraction map. The identity follows because the operator preserves constant paths and commutes with integration. There is no positivity hypothesis on $T$ in this algebraic statement; orthogonality of mean subtraction is established separately.
TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift_commutes_endp.summary: Spatial action commutes with subtracting the time average

TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift_isSymmetricPr.text: If the spatial operator is a symmetric projection, its lifted action is a symmetric projection on the real $L^2$ path space. Idempotence holds almost everywhere and symmetry is integrated through the path inner product. No positive-duration assumption is needed for this lifting statement.
TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift_isSymmetricPr.summary: A symmetric spatial projection remains one on paths

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_centeredLab.text: The coordinatewise centered-label representative is unchanged when an integer lattice vector is added. This follows from periodicity of the fractional-part operation. The result is a statement about values only: the representative jumps at cell boundaries, so it is not by itself a smooth map.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_centeredLab.summary: The centered representative is invariant under lattice translation

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_closedSlab_.text: Smooth periodic slices of velocity and pressure give a periodic momentum residual at each slab time, with velocity periodicity assumed over the full time interval to handle the time derivative.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_closedSlab_.summary: The momentum residual remains spatially periodic

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_curl.text: The curl of a spatially periodic vector function is also spatially periodic. The statement itself has no differentiability assumption because Lean’s total derivative respects translation identities even outside the differentiable case. Classical smoothness and the divergence-of-curl identity are established separately before physical applications.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_curl.summary: Curl respects the periodic translation identity

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_dyadicPerio.text: The double dyadic and lattice kernel expression is spatially periodic by reindexing the lattice translates. No separate convergence argument is part of this theorem. Its analytic use together with smoothness requires the later off origin summable-majorant estimates.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_dyadicPerio.summary: The full kernel respects the unit periods

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_endpointFin.text: The real pressure formed from the finite Fourier sum is spatially periodic for every frequency set and coefficient family. Its argument passes through the unit torus, so integer lattice translations do not change the value. This is a periodicity assertion independent of whether its gradient reconstructs a chosen vector field.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_endpointFin.summary: Finite Fourier pressures have the prescribed periods

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_endpointPar.text: If a field is invariant under integer lattice shifts, its reflection average has the same periodicity for any real sign. Reflection sends a lattice shift to the opposite shift, which is still available in the periodicity hypothesis. This result does not require the sign to be a genuine parity value.

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_firstWaveLo.text: The constructed first-wave velocity is periodic for every real choice of its scalar parameters and every time. Centered periodization gives periodicity of the potential, and the inverse shear map respects lattice translations. This algebraic periodicity statement is weaker than the separate smoothness theorem and does not require its collar hypotheses.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_firstWaveLo.summary: The completed first velocity is spatially periodic

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_firstWaveSm.text: For every shear ratio $s$, amplitude scale $c$, and time $t$, the vector seed is spatially periodic. Its label dependence enters through the periodic sweep. The result concerns the unlocalized seed; localization and the twisted periodization used for the physical oscillation are separate constructions.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_firstWaveSm.summary: The explicit seed is periodic in its label

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_fourierMode.text: For every integer frequency, the lifted Fourier mode is invariant under translation by an integer lattice vector. The proof uses equality in the torus quotient. This connects the library character with the periodicity predicate used throughout the Euler formalization on Euclidean space.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_fourierMode.summary: Integer Fourier characters are spatially periodic

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_halfHolderP.text: For any input function and any bounded torus operator, the projected lift is spatially periodic. On its admissible branch it is evaluation through the torus quotient; otherwise the definition returns zero. This unconditional periodicity theorem therefore does not certify that the input had a valid half-Hölder descent or that the output is its mathematical projection.

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_liftConvolu.text: If the input field is invariant under all lattice translations, its convolution has the same periodicity for any kernel. The proof compares the integrands pointwise after a lattice shift. No convergence assumption is needed for this identity of total integral expressions; the analytic existence of convolution is established separately.

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_lift_realVe.text: The real vector Fourier cutoff, composed with the quotient map, is a spatially periodic field. Periodicity follows from being a function on the torus, regardless of approximation estimates.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_lift_realVe.summary: The truncated torus field lifts periodically

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_lift_smooth.text: The Fourier cutoff composed with the quotient map is invariant under integer lattice translations. This periodicity holds for arbitrary symbol, scale, and input because the output is defined on the quotient torus. Separate hypotheses establish norm estimates or agreement with a prescribed smooth multiplier.

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_localizedTr.text: Fix a time and suppose $A(x+n)=A(x)+n$ for all $n\in\mathbb Z^3$. For arbitrary $k_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and any profile $f$, the formal statement proves spatial periodicity of the field obtained by evaluating $f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ in the centered cell, extending it periodically and composing with $A$. The result needs no smoothness, transversality or support assumptions and applies to arbitrary values of the profile. It is the periodicity part of the construction in §3.1. Vanishing near the boundary is still needed for smoothness; integer coordinates of $k_*$ are unnecessary for this extended field.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_localizedTr.summary: Integer-translation equivariance of the inverse map suffices

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_modOne_line.text: For an arbitrary $k_*\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal theorem proves that the circle-valued phase $a\mapsto k_*\cdot a\pmod1$ is invariant under every integer translation exactly when $k_*\in\mathbb Z^3$. The phase takes values in $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, rather than being a real-valued periodic function. This is the precise lattice restriction discussed in §3.1. It is a statement about the phase itself; a particular scalar profile could have additional symmetries. The localized construction avoids requiring a global periodic linear phase by cutting the field off inside one label cell and extending that field periodically.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_modOne_line.summary: A phase modulo one is periodic exactly at lattice frequencies

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_operatorLif.text: A spatially periodic input field remains periodic after convolution with any operator-valued kernel. The identity follows from periodicity of the integrand under lattice translation of the output point. It is valid as an equality of total integral expressions; convergence and norm estimates are separate assertions.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_operatorLif.summary: Operator convolution preserves the lattice period

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_periodicLer.text: Specializes the unconditional periodicity property of the general projection lift to the spatial Leray operator. It remains true for inadmissible inputs because the underlying definition then returns zero. The theorem should be read as a property of the total extension; meaningful projection and regularity claims require the hypotheses supplied by the neighbouring estimates.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_periodicLer.summary: The Leray lift is periodic for every input

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_periodizeCe.text: Extending a function by evaluating it at the centered representative produces a spatially periodic function. This statement alone does not assert continuity at cell walls.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_periodizeCe.summary: The centered extension is spatially periodic

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_stationaryS.text: The stationary shear is spatially periodic for every real parameter. Translating the second coordinate by an integer changes its sine phase by an integer multiple of $2\pi$, leaving the velocity unchanged. This verifies the periodicity requirement for the initial parent on the torus.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_stationaryS.summary: The sinusoidal shear is periodic under integer translations

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_transported.text: Affine lattice equivariance of the inverse-label map and the corresponding joint label-phase shift law for the profile imply spatial periodicity after graph evaluation. This statement works for any target type and needs no smoothness or integrality of the carrier vector. Compatibility of the profile absorbs the carrier’s phase shift.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_transported.summary: A compatible phase twist produces a periodic physical field

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_truncatedPa.text: Shows that the slice pressure is invariant under every integer spatial translation, for every radius and input. Each Fourier mode is periodic, so the finite synthesis has the same property. This supplies the periodicity needed to package the potential for the Leray and pressure-recovery arguments.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_truncatedPa.summary: The finite pressure respects lattice translations

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_tsum_lattic.text: The double sum over dyadic grades and all integer translations is spatially periodic for any family $K$. Translating the observation point simply reindexes the lattice by a bijection. This identity holds for the infinite sum as defined in the formalization, which takes the value zero on non-summable families, so no summability premise is needed; later estimates are needed to interpret it as a convergent kernel.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_tsum_lattic.summary: Summing all lattice translates gives a periodic expression

TorusEuler.stage_spatial_jets_of_joint_s.text: A jointly smooth velocity on a nondegenerate closed time slab has smooth spatial slices and jointly continuous spatial derivatives of every order, including at the time endpoints. The proof restricts the joint within derivative to spatial directions. This supplies the continuity assumptions required before passing stage jets to a uniform limit.
TorusEuler.stage_spatial_jets_of_joint_s.summary: Closed slab smoothness controls all spatial jets

TorusEuler.stationaryInductiveEulerStage.text: Builds the full stage-zero record using the sine shear tilted by the scheduled gain ratio, zero pressure and the explicit two-time shear flow. It assumes that the ratio has absolute value at most one and that the initial frequency is at least $1+4\pi$. These hypotheses justify the velocity, Fourier, deformation and residual bounds.
TorusEuler.stationaryInductiveEulerStage.summary: The scheduled stationary shear supplies the zero stage

TorusEuler.stationaryInductiveEulerStage.text: Computes the velocity field of the constructed zero stage as the explicit stationary shear with the scheduled ratio. The equality holds pointwise for every real time and spatial point because that stage is time independent. The same parameter hypotheses required by the constructor remain arguments of this identity.
TorusEuler.stationaryInductiveEulerStage.summary: The base-stage velocity is the prescribed tilted shear

TorusEuler.stationaryShear.text: The formal velocity is $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$ for a real parameter $\rho$. Its values lie in the plane spanned by $e_1,e_3$ and depend only on the transverse coordinate $x_2$. This formula defines a field on all of $\mathbb R^3$ that is invariant under integer translations and odd under $x\mapsto-x$. It is the initial shear of §1.1 and (6.1). The definition permits any real tilt, whereas the amplification construction chooses $\rho>0$ small. The assertion that this field solves Euler with zero pressure is supplied separately.
TorusEuler.stationaryShear.summary: A one-dimensional sine shear initializes the construction

TorusEuler.stationaryShearComplexTorus.text: This torus field is the finite Fourier sum over the positive and negative second-coordinate unit frequencies with the prescribed sine coefficients. It is a complex Euclidean-valued representation of the stationary parent. The lift theorem proves that its values are exactly the complexification of the real sinusoidal shear.
TorusEuler.stationaryShearComplexTorus.summary: Synthesizing the stationary parent from its two Fourier modes

TorusEuler.stationaryShearComplexTorus_l.text: The complex torus field evaluated on a Euclidean label equals coordinatewise complexification of the stationary sinusoidal shear at that label. The proof expands both distinct frequencies and uses the sine identity. Thus later Fourier support statements refer to the actual parent velocity, not an unrelated model field.
TorusEuler.stationaryShearComplexTorus_l.summary: The two mode field is the actual stationary shear

TorusEuler.stationaryShearDeformation_in.text: Let $G$ be the stationary shear gradient $v\mapsto2\pi v_2(e_1+se_3)$. For every real $s$ and $c$, the maps $I+cG$ and $I-cG$ are two-sided inverses: $(I+cG)(I-cG)=I$ and $(I-cG)(I+cG)=I$. This uses $G^2=0$ and needs no smallness of $c$ or $s$.
TorusEuler.stationaryShearDeformation_in.summary: The shear deformation inverse reverses its nilpotent correction

TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow.text: For $U_0(a)=\sin(2\pi a_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$, the formal flow formula is $X_0(t,a)=a+tU_0(a)$, for all real $t$ and $\rho$. The second coordinate remains $a_2$, so $U_0(X_0(t,a))=U_0(a)$ and the formula describes trajectories of the stationary shear. Its displacement is periodic under integer translations of the label $a$. This is the explicit flow used in the first-wave construction. The displayed definition gives particle positions; its inverse, derivatives and volume-preserving properties are proved separately and should not be read as additional conclusions of the formula itself.
TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow.summary: Particles keep their second coordinate while moving along the shear

TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_inverse.text: Let $X_t(a)=a+t\,\sin(2\pi a_2)(e_1+se_3)$ be the explicit stationary shear flow. For all real $s,t$ and labels $a$, $X_{-t}(X_t(a))=a$. The velocity is constant along each trajectory, so the two displacements cancel exactly, with no restriction on the size of $t$.
TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_inverse.summary: Reversing time inverts the shear flow

TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_jacobian_.text: Let $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$ with $|\rho|\le1$, and let $X_0(t,a)=a+tU_0(a)$. For every $t\in[0,1]$ and label $a\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal statement bounds both $\|D_aX_0(t,a)\|$ and $\|D_xX_0(-t,X_0(t,a))\|$ by $1+4\pi$. These are Euclidean operator norms. The second derivative is evaluated at the transported point and is the inverse of the first. Thus the result supplies the deformation and inverse-deformation bounds for the base interval $S_0=1$. It permits a larger tilt range than the construction's positive $\rho$.
TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_jacobian_.summary: The flow derivative and its inverse have a common bound

TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_jacobians.text: For any real $\rho,t$ and label $a\in\mathbb R^3$, take $X_0(t,a)=a+t\sin(2\pi a_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$ and $B_\rho=2\pi(e_1+\rho e_3)\otimes e_2$. The formal theorem proves $D_aX_0(t,a)=I+t\cos(2\pi a_2)B_\rho$ and $D_xX_0(-t,X_0(t,a))=I-t\cos(2\pi a_2)B_\rho$. The inverse derivative is taken at the image of the original label, not at an unrelated point. These are the deformation formulas in (6.2); the flow itself is a separate definition. No small-time or tilt restriction is needed, because $B_\rho^2=0$.
TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_jacobians.summary: Computes both derivatives at corresponding particle positions

TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_jacobians.text: The spatial derivative of the forward shear flow and the derivative of its inverse evaluated at the corresponding particle are two-sided inverse operators. The proof inserts their explicit identity-plus-or-minus-nilpotent formulas. This is a statement about the actual Jacobians, not arbitrary matrices chosen to satisfy inverse identities.
TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_jacobians.summary: The actual forward and inverse shear Jacobians cancel

TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_lattice_e.text: Translating a starting label by an integer lattice vector translates its evolved position by the same vector. The stationary shear velocity is periodic, so the velocity increment is unchanged. This verifies that the explicit lifted flow descends to the torus while retaining its concrete Euclidean formula.
TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_lattice_e.summary: The shear flow respects integer lattice translates

TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_origin.text: For the shear flow $X_0(t,a)=a+t\sin(2\pi a_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$, the formal statement proves $X_0(t,0)=0$ for every pair of real numbers $\rho,t$. This is an exact identity for the flow lifted to $\mathbb R^3$, and therefore also fixes the origin of $\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$. It follows from the zero value of the sine at the origin. No smallness, positivity or frequency condition is required. The assertion concerns this explicit stationary shear, not every particle of the flow or every later velocity in the induction.
TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_origin.summary: The shear flow fixes the origin for every time

TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_second.text: For every real $\rho,t$ and label $a\in\mathbb R^3$, let $X_0(t,a)=a+t\sin(2\pi a_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$. The formal theorem states $(X_0(t,a))_2=a_2$. It is an equality for the lifted trajectories in Euclidean space, so it is stronger than equality only modulo integers on the torus. The formal coordinates are numbered starting at zero; its coordinate numbered one is the paper's second coordinate.
