This is the quotient map identifying lattice translates, not a choice of a representative. No inverse is claimed; surjectivity and the exact lattice equivalence are proved separately.
TorusEuler.toUnitTorus.summary: Passing from a periodic lift to the unit torus

TorusEuler.toUnitTorus_add.text: The quotient map from $\mathbb R^3$ to the product of three unit circles sends a vector sum to the sum of the corresponding labels. This identity translates Euclidean increments into torus translations. It supports directional difference quotients of periodic lifts without choosing a fundamental-domain representative for each point.
TorusEuler.toUnitTorus_add.summary: The quotient map to the torus is additive

TorusEuler.toUnitTorus_eq_iff.text: Two lifted positions have the same torus image exactly when their difference is an integer lattice vector. This identifies the quotient relation used by periodic functions.
TorusEuler.toUnitTorus_eq_iff.summary: Equal torus points differ by an integer translation

TorusEuler.toUnitTorus_surjective.text: The quotient map from Euclidean space onto the unit torus is surjective. This permits pointwise statements on torus fields to be checked on their lifts.
TorusEuler.toUnitTorus_surjective.summary: Every torus point has a Euclidean representative

TorusEuler.toUnitTorus_zero.text: The Euclidean zero vector maps to zero in the unit torus. This normalization is used when comparing directional derivatives at zero line parameter.

TorusEuler.torusEuclideanDistance.text: Defines a geodesic Euclidean distance on the three-torus by taking the square root of the sum of the three squared circle distances. This auxiliary distance matches the length of a shortest Euclidean lift. It is distinguished from the default product distance used by the formal half-Hölder space, and comparison lemmas connect the two.
TorusEuler.torusEuclideanDistance.summary: Euclidean distance from coordinate circle distances

TorusEuler.torusEuclideanDistance_le_lif.text: For arbitrary Euclidean representatives $x,a$, the torus Euclidean distance between their images is at most $\|x-a\|$. Each circle distance is bounded by the corresponding real-coordinate separation. This transfers vanishing of a torus source on a Euclidean torus ball to vanishing of its periodic lift on an ordinary Euclidean ball.
TorusEuler.torusEuclideanDistance_le_lif.summary: Every lift bounds torus Euclidean distance

TorusEuler.torusEuclideanDistance_le_two.text: Bounds the auxiliary Euclidean torus distance by twice the default product distance. The proof bounds all three squared coordinate distances by the squared product distance and uses $3\le4$. The convenient factor two converts the off-support estimate to the chosen Hölder metric; it is a sufficient comparison constant, not an optimality assertion.
TorusEuler.torusEuclideanDistance_le_two.summary: Euclidean distance is bounded by twice product distance

TorusEuler.torusHalfHolderDerivativeOper.text: Extends a bounded operator $P$ on vector-valued half-Hölder fields to fields valued in continuous linear maps. It evaluates the derivative in each coordinate direction, applies $P$, then reconstructs the linear map using coordinate functionals. This is a finite linear construction. Commutation with differentiation is a separate property of $P$, not a consequence of this definition.

Identifies the bundled continuous linear operator on derivative fields with the earlier pointwise construction that applies $P$ to each coordinate column and reassembles the linear map. The result holds for every bounded $P$ and every half-Hölder linear-map field $H$. It is an equality of constructions, with no assumption that $H$ actually differentiates another field.

TorusEuler.torusHalfHolderDirection.text: Applies a fixed vector $v$ to each continuous linear map in a half-Hölder operator field, producing a half-Hölder vector field. This packages a candidate directional derivative while preserving the quotient-space representation. The definition itself does not establish that the operator field is the derivative of any function.
TorusEuler.torusHalfHolderDirection.summary: Evaluating a derivative field in one direction

TorusEuler.torusHalfHolderProjectedDeriv.text: Forms an operator-valued half-Hölder field by applying $P$ to each coordinate column of $H$ and reconstructing the linear map with coordinate projections. The construction uses the three standard Euclidean directions. It is meaningful for any continuous linear operator $P$ on fields; no commutation with differentiation is built into the definition.
TorusEuler.torusHalfHolderProjectedDeriv.summary: Applying a spatial operator to derivative columns

TorusEuler.torusIntegral_eq_centeredCell.text: The standard torus probability integral is the lift's integral over the centered unit cube.
TorusEuler.torusIntegral_eq_centeredCell.summary: The torus integral equals the fundamental-cube integral

TorusEuler.torusLInf.text: The formal quantity is the essential supremum of $|f(x)|$ over $[-1/2,1/2]^3$ with respect to Lebesgue measure, taking values in $[0,\infty]$. For a continuous periodic field it equals the ordinary spatial supremum. Vector values use the Euclidean norm; when $f=D_xu$, the pointwise norm is the induced operator norm. Theorem 1.1 integrates these nonnegative extended-valued quantities over $[0,T_*)$, allowing the result to be infinity. The definition itself neither imposes periodicity nor asserts finiteness or divergence. Integrating over the closed cube does not duplicate boundary mass because its faces have measure zero.
TorusEuler.torusLInf.summary: The norm may take the value positive infinity

TorusEuler.torusLInf_curl_le.text: For a spatial field $v$, the formal inequality is $\|\operatorname{curl}v\|_\infty\le C\|\nabla v\|_\infty$, with $C$ the operator norm of the fixed linear map taking a derivative matrix to its coordinate curl. Both spatial norms are essential suprema over $[-1/2,1/2]^3$, and the gradient is measured in operator norm. No Euler equation, periodicity or separate differentiability assumption occurs in the formal inequality. In its application to Corollary 8.3, $v=u(t)$ is smooth and periodic, so these expressions are the usual torus norms of the genuine derivatives. The constant is independent of $v$ and time, allowing integration to transfer divergence from vorticity to gradient. At a spatial point without a derivative, the derivative expression is assigned zero; this convention does not assert differentiability.
TorusEuler.torusLInf_curl_le.summary: A fixed linear map controls the essential supremum of vorticity

TorusEuler.torusLInf_stationaryShear_le_.text: If $|s|\le1$, the torus essential-supremum norm of the stationary shear is at most two, as a value in $[0,\infty]$. The bound follows from the pointwise velocity estimate. No representative or exceptional null set is needed because the estimate already holds everywhere.
TorusEuler.torusLInf_stationaryShear_le_.summary: The parent velocity has essential supremum at most two

TorusEuler.torusLiftConvolution.text: For integrable scalar kernel $K$ and continuous torus field $g$, define the continuous field obtained by integrating $K(y)g(z-[y])$. Compactness bounds $g$, and the $L^1$ kernel provides an integrable dominating function. The complete complex target ensures the vector-valued integral has its usual value.
TorusEuler.torusLiftConvolution.summary: Convolve a torus field using a Euclidean kernel

TorusEuler.torusLiftConvolution_toUnitTo.text: Evaluating the torus convolution at the image of $x$ equals the Euclidean lift convolution applied to $z\mapsto g([z])$ at $x$. The equality follows from the quotient subtraction identity. It connects the torus operator to the real-space kernel estimates without changing the actual integrand.
TorusEuler.torusLiftConvolution_toUnitTo.summary: Torus convolution agrees with convolution of the periodic lift

TorusEuler.trace_deriv_comp_inverse_eq_z.text: Let $F$ be a field of linear maps of $\mathbb R^3$ with derivative $DF$ at $a$, let $G$ satisfy $G\,F(a)=I$, and suppose $\det F(b)=1$ for all $b$ near $a$. Then for every direction $w$, $\operatorname{tr}\bigl(DF(w)\,G\bigr)=0$. This is the derivative of the constant determinant along the line $a+sw$ at $s=0$.
TorusEuler.trace_deriv_comp_inverse_eq_z.summary: A locally unit determinant gives zero trace of the variation

TorusEuler.trace_endpointPhysicalMean_eq.text: This is pointwise at a label $a$: $X$ is twice differentiable, $v$ differentiable, $\det D_aX=1$ in a neighbourhood and $G(D_aX)=I$. If $X$ preserves volume, $v$ is divergence free in label coordinates and $B=D_aXv$, then $\mathbf d\cdot B=0$. The statement assumes the necessary spatial derivatives and inverse deformation. This identifies the divergence condition in the endpoint formulation with the mean equation (5.11), using the volume-preserving change of variables.
TorusEuler.trace_endpointPhysicalMean_eq.summary: Volume preservation carries divergence freedom to physical coordinates

TorusEuler.trace_piola_coframe.text: Assume $F$ has a symmetric spatial derivative, determinant one near $a$, and a left inverse $G$ at $a$. The trace of the derivative of $Fv$, composed with $G$, equals the divergence of $v$. The extra derivative of $F$ has zero trace by the determinant identity, while cyclicity of trace cancels the inverse in the remaining term.
TorusEuler.trace_piola_coframe.summary: A volume preserving coframe preserves divergence

TorusEuler.trace_piola_coframe_of_contDi.text: For a twice differentiable spatial map $X$, determinant one in a neighborhood and a left inverse of its derivative give the coframe divergence identity for a differentiable field $v$. Second derivative symmetry is obtained from the twice-differentiability of $X$, rather than assumed separately. The result is pointwise at the label $a$ and does not assert global invertibility of $X$.
TorusEuler.trace_piola_coframe_of_contDi.summary: The flow deformation gives the divergence identity

TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_joint_contDi.text: In finite-dimensional parameter and state spaces, a jointly continuous family solving a smooth vector-field ODE with a smooth initial map is jointly smooth on a positive closed slab. The proof bootstraps using the spatial variational equation and the combined time-parameter derivative. It is a regularity theorem for an existing family, not a global existence result.
TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_joint_contDi.summary: A continuous smooth-flow family is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_spatialDeriv.text: For a finite-dimensional trajectory family of a smooth time-dependent ODE, assume joint continuity of the family in time and initial point, that each trajectory solves the ODE within $[0,T]$, and smooth dependence of the initial values on the initial point. Every time slice is then spatially differentiable; its derivative is jointly continuous and solves the first variational equation within $[0,T]$. The theorem derives regularity of an existing family rather than constructing trajectories.
TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_spatialDeriv.summary: A trajectory family has a continuous variational derivative

TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_spatialJets.text: Under smooth finite-dimensional ODE data, joint continuity of the trajectory family, and smooth initial values, the spatial derivative of any order $n$ exists continuously across the slab. Both the trajectory derivative and the differentiated right-hand side are jointly continuous. The time derivative of the former is exactly the latter, expressed as a within-interval derivative.
TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_spatialJets.summary: Every spatial derivative satisfies its differentiated ODE

TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyMean_freq.text: For a phase-independent mean $\bar f$ transported through a smooth inverse chart $A(t,\cdot)$, only the explicit parent-parameter power in its jet bound grows; the input frequency exponent $\alpha$ is unchanged. Assume positive frequency $\lambda>0$, $\ell>0$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, $L\ge1$, $C\ge0$ and $\ell^{-1}\le\mathsf D^e$ for a natural number $e$; the actual coframe $B$ is smooth with $B(A(t,x))=D_xA(t,x)$ and weighted derivatives $\ell^j\|D^jB(x)\|\le L\mathsf D$ for $j\le n$; and the scaled mean jets, the derivatives of order at most $n$ of $(a,s)\mapsto\bar f(\ell a)$, are bounded by $C\mathsf D^p\lambda^\alpha$. Then the derivatives of order at most $n$ of $\bar f\circ A(t,\cdot)$ are bounded by $(3\cdot2^nL)^nC\mathsf D^{(e+1)n+p}\lambda^\alpha$. There is no carrier-size or phase-width assumption.
TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyMean_freq.summary: A transported phase-independent mean keeps its frequency exponent

TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyMean_jetB.text: A phase-independent mean composed with the inverse labels satisfies the chain-rule estimate with no carrier term. Assume $\ell>0$, $C\ge0$, $M\ge0$ and a number $Q\ge1$ bounding the label cost alone, $\ell^{-1}C\le Q$; $A(t,\cdot)$ smooth, with coframe $B$ smooth and $B(A(t,x))=D_xA(t,x)$; weighted coframe jets $\ell^j\|D^jB(a)\|\le C$ for $j\le n$; and scaled jets of the mean, the derivatives of order at most $n$ of $(a,s)\mapsto\bar f(\ell a)$, bounded by $M$, with $\bar f$ smooth. Then the derivatives of order at most $n$ of $x\mapsto\bar f(A(t,x))$ are bounded by $(3\cdot2^n)^nQ^nM$. This is the general transported-profile estimate specialized to zero carrier and unit amplitude.
TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyMean_jetB.summary: A phase-independent field pays only the label cost under transport

TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyProfile_f.text: Let $\ell>0$, $h>0$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, $\lambda\ge1$, $L\ge1$, $C\ge0$, $\gamma\ge0$, real $\alpha$, nonnegative integers $e,p,n$, $\ell^{-1}\le\mathsf D^e$, $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$ and $|k|\le\mathsf D\lambda$. Assume $A(t,\cdot)$ is smooth, $B$ is a smooth field of linear maps with $B(A(t,x))=D_xA(t,x)$ and $\ell^j\|D^jB(x)\|\le L\mathsf D$ for $j\le n$, $(a,s)\mapsto f(t,a,s)$ is smooth, and every derivative of order at most $n$ of $(a,s)\mapsto f(t,\ell a,hs)$ is bounded by $\gamma C\mathsf D^p\lambda^\alpha$. Then every derivative of order at most $n$ of $x\mapsto f(t,A(t,x),k\cdot A(t,x))$ is bounded by $(3\cdot2^n\cdot2L)^nC\mathsf D^{(\max(e,1)+1)n+p}\gamma\lambda^{3n/2+\alpha}$.
TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyProfile_f.summary: Each physical derivative of the transported profile costs $\lambda^{3/2}$

TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyProfile_j.text: Given a smooth inverse-label map $A(t,\cdot)$, its actual coframe field $B$ (smooth, with $B(A(t,x))=D_xA(t,x)$), weighted coframe jets $\ell^j\|D^jB(a)\|\le C$ for $j\le n$, and scaled profile jets, the derivatives of order at most $n$ of $(a,s)\mapsto f(t,\ell a,hs)$, bounded by $\gamma M$, the graph evaluation $x\mapsto f(t,A(t,x),k\cdot A(t,x))$ has all derivatives of order at most $n$ bounded by $(3\cdot2^n)^nQ^n\gamma M$. Here $\ell,h>0$, $C,\gamma,M\ge0$, the profile is smooth, and the supplied number $Q\ge1$ bounds the combined label and phase cost, $(\ell^{-1}+h^{-1}|k|)C\le Q$. The order constant and $Q^n$ record repeated spatial differentiation.
TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyProfile_j.summary: A rescaled profile jet bound gives an Eulerian jet bound

TorusEuler.transportedProfile.text: Given maps $A(t,x)$, a fixed $k_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and a profile $f(t,a,s)$, the formal definition is $f^\natural(t,x)=f(t,A(t,x),k_*\cdot A(t,x))$. For the parent flow, $A(t,\cdot)=X(t,\cdot)^{-1}$, so it is exactly the evaluation convention of §3.1. The formula itself does not assume that $A$ is an inverse or solves a transport equation. It is defined on all arguments and imposes no regularity, spatial periodicity or label support. Those properties must be established before this evaluated expression is used as a smooth field on the torus.
TorusEuler.transportedProfile.summary: The inverse label map determines both label and phase

TorusEuler.transportedProfile_chainRule.text:
At $(t,x)$, assume the inverse label map and profile have their indicated joint derivatives, and that $A_t+D_xA\,U=0$. Let $a=A(t,x)$, $s=k_*\cdot a$ and $\kappa=(D_xA)^Tk_*$. The formal statement gives $D_xf^
atural=D_af\,D_xA+(\partial_sf)\kappa^T$ and $(\partial_t+U\cdot
abla_x)f^
atural=\partial_tf$, with the profile derivatives evaluated at $(t,a,s)$. These are (3.1). Time derivatives are taken within the given time set, which must determine a unique derivative at $t$; a nondegenerate closed interval includes the appropriate one-sided endpoints. Periodicity and nonvanishing of the wave vector are unnecessary for the chain rule.
TorusEuler.transportedProfile_chainRule.summary: Spatial differentiation sees the phase; material differentiation does not

TorusEuler.transportedProfile_neg_equiva.text: If the inverse-label map is odd and the profile transforms by a supplied map $R$ under simultaneous label and phase negation, its graph evaluation transforms by the same $R$ under spatial reflection. The result is algebraic and allows an arbitrary target type and transformation, beyond the later even and odd specializations.
TorusEuler.transportedProfile_neg_equiva.summary: Spatial reflection reflects both label and phase

TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_traject.text: At a fixed time, suppose $A(t,X(t,a))=a$. For any profile $f$ and any real wave vector $k_*$, the formal statement proves $f^\natural(t,X(t,a))=f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$, where $f^\natural(t,x)=f(t,A(t,x),k_*\cdot A(t,x))$. This is the evaluation convention used for the leading oscillation in §3.1. Only the inverse relation at the label in question is required; there is no derivative, trajectory equation, periodicity or nonzero-covector hypothesis. Constancy of the phase along the parent follows by applying this identity with the phase profile itself.
TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_traject.summary: The profile sees the initial label and its fixed phase

TorusEuler.transverseModeSpace.text: This complex subspace is the orthogonal complement of the complex line spanned by the real wave vector embedded in Euclidean coefficient space. At nonzero frequency it is the transverse plane. At zero frequency the span is zero and the transverse space is the whole coefficient space.
TorusEuler.transverseModeSpace.summary: Coefficients orthogonal to the frequency span

TorusEuler.transversePlane.text:
The real linear plane transverse to a wave vector.

At k=0 the kernel of the zero functional is the whole ambient space. The intended codimension-one transverse plane requires k≠0.

TorusEuler.transversePressureIdentity.text: At one time, the wave-vector and forced amplitude derivative equations, together with hperp, the zero derivative of their inner product, imply $\|\kappa\|^2p_s=\langle\kappa,f\rangle-2\langle\kappa,MV\rangle$. The theorem works in any complete real inner-product space. It neither divides by $\|\kappa\|^2$ nor requires a nonzero wave vector, so it does not by itself determine a unique pressure when $\kappa=0$.

TorusEuler.truncatedEulerLerayProjectedR.text: Inserts the proved periodic Leray estimate into the abstract time-uniform residual theorem. It obtains one nonnegative residual coefficient $C_r$ before choosing depth $P$, and a tail coefficient $C_t$ that may depend on $P$. The inputs require bounded time-indexed Hölder norm ranges. The output estimates the defined projected residual expression; its equality with the physical Euler residual is proved separately.
TorusEuler.truncatedEulerLerayProjectedR.summary: The actual Leray residual obeys the uniform truncation bound

TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.text:
The projected cutoff residual in (5.58) with the Euclidean momentum tensor and its divergence.

The tensor operations are fixed to the physical ones, but the projection remains an arbitrary function parameter. The actual residual identification chooses the periodic Leray projection and proves its domain conditions.
TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.summary: The projected residual with the physical momentum tensor

TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.text: Specializes the abstract residual bound to the actual Euclidean momentum tensor and its column divergence. A first-order bound for the chosen projection is still an explicit hypothesis. The result controls the second-order cutoff error and first-order residual expression with the common tail budget, while keeping the coefficient of the input residual independent of expansion depth.
TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.summary: The momentum residual has a uniform Hölder estimate

TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.text: For any nonempty index type, applies the slice estimates with one common set of constants and takes real suprema over the family. Boundedness of the input velocity and residual norm ranges is required explicitly. The index can represent time, but no temporal derivative or time continuity is assumed by this norm-aggregation theorem.
TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.summary: The residual estimates hold uniformly over an index family

TorusEuler.truncatedParentProjectedResid.text:
The right-hand side of (5.58), formed using the real velocity and tensor cutoffs.

The projection, tensor pairing and contraction are parameters. This expression is the physical residual only after their concrete identities and the smooth cutoff hypotheses are supplied; it is not a PDE assertion by definition.
TorusEuler.truncatedParentProjectedResid.summary: The residual after velocity and tensor truncation

TorusEuler.truncatedParentProjectedResid.text: Assuming a first-order Hölder bound $\|\mathcal Pf\|_{C^{1,1/2}}\le C\|f\|_{C^{1,1/2}}$ for the supplied projection $\mathcal P$ on periodic fields, a bilinear tensor product, a derivative contraction and compatible real-complex maps, obtains uniform bounds for the second-order velocity tail and first-order projected residual. The error is $\Lambda^{2-P}(1+\|V\|_{C^{P,1/2}})^2$ with $P\ge2$. The coefficient on the supplied residual is independent of $P$; this theorem estimates the defined expression, not its identification with a PDE residual.
TorusEuler.truncatedParentProjectedResid.summary: The abstract projected residual satisfies the truncation estimate

TorusEuler.truncatedParentSlicePressure.text: Takes the negative real Fourier pressure potential of the coefficients of a continuous torus vector field $A$, retaining the finite band of radius $r$. In the child construction $A$ represents advection. Smoothness and zero mean hold for every input, but the equation with the full divergence of $A$ requires the separate band hypothesis.
TorusEuler.truncatedParentSlicePressure.summary: The finite-band pressure potential of a continuous periodic field

TorusEuler.truncatedParentSlicePressure_.text: If the input torus field represents the advection of the stationary shear, its slice pressure is identically zero for every cutoff radius and shear parameter. The shear advects itself trivially, so the represented source and every Fourier coefficient vanish. This confirms the pressure normalization used by the explicit zero-stage construction.
TorusEuler.truncatedParentSlicePressure_.summary: The stationary shear has zero normalized pressure

TorusEuler.truncatedParent_residual_rate.text: If $C\ge0$ and the next frequency is at least $\max(2,(2C)^2)$, then $C\,\mathrm{next}^{-7/2}+\mathrm{next}^{-5}\le\mathrm{next}^{-3}$. The explicit threshold absorbs the fixed constant and allocates room for both error terms. This is a rate comparison, not an independent bound on any velocity or residual.
TorusEuler.truncatedParent_residual_rate.summary: Two residual terms fit below a third inverse power

TorusEuler.tsupport_radialEnvelope_subse.text: For the chosen radial envelope $g(a)=\chi(|a|/\ell_*)$ with $\ell_*>0$, the closure of the set where $g\ne0$ lies in $\{a:|a|\le2\ell_*\}$. This is a closed-support statement, so it includes possible boundary points where the function itself is zero. The theorem does not mention the periodic cell. To obtain the sentence in §5.1, also use $\ell_*\le\mathsf D^{-3}$ and $\mathsf D\ge2$, which give $2\ell_*\le1/4<1/2$; hence the support lies strictly inside the centered unit cell. The envelope acts in label space, before transport to physical space.
TorusEuler.tsupport_radialEnvelope_subse.summary: The closed support lies inside the ball of twice the radius

TorusEuler.uniformPhysicalEstimates_of_l.text: From a record of the later-wave primary costs, proves the uniform physical estimates: cutoffs chosen before the common frequency and order schedule, for the first and every later stage. It combines first and later seed estimates, recurrence bounds, pressure geometry, Fourier cutoff constants and residual estimates, then takes maxima and sums to choose common exponents and nonnegative costs. The first case uses zero switches; the later case uses the actual activation profile and its weighted switch bound.
TorusEuler.uniformPhysicalEstimates_of_l.summary: The first and later bounds share one common cost table

TorusEuler.uniqueDiffOn_hierarchyProfile.text: For T > 0, the closed time–label–phase slab satisfies the unique-differentiability condition used by within-set derivatives. The positivity excludes a slab reduced to a single time.
TorusEuler.uniqueDiffOn_hierarchyProfile.summary: The nondegenerate slab determines derivatives uniquely

TorusEuler.unitInverseFourthPowerTail.text: Defines the real constant obtained by integrating $|z|^{-4}$ over the complement of the open unit ball in three-dimensional Euclidean space. This records the finite tail mass used in all later off-support estimates without choosing a numerical spherical-coordinate evaluation. Scaling then gives the radius dependence $r^{-1}$.

TorusEuler.unitInverseFourthPowerTail_no.text: The unit inverse-fourth-power tail constant is nonnegative because its integrand is nonnegative on the integration set. This sign is subsequently needed when multiplying inequalities by the tail constant and replacing Euclidean torus distance by a larger multiple of the product distance. The statement claims neither strict positivity nor an exact numerical value.

TorusEuler.unitTorusMeasure.text:
Product Haar probability measure on the unit three-torus.

The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.unitTorusMeasure.summary: Probability Haar measure on the unit three-torus

TorusEuler.unitTorusMeasure_closedBall.text: For a nonnegative radius $r$, the Haar measure of the closed ball about any torus point is $(\min(1,2r))^3$, expressed as an extended nonnegative real number. The formula uses the product metric on three unit circles. It is not the Euclidean three-dimensional ball-volume formula, and this distinction matters when reading the interpolation constants.
TorusEuler.unitTorusMeasure_closedBall.summary: Small torus balls have an explicit volume

TorusEuler.unitTorus_sup_le_holderHalf_a.text: Let $v$ be a continuous normed-space-valued field on the unit torus and suppose $\|v(a)-v(b)\|\le H\sqrt{d(a,b)}$ with $H\ge0$. For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $\|v\|_\infty\le\varepsilon H+\varepsilon^{-3}(\int\|v\|^2)^{1/2}$. Measure is normalized to total mass one. This is the averaging inequality used in Lemma A.2; the exponent three reflects the spatial dimension. The paper writes a full half-Hölder norm and an unspecified constant, whereas this formal estimate uses the supplied seminorm bound and explicitly restricts the small parameter.
TorusEuler.unitTorus_sup_le_holderHalf_a.summary: Control the supremum by a small Hölder term and energy

TorusEuler.velocityPressureTensor.text: This continuous real bilinear map sends two vectors to the complex tensor with entry $u_i v_j$. Its norm is bounded by the product of the two Euclidean norms using coordinate estimates. On the diagonal it supplies the velocity tensor for pressure, while no symmetry is claimed for two different inputs.
TorusEuler.velocityPressureTensor.summary: Real velocities give a bounded bilinear complex tensor

TorusEuler.velocityPressureTensor_apply.text: The entry $(i,j)$ of the tensor made from two real vectors is the complex number $u_iv_j$. This definitional identity fixes the coordinate order used in double divergence and the pressure Poisson equation. It introduces no approximation or transpose convention.
TorusEuler.velocityPressureTensor_apply.summary: The velocity tensor has the expected coordinate product

TorusEuler.vorticityForm.text: For bounded operators $F,M$ on a real Hilbert space, define $\Omega=F^*(M^*-M)F$. In the three-dimensional application, the adjoints are transposes, $F=D_aX$ and $M=(\nabla u)\circ X$, so this is precisely (4.1). The sign is $M^T-M$, consistent with the paper's velocity-gradient convention. No invertibility, flow equation or Euler equation is assumed in this definition. The time evolution relation with $K=F^*F$ is established separately using $F_t=MF$.
TorusEuler.vorticityForm.summary: Pull back the skew part of a velocity gradient

TorusEuler.waveBump.text: The formal construction fixes $\psi(s)$ by applying a smooth transition function to $1-64s^2$. The resulting even smooth function satisfies $0\le\psi\le1$, $\psi(0)=1$, and vanishes for $|s|\ge1/8$, as proved in the same file. Its support therefore lies compactly inside $(-1/4,1/4)$, the interval allowed in the proof of Lemma 3.1. The linked definition specifies this particular bump; it does not quantify over all bumps satisfying the paper's assumptions. Subsequent estimates use its narrower support to obtain the explicit bounds $-h/2\le F_h'\le1$ and $|F_h|\le h/2$.
TorusEuler.waveBump.summary: A particular even bump is supported inside the paper’s allowed interval

TorusEuler.waveBump_zero.text: The bump has value one at phase zero because the smooth transition is evaluated at one. This is the normalization needed before subtracting its mean. Dividing the mean-free slope by its value at zero then makes the eventual wave profile derivative equal exactly one there.
TorusEuler.waveBump_zero.summary: The compact bump equals one at its center

TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal.text: If the phase derivative of $\langle\kappa,C\rangle$ equals $-g$ for a scalar function $g$ (the divergence term), if $g$ is continuous, and if that scalar component has zero phase mean, obtains $\langle\kappa,C(s)\rangle=-\mathcal Ig(s)$, where $\mathcal I$ is the normalized phase primitive. The theorem assumes the derivative identity; it does not derive it from commuting spatial operators or a curl construction. No nonvanishing condition on $\kappa$ is needed here.
TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal.summary: Recover the correction along the wave vector

TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal_o.text: Let $\kappa$ be independent of phase, let $C(s)$ and a scalar function $d(s)$ be continuous, and suppose $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C)=-d$ for every $s$, with $\int_0^1C=0$. The formal statement proves $\kappa\cdot C(s)=-\partial_s^{-1}d(s)$, where the primitive has zero phase mean. Substituting $d=\mathbf d\cdot V$ gives the second identity of (3.6). This theorem assumes the longitudinal derivative identity; it does not prove that $C$ was formed by a curl. Periodicity and nonvanishing of $\kappa$ are not needed for this integration step.
TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal_o.summary: Zero phase mean fixes the integration constant

TorusEuler.wavePotential.text: At fixed time and label, the formal definition is $Q[V]=-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V/|\kappa|^2)$, with the covector held fixed during phase integration. The primitive means the integral from zero with its average over $[0,1]$ subtracted. A continuous transverse $V$ and $\kappa\ne0$ give $\kappa\times\partial_sQ[V]=V$; period one and zero mean of $V$ make the potential periodic. These are separate hypotheses, not requirements of the definition. Division by zero is assigned zero, so the displayed formula gives $Q[V]=0$ at $\kappa=0$; it cannot then recover a nonzero oscillation by its fast curl.
TorusEuler.wavePotential.summary: The normalized phase primitive supplies the potential for a curl

TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource.text: For a linear map $M:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and vectors $\kappa,V,f$, define $\mathcal Q=[(M^T\kappa)\times V+\kappa\times MV-\kappa\times f]/|\kappa|^2-2(\kappa\times V)(\kappa\cdot M\kappa)/|\kappa|^4$. This is precisely the vector inside the phase primitive in (5.33). The expression is defined for arbitrary inputs and contains no time derivative of $M,f$ or any mean. At $\kappa=0$, reciprocals are assigned zero, hence $\mathcal Q=0$. This definition does not assert a time evolution equation. For a nonzero transported covector $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ and $V_t+MV+\kappa\mathsf p_s=f$, the separate differentiation statement gives $\partial_tQ[V]=\partial_s^{-1}\mathcal Q$, with the zero-mean phase primitive.
TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource.summary: Collect the terms inside the time-differentiated phase primitive

TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_eq_co.text: An algebraic identity splits the potential-time source into its amplitude coefficient applied to v and its vector-potential coefficient applied to the forcing. This does not itself differentiate a time-dependent solution.
TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_eq_co.summary: The potential time derivative separates amplitude and forcing

TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_frequ.text: Replacing the normalized covector $k$ by $\lambda k$ multiplies the time source of the wave potential by $\lambda^{-1}$, assuming positive frequency. Strain, velocity, and forcing remain fixed. This is an exact algebraic homogeneity identity, independent of time regularity and valid even for a zero normalized covector because division by zero is assigned the value zero.
TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_frequ.summary: The time source scales by inverse carrier frequency

TorusEuler.wavePotential_fast_curl.text: Let $\kappa\ne0$ and let $V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous with $\kappa\cdot V(s)=0$ for every phase. The formal statement proves $\kappa\times\partial_sQ[V](s)=V(s)$ for every real $s$, where $Q[V]=-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V/|\kappa|^2)$. Differentiating the normalized primitive removes its additive constant, and the vector triple product gives the result. This is the fast part of the curl in (3.5). The theorem does not require periodicity or zero phase mean; those ensure a periodic potential in the application. The nonzero-covector assumption excludes the default zero value of the quotient.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_fast_curl.summary: Transversality and a nonzero covector give an exact algebraic recovery

TorusEuler.wavePotential_firstWaveLeadin.text: For the selected first-wave amplitude $\mathbf a(t,a)$, transported wave vector $\kappa(t,a)$ and radial envelope $g(a)$, the formal theorem identifies the phase potential of $g(a)F_h(s)\mathbf a(t,a)$ with $g(a)P_h(s)(\mathbf a\times\kappa)/|\kappa|^2$, assuming $0<h\le1$. Here $P_h$ is the mean-zero periodic primitive of $F_h$, and $s$ is an independent phase variable. The statement concerns this particular first-wave construction; it does not quantify over arbitrary amplitudes and parent flows from §3.1. It allows zero frequency: at $\kappa=0$ the inverse squared norm is assigned zero, so the identity still holds algebraically but does not assert a nonzero wave or an inverse curl relation.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_firstWaveLeadin.summary: The phase primitive gives the explicit first-wave potential

TorusEuler.wavePotential_frequency_scale.text: The identity holds for every phase field and every vector, including zero, because the potential assigns zero to reciprocal powers at a zero wave vector. Rescaling the wave vector by a positive frequency rescales its vector potential by the inverse frequency. This separates the factor $\lambda^{-1}$ from the normalized coefficients $\kappa/\lambda$ and $\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2$ in the proof of Lemma 5.5. Product, derivative, and phase primitive estimates are then needed to bound the curl correction.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_frequency_scale.summary: Normalize the wave vector and extract the small factor

TorusEuler.wavePotential_neg_reflected.text: The normalized potential of the reversed, negated velocity is the reversed potential of the original velocity.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_neg_reflected.summary: Reflection of the normalized vector potential

TorusEuler.wavePotential_zero_of_profile.text: At a fixed time and label, suppose $V(s)=0$ for every real phase. The formal statement gives $Q[V](s)=0$ for every phase, for any covector $\kappa$, including zero. Phase integration and subtraction of a phase mean act only on that label's profile and cannot create a nonzero value elsewhere. This is the potential part of the support assertion following (3.6). The theorem does not itself address $C[V]$: vanishing of the spatial curl outside the support additionally uses locality of differentiation on an open set where the potential is zero.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_zero_of_profile.summary: Zero input at every phase gives zero potential at that label

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient.text: For a real scalar $c$, phase gradient $\kappa$, amplitude $\mathbf a$ and linear map $M$ on $\mathbb R^3$, the formal expression is $2c(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$. In the localized wave, $c=\widetilde\chi(t)g(a)$ is the product of the time cutoff and spatial envelope. At the central label $a=0$, the condition $g(0)=1$ gives $c=\widetilde\chi(t)$; it equals one only when the time cutoff equals one. The definition permits arbitrary real $c$ and imposes no evolution equation or sign condition. Division by zero is assigned zero, so the expression is zero at $\kappa=0$. For a nonzero phase gradient its sign depends on both $c$ and $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a$.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient.summary: A scalar cutoff multiplies the usual wave pressure coefficient

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_cente.text:
Let $\kappa,\mathbf a
e0$ in Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$, let $M$ be a linear map and $c\in\mathbb R$. Put $E_{1,+}=\kappa/|\kappa|$, $E_{2,+}=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$ and $
u_+=E_{1,+}\cdot ME_{2,+}$. The formal identity is $-[2c(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2]\,\kappa\otimes\kappa=-2c|\mathbf a||\kappa|
u_+\,E_{1,+}\otimes E_{1,+}$. It is the tensor form of the scalar pressure normalization used for the wave coupling. Nonzero vectors justify the normalizations, but perpendicularity and positive coupling are not assumed. Consequently the identity alone gives neither a sign nor an upper bound for the pressure Hessian.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_cente.summary: Normalizing the wave directions expresses the pressure tensor through the coupling

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_eq_ne.text: The positive coefficient used to write the leading pressure as $-cP_h$ equals minus the oscillatory pressure slope for zero source and cutoff-scaled amplitude. This is an exact algebraic identity for arbitrary inputs, including a zero covector under Lean’s totalized division. Nonnegativity and geometric use of the coefficient require additional hypotheses.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_eq_ne.summary: The leading pressure uses the opposite slope sign

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_first.text: When $\lambda\ne0$, substituting the transported covector, explicit seed, and stationary-shear gradient into the wave-pressure coefficient yields $c/\lambda$ times the normalized coefficient. The shear ratio cancels. Nonzero frequency is needed for the inverse-length calculation; the theorem does not extend its stated factorization by removing that hypothesis.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_first.summary: The first pressure separates scale and frequency

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_mul_n.text: Let $\kappa\ne0$, $0\le\theta\le1$, and $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge0$. For $c_{\mathbf a}=2\theta(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$, the formal statement proves $c_{\mathbf a}\ge0$ and $c_{\mathbf a}|\kappa|^2\le2|\kappa|\|M\||\mathbf a|$. In Lemma 5.9, $\theta=\widetilde\chi g$ and the localized positive coupling supplies the sign. Together with $F_h\,{}^{\prime}\ge-Ch$, this yields an upper bound for $-c_{\mathbf a}F_h\,{}^{\prime}\kappa\otimes\kappa$. The theorem itself is a pointwise coefficient estimate; it does not include the other Hessian tensors or assert an absolute bound for the leading pressure Hessian.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_mul_n.summary: Positive coupling makes the leading pressure coefficient nonnegative

TorusEuler.wavePressurePrimitive.text: For any real width parameter, the formal definition sets $P_h=\partial_s^{-1}F_h$: integrate $F_h$ from phase zero, then subtract the mean of that integral over $[0,1]$. For $0<h\le1$, the constructed $F_h$ is smooth, odd, periodic and of zero mean, so $P_h$ is a smooth periodic primitive with $\int_0^1P_h=0$. This is the scalar factor in the leading pressure (3.3). The normalization does not generally give $P_h(0)=0$. The definition is assigned values outside the admissible width range as well, but those values carry none of the stated profile guarantees.
TorusEuler.wavePressurePrimitive.summary: The scalar pressure profile is the normalized primitive of the velocity profile

TorusEuler.wavePressure_hessian_quadrati.text: If a total operator decomposes into four contributions, a one-sided quadratic bound for its leading part and operator norm bounds for the other three add to a one-sided bound for the total. Symmetry is not assumed or needed for this inequality. The theorem preserves the favorable sign of the leading pressure instead of replacing it by its norm.
TorusEuler.wavePressure_hessian_quadrati.summary: Combine one signed bound with three norm bounds

TorusEuler.wavePressure_hessian_upper_of.text: Combines a leading quadratic bound at order $N^{-1/4}$ with norm bounds for geometric, higher oscillatory and mean terms at orders $N^{-3/4}$, $N^{-5/12}$ and $N^{-5/2}$. Since $N\ge1$, all three faster decays are bounded by the quarter power. The nonnegative constants $b$, $c$ and $d$ of those three bounds justify these exponent comparisons.
TorusEuler.wavePressure_hessian_upper_of.summary: All pressure contributions fit the quarter power upper bound

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_center_le.text: A nonnegative pressure coefficient makes the quadratic form of $-c\,\kappa\otimes\kappa$ nonpositive in every direction. The proof reduces it to minus a nonnegative scalar times a square. This sign statement concerns only the leading rank-one contribution; the geometric remainder is bounded separately in operator norm.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_center_le.summary: The central rank one contribution is nonpositive

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian.text:
Let $0<h\le1$ and let $c,\phi:\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. For the constructed profile $F_h$ and primitive $P_h$, write $\kappa=
abla\phi$. The formal statement gives $
abla^2(-cP_h(\phi))=-cF_h'(\phi)\kappa\otimes\kappa-F_h(\phi)(
abla c\otimes\kappa+\kappa\otimes
abla c+c
abla^2\phi)-P_h(\phi)
abla^2c$. All terms are evaluated at the same spatial point. When $c$ is constant and $\phi$ is linear, only the rank-one term remains, recovering the affine pressure calculation in §1.2. The formal identity permits varying coefficients and curved phase, but uses the particular constructed family; it is not a statement for every smooth profile without further hypotheses.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian.summary: The Hessian separates the leading rank-one term from coefficient and phase derivatives

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian_c.text: If the transported phase vanishes at the origin, the leading pressure Hessian there is $-c(0)\kappa\otimes\kappa-P_h(0)D^2c(0)$. The mixed and phase-curvature terms vanish because $F_h(0)=0$, while the slope is one. The coefficient-Hessian term remains: a zero-mean primitive need not vanish at phase zero.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian_c.summary: The central Hessian retains a slow coefficient term

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u.text: For $0<h\le1$, $c\ge0$, any phase value $s$ and vectors $\kappa,v\in\mathbb R^3$, the formal statement proves $v\cdot[-cF_h'(s)\kappa\otimes\kappa]v\le(hc|\kappa|^2/2)|v|^2$ for the constructed profile. It uses the lower slope bound $F_h'\ge-h/2$. With $c=p_{\rm w}$ and linear phase $\kappa=k$, this yields (1.11) with the explicit factor $1/2$. It is an upper quadratic-form bound and permits a large negative eigenvalue. It controls the leading rank-one term only; if the coefficient or phase varies spatially, the additional Hessian terms require separate estimates.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u.summary: The profile’s lower slope bound controls the positive part of the pressure Hessian

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u.text: For $N\ge1$, cutoff in $[0,1]$, nonnegative coupling and a nonzero covector, the scale bounds on $\kappa$, strain and amplitude yield a quadratic upper bound $2D^3N^{-1/4}|v|^2$. The profile width is fixed to $N^{-1/2}$. This bounds the largest quadratic contribution, not the operator norm of a potentially large negative rank-one tensor.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u.summary: The signed leading Hessian has quarter power decay

TorusEuler.waveProfile.text: The formal definition is $F_h(s)=\int_0^s S_h(r)\,dr$, where $S_h$ is the periodized scaled bump after removing its phase mean and normalizing its value at zero. It fixes $F_h(0)=0$ for every real $h$. For $0<h\le1$, the slope is smooth, even and has zero integral over one period; the proved consequences are smoothness, oddness and period one of $F_h$. These hypotheses matter: the formula alone is defined for arbitrary widths and does not assert those regularity properties there. The construction realizes the family used in Lemma 3.1, rather than leaving the primitive's additive constant unspecified.
TorusEuler.waveProfile.summary: Integrating the normalized slope fixes the profile at phase zero

TorusEuler.waveProfile_zero.text: The profile defined by integrating its slope from zero has value zero at zero for every real scale. The equality uses the integral over a degenerate interval. It is the base-point condition that combines with oddness and unit central derivative in the localized wave construction.
TorusEuler.waveProfile_zero.summary: The primitive profile vanishes at phase zero

TorusEuler.waveSlope.text: Let $\psi$ be the chosen even bump and extend $\psi(s/h)$ with period one by reducing the phase to the centered unit cell. If $c_h$ denotes its phase mean, the formal definition is $S_h(s)=(\psi_{\mathrm{per},h}(s)-c_h)/(1-c_h)$. For $0<h\le1$, the proved bound $0\le c_h\le h/4$ makes the denominator positive; the slope is smooth, mean zero and equals one at zero. On $|s|\le1/2$ this is the formula in Lemma 3.1. The formula is also assigned values at other widths: division by zero then gives zero, and no profile conclusions are asserted without the admissible-width hypotheses.
TorusEuler.waveSlope.summary: Remove the bump mean and normalize the central value

TorusEuler.waveSwitch.text: The switch is the smooth transition evaluated at $r(t-t_0)$. The definition accepts arbitrary real $r$; activation after $t_0$ with duration $1/r$ requires the positive-rate hypotheses in later lemmas. This scalar factor multiplies the leading wave and its divergence correction without changing their spatial cancellation.

TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_of_activati.text: Let $r>0$ and let $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$, where the fixed smooth transition $\theta$ equals one for arguments at least one. If $t\ge t_0+1/r$, then $\widetilde\chi(t)=1$. Since $\tau=r(t-t_0)$, this is precisely the statement that the cutoff equals one for $\tau\ge1$. Positivity of $r$ is essential for this conversion of the time inequality. The theorem applies at the endpoint $t=t_0+1/r$ as well as afterward, and imposes no condition on the amplitude of the wave being switched on.
TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_of_activati.summary: The wave is fully present after one normalized time unit

TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_sub_envelop.text: Write $\theta$ for the fixed smooth transition and define the envelope profile by $\chi(s)=1-\theta(s-1)$. The formal theorem proves $\widetilde\chi(t)=1-\chi(1+r(t-t_0))$ for every real $t_0,r,t$, where $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$. Thus the paper's spatial-envelope profile also gives its time transition. This identity alone does not require $r>0$ and does not state the zero-before-activation branch. With $r\ge0$, the transition is zero for $t\le t_0$, giving that branch, including the activation time itself.
TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_sub_envelop.summary: Identifies the time transition with the fixed envelope profile

TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_zero_of_le.text: For any $r\ge0$ and real $t_0$, take $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$, where the fixed smooth transition is zero for nonpositive arguments. The formal theorem proves $\widetilde\chi(t)=0$ whenever $t\le t_0$. It therefore includes equality at the activation time, while the piecewise display in §6.2 explicitly gives the zero branch only for $t<t_0$. The result also allows $r=0$, in which case the cutoff is identically zero. It does not assert vanishing of every higher oscillatory profile; those profiles require their own initial conditions.
TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_zero_of_le.summary: The cutoff is zero up to and including activation

TorusEuler.waveSwitch_weighted_derivativ.text: There is a constant $C\ge0$, depending only on the fixed smooth transition, such that the following holds. Let $r>0$, $G\ge0$ and let $\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\gamma(t)|\le G$ on $[t_0,t_0+1/r]$. For $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$, the formal theorem gives $|\widetilde\chi'(t)\gamma(t)|\le CrG$ for every real $t$. No continuity or measurability of $\gamma$ is needed; outside that interval the derivative of the cutoff vanishes. Taking $\gamma=1$ and $G=1$ gives $|\widetilde\chi'|\le Cr$. Taking $G=e^{3-\varepsilon^{-1/2}}$ after the early-gain estimate gives the residual factor following (6.8).
TorusEuler.waveSwitch_weighted_derivativ.summary: Only the weight on the switching interval affects the bound

TorusEuler.weightedLabelWord_holderQuoti.text: Under the same positive-word and adjacent-jet assumptions, dividing the increment by $\sqrt{\operatorname{dist}(x,y)}$ gives the stated Hölder quotient bound. The hypothesis $x\ne y$ makes the denominator strictly positive. This theorem covers distinct labels; the jet-range proofs handle equal labels separately using the convention that division by zero gives zero.
TorusEuler.weightedLabelWord_holderQuoti.summary: Divide the increment estimate at distinct labels

TorusEuler.weighted_endpointIntegratedFo.text: For positive duration and radius, assume smooth coframe and force, bounded Hölder jet sets, and actual torus derivative words for their product whose negative primitives equal the source words. Each weighted source time norm is bounded by $T\sqrt2$ times the finite product estimate. The argument includes both integration duration and the Euclidean-to-torus Hölder comparison.
TorusEuler.weighted_endpointIntegratedFo.summary: The integrated source is bounded by the coframe product

TorusEuler.weighted_fixedTransverse_forw.text: The physical center growth estimate gives the fixed-coordinate estimate on the same slab. Reading and lifting coordinates cost the two deformation bounds, so a physical constant $D$ becomes $D^3$ when both are at most $D$.
TorusEuler.weighted_fixedTransverse_forw.summary: Fixed transverse coordinates cost two deformation bounds

TorusEuler.weighted_homogeneous_jetBound.text: On a nondegenerate interval $[l,r]$, consider a smooth homogeneous linear equation $\partial_ty=A(t,p)y$ with parameter $p$ in a finite-dimensional space $P$, values in a finite-dimensional space $E$, and $y$ jointly smooth on $[l,r]\times P$. Assume a strictly positive weight $g$ with continuous derivative, weighted homogeneous stability on a parameter set $S$ (every solution $z$ satisfies $|z(v)|/g(v)\le K|z(u)|/g(u)$ for $l\le u\le v\le r$, $p\in S$), initial jets $\|D_p^my(l,p)\|/g(l)\le B$ for $m\le N$, and positive-order coefficient jets $\|D_p^mA(t,p)\|\le C$ for $0<m\le N$, with $K,C,B\ge0$. Then all solution jets through order $N$ satisfy $\|D_p^my(t,p)\|\le\Phi_N(K(r-l)C)\,KB\,g(t)$ for $p\in S$, $t\in[l,r]$, where $\Phi_0(q)=1$ and $\Phi_{n+1}(q)=1+2^{n+1}q\,\Phi_n(q)$.
TorusEuler.weighted_homogeneous_jetBound.summary: Homogeneous stability controls every parameter derivative

TorusEuler.weighted_linearODE_forced_nor.text: The weighted forward estimate for a forced linear ODE in fixed coordinates, with the exact time integral of the normalized forcing.
TorusEuler.weighted_linearODE_forced_nor.summary: Weighted variation of constants for forced linear evolution

TorusEuler.weighted_linearODE_perturbati.text: For a positive differentiable weight, a continuous perturbation bounded by $\rho$ changes the weighted forward estimate by $e^{KD}$, where $D$ is the integral of $\rho$ up to the observation time. A second conclusion bounds the difference from an unperturbed solution, including the initial mismatch. Both constants and the actual perturbed equations are explicit hypotheses.
TorusEuler.weighted_linearODE_perturbati.summary: An integrated coefficient error controls weighted propagation

TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_differenc.text: Compares solutions of the center operator $A$ and a nearby operator $A_1$ using a positive differentiable weight $g$. If every center solution has weighted growth at most $K$, the interval has length at most one, and the operator gap is at most $d$ with $Kd\le1$, the relative error is bounded by the propagated initial mismatch plus $eK^2d$ times the initial relative size.
TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_differenc.summary: Nearby solutions remain close relative to the center

TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forced_no.text: Let $E$ be a real normed space, $A,A_1$ continuous families of bounded linear operators on $[a,b]$ and a continuous forcing $f$, and $\gamma>0$ continuously differentiable there, with endpoint derivatives taken from within the interval. Assume $K>0$, $b-a\le1$, and $\|A_1(u)-A(u)\|\le K^{-1}$ throughout. For every solution $z_t=Az$ and all $a\le u\le v\le b$, require $|z(v)|/\gamma(v)\le K|z(u)|/\gamma(u)$. Then every solution $x_t=A_1x+f$ satisfies $|x(t)|/\gamma(t)\le eK\bigl(|x(a)|/\gamma(a)+\int_a^t|f(u)|/\gamma(u)\,du\bigr)$ for $t\in[a,b]$. The stability hypothesis quantifies over all solutions of the central homogeneous equation. Taking $K=\mathsf D^3$ gives the factor in the nearby-label estimate used for Lemma 5.3.
TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forced_no.summary: Weighted variation of constants controls the forced transverse equation

TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forward.text: Let $E$ be a real normed space, $A,A_1$ continuous families of bounded linear operators on $[a,b]$, and $\gamma>0$ continuously differentiable there, with endpoint derivatives taken from within the interval. Assume $K>0$, $b-a\le1$, and $\|A_1(u)-A(u)\|\le K^{-1}$ throughout. For every solution $z_t=Az$ and all $a\le u\le v\le b$, require $|z(v)|/\gamma(v)\le K|z(u)|/\gamma(u)$. Then every solution $x_t=A_1x$ satisfies $|x(t)|/\gamma(t)\le eK|x(a)|/\gamma(a)$ for $t\in[a,b]$. The stability hypothesis quantifies over all solutions of the central homogeneous equation. Taking $K=\mathsf D^3$ gives the factor in the nearby-label estimate used for Lemma 5.3.
TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forward.summary: Small coefficient variation preserves weighted forward control

TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_stability.text: A uniform coefficient comparison with the center gives stability at a label for every pair of ordered times on the slab.
TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_stability.summary: Near-center coefficient control gives weighted stability

TorusEuler.weighted_stability_restrict_I.text: For continuous linear coefficients on $[l,r]$, a weighted stability estimate for every solution on that interval also holds for solutions launched at any $a \in  [l,r]$. The proof extends the later solution backward using linear ODE existence and identifies the extensions by uniqueness. Positivity or regularity of the weight is not separately needed because the comparison is already assumed.
TorusEuler.weighted_stability_restrict_I.summary: Restrict weighted stability to a later launch time

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: For a hierarchy-regular seed at an active time, a scaled jet bound for the unwrapped unswitched leading wave transfers unchanged to its centered skew-periodization. The wrapped profile is jointly smooth in label and phase, one-periodic, and has zero phase mean. Envelope support inside the centered cell supplies boundary smoothness; phase translation preserves the mean, and the centered-cell jet theorem transfers the budget.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: Centered wrapping preserves the unswitched leading jet budget

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: Defines the continuous linear operation that sends a derivative on label-and-phase space to its composition with the inclusion $v \mapsto  (v,0)$. It extracts label differentiation while holding phase fixed. The operation is used to express the unscaled slow curl in terms of derivatives of the jointly scaled potential.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: Restrict a joint derivative to label directions

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: The linear operation restricting a joint derivative to label directions has operator norm at most one. The proof bounds composition with the inclusion $v \mapsto  (v,0)$, whose norm is at most one for the product norm. This prevents an extra coefficient when extracting label derivatives from the scaled phase profile.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: Forgetting the phase direction does not increase operator norm

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: Proves that the operator-valued cross-product map has norm at most one by applying the usual cross-product norm inequality twice through operator-norm bounds. The estimate has no nonzero-vector hypothesis and includes the zero operator. It supplies the unit operator cost used when differentiating the potential coefficient.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: Cross-product insertion has operator norm at most one

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: For any one-periodic vector function, translation of the phase leaves its mean over one period unchanged. The proof changes variables in the interval integral and applies periodicity. No continuity hypothesis appears in this identity; it is used to preserve the zero-mean condition when the centered wrapping introduces a label-dependent phase translation.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: A phase translation preserves the periodic mean

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: For a continuous one-periodic function with zero phase mean, the normalized primitive of its phase translate evaluated at zero equals the original normalized primitive at the translating phase. The proof compares derivatives and uses the zero mean of the primitive. This formulation turns a moving evaluation phase into a parameter of the integrand.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: The normalized primitive commutes with phase translation

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: Packages $v \mapsto  (x \mapsto  v \times  x)$ as a continuous linear map from vectors to continuous linear operators. Linearity follows from the cross product identities, and continuity follows from the estimate $\lVert v \times  x\rVert  \le  \lVert v\rVert \cdot \lVert x\rVert$. This representation lets iterated derivative estimates treat the potential coefficient through ordinary operator composition.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: The cross product as an operator-valued linear map

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: For a smooth label-and-phase potential and nonzero label scale, its ordinary label derivative at the scaled label equals $\ell^{-1}$ times the label restriction of the derivative of the scaled profile. The phase scale may be arbitrary. Uniqueness of the derivative compares two chain-rule expressions; the nonzero radius is essential when cancelling the scale.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: Recover a label derivative from the scaled joint derivative

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationProfiles.0.text: If $s\notin[0,1]$, the derivative of the smooth transition at $s$ is zero. The proof uses local constancy on the left and right plateaus. The endpoints themselves are excluded from this statement, although the underlying transition is smooth there as well.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationProfiles.0.summary: The transition derivative vanishes outside its interval

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationProfiles.0.text: There exists a nonnegative real constant bounding the absolute derivative of the smooth transition at every real input. Compactness supplies a maximum on $[0,1]$, and the preceding plateau lemma handles the complement. The bound is existential; no numerical value or optimality is claimed.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationProfiles.0.summary: One constant bounds the transition derivative

_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationAssembl.text: Deduces $T\delta\le1$ from the window hypotheses $T\ge2$, $\delta\ge0$ and $240\delta T^6\le1$. The proof compares the first and sixth powers of $T$. This estimate is used in the logarithmic strength calculation to convert an integrated older-strain bound into a small relative change of the preceding shear.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationAssembl.summary: The window budget controls integrated older strain

_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationCouplin.text: For two continuous three-dimensional vector paths on the same set, proves continuity of their cross product. There are no nonzero, length or perpendicularity assumptions. The coordinate formula makes each component a difference of products, and the Euclidean-space wrapper preserves continuity. Applied to normalized wave directions, it provides continuity of the third new-frame axis.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationCouplin.summary: Crossing continuous paths gives a continuous path

_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationCouplin.text: If a vector path is continuous on a set $J$ and nonzero at every member of $J$, its normalized direction is continuous there. The nonvanishing assumption ensures continuity of the reciprocal norm. This does not extend the direction continuously through zero vectors; such values remain assigned in the formalization but are excluded from the theorem's domain of control.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationCouplin.summary: A nonvanishing vector path has a continuous direction

_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationCouplin.text: Introduces $\kappa=(64C+143)T^{p+9}\delta$ and shows it dominates the wave-vector error, inverse-shear contribution and amplitude-ratio error while remaining at most $1/2$. It assumes the stated lower bounds on $C_0$ and the polynomial smallness condition. This is finite arithmetic bookkeeping for the coupling comparison; it supplies no wave or coupling equation on its own.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationCouplin.summary: One error allowance controls coordinates and coupling inputs

_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationTimeRes.text:
With positive $r,\sigma,
u$ and the defining relation $r^2=2\sigma
u$, proves $(\sigma/r)(1/r)=1/(2
u)$. This is the conversion $S/r=1/(2
u)$ used to measure the matrix error against the older coupling. All three positivity assumptions appear in the source, although the equality is algebraic once the relevant denominators are nonzero.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationTimeRes.summary: The shear factor converts growth rate to coupling

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeDenominator.text: For positive real numbers $a$ and $b$, the absolute difference of their reciprocals equals $|a-b|/(ab)$. Both positivity assumptions matter when removing the absolute value from the denominator. The identity is the algebraic step that turns lower denominator bounds into reciprocal stability estimates.

For $T\ge2$, $0\le\tau\le T$, $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, and total coordinate error at most $d\le1/2$, the actual coordinates satisfy $|X|,|Q|\le T^2$ and $|Z|\le3/2$. The reference first coordinate is also bounded by $T^2$, while $|\varepsilon\tau|\le T$. This is a scalar consequence of the closeness hypothesis $|X-x|+|Z-1|\le d$, before any wave equation is used.

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.text: Evaluating a matrix entry built from formal multivariate variables at real coordinates $\chi$ gives the corresponding entry built directly from $\chi$. The proof splits the four matrix positions and simplifies polynomial evaluation. This connects the generic polynomial theorem to the concrete reduced amplitude matrix.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.summary: Evaluate a formal amplitude entry at real inputs

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.text: Given values $\chi$ indexed by the combined strain and scalar coordinates, this definition feeds the two nine-entry blocks and six scalars into the polynomial two-by-two amplitude matrix. It is valid over any commutative ring. The last three scalars are independent inputs here; only later substitutions identify them with physical reciprocals.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.summary: Build the amplitude matrix from all coordinates

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.text: Packing two strain arrays and six scalar inputs into one coordinate vector, then reading them back into the amplitude matrix, gives exactly the polynomial amplitude matrix with those arguments. This equality holds by definition. It certifies the bookkeeping used to apply polynomial bounds, without adding positivity or denominator assumptions.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.summary: Packing the inputs leaves the matrix unchanged

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.text: There exist a common nonnegative constant $C$ and natural exponent $n$ such that every matrix entry changes by at most $CM^nd$ on a coordinate box of radius $M\ge1$. The proof combines the four individual polynomial estimates by summing constants and taking the largest exponent. The input differences are hypotheses, not conclusions of this helper.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.summary: One polynomial bound controls every matrix entry

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeScaledStrai.text: In an orthonormal frame, omitting the error strain leaves the older matrix plus a single entry $S\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ratio}}$ in position $(2,1)$ (paper indices). The theorem is pointwise and accepts any continuous linear map $B$. It uses the rank-one form of the preceding wave's gradient and does not assume an evolution equation for $B$.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeScaledStrai.summary: The preceding shear changes one matrix entry

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeScaledStrai.text: The full reference matrix equals the older reference matrix plus the elementary matrix with unit entry at $(1,0)$. The proof checks the nine possible positions. This exact decomposition mirrors the no-error physical strain identity and makes the strength-ratio error easy to isolate.

For $S\ne0$, the full no-error strain has the same scaled entries as the older strain except at position $(2,1)$, where it adds $\sigma_{\mathrm{ratio}}$. This identity uses an orthonormal frame and cancels the shear factor only under $S\ne0$. It isolates the single changing strength coefficient in the amplitude comparison.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeScaledStrai.summary: Rescaling turns the shear entry into a strength ratio

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: This map sends a vector $w$ to $(-S\langle E_1,w\rangle,\langle E_2,w\rangle)$. It uses the sign convention $U=-\alpha_1$ and $V=\alpha_2$. Its norm estimate later costs a factor $S$, explaining how a small physical strain error enters the reduced amplitude equations.

The vector is $(-u/S)E_1+vE_2+((xu-qv)/(Sz))E_3$. Here $u$ corresponds to $U=-\alpha_1$ and $v$ to $V=\alpha_2$. For nonzero $S,z$ this is the amplitude determined by transversality to the coordinate wave. The definition itself does not enforce those hypotheses or orthonormality.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: An amplitude reconstructed from two transverse coordinates

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: For any frame vectors and continuous linear map $E$, the pairing with the $i$th axis is the linear combination of the three matrix entries weighted by the reconstructed amplitude coefficients. No orthonormality or nonzero denominator hypothesis is needed for this expansion. It prepares the pressure pairing for the added-strain calculation.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: Apply the strain to each amplitude component

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: For nonzero $S$ and $z$, pairing the coordinate wave with $E$ applied to the coordinate amplitude gives $(F_Uu+F_Vv)/S$, where $F_U,F_V$ are the rational pressure coefficients of the two amplitude coordinates. The result uses the entries of $E$ in the supplied frame. It does not require orthonormality because it expands the same pairings on both sides.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: The reconstructed pressure pairing has two coefficient rows

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: The vector is $xE_1+(q/S)E_2+zE_3$, without the physical frequency factor $\lambda$. It is defined for any three vectors $E_1,E_2,E_3$, and orthonormality is supplied by the lemmas computing its pairings and norm. This reconstruction isolates the wave direction used to estimate the added strain.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: A wave vector reconstructed from scaled coordinates

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: For an orthonormal frame, pairing the reconstructed wave with its three axes returns $x$, $q/S$ and $z$. Orthogonality cancels all cross terms. No nonzero shear hypothesis is required for this algebraic identity, so its interpretation remains consistent with the total definition at $S=0$.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: Pairings recover the reconstructed wave components

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: The difference between the full amplitude error operator and the operator with $E=0$ equals the raw matrix generated by $E$ alone with zero older strain. The reference matrix cancels. This identity holds for arbitrary coordinates and parameters because the strain contribution is linear, even before nondegenerate physical interpretation is imposed.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: Subtracting the zero-error operator isolates the added strain

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: For an orthonormal frame and $S\ge1$, the maximum norm of the extracted amplitude pair is at most $S\|w\|$. Each inner product is bounded by the vector norm, and the first component carries the shear factor. This is the reverse coordinate cost in the added-strain estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: Extracting raw coordinates costs one shear factor

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: When the frame is orthonormal, $S\ge1$, $|x|,|q|\le S$ and $z\ge1/2$, the reconstructed amplitude has norm at most $6\|(u,v)\|$. The pair norm is the maximum norm. The proof bounds the three physical coefficients separately, so no Riccati equation or growing-mode assumption is used.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: Reconstruction has a uniform amplitude bound

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: With an orthonormal frame, the squared norm of the reconstructed wave $xE_1+(q/S)E_2+zE_3$ equals $x^2+q^2/S^2+z^2$. The proof uses its three pairings and the inner product of the vector with itself. This equality holds for all $S$, including $S=0$ where $1/0=0$; positivity comes separately from the third coordinate.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: The reconstructed wave has the expected squared norm

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: The vector $-w+2\langle k,w\rangle k/\|k\|^2$ has exactly the same norm as $w$. Lean identifies it with reflection in the span of $k$. The equality also covers $k=0$: the totalized correction term vanishes and the result is $-w$, whose norm is unchanged.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: The pressure reflection preserves vector length

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: Assuming an orthonormal frame and nonzero $S,z$, the raw matrix with zero older strain acts on $(u,v)$ by reconstructing an amplitude, applying $E$, reflecting the result across the wave direction, and extracting its two components. The squared wave norm is proved nonzero from $z\ne0$. This identity makes the operator estimate geometric.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: The error matrix acts by reflection and projection

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: At a nonzero frequency $\xi$, the angular Leray map is differentiable to every requested order $n$. The reciprocal norm in the normalized-frequency formula is smooth only away from zero. The result is local ambient smoothness; it does not assert continuity at the separately assigned zero-frequency value.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: The angular projection is smooth away from zero

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: For each order $n$, there is a nonnegative constant bounding the derivative norm by $C/\|\xi\|^n$ at every nonzero frequency. Compactness bounds derivatives on the unit sphere, and homogeneity transfers the bound to other radii. The theorem supplies existence of constants, not explicit numerical values.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: Angular derivative bounds decay with frequency order

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: The $L^2$ inner product of a constant vector path with a path $v$ equals the vector inner product of that constant with the time integral of $v$. The restricted interval has finite measure. This identity proves symmetry of the operation that removes the time average.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: Pairing with a constant path extracts the time integral

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: For $T>0$, the operator-valued lift that also subtracts time means has norm at most one. The proof combines the contractive spatial lift with the norm-one bound for the orthogonal time projection. This estimate is uniform in duration and is used in angular derivative transfer.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: Adding time mean subtraction does not increase operator norm

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: The real inner product of the embedded integer frequency with a vector equals the sum of its integer coordinates times the vector coordinates. This unfolds the Euclidean representation. It is used to show that restricting the complex Leray symbol to real coefficients agrees with the real angular operator.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: The real frequency pairing is a coordinate contraction

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: The squared Euclidean norm of the embedded real Fourier frequency equals the sum of the squared integer coordinates, $k_1^2+k_2^2+k_3^2$. This is the real counterpart of the complex Euclidean identity. It ensures that both versions of the Leray formula use exactly the same denominator.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: The real frequency norm matches the coordinate sum

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: Applying the lifted spatial operator to a constant $L^2$ path gives the constant path with the transformed value. This is equality of path-space elements, proved from their almost-everywhere representatives. It supports the algebraic commutation between spatial action and subtraction of the time average.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: Constant paths remain constant under spatial operators

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: Time integrating the path after applying a fixed bounded spatial operator gives the operator applied to the original time integral. The path belongs to $L^2$ on a finite measure interval, hence is integrable. This identity is the key reason the spatial action preserves the zero-time-mean condition.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: Spatial operators commute with path integration

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: This bounded linear map sends a spatial operator to its lifted action composed with the time mean projection. It isolates all time-path structure from the frequency-dependent angular symbol. Consequently angular differentiation can be transferred by postcomposition with one fixed bounded linear map.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: Lifting a spatial operator together with time mean subtraction

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: The positive and negative shear Fourier modes are the exponentials with phases $\pm2\pi i x_2$. The result expands the general integer-character formula at the specific unit frequency. It fixes the signs needed to reconstruct the real sine shear from its pair of complex coefficients.
_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.summary: The two shear characters are opposite complex exponentials

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: The Euclidean norm of the real lattice vector corresponding to the stationary shear mode is one. It is exactly the second coordinate unit vector. This numerical identity ensures that both active frequencies fit within the initial frequency band once the chosen base frequency is sufficiently large.
_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.summary: The initial shear frequency has unit length

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: For positive envelope scale $r$, if some coordinate lies beyond the stated collar threshold, the radial envelope is zero. The threshold simplifies to twice the scale. A coordinate absolute value is bounded by the Euclidean norm, so the outer-radius cutoff lemma applies.
_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.summary: A coordinate outside the envelope radius forces the cutoff to vanish

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: This is coordinatewise complexification of the vector $(1,0,s)$. The same direction multiplies both sine Fourier coefficients. It keeps the real velocity geometry while allowing the finite complex Fourier synthesis used to certify the parent's spectral support.
_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.summary: The shear direction embedded in complex Euclidean space

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: The complexified shear direction is nonzero for every real parameter. Its first coordinate is always one, independently of $s$. This ensures both signed sine coefficients are nonzero, so the later Fourier-support theorem identifies exactly two frequencies rather than merely bounding the support.
_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.summary: The Fourier shear direction never vanishes

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: The scalar factor is $1/(2i)$, the coefficient multiplying the positive exponential in the sine identity. The negative frequency uses its negative.
