The value is independent of that representative up to null sets. This identity converts integral energy bounds into operator-norm estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointPrimitive.0..summary: The L² norm equals its squared time integral

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointPrimitive.0..text: If a velocity is square-integrable on the full slab and $0\le a\le b\le T$, its integral over $[a,b]$ has squared norm at most $(b-a)$ times the full-slab squared norm integral. The theorem deliberately uses the larger energy integral, producing one bound uniform over all subintervals.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointPrimitive.0..summary: A subinterval integral is controlled by the full energy

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointPrimitiveAdj.text: For two absolutely continuous paths in a real Hilbert space, their pointwise inner product is an absolutely continuous scalar function on the interval. This supplies the scalar function to which the fundamental theorem for absolutely continuous functions can be applied. No classical pointwise differentiability of the original paths is assumed everywhere.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointPrimitiveAdj.summary: Pairing absolutely continuous paths preserves absolute continuity

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointPrimitiveAdj.text: The norm of an absolutely continuous path is absolutely continuous on the same interval. The norm map is Lipschitz, so its increments are controlled by those of the original path. This auxiliary result is used in constructing the integration-by-parts identity for Hilbert-valued time primitives.

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointRealFourierT.text: Multiplying an embedded real vector by a complex scalar splits into the embedded real multiple and $i$ times the embedded imaginary multiple. The supplied complexification structure provides the real embedding and its linearity. This algebraic identity is the first step in translating real Fourier moments into the complex coefficient convention.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointRealFourierT.summary: Separate a complex scalar into real parts

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointRecoverTime..text: An $L^2$ time path has primitive increments bounded by $\sqrt{t-s}\,\|v\|$ whenever $s\le t$ and both times lie in the slab. This is Cauchy–Schwarz expressed in the quotient norm. It provides a pointwise time modulus for the integral even though the velocity representative itself need not be continuous.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointRecoverTime..summary: Primitive increments gain the square root of elapsed time

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointRecoverTime..text: For an $L^2$ time path on a nonnegative interval, its norm squared is the interval integral of the squared norm of its representative. The restriction measure ignores endpoint null sets. This identity is used to express Cauchy–Schwarz bounds directly in the Hilbert norm of a time path.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointRecoverTime..summary: The time-path norm is its integral energy

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSmoothSlices.text: The centered Euclidean fundamental cell equals the preimage of the coordinate box $[-1/2,1/2]^3$ under the map sending a Euclidean vector to its coordinate triple. This identifies the Euclidean norm model with ordinary coordinate functions. It lets the periodic divergence theorem be applied through the box integral theorem without changing the domain of integration.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSmoothSlices.summary: The centered cell is the coordinate box

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSmoothSlices.text: If a Euclidean vector field is smooth of all orders, so is its divergence. The statement uses infinite differentiability order and obtains the result by differentiating the field once and summing its diagonal components. This permits divergence itself to serve as a smooth test potential in the converse weak-solenoidal argument.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSmoothSlices.summary: Smooth vector fields have smooth divergence

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSmoothSlices.text: For a $C^1$ vector field $v$, divergence is a continuous scalar function. The proof expresses divergence as the finite sum of diagonal coordinate derivatives of $v$. This supplies integrability on the compact fundamental cell for the periodic integration-by-parts argument; no divergence-free assumption is needed.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSmoothSlices.summary: A continuously differentiable field has continuous divergence

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSmoothSlices.text: At a point where $p$ and $v$ are differentiable, the divergence of $pv$ equals $\langle\nabla p,v\rangle+p\,\mathrm{div}\,v$. The hypotheses are local differentiability assumptions, not global smoothness. This coordinate calculation is the algebraic step in the later periodic integration-by-parts formula.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSmoothSlices.summary: The divergence product rule for a scalar factor

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSmoothSlices.text: For a differentiable periodic vector field, divergence is periodic with the same lattice. The proof differentiates the equality between a lattice translate and the original field, then compares traces. Differentiability is explicit because equality of functions alone does not provide the derivative formula used here.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSmoothSlices.summary: Divergence inherits periodicity from a differentiable field

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpace.0.Toru.text: The gradient of the smooth periodic lift of the potential $p$ is spatially periodic. Differentiating the translation identity preserves the derivative because the translating map has identity derivative. Smoothness is essential here: this theorem supplies a legitimate gradient that can descend to a continuous torus test field.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpace.0.Toru.summary: A smooth periodic potential has a periodic gradient

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpace.0.Toru.text: For a square-integrable test field $f$, its bounded Hilbert functional on an endpoint path equals the integral of their real inner product. The proof replaces the chosen $L^2$ representative of the test by its original function almost everywhere. This validates the concrete formulas for both endpoint constraints.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpace.0.Toru.summary: A Hilbert test equals its integral pairing

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpace.0.Toru.text: For an integrable real function $f$, vanishing of its product integral against every bounded measurable scalar test is equivalent to being zero almost everywhere. Measurable-set indicator tests give the forward implication. The integrability premise is essential to identify the function through these integral conditions.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpace.0.Toru.summary: All bounded tests detect an almost everywhere zero function

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpace.0.Toru.text: If the test field $f$ is square integrable, its real inner product with any endpoint $L^2$ path is integrable over the product measure. The proof uses the Hilbert-space Cauchy–Schwarz result and almost-everywhere representative equality. This is the integrability needed before exchanging time and spatial integrals.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpace.0.Toru.summary: The pairing of two square integrable fields is integrable

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpace.0.Toru.text: A bounded measurable time factor multiplied by the torus gradient of a smooth periodic potential belongs to joint $L^2$. The gradient is bounded because it is continuous on a compact torus. This makes its Hilbert inner product with any endpoint path a well-defined bounded linear divergence test.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpace.0.Toru.summary: Separated divergence tests are square integrable

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpace.0.Toru.text: A bounded measurable spatial scalar test multiplied by a coordinate unit vector belongs to the joint $L^2$ endpoint space. Its value is independent of time. Finite product measure and the supplied bound on the test justify this assertion, enabling continuous linear tests for the coordinate time mean.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpace.0.Toru.summary: Bounded spatial tests define square integrable joint fields

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: For the product of the restricted time measure and the label measure, the first coordinate belongs to $(0,T]$ almost everywhere. This is a support property of the measure, rather than a statement about all product points. It permits later primitive identities to use their time-domain hypotheses.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: Almost every product point lies in the time interval

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: Construct time integration as a real linear map between joint $L^2$ spaces. Addition and scalar multiplication are checked by moving quotient equalities to almost-everywhere label slices and then into the integral. The assumption $T\ge0$ supplies the square-integrable output; boundedness is established separately.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: Time integration is linear on the joint space

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: For $T\ge0$, the linear primitive satisfies $\|Jv\|_2\le T\|v\|_2$ on the joint space. Squaring reduces the estimate to the labelwise energy majorant; Fubini contributes the second factor of $T$. This bound certifies continuity of the subsequently bundled operator.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: Time integration costs at most the interval length

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: Assuming $T\ge0$, the squared norm of the primitive is at most $T$ times the full time-slice energy, almost everywhere in the product measure. The estimate combines the one-dimensional primitive bound with slice square integrability obtained from Fubini; exceptional labels are excluded by the conclusion.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: The squared primitive is bounded by T times the slice energy

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: Package the primitive representative as a joint $L^2$ equivalence class, using the square-integrability theorem and the assumption $T\ge0$. The construction forgets changes on product null sets. Its chosen pointwise representative is identified with the original time integral only almost everywhere in the next theorem.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: The primitive as a joint square integrable field

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: The representative chosen for the $L^2$ class of the joint primitive agrees almost everywhere with the pointwise labelwise primitive $\int_0^t v(s,a)\,ds$. The nonnegative-time assumption is inherited from the construction. This theorem is the representative bridge used when proving linearity and bounds; it does not upgrade quotient equality to pointwise equality on exceptional product points.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: The square integrable primitive has the expected representative

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: If two paths $u$ and $v$ lie in time $L^2$, their real inner product is integrable on the restricted interval. The proof passes through the corresponding $L^2$ classes and then returns to the given representatives. This ensures later integration-by-parts identities use genuine integrals of products.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: Two square integrable paths have an integrable pairing

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: The function that assigns $T$ times the integrated squared norm of a label slice to every product point is integrable. Joint square integrability of $v$ and Fubini provide this majorant. No positivity of $T$ is needed for integrability, unlike the preceding pointwise inequality.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: The slice energy bound is jointly integrable

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: For square-integrable paths $u$ and $v$, with $v$ having zero time integral, the pairing of $Ju$ with $v$ equals minus the pairing of $u$ with $Jv$. The zero-mean assumption applies to $v$, not both paths. The result converts the integrated operator into the displacement energy form.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: A zero mean test path reverses the primitive

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: For square-integrable $v$, $w$, and $k$, with zero mean for $v$, rewrite the integral of $\langle k-Jw,v\rangle$ as that of $\langle k,v\rangle+\langle w,Jv\rangle$. The lemma isolates the sign change from the adjoint identity. Substituting $k=Kv$ and $w=\Omega v$ gives the energy expression used for coercivity.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: The primitive term becomes the displacement pairing

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: For an element of $L^2(\mu;E)$, its squared norm equals the integral of the squared norm of its chosen representative. The real inner-product-space structure supplies the identity through the $L^2$ inner product. The theorem is generic in the underlying measured space and is not a new PDE estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: The Hilbert norm equals the integrated square

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: For nonnegative $T$, the chosen primitive representative belongs to joint $L^2$. Strong measurability and the integrable slice-energy majorant establish the claim. This is the proof needed before turning an everywhere-defined vector-valued integral into an element of the quotient space $L^2$ over time and labels.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: Time integration preserves joint square integrability

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: The labelwise time integral is strongly measurable as a function of the pair of time and label. The proof inserts the indicator of $0<s\le t$ before integrating in $s$. It applies to the measurable representative supplied by the $L^2$ class, including exceptional slices where the integral takes its assigned value zero.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: The primitive has a measurable joint representative

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: When $T$ is nonnegative, the real-valued mass of the whole space for Lebesgue measure restricted to $(0,T]$ equals $T$. This elementary normalization is used after Fubini to obtain the joint primitive bound. At $T=0$, both sides vanish and the identity remains valid.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: The time measure has mass equal to its length

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialDeriv.text: If the families $v$ and $w$ agree at every word shorter than $t$, their mixed corrections at $t$ are equal. The coefficient family $B$ is unchanged. The proof uses the strict lower-order property of correction pairs, which ensures that the recursive construction never depends on an unknown derivative of the current order.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialDeriv.summary: Lower order agreement determines the commutator

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialDeriv.text: Assume coefficient derivatives through the length of the word $t$ and unknown derivatives strictly below that length. Differentiating the mixed correction in direction $u_i$ gives the sum of the two product-rule terms for each correction pair. The two different length thresholds are explicit and are what allow induction on derivative order.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialDeriv.summary: Differentiate all lower order correction products

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialDeriv.text: For a finite list $l$, if each indexed function has the stated derivative at $s$, the sum of those functions has derivative equal to the list sum of their derivatives. Repeated list elements remain repeated, preserving multiplicities. This is used in the product-rule expansion of the higher spatial commutator.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialDeriv.summary: Differentiate a finite list sum term by term

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.text: Evaluating a half-Hölder derivative field $f'$ along the path $s\mapsto a+[shu]$, where $[shu]$ is the torus image of $shu$, is continuous as a function of $s$. The argument composes the continuous value field with the Lipschitz quotient map and a linear path. This continuity permits the fundamental theorem of calculus along each directional segment.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.summary: A derivative field stays continuous along a translated line

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.text: The private translated-field constructor evaluates exactly to the original field at $a+b$. This definitional identity is used to prove linearity and norm bounds for the translation operator. It is a pointwise statement on the torus and involves no almost-everywhere representative choice.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.summary: Evaluate a translated field at the shifted label

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.text: If the norm of $g$ is at most $C$ on $(0,1]$, the norm of its interval integral from zero to one is at most $C$. This norm inequality is used after expressing a directional difference quotient as an averaged derivative. It does not itself identify any function as a derivative or require such an interpretation.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.summary: A unit interval integral inherits its uniform bound

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.text: The norm of the constructed translated field is no larger than the original half-Hölder norm. Translation preserves both value bounds and distances between labels, so the same increment estimate applies. This preliminary inequality is later strengthened to equality by translating back by the negative increment.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.summary: Translation preserves the available Hölder bound

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.text: For each lattice mode, the Fourier character at the sum of two torus points is the product of its values at those points. This is the character homomorphism law. It is the algebraic input that makes translation diagonal on Fourier coefficients and allows Fourier multipliers to commute with spatial translation.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.summary: A Fourier character turns addition into multiplication

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.text: For a torus increment $b$, the constructed field takes the value of $f$ at $a+b$. Translation preserves the torus distance, so the same value and square-root increment bounds certify the new bundled field. This is the underlying field construction before it is packaged as a bounded linear operator.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.summary: Translate a half Hölder field on the torus

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointStrongWeakAg.text: For positive $T$, suppose the bounded mixed operator $P$ acts by the combined angular-time symbol on all real-character moments. Embedding $Pw$ into joint $L^2$ then gives the orthogonal joint constraint projection of the embedded field. The Fourier law is the evidence identifying the strong and weak projections.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointStrongWeakAg.summary: The mixed Fourier projection matches the joint constraint projection

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.text: Almost every point for the endpoint product measure lies in the closed time and label slab. The time factor is Lebesgue measure restricted to $(0,T]$, and the label factor is torus Haar measure. The proof projects to time and uses $(0,T]\subseteq[0,T]$; no regularity of a field is involved.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.summary: The product measure stays inside the closed slab

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.text: Continuity of the deformation field $F$ on the slab implies continuity of $F^*F$. The proof combines continuity of adjoint with composition of continuous linear maps. No inverse deformation is needed for this regularity statement; positivity bounds are supplied separately when the kinetic coefficient enters the endpoint equation.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.summary: The kinetic coefficient is continuous on the slab

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.text: Continuous deformation and gradient fields on the slab give a continuous pulled-back vorticity coefficient $F^*(M^*-M)F$. All dependence is through continuous operator algebra. This provides the measurable, bounded coefficient required by the weak product operator, while leaving the flow identities and Hessian upper bound to the coercivity theorem.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.summary: Continuity of the space-time vorticity coefficient

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.text: Continuity of an operator coefficient on the compact slab gives almost-everywhere strong measurability for the endpoint space-time measure. Outside-slab values need no continuity assumption, because that measure is concentrated on the slab. This is the measurability obligation for constructing the bounded product multiplier used in the weak inverse.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.summary: Continuous slab coefficients are strongly measurable almost everywhere

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.text: A coefficient continuous on the closed time and torus slab has an almost-everywhere finite operator-norm bound for the endpoint product measure. The bound is existential and depends on the coefficient and duration. It does not supply the explicit uniform polynomial estimate required later for the physical inverse.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.summary: Continuous slab coefficients have a finite essential bound

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.text: The product of $[0,T]$ with the entire three-dimensional unit torus is compact. This holds for every real $T$, including an empty time interval. It supplies the compact domain on which continuous kinetic and vorticity coefficients acquire finite bounds before being used as space-time $L^2$ multipliers.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.summary: The closed time and label slab is compact

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: If the joint residual is orthogonal to every zero-time-mean solenoidal test, its pairing with each fixed solenoidal $y$ equals the pairing with its time average almost everywhere. The strict condition $T>0$ licenses $T^{-1}$. This theorem fixes one test at a time, before the later simultaneous projection identity.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.summary: An orthogonal residual has constant solenoidal moments

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: Pairing the weak spatial Leray projection of $r$ with a vector $y$ in the solenoidal subspace gives the original ambient $L^2$ pairing. The vector $y$ is taken from the solenoidal subspace itself. Orthogonality of the projection is the reason pressure and other complementary components disappear in this test.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.summary: Remove a projection against a solenoidal test

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: Pair a joint $L^2$ residual $r$ with a spatial $L^2$ field $y$ pulled back along the second coordinate. The scalar pairing is integrable for the endpoint product measure. This is an integrability statement, allowing Fubini in the weak argument; it does not assert pointwise continuity of a residual representative.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.summary: The residual pairing is integrable in space and time

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: Under $T\ge0$, integrating the spatial pairing of $r$ with $y$ over time equals pairing the weak time integral of $r$ with $y$. Fubini and bounded linearity of the inner product justify the exchange. The identity is formulated through $L^2$ classes so it is independent of representative choices.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.summary: Move the time integral outside the spatial pairing

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: An essentially bounded scalar time function $\eta$ may multiply an arbitrary spatial $L^2$ field $y$ to give a joint space-time $L^2$ field. The product measure and separated variables are essential here. This builds admissible probes without requiring pointwise regularity of either factor.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.summary: Separate a bounded time test from a spatial field

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: The product of an essentially bounded time function with a weakly solenoidal spatial field belongs to the endpoint subspace of zero-time-mean, weakly solenoidal paths when the time function has vanishing integral. The proof checks zero time mean and the spatial gradient pairing separately. These tests isolate the time-independent part of an orthogonal residual.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.summary: A centered separated test satisfies both constraints

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: For $T\ge0$, the real mass of Lebesgue measure restricted to $(0,T]$ is exactly $T$. The nonnegative-length condition includes the zero interval. This normalization justifies the time average in the weak endpoint argument; division by $T$ is used later only with a strictly positive length.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.summary: The restricted time measure has mass T

_private.TorusEuler.EulerAdvectionBounds.text: The centered periodic cell has strictly positive real volume. The proof exhibits a nonempty interior and uses finite volume of the compact cell. This justifies dividing by the cell volume when subtracting the average from a reconstructed pressure, ensuring that the mean-zero normalization uses a nonzero denominator.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerAdvectionBounds.summary: The normalization cell has positive volume

_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.text: The supplied bounded jets $J$ obey the next order derivative relation whenever they are, by hypothesis, the iterated spatial derivatives of a spatially smooth field. Reading the next multilinear derivative as a map into multilinear maps turns it into the derivative map of the current jet. This is a representation lemma, not a source of smoothness for the velocity.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.summary: Actual velocity jets satisfy the compatibility equations

_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.text: For a continuous family of bounded continuous functions and a continuous bounded derivative family $D$, the spatial derivative of the evaluated time primitive equals the primitive of $D$. The relation that $D$ is the spatial derivative at $x$ is assumed at every time in the slab. Compactness in time supplies the domination needed to differentiate under the integral.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.summary: Spatial differentiation passes through the time primitive

_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.text: For a time dependent bounded continuous function, a within time derivative in the uniform norm and a spatial derivative at $x$ combine into a joint within derivative on $I\times\mathbb R^3$. The resulting linear map adds the time contribution and spatial contribution. Uniform control of the time remainder is what makes evaluation at varying spatial points legitimate.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.summary: Time and spatial derivatives combine under evaluation

_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.text: Given a tower smooth in the uniform time norm and compatible under spatial differentiation, the time differentiated tower remains spatially compatible. The original derivative relation, that each jet has the next as spatial derivative, is a hypothesis. Difference quotients converge uniformly as bounded continuous functions, allowing the derivative relation to pass to the limit even at closed slab endpoints.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.summary: Spatial differentiation commutes with bounded jet time derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.text: If the tower $U$ is continuous in time and successive entries are spatial derivatives, its time primitives satisfy the same derivative relation. The derivative of the order-$m$ primitive is the order-$(m+1)$ primitive, read as a map into $m$-linear maps. Bounded evaluation and this identification commute with integration, allowing the previous integral differentiation result to apply.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.summary: Time integration preserves compatibility of spatial jets

_private.TorusEuler.EulerLimitClosure.0..text: A jointly smooth integrand on a closed convex parameter domain remains $C^m$ after integration over a fixed compact set, for every natural $m$. The hypotheses include unique differentiability of the domain, a proper parameter space and a locally finite measure. Induction differentiates under the integral, supporting the normalized pressure formula at the initial time.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerLimitClosure.0..summary: Compact integration preserves every finite smoothness order

_private.TorusEuler.EulerLimitClosure.0..text: On a closed convex parameter set in a proper normed space, a jointly continuous integrand and supplied continuous parameter derivative over a compact integration set may be differentiated under the integral. The measure is locally finite and the target is complete. The conclusion is a within-set derivative, so it applies at boundary parameters as well.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerLimitClosure.0..summary: Differentiate a compact integral with a continuous derivative

_private.TorusEuler.EulerLimitClosure.0..text: For a smooth integrand on a closed convex parameter domain times the whole integration space, this identifies the derivative of its compact-set integral as the integral of the parameter component of its joint within-derivative. Unique differentiability on the convex domain fixes that derivative there. The argument inherits properness and local finiteness from the surrounding section.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerLimitClosure.0..summary: Smooth joint integrands supply the compact integral derivative

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: The private level record combines a transverse output, a completion $C$ with zero average, and a mean output. It packages exactly the information needed by the recursion. The record does not assert that $C$ is the completion of the transverse velocity $V$; that equality is a property of the constructed levels proved later.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Store one completed oscillation and its mean

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: If averaging is idempotent and fixes the parent residual, then the mean source at every level $p$, built from the preliminary source $H$ and the parent residual, is fixed by averaging. The proof distinguishes $p=2$ from other levels. This gives the exact admissibility proof required by the mean solver.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: The mean source is fixed by averaging

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: Assume every mean $B_i$ is fixed by averaging. Idempotence removes the averaged part of $H$, while the solver property that phase advection by an averaged mean has zero average makes each supplementary mean-advection term average to zero. The resulting source therefore satisfies the zero-average admissibility condition required by the transverse solver, at any indices $P,p$.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: The supplementary source has zero phase mean

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: The family of previously built records is available only for indices $i<p$. This definition turns it into a sequence defined at every index, using the earlier record at $i<p$ and the zero record at all other indices. It ensures the preliminary source cannot read unresolved values from the current or later levels.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Expose only the levels already constructed

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: At index one the recursion returns the prescribed leading wave, its completion, and zero mean. At indices $2\le i\le P$ it calls the single-level solver, which solves the mean and then the transverse equation; every other index receives zero. The leading branch is tested first, so depth zero still stores a leading record even though its finite velocity sum is empty.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Build the finite expansion by strong recursion

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: The recursively defined index-one record is exactly the supplied leading transverse output, its completion under the supplied completion map, and the zero mean. This identity holds for every depth $P$, because the index-one branch precedes the depth test. It identifies the base data without asserting the leading momentum equation.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: The prescribed leading wave starts the recursion

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: For $2\le p\le P$, the recursive level equals the output of the single-level solver supplied with the same recursion at earlier indices. Strong recursion is unfolded at the current index. This equation enables later proofs to read the mean and transverse equations from the solver output.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Retained correction levels use the ordered solver

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: At positive depth $P\ge1$, any index equal to zero or larger than $P$ carries the zero record. The positive-depth condition excludes the exceptional index-one branch when $P=0$. This supplies the zero conventions needed to close the final interaction sums.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Zero and unretained levels carry no profiles

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: The source for the mean equation is minus the average of the preliminary source $H$, with the parent residual subtracted only when $p=2$. The same expression is defined at every natural index. Admissibility under averaging requires the separate hypothesis that the parent residual is fixed by the average.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: The mean source includes the parent residual once

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: Taking a level sequence, retaining its values below $p$, and filling the rest with zeros produces profiles that agree with the original profiles before $p$. The proof unfolds the conditional branch for each $i<p$. It justifies discarding provisional padding when rewriting the constructed sources.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: The recursion prefix agrees where it is used

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: A sequence of level records is converted into a family of hierarchy profiles by taking its oscillatory velocity, completion, mean velocity, oscillatory pressure, and mean pressure at each index. This conversion adds no mathematical property. It exposes the recursively constructed records to the algebraic source and cancellation formulas.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Read five profile sequences from the levels

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: This changes only the mean sequence $B$ of a profile family, replacing its value at $p$ by the newly solved mean. Every other sequence and every other mean index is unchanged. The transverse source can therefore include $B_p$ while its oscillatory inputs still come from earlier levels.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Insert the newly solved mean at one level

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: Given earlier levels and a parent residual fixed by averaging, this first solves the mean equation, inserts its velocity at the current index, and then solves the transverse equation with that updated source. The returned record comes with proofs of both equations. The completion is obtained by applying the supplied completion map to the new oscillation.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Solve the mean and then the transverse equation at one level

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: This defines the transverse source as $-(H-\langle H\rangle)$ minus the filtered phase-advection contribution of the means. The latter includes the newly computed $B_p$ acting on the leading oscillation. The formula is algebraic; the proof that its phase average vanishes uses compatibility supplied by the solvers.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Subtract the mean and the current mean transport

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: This private record puts zero in the oscillation, both pressures, completion, and mean. Operator linearity discharges its compatibility proofs. It fills indices unavailable to strong recursion and indices outside the retained depth, so source formulas remain total functions on natural numbers.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: The zero level outside the retained expansion

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: This provides the mean-output record with both velocity and pressure equal to zero. Linearity of the hierarchy operators proves all required compatibility fields. It is used at the leading level and in absent levels, rather than as an analytic solution of a nonzero mean source.

If two profile families agree at every index below $p$ in their oscillations $V$, completions $C$, means $B$ and pressures, and $i<p$, their blocks $Y_i=V_i+C_{i-1}$ agree. The proof uses equality of $V_i$ and $C_{i-1}$. Since natural subtraction gives $i-1\le i$, the completion is still among the earlier inputs.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Earlier oscillatory blocks agree with the prefix

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: Agreement of profile families before $p$ gives equality of the full block $Z_i=Y_i+B_i$ for each $i<p$. The earlier $Y_i$ identity supplies the oscillatory part, and the stored equality of $B_i$ supplies the mean. This lets quadratic source sums use the final family.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Earlier full blocks agree with the prefix

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: Membership of an index pair $(i,j)$ in a filtered level sum with shift $\delta$ implies that $i\ge\delta+1$, $j$ is positive, and $i+j=p+\delta$. These inequalities justify later uses of natural subtraction and show which profile indices lie before the current recursion level.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Recover the positive indices of one interaction

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: For nonzero frequency $\lambda$, the first-wave pressure coefficient formed from the explicit seed and material gradient is smooth in the label at any fixed time. The proof rewrites it using the normalized coefficient, whose denominator never vanishes. This checks regularity of the coefficient before its phase primitive and envelope are inserted.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: The raw pressure coefficient is spatially smooth

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: The normalized scalar pressure coefficient is globally smooth as a function of the pair $(t,a)$. The shear rate is a cosine, the sweep is smooth, and the denominator is strictly positive. The result supplies joint regularity before compactness is used to obtain constants independent of time and label.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: The normalized pressure is smooth in time and label

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: For each finite order $n$, the unit radial envelope admits a constant $C\ge1$ with $\|D^jg\|\le C$ everywhere for all orders $j\le n$. Its derivatives are bounded on a compact ball and vanish outside the envelope support. The bound controls all orders up to $n$; it is not a single constant for every derivative order simultaneously.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: A fixed envelope has bounded derivatives at every order

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: Fixing a parameter cannot increase the norm of an iterated Fréchet derivative. For globally smooth $f:P\times\mathbb R^3\to E$, the spatial derivative of $a\mapsto f(p,a)$ is bounded by the joint derivative at the same point. The proof composes with an isometric inclusion, so the comparison has constant one.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: Spatial derivatives inherit the joint derivative bound

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: This scalar is twice the initial shear rate divided by the square of $1+\mathrm{firstWaveSweep}^2$. The shear ratio and amplitude are absent: they have been separated from the first-wave pressure calculation. Its globally positive denominator makes it suitable for uniform compact-time derivative estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: The pressure coefficient after amplitude normalization

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: If a smooth map satisfies $\|D^jf\|\le A$ everywhere for all orders $j\le n$, precomposing it with a continuous linear map of norm at most one preserves the same bound. The chain rule contributes a power of the linear-map norm at each order, which can only decrease the estimate. No invertibility of the contraction is required.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: A linear contraction preserves the derivative budget

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: For a globally smooth function and a list $w$ of constant directions, the repeated directional derivative equals the iterated Fréchet derivative evaluated on those directions in the same order. The list length sets the derivative order. This identity converts the coordinate-word representation of hierarchy norms into an operator-norm estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: Ordered constant derivatives equal Fréchet derivative evaluation

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: The cosine factor $\cos(2\pi a_2)$ of the second label coordinate is unchanged by any integer lattice translation of the label. The formalization numbers coordinates from zero, so this coordinate carries index one there. This scalar periodicity is the starting point for periodicity of the shear sweep and the explicit first-wave seed.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: The initial shear repeats across the lattice

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: At each fixed time $t$, the scalar sweep $t\cdot2\pi\cos(2\pi a_2)$ is spatially periodic in the label $a$. Multiplication of the periodic cosine by its time-dependent scalar preserves every integer translation. This statement places no restriction on time and does not assert periodicity in time; it supplies the spatial hypothesis for later uniform derivative bounds.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: The shear sweep repeats across the lattice

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: At every real time, the normalized pressure coefficient is spatially periodic. The proof combines periodicity of the sweep with periodicity of the cosine in the numerator. This concerns the scalar coefficient before multiplication by the envelope and the phase primitive, rather than the complete physical pressure.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: The normalized pressure repeats across the lattice

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: The centered label cell has uniquely determined derivatives within it at every one of its points. The argument uses convexity and a nonempty interior containing a ball around the origin. This property permits equality of smooth functions on the entire closed cell to identify their ambient derivatives even at its boundary.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: Derivatives on the closed cell are uniquely determined

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: A time-label field smooth on the slab and spatially periodic at every time is embedded as a phase-independent twisted profile. The carrier $k$ is arbitrary because the function ignores the phase shift. The constructor composes with the time-label projection and then takes the established zero-extension representative.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: Insert a periodic material coefficient into the hierarchy

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: At a slab point $(t,a,s)$, the embedded twisted coefficient evaluates to $f(t,a)$. The phase coordinate disappears because the construction uses only time and label. This equality removes the zero-extension branch using the assumption that the point lies in the slab, and makes the original coefficient available in concrete hierarchy equations.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: Read the original time-label coefficient on the slab

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The twisted profile obtained from a global time-label field is phase independent on the slab. Evaluating at any two phases gives the same original field value. This theorem supplies the independence hypothesis used to interpret means and prove cancellation of mean-driven phase advection.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: Embedded material coefficients do not depend on phase

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: If a smooth spatially periodic time-label field is even in labels at each slab time, its phase-independent twisted embedding has joint reflection multiplier one. The phase component contributes nothing because the embedding ignores it. Off-slab zero extension preserves the same symmetry.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: Even material coefficients remain even in the joint coordinates

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The explicit inverse deformation is infinitely differentiable as a function of time and label. The proof combines the smooth material-gradient field with multiplication by time and subtraction from the identity. No inverse-function theorem or determinant lower bound is needed for this explicit polynomial-in-time formula.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The inverse shear deformation is jointly smooth

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The label-dependent material gradient is infinitely differentiable for every shear parameter $s$. It is a smooth cosine factor times a fixed bounded linear map. This coefficient regularity is used when embedding the first-wave hierarchy data into the smooth time-label-phase profile space.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The material shear coefficient is smooth in labels

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The explicit primary pressure is jointly smooth when $\lambda\ne0$ and $0<h\le1$. Nonzero frequency makes the transported covector nonzero everywhere, so its squared norm can be divided into a smooth coefficient. Smoothness of the phase primitive then gives the full pressure regularity.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The unwrapped primary pressure is jointly smooth

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: Under $0<h\le1$, the primary velocity before localization is infinitely differentiable jointly in time, label, and phase. The smooth seed depends on time and label, while the scalar wave profile depends on phase. Multiplication preserves smoothness, independently of any frequency or support choices.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The unwrapped primary velocity is jointly smooth

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The first-wave material gradient is unchanged by label negation. Its only label dependence is through a cosine of the second coordinate, and cosine is even. This supplies the symmetry of the parent coefficient needed for the hierarchy’s reflection propagation, without imposing a bound on the shear parameter.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The material shear gradient is even in the label

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The explicit amplitude operator, material-gradient term, and pressure-gradient coefficient sum to zero at every label and phase. This is an algebraic identity in the total definitions and requires no nonzero-frequency hypothesis. Analytic identification of its first term with a time derivative is established separately under nonzero frequency.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: Cancel the affine amplitude and pressure terms at one label

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: For $0<h\le1$, the phase derivative of the localized leading pressure at phase $z$ is its phase-independent coefficient times the scalar wave profile at $z$. The radius and frequency are otherwise unrestricted in this derivative statement. It differentiates only the phase primitive, so no covector denominator is being differentiated.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The pressure primitive differentiates back to the wave

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: For nonzero frequency, the time derivative of the localized leading profile is the fixed radial and phase factors times the affine amplitude operator $b\mapsto-Mb+2\langle k,Mb\rangle k/|k|^2$ applied to its seed, with $M$ the material shear gradient and $k$ the transported covector. The label and phase are held fixed. This supplies the time part of the first-wave momentum identity before lattice wrapping.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The leading velocity evolves by the seed equation

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: This pressure is minus the first-wave pressure coefficient times the mean-zero phase primitive of the wave profile. The coefficient uses the actual transported covector, smooth seed, and material gradient. The radial envelope is omitted here and applied before wrapping the profile into the lattice-compatible space.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The primary pressure before spatial localization

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: This is the scalar wave profile in phase multiplied by the explicit smooth first-wave seed at the chosen time and label. The radial envelope has not yet been applied. The definition also carries no activation switch, because the first wave is fully present at time zero.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The primary oscillation before spatial localization

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: A spatially periodic field has the same value at a label $a$ and at its centered representative in the unit cell. The centered representative differs from the original label by an explicit integer lattice vector. This identity allows wrapped oscillatory profiles to interact with coefficient fields evaluated at the original label.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: A periodic coefficient agrees at its centered label

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: For $0<h\le1$, the unwrapped pressure has period one in phase. Its coefficient is independent of phase, while the pressure primitive is periodic. The theorem does not require nonzero frequency because it proves periodicity of the total expression, rather than smoothness of its coefficient in the labels.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The unwrapped primary pressure has unit phase period

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: For $0<h\le1$, the unwrapped primary velocity is periodic in its phase variable with period one. Time and label are fixed, so the smooth seed is a constant vector in this assertion. Periodicity is inherited solely from the scalar wave profile.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The unwrapped primary velocity has unit phase period

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: For $0<h\le1$, translating the scalar wave profile by any real phase offset preserves its zero phase mean. Integration over a whole period is unchanged by the starting point. This removes the carrier-dependent phase shift when the wrapped leading velocity is averaged.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: A shifted phase profile still has zero mean

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The transported covector is spatially periodic at every time. The inverse-deformation matrix repeats on the label lattice, and its adjoint is applied to the same constant launch covector. This provides ordinary coefficient periodicity before the oscillatory velocity is placed in the carrier-twisted space.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The transported first-wave covector is label periodic

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: At each fixed time, the explicit inverse deformation is spatially periodic in the label. The identity term is constant and the material-gradient term is periodic. This property concerns the derivative matrix; the shear flow itself is lattice equivariant rather than a spatially periodic map.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The inverse deformation repeats with the label lattice

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The material gradient is spatially periodic for every shear parameter. Translating the second label coordinate by an integer changes the cosine angle by an integer multiple of $2\pi$, leaving the matrix unchanged. This periodicity permits the coefficient to be embedded into any carrier-twisted profile space.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The material shear coefficient repeats on the lattice

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: For a nonzero vector $a$, the absolute value of $-\langle a,Ba\rangle/|a|^2$ is at most the operator norm of $B$. Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator norm bound give the numerator estimate. The explicit nonzero assumption guarantees the denominator is positive before cancellation.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: The logarithmic amplitude rate is bounded by the operator norm

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: A nonzero transverse solution of the affine amplitude equation satisfies $|a(u)|e^{-\|B\|(v-u)}\le|a(v)|$ for ordered slab times. The proof integrates a bound on the logarithmic norm derivative. Unlike the upper estimate, this statement explicitly assumes, at every slab time, that the amplitude is nonzero and perpendicular to the covector.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: A transverse amplitude cannot decay too quickly

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: Any solution of the affine amplitude equation with constant matrix $B$ satisfies $|b(v)|\le|b(u)|e^{\|B\|(v-u)}$ for ordered times in $[0,T]$. The reflected-vector identity bounds the derivative norm, and Grönwall gives the estimate. No transversality or nonvanishing hypothesis is required for this upper bound.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: The amplitude grows at most exponentially

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: The local abbreviation denotes the $i$th Euclidean coordinate vector with coefficient one. The formalization indexes these three directions by $0,1,2$, so index zero corresponds to the paper’s $e_1$. This supplies the initial wave vector and transverse amplitude in the stationary-shear construction, without making any claim about their subsequent evolution.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: Coordinate directions for the first shear

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: Every coordinate axis used for the initial wave is nonzero. The proof applies the preceding unit-norm identity, so no geometric nondegeneracy assumption is needed. The result discharges the initial-data requirements of the affine wave existence theorem before frequency and amplitude scales are attached.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: The initial coordinate directions are nonzero

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: For a real number between zero and one quarter, its exponential is at most two. The proof uses a quantitative bound on $|e^x-1|$. In the first-wave estimate the argument is twice the accumulated shear norm, so the short-time hypothesis turns exponential comparison into the fixed factor two.

At a point where the amplitude is nonzero and perpendicular to the covector, the derivative of $\log|a|$ is $-\langle a,Ba\rangle/|a|^2$. The amplitude equation is supplied as a derivative within an arbitrary set. Transversality cancels the covector correction in the derivative of $|a|^2$, and nonvanishing justifies differentiating the logarithm.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: The logarithmic amplitude has a quadratic rate

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: The chosen Euclidean coordinate vector has norm one for every index $0,1,2$. The statement concerns the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^3$, not a componentwise bound. It provides the nonzero initial directions and the exact normalization used to compute the first wave’s initial strength and frame.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: Every coordinate direction has unit length

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: The vector $-w+2(k\cdot w)k/|k|^2$ has the same norm as $w$. The formalization proves the identity using reflection in the span of $k$. No nonzero hypothesis on $k$ appears: at $k=0$, the quotient by $|k|^2$ is assigned the value zero and the expression is simply $-w$, whose norm is still correct.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: Reflecting the amplitude preserves its length

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: Given orthonormal vectors $x$ and $y$, a linear combination whose coefficients have the same squares as the corresponding components of $z$ has norm at most $|z|$. Independent sign changes are allowed. This finite-dimensional estimate controls the moving-frame derivatives by the norm of the shear acting on a unit vector.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: Two signed orthogonal components do not increase length

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: The constant gradient matrix of the stationary shear has trace zero for every real shear parameter. The proof expands the trace in the Euclidean basis. This algebraic form of incompressibility allows the affine moving-frame equations to be applied when estimating the first coupling throughout the initial wave window.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: The stationary shear matrix has zero trace

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Names the Euclidean coordinate vector with unit coefficient at the chosen index $0$, $1$ or $2$. The explicit seed formulas use these vectors to separate the rational first two components from the arctangent third component. Indices zero, one and two represent the paper’s first, second and third coordinate directions.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: The coordinate vectors of the first-wave formulas

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: The $j$th component of the $i$th coordinate vector is one when $j=i$ and zero otherwise. This identity unfolds the Euclidean-space representation used for $\mathbb R^3$. It lets the explicit stationary-shear calculations work component by component without changing the normed vector space in which the ODE is formulated.

The pointwise cross product of two smooth vector fields on time and label space is smooth. The proof expands each component into products and differences of scalar coordinate functions. This is the elementary regularity step for the numerator of the localized vector potential.

Fixing a time in the jointly smooth first-wave potential gives a smooth spatial vector potential. The assumptions remain nonzero frequency, positive radius, a strict cell collar and $0<h\le1$. This slice result supplies the twice differentiable potential needed for the divergence-of-curl identity.

At a fixed time, the first potential profile is smooth jointly in its label and independent phase. Nonzero frequency controls the inverse-square covector, while positive radius and $0<h\le1$ provide smooth envelope and primitive. A cell collar is unnecessary here because this statement precedes periodization.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: The first potential is smooth in label and phase

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Lists the three components of the first coordinate vector as $(1,0,0)$. The statement uses index zero in the formalization's numbering $0,1,2$ of coordinates, corresponding to $e_1$ in the manuscript. These component identities enter the explicit transported-covector formula and the computation of the first component of the smooth seed.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: Components of the first coordinate direction

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Defines the vector with components $cz/(1+z^2)$, $c/(1+z^2)$ and $-sc\arctan z$. Here $s$ is the shear parameter and $c$ is the initial amplitude scale. The formula supplies a smooth label-dependent solution once the accumulated shear is substituted; its ODE identity is proved later.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: An explicit amplitude in the shear variable

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Expands the vector-valued seed at sweep $z$ into its two rational components and its arctangent component. The identity holds for all real parameters, because the denominator $1+z^2$ never vanishes. It is used both in the ODE calculation and in the direct proof that a nonzero scale gives a nonzero seed.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: Read the three explicit amplitude components

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Computes the derivative of the explicit amplitude with respect to $z$: the first two entries have denominator $(1+z^2)^2$, and the third is $-sc/(1+z^2)$. All real parameters are allowed. The time-derivative proof later multiplies this vector by the local shear rate through the chain rule.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: Differentiate the explicit amplitude in the shear variable

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Lists the three components of the second coordinate vector as $(0,1,0)$. This is the initial amplitude direction for the first wave, represented by index one in Lean. The explicit seed’s second component then gives a direct nonvanishing proof whenever its scale is nonzero.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: Components of the initial amplitude direction

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Lists the three components of the third coordinate vector as $(0,0,1)$. The statement supplies the component simplifications for the arctangent term of the explicit seed. This direction carries the shear parameter in the first-wave amplitude, while the transported covector has no component in it.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: Components of the third coordinate direction

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Multiplies the smooth raw coefficient by the smooth radial envelope to obtain smoothness of the localized coefficient at each fixed time. Nonzero frequency and positive radius are explicit assumptions. This is the regularity needed by the pressure product rule; the separate support restriction for its sign is not needed for smoothness.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The localized first pressure coefficient is smooth

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: For a nonzero carrier frequency, proves smoothness in the spatial labels of the first pressure coefficient before multiplication by the radial envelope. The explicit stationary formula has denominator $(1+\mathrm{sweep}^2)^2$, which is everywhere positive. The result is for each fixed time and does not supply a uniform derivative bound.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The uncut first pressure coefficient is smooth

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Chooses a nonnegative constant bounding the coefficient and its first two derivatives after rescaling labels by the envelope radius. For normalized first-wave data, positive frequency, radius in $(0,1]$ and a slab of duration at most one, the bound is $K\lambda^{-7/4}$. The constant is selected before the first-wave data, radius and time.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: Two scaled label derivatives retain the pressure decay

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Defines the scalar coefficient multiplying the first pressure primitive, from the radial envelope, transported covector, smooth seed and stationary material gradient. All arguments are arbitrary reals at this definition site. Its sign and smoothness are proved later under explicit carrier and support assumptions; they are not consequences of the name or of the bare formula.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The envelope multiplies the first pressure coefficient

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Factors the radial envelope from the pressure coefficient, leaving the same coefficient evaluated with envelope value one. The statement is an algebraic identity and has no positivity or nonvanishing hypotheses. It allows the subsequent sign argument and scaled derivative estimate to treat the cutoff and raw stationary-wave coefficient separately.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The envelope factors out of the pressure coefficient

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Proves nonnegativity for nonnegative seed scale, positive frequency and radius, with $2r\le1/4$. Outside the envelope the coefficient vanishes. Inside it, the second label coordinate lies where the stationary shear's cosine is nonnegative. This smaller support requirement is stronger than the condition needed merely to periodize the envelope.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The first pressure coefficient is nonnegative on its envelope

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Sets the fixed geometric constant to $(1+8\pi^2)(1+4\pi)$. The two factors bound a derivative of the stationary inverse deformation and the deformation itself on the unit time interval. This is a constant used to estimate the first pressure phase and the rescaled inverse flow, not a bound containing the wave frequency.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: A fixed constant controls the first inverse flow

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: For tilt of absolute value at most one and time in $[0,1]$, bounds the label derivative of the inverse-flow Jacobian pulled back along the forward flow by $1+8\pi^2$. The proof differentiates the explicit cosine factor in the stationary shear. This is a bound for one derivative of the coframe, not for the whole hierarchy.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The first inverse deformation has a uniform label derivative

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Given a smooth coefficient $p$, a smooth inverse-label map $A$, a two-jet bound for the scaled labels and derivative bounds for the scaled inverse map, bounds $p\circ A$, its gradient and Hessian by $2KB^2r^{-2}\lambda^{-7/4}$. Positive radius and frequency make the rescaling identities valid. This theorem is conditional calculus, independent of the choice of first wave.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: Label pressure bounds transfer through the inverse flow

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: For a positive slab of duration at most one, small tilt, positive frequency and radius at most one, bounds the physical phase gradient and Hessian by a fixed constant times frequency. It also controls the first two derivatives of the radius-rescaled inverse flow. These estimates supply the chain-rule factors when the label pressure is read in Eulerian coordinates.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The first pressure phase and inverse labels have two-jet bounds

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Identifies the entire phase-dependent first pressure profile with the negative of the label coefficient times the periodic pressure primitive. This separates slow label dependence from rapid phase dependence. The equality itself is algebraic and holds without the positivity assumptions used later to derive a one-sided Hessian bound.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The first pressure is a signed coefficient times a primitive

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: For times on the closed slab, identifies the graph readout of the first pressure profile with its localized transported expression. The inverse-label map $A$ is arbitrary here. Positive radius, cell margin, nonzero frequency and phase width in $(0,1]$ are the hypotheses needed by the wrapped pressure representation.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: Reading the first pressure gives the localized pressure

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Shows that each factor of the chosen inverse-flow constant is at least one, hence so is their product. The estimate allows uniform use of monotonicity for low-order powers in the pressure composition argument. It is a numerical fact about the fixed constant and has no wave or stage hypotheses.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The fixed inverse-flow constant is at least one

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: For a nonnegative coefficient at the point, two derivatives of the coefficient of size $K\lambda^{-7/4}$, and phase derivatives bounded by $B\lambda$, proves an upper quadratic-form bound of order $K\lambda^{-1/4}$. The leading rank-one tensor uses the lower bound for the profile slope. This is one-sided control; it does not bound the absolute Hessian norm by the same rate.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The Hessian of the signed pressure product is bounded above by a multiple of $K\lambda^{-1/4}$ as a quadratic form

_private.TorusEuler.FlowDeterminant.0.To.text: Represent a continuous linear endomorphism of three-dimensional Euclidean space by its matrix in the standard coordinate basis. This finite-dimensional conversion allows determinant and trace calculations to use matrix identities before returning to the coordinate-free linear map. No invertibility or determinant condition is built into the definition.

The $(i,j)$ entry of the coordinate matrix of $A$ is the $i$th component of the image of the $j$th standard basis vector under $A$. This makes the matrix convention explicit and fixes which index is the input coordinate when translating the variational equation to entries.

The coordinate matrix of the composition $A\circ F$ is the product of the matrices of $A$ and $F$, in that order. This identity holds for arbitrary continuous linear endomorphisms. It lets the vector-space variational equation $F'=MF$ be read as the matrix equation needed by the determinant computation.

If every matrix entry has within-set derivative given by the corresponding entry of $Af(t)$, then the determinant has derivative $\operatorname{tr}(A)\det f(t)$. This three-dimensional identity does not assume the matrix is invertible. It therefore establishes the volume evolution before a determinant-one conclusion is available.

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: A jointly smooth function on $[0,T]$ times a normed spatial domain has a jointly smooth spatial derivative on the same slab, provided $T>0$ makes the interval nondegenerate. Spatial increments remain inside the domain even at temporal endpoints. The result concerns the derivative of each spatial slice, not an arbitrary extension in time.

A jointly smooth field on the product slab remains smooth as a function of space after fixing any time in the slab. The conclusion is smoothness of all orders on the full spatial space. It is stronger than pointwise differentiability but makes no assertion outside the supplied time interval.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: Every time slice retains all spatial derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: Joint smoothness on the time slab implies ordinary differentiability of the spatial slice at every time $t$ of the slab. Time is fixed before differentiating, so the conclusion is valid on all spatial points and does not require an interior time. This supplies elementary differentiability for the higher variational chain rules.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: Every smooth time slice is differentiable

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: Any ordered partition of a positive number of slots with exactly one block is the explicitly constructed whole-slot partition. The statement is combinatorial and carries the positive-order hypothesis $n\ge1$. It lets the composition expansion remove exactly one linear term, with no ambiguity about its block embedding or ordering.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: A one-block partition is uniquely determined

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: For a strictly positive order $n$, construct the ordered partition with a single block containing all derivative slots. This isolates the term linear in the highest derivative of the inner function in the Faà di Bruno formula. The hypothesis $n\ge1$ guarantees that the sole block is nonempty.

For a positive order $n$, the one-block contribution to composition of formal Taylor series is the first derivative of the outer function composed with the $n$th derivative of the inner function. This is an identity between total derivative expressions. Smoothness assumptions enter later when those formal terms are identified with an actual composition derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: The one-block term is the highest linear variation

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: The Grönwall expression is homogeneous when its initial bound and forcing bound are multiplied by the same scalar $d$. This exact identity includes the zero-rate case. It isolates the size of a parameter increment from the remaining constants in the local trajectory comparison used for spatial differentiability.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: The Grönwall bound is homogeneous in its data

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: Applying a continuous linear map $L$ to a curve with within-set derivative $u'$ gives within-set derivative $Lu'$. The source and target are arbitrary real normed spaces. This transports ODE identities for operator-valued or multilinear-valued curves to their fixed evaluations without changing the time domain.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: Linear evaluation commutes with time differentiation

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: For a function differentiable on a closed slab, fixing any time in the slab yields a Fréchet derivative in the spatial variable. The derivative is the within-slab derivative composed with the spatial inclusion. This permits higher spatial differentiation without requiring the time coordinate to lie in the interior.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: Fixing time leaves an ordinary spatial derivative

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: On a convex set $s$, differentiability and a Lipschitz derivative bound imply a quadratic first-order Taylor remainder between any two points of $s$. The derivative is an ordinary Fréchet derivative, while the Lipschitz hypothesis restricts its estimate to the set. This local form supports the compact-neighborhood argument for differentiating trajectory families.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: Quadratic Taylor control on a convex domain

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: For an ordered partition of $n$ derivative slots, summing the sizes of all blocks gives exactly $n$. The covering and disjointness properties of the partition supply this identity. It is the exponent-counting input that turns a product of lower-order deformation estimates into the required bound at order $n$.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: Partition block sizes exhaust the derivative order

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: For a normed-space curve with a within-interval derivative satisfying the stated affine growth inequality, its norm at every allowed time is bounded by the Grönwall expression at the full terminal time $T$. Nonnegativity of $K$ and $\varepsilon$ allows this replacement. The initial norm bound is retained as the parameter $\delta$.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: A full-interval bound for vector-valued growth

_private.TorusEuler.FlowSecondVariation..text: Integer lattice translation leaves the Fréchet derivative of a periodic function unchanged. The statement needs no differentiability assumption because it follows from equality of translated functions and the derivative’s translation rule. Later applications separately establish smoothness before interpreting these derivatives as classical spatial gradients.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowSecondVariation..summary: The derivative of a periodic field is periodic

_private.TorusEuler.FlowSecondVariation..text: For operator-valued functions, differentiating $f(q)g(q)$ at a point with $f(p)=0$ needs a derivative only for $f$ and continuity for $g$. The derivative is the derivative of $f$ postcomposed with the fixed operator $g(p)$. This removes a circular differentiability assumption when differentiating the fundamental solution’s parameter-difference formula.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowSecondVariation..summary: A vanishing factor needs only continuity of its partner

_private.TorusEuler.FlowSecondVariation..text: For a field differentiable on a closed time slab, its spatial slice at an admissible time has a Fréchet derivative obtained by composing the within-slab derivative with the spatial inclusion. Spatial points are unrestricted. This isolates spatial differentiation from the one-sided time behavior at the slab endpoints.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowSecondVariation..summary: A spatial slice inherits the slab derivative

_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.text: The lifted torus mode at $-y$ equals the complex exponential with phase $-2\pi\langle y,k\rangle$. This fixes the sign and normalization matching the whole-space Fourier transform. It is the algebraic bridge between a periodic character and the Fourier multiplier obtained by integrating the Euclidean kernel.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.summary: The reversed character is the Fourier-transform factor

_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.text: The Fourier character at $x-y$ is the product of its values at $x$ and $-y$. This identity uses the integer lattice frequency $k$ and the exponential definition of the lifted torus mode. It separates the output location from the integration variable in the convolution calculation.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.summary: A translated Fourier mode factors into two characters

_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.text: If a real symbol vanishes whenever the frequency norm exceeds two, its complex-valued version has compact support. The proof contains the support in the closed radius-two ball of Euclidean three-space. This creates the compactness input needed to regard a smooth cutoff symbol as a Schwartz function.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.summary: A bounded support condition survives complexification

_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.text: For positive $\Lambda$, the integral of $\Lambda^3g(\Lambda y)$ over Euclidean three-space equals the integral of $g$. The declaration is an equality of vector-valued integral expressions and has no explicit integrability premise. It supplies the change-of-variables identity underlying all normalized kernel scaling formulas.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.summary: Dimensionally normalized dilation preserves the integral
