_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.text: For a positive cutoff frequency $\Lambda$ and a symbol $\psi$ supported in the radius-two ball, applying the smooth Fourier cutoff to a finite Fourier sum multiplies its $k$th coefficient by $\psi(k/\Lambda)$, the symbol at the rescaled lattice frequency. This statement concerns a finite polynomial and does not yet identify a convolution kernel.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.summary: The cutoff weights each Fourier coefficient by its symbol

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: A finite sum of torus Fourier characters with fixed amplitudes is continuous in any complex normed target. Each term is a continuous scalar character multiplying a constant vector, and finite addition preserves continuity. This supplies the continuous-map packaging used in Fourier uniqueness arguments for spectral cutoffs.

The map from Euclidean three-space to the product unit torus is continuous because every coordinate map to the additive circle is continuous. This structural fact supplies measurability and continuity for lifted or translated torus fields inside convolution integrals. It does not assert differentiability of the quotient map as a Euclidean-valued function.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: The Euclidean to torus quotient map is continuous

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: Two complex continuous torus functions are equal if all their Fourier coefficients agree. The proof embeds them into scalar L² and uses injectivity of Fourier coordinates, then returns to continuous functions using full support of Haar measure. This provides pointwise function equality, not only an almost-everywhere identification.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: Complex continuous torus functions are determined by coefficients

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: The Fréchet derivative of a Euclidean Fourier wave at $x$, applied to $v$, equals the same wave multiplied by $2\pi i\langle k,v\rangle$. The integer frequency is read as the corresponding vector of $\mathbb R^3$. This formula links the torus character convention to the real-space kernel derivative symbol.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: Differentiating a Fourier wave yields its directional frequency factor

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: The Euclidean Fourier transform of $K$ at lattice frequency $k$ equals the integral of $K$ multiplied by the negative-frequency torus character of the Euclidean integration variable. The formula fixes the transform sign convention. It is an identity between integral expressions and does not itself certify integrability of an arbitrary $K$.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: Sampling the Euclidean transform uses the negative torus character

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: For a list of $j$ directions, the Fourier transform of the iterated Schwartz-kernel derivative is the original transform times the product of all directional symbols. The empty list gives the original transform. Induction preserves the order convention and supplies the Fourier calculation underlying higher-order Bernstein estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: Repeated kernel derivatives multiply all directional symbols

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: The Fourier transform of a directional derivative of a Schwartz kernel in direction $v$ equals its transform at $\xi$ multiplied by $2\pi i\langle\xi,v\rangle$. Schwartz regularity and decay justify the derivative-transform identity. The result tracks the sign and $2\pi$ convention needed when derivatives are moved from a band-limited function to its convolution kernel.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: A directional kernel derivative multiplies the Fourier transform

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: The scalar symbol is $2\pi i\langle\xi,v\rangle$, using the Fourier convention of the paper. It records the factor obtained when differentiating in direction $v$. The definition accepts arbitrary real frequency and direction vectors and contains no projection, denominator, or nonzero-frequency condition.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: The Fourier factor for one directional derivative

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: Differentiate the Euclidean lift of a finite Fourier synthesis in direction $v$. The result is the same finite synthesis with each amplitude multiplied by its directional symbol. The input is a finite set of frequencies, so no convergence or interchange of infinite series is required.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: A directional derivative acts on every finite Fourier amplitude

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: A continuous complex-linear scalar functional applied to a continuous torus field commutes with taking its Fourier coefficient. The proof moves the functional through the Bochner integral and uses complex linearity for the character factor. This reduces vector-valued Fourier uniqueness to scalar Fourier uniqueness.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: Scalar linear functionals commute with Fourier coefficients

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: For each lattice frequency, evaluating the torus character at $z+w$ gives the product of its values at $z$ and $w$. This character law is used when translating the Haar integration variable in the convolution coefficient calculation. It is an exact algebraic identity valid at every torus point.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: Fourier characters turn spatial addition into multiplication

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: Taking the torus image of $x-y$ equals subtracting their torus images. The coordinate quotient homomorphisms supply the equality. This identifies a Euclidean convolution evaluated on periodic lifts with torus translation by the image of its integration variable, without choosing special representatives of torus points.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: The quotient map preserves subtraction of spatial points

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: An increment bound $\|f(x+v)-f(x)\|\le D\sqrt{\|v\|}$ with $D\ge0$ proves both boundedness of the quotient range and seminorm at most $D$. The proof separates the zero-increment case from positive denominators. It converts convolution increment estimates into the Hölder bounds in the form the regularity condition requires.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: A uniform increment estimate bounds the seminorm

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: If $k\le M$, the loss-$k$ tail constant is bounded by one plus the sum of absolute kernel moments through order $M$. Nonnegativity allows the relevant moment to be selected from the finite sum. This produces one constant valid for every output order below a fixed input regularity.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: One finite moment sum controls every smaller loss

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: The tail constant is nonnegative for every loss order. The proof combines nonnegativity of the absolute kernel moment with the extra zero-order term, which is either zero or one. This supplies a sign needed when comparing the derivative-level norm to the total input norm.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: The loss-dependent tail constant is nonnegative

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: The absolute moment of any order of a Schwartz kernel is nonnegative because both the distance power and kernel norm are nonnegative pointwise. This sign fact permits comparison and summation of the kernel constants in the uniform tail bound. It does not assert strict positivity for a potentially zero kernel.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: Every absolute kernel moment is nonnegative

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: The norm of the $n$th iterated derivative of the $j$th derivative equals the norm at total order $j+n$. The equality uses the isometric identifications between nested multilinear-map spaces. It is stated without differentiability hypotheses, as an identity of the derivative expressions, which are zero where no derivative exists; substantive derivative estimates still require regularity.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: Nested derivative norms equal the combined-order norm

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: Under $C^{j+n}$ regularity, differences of nested iterated derivatives at two points have the same norm as differences of the derivative of total order $j+n$. The proof applies the norm identity to a translated difference of functions. This preserves the half-Hölder increment estimate when derivatives are regrouped in the cutoff argument.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: Nested derivative increments preserve their norm

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: For a continuous torus field whose lift has order-$(s+k)$ half-Hölder regularity, the cutoff tail has order $s$ and norm bounded by $C_{s+k}\Lambda^{-k}$ times the input norm. The symbol is smooth, compactly supported and one near zero, while $\Lambda$ is positive. The proof applies the lifted remainder estimate to every derivative through order $s$.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: The tail loses a prescribed number of derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: For a field $f$ with order-$m$ spatial half-Hölder regularity, the supremum norm plus half-Hölder seminorm of the $j$th derivative is bounded by the full order-$m$ norm whenever $j\le m$. Every summand is nonnegative because the regularity condition provides boundedness. This permits a tail estimate at one derivative order to use the common input norm.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: Each derivative level is controlled by the full norm

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: For a field with bounded half-Hölder quotient range, the real seminorm is nonnegative. The zero increment contributes quotient zero, and the conditional supremum is at least this value. This supplies the sign condition needed when multiplying or summing the derivative-level bounds in the tail estimate.

For a smooth cutoff equal to one on the unit ball and supported in radius two, bounds the supremum and half-Hölder seminorm of $g-K_\Lambda*g$ by $\Lambda^{-k}$ times the corresponding top-derivative norm and a kernel moment constant. Positive $\Lambda$, bounded input, and bounded top derivative and increment quotients are explicit hypotheses. The zero-loss case uses the elementary convolution bound.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: Taylor cancellation bounds the lifted convolution tail

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: For a field with bounded norm range, its real supremum norm is nonnegative. The proof compares the supremum with the norm at the origin. The boundedness hypothesis is kept explicit because the definition uses a conditional real supremum, not an extended-real supremum that automatically records infinity.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: A bounded spatial supremum is nonnegative

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: Multiply a Schwartz kernel by a coordinate monomial $y_{\iota_1}\cdots y_{\iota_j}$, with each $\iota_m\in\{1,2,3\}$; the result is integrable. Repeated coordinates are allowed. The proof bounds the absolute product by $\|y\|^j$ and uses Schwartz moment integrability, providing the integrability needed before expanding and integrating Taylor terms.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: Every coordinate monomial is integrable against a Schwartz kernel

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: For the normalized smooth cutoff kernel at positive scale, its product with the finite Taylor polynomial is integrable and has integral $f(x)$. This theorem does not require smoothness of $f$: every positive homogeneous term cancels regardless of its coefficient, and the degree-zero term is the value. A genuine remainder estimate needs additional regularity.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: Integrating the Taylor polynomial returns the center value

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: For any continuous multilinear map $A$, the function $K(y)A(y,\ldots,y)$ is integrable when $K$ is Schwartz. The operator norm bounds the multilinear evaluation by $\|A\|\|y\|^j$. This result applies even when $A$ is not the derivative of a function, which is useful for the algebraic Taylor-polynomial integration step.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: Schwartz kernels make every homogeneous multilinear term integrable

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: For a function of class $C^n$ and $j\le n$, the $j$th derivative of $t\mapsto f(x+ty)$ equals the $j$th Fréchet derivative of $f$ at that point evaluated repeatedly on $y$. The explicit order hypothesis prevents reading derivative expressions outside their justified regularity range.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: Derivatives along a line are repeated directional derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: Form the finite sum through degree $n$ of $1/j!$ times the order-$j$ Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$, evaluated on copies of $-y$. This defines the polynomial used to approximate $f(x-y)$. The definition accepts arbitrary $f$; smoothness enters the remainder estimate, not the finite algebraic expression.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: The Taylor polynomial for translating by minus y

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: A continuous $j$-linear map evaluated on $j$ copies of $y$ equals the sum over all coordinate selections of the corresponding monomial times its basis evaluation. This is a finite algebraic identity with no differentiability requirement. It converts directional Taylor terms into coordinate moments whose cancellation is already available.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: Expand a diagonal multilinear term into coordinate monomials

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: If $f$ is $C^{n+1}$ and its order-$(n+1)$ derivative has global norm bound $M$, the error in the translated Taylor polynomial is at most $M\|y\|^{n+1}$. The proof reduces to a one-dimensional line segment and discards a favorable factorial denominator. The estimate is valid globally because the derivative bound is assumed at every point.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: A bounded next derivative controls the Taylor remainder

_private.TorusEuler.FrameCouplingVariati.text: An orthonormal frame whose axes have speed at most $2M$ on $[t_0,t_1]$, together with a matrix field bounded by $M$ and derivative bounded by $D$, has each frame entry vary by at most $(4M^2+D)(t_1-t_0)$. Derivatives are taken within the closed interval. The theorem assumes the frame-speed bounds rather than deriving them from the wave ODEs.
_private.TorusEuler.FrameCouplingVariati.summary: Frame coefficients vary by the gradient and frame-speed budget

_private.TorusEuler.FreezingConcreteMult.text: If $P$ is smooth on a set $s$ and every frozen operator $P(\xi)BP(\xi)+I-P(\xi)$ is a unit there, then its real ring inverse depends smoothly on $\xi$ within $s$. The argument first builds the direct frozen symbol from products and sums, then composes with smooth inversion on the unit set. The unit hypothesis excludes the inverse's default values.

For a symbol smooth away from zero, the constructed real multiplier satisfies an off-support Lipschitz bound when $f$ vanishes on a product-metric ball of radius $r>0$ and the second point lies within $r/4$. The constant is explicit in the annular symbol's derivative mass and the inverse-fourth-power tail. The input factor is the supremum norm $\|f.val.1\|$, not its full half-Hölder norm.
_private.TorusEuler.FreezingConcreteMult.summary: A real multiplier gains local Lipschitz control

_private.TorusEuler.FreezingConcreteSolv.text: For $s\in[0,1]$, a pointwise coercivity bound for $B$ on one vector $v$ gives a bound with constant $\min(1,\mu)$ for the affine coefficient on that vector. No symmetry of $B$ is required by this statement. It is applied on the ranges of the relevant Fourier projections.
_private.TorusEuler.FreezingConcreteSolv.summary: Affine coefficients preserve coercivity on each projected vector

_private.TorusEuler.FreezingConcreteSolv.text: The hypotheses bound the localization remainder by $J₀Q^{36}$ and the reciprocal coercivity factor by $Q$, with all constants nonnegative and $Q\ge1$. The resulting inverse expression is bounded by $4(C+64J₀^4)Q^{145}$. This algebraic estimate explains the concrete exponent used later to realize the paper’s unspecified fixed power.
_private.TorusEuler.FreezingConcreteSolv.summary: The assembled inverse bound has exponent one hundred forty five

_private.TorusEuler.FreezingConcreteSolv.text: Assume the nonnegative constants $C,K,L,M$ and the size conditions $Q\ge1$, $L\le Q$ and $1+M\le Q$. For the radius $r=R^{-2}$ with $R=1+16CQ^{11}L$ and the distant bound, the lower-order localization constant is at most the displayed coefficient $J=1+2K(1+16C)^2+4(1+16C)$ times $Q^{36}$. The theorem accounts for this exponent explicitly; it is a sufficient bound rather than an optimal growth claim.
_private.TorusEuler.FreezingConcreteSolv.summary: Bound the localization remainder by a fixed power

_private.TorusEuler.FreezingConcreteSolv.text: For nonnegative $C$ and $L$, set $R=1+16CL$ and $r=R^{-2}$. The theorem proves $R\ge1$, $0<r\le1$, and $8CL\sqrt r\le1/2$. This explicit choice simultaneously guarantees a meaningful radius and the smallness required by the absorption lemma; no asymptotic choice of radius remains.
_private.TorusEuler.FreezingConcreteSolv.summary: Choose a positive radius that makes the nearby error small

_private.TorusEuler.FreezingContinuation.text: Start from an invertible $A$ with the a priori estimate $\|v\|\le M\|Av\|$ for a nonnegative $M$. If $M\|A-B\|<1$, then $B$ is invertible as a bounded operator. The strict smallness condition is what permits the Neumann argument; a merely non-strict bound is not claimed.
_private.TorusEuler.FreezingContinuation.summary: A sufficiently small step preserves invertibility

_private.TorusEuler.FreezingContinuation.text: Assuming $A$ is invertible, $M\ge0$, and $\|v\|\le M\|Av\|$ for every $v$, the inverse $A^{-1}$ has operator norm at most $M$. The proof applies the estimate to inverse images. The invertibility hypothesis matters: this theorem bounds an already invertible operator and does not infer surjectivity from a lower bound alone.
_private.TorusEuler.FreezingContinuation.summary: An a priori estimate bounds an existing inverse

_private.TorusEuler.FreezingLocalization.text: A continuous field whose values have norm at most a nonnegative $M$, and whose increments satisfy $\|f(x)-f(y)\|\le M\,d(x,y)^{1/2}$, defines a half-Hölder field of norm at most $M$. The value bound and the increment bound control the two components of the endpoint half-Hölder norm. This helper records the bound for the field built from those two bounds.
_private.TorusEuler.FreezingLocalization.summary: Pointwise bounds control the half Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.FreezingSymbol.0.Tor.text: With a symmetric projection $r$, $\mu>0$, and the lower bound $\langle Bv,v\rangle\ge\mu\|v\|^2$ on its range, the bilinear form induced by the frozen operator is coercive. The explicit constant is $\min(1,\mu)$. This packages the preceding quadratic estimate in the form required by the Lax–Milgram theorem.
_private.TorusEuler.FreezingSymbol.0.Tor.summary: Positive projected energy makes the frozen form coercive

_private.TorusEuler.FreezingSymbol.0.Tor.text: For a symmetric projection $r$, the vectors $rv$ and $v-rv$ have zero real inner product. Symmetry transfers one projection across the inner product, and idempotence annihilates the complement. This establishes the orthogonal decomposition needed for the frozen operator energy identity.
_private.TorusEuler.FreezingSymbol.0.Tor.summary: A projected vector is orthogonal to its complement

_private.TorusEuler.FreezingSymbol.0.Tor.text: A symmetric projection $r$ satisfies $r(rv)=rv$ for every vector $v$. This extracts idempotence from the symmetric-projection hypothesis and identifies the range as a space of fixed vectors. It is used to apply coercivity assumptions that are stated only on the projected subspace.
_private.TorusEuler.FreezingSymbol.0.Tor.summary: Every projected vector is fixed by the projection

_private.TorusEuler.FrequencyLattice.0.T.text: The assumption $b\ge1$ implies $15\le K(q)$ for every natural order $q$. This deliberately weak bound follows from the much larger factor $320$ in the exponent definition. It is sufficient for the later comparison of cutoff-tail powers, without requiring positivity of the order itself.
_private.TorusEuler.FrequencyLattice.0.T.summary: Every admissible exponent exceeds the tail threshold

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingAmplitudeNorm.text: If the normalized state is within $\delta\le1/2$ of $(1,0)$ in the product maximum norm, then $|h-1|\le\delta$, $|l|\le\delta$ and $h\ge1/2$. The estimate is pointwise and needs no differential equation. In applications the comparison theorem supplies this closeness, which then prevents the physical second amplitude component from vanishing.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingAmplitudeNorm.summary: Closeness gives a positive normalized amplitude

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingAmplitudePeak.text: For positive $\varepsilon$ and successor ratio $\varepsilon_+$, assume $1/(4\varepsilon_+)\le x\le3/(2\varepsilon_+)$. Then $\sqrt{x/\varepsilon}$ lies between one half and twice $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$. This scalar comparison extracts the time scale needed in the strength estimate once a crossing has provided bounds on $x$.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingAmplitudePeak.summary: The crossing scale controls the square-root factor

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingAmplitudeProp.text: Let $a\in[0,T]$ and $t\in[a,T]$. For a Riccati reference solution initialized by $Y(0)=1$, a continuous triangular-system perturbation bounded by continuous $\rho$, every solution satisfies $\|z(t)\|\le2\|z(a)\|\exp(2\int_a^t\rho)$. The reference data still begin at zero; only the comparison interval begins at $a$.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingAmplitudeProp.summary: The normalized bound starts at any interior time

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.text: For arbitrary vectors, crossing a sum in the first input gives the sum of the two cross products. The result is transported from coordinate linearity to the Euclidean-space representation. It allows expansion of each wave-vector component in the rational coupling formulas.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.summary: The cross product distributes over its first input

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.text: The cross product is additive in its second vector argument. No frame or nonzero-vector hypotheses are needed. The proof rewrites through the coordinate representation, and the resulting identity expands the amplitude components when calculating the new third-axis coupling.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.summary: The cross product distributes over its second input

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.text: Let $(E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be an orthonormal frame in $\mathbb R^3$ with $E_1\times E_2=E_3$. For arbitrary real coordinates $k_i,a_i$, the formal statement proves $(\sum_i k_iE_i)\times(\sum_i a_iE_i)=(k_2a_3-k_3a_2)E_1+(k_3a_1-k_1a_3)E_2+(k_1a_2-k_2a_1)E_3$. Substituting $(k_1,k_2,k_3)=(\zeta_1,\zeta_2/S,\zeta_3)$ and $(a_1,a_2,a_3)=(q/S,1,z/S)$ gives the cross product used in Lemma 2.7. The orientation hypothesis fixes the signs. No differential equation, transversality or nonzero vector hypothesis is required for this coordinate identity. Interpreting these two triples as $k/\lambda$ and $\mathbf a/\alpha_2$ additionally requires nonzero $\lambda,\alpha_2,S$.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.summary: Computes the cross product from six frame coordinates

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.text: The cross product of any Euclidean vector with itself is zero. The proof reduces the statement to the corresponding identity for the coordinate cross product. This removes diagonal terms when expanding the wave vector crossed with the amplitude in the preceding orthonormal frame.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.summary: A vector has zero cross product with itself

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.text: Multiplying the first vector by a real scalar multiplies the cross product by the same scalar. This holds for every scalar, including zero and negative values. The identity extracts wave-coordinate coefficients during the oriented-frame expansion used to compute the coupling numerator.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.summary: A scalar leaves the first cross-product input

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.text: Multiplying the second vector by a real scalar multiplies the cross product by that scalar. The proof uses the coordinate cross product’s linearity. Applied to the amplitude expansion, it separates the component coefficients from the oriented basis-vector cross products.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.summary: A scalar leaves the second cross-product input

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.text: For arbitrary three-dimensional Euclidean vectors, swapping the arguments of the cross product negates the result. The proof transfers the statement to the coordinate cross product on $\mathbb R^3$. This orientation identity is used when expanding the new frame’s third direction in the preceding frame.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.summary: Reversing the cross product reverses its sign

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.text: If $a=c\,v$, both $c$ and $n$ are nonzero, and the supplied norm identity is $\|a\|=cn$, then normalizing $a$ gives $n^{-1}v$. Positivity of $c$ is not assumed here. The norm equality itself supplies the sign consistency needed for cancellation.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.summary: Normalize a vector after factoring its signed scale

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.text: For $S\ne0$, apply a continuous linear map $M$ to the vector $(-w/S)e_0+e_1+(z/S)e_2$. Pairing with the three supplied frame vectors gives $f_0/S,f_1,f_2/S$, where $f$ is the vector of scaled forcing components of $M$ in that frame. Orthonormality is unnecessary for this linear expansion because the matrix entries use the same pairings.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingBound.summary: Strain pairings recover the three forcing coordinates

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.text: Bounds on $|a-a_0|$, $|b|$, $|a_0|$ and $|b-b_0|$ give $|ab-a_0b_0|\le d_A b_{\max}+a_{\max}d_B$. The proof splits the difference into $(a-a_0)b+a_0(b-b_0)$. Nonnegativity needed for multiplication follows from the supplied absolute-value bounds. This avoids separately assuming signs for the error budgets.

The absolute value of $a+b+c$ is at most $|a|+|b|+|c|$ for arbitrary real inputs. The proof applies the triangle inequality twice. This local helper combines the three coordinate contributions to the second normalized coupling numerator.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.summary: Three summands obey the triangle inequality

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.text: For arbitrary real factors, the difference $ab-a_0b_0$ is bounded by $|a|\,|b-b_0|+|a-a_0|\,|b_0|$. This unconditional inequality chooses the actual first factor and reference second factor. It supplies a convenient form of the product rule for the longer second numerator.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.summary: A product difference splits into two absolute errors

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.text: The difference between $a-b+c$ and $a_0-b_0+c_0$ is bounded by the sum of the three component differences. The middle minus sign contributes no additional factor after taking absolute values. This form matches the three signed products in the second coupling numerator.

For positive $a$ and $b$, this auxiliary identity rewrites $|a^{-1}-b^{-1}|$ as $|a-b|/(ab)$. The two strict positivity assumptions justify clearing denominators and removing their absolute values. It is used for the square-root denominators of the normalized couplings.

For $a\ge1$, the reciprocal error satisfies $|a^{-1}-1|\le a-1$. The lower bound makes $a$ positive and limits division by it. Applied to the amplitude normalization factor and its square, this controls both coupling denominators from their squared-norm corrections.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.summary: Reciprocals near one have no larger error

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.text: If the reference coordinates lie in a box of radius $R/2$, $|y|\le1$, $R\ge4$ and actual errors are at most $0\le\kappa\le1/2$, then $Z\ge1/2$. The derived coordinate $z=(Xw-Q)/Z$ satisfies $|z|\le6R$ and $|z-(xy-q_0)|\le8R\kappa$. Additional bounds on $X,Q,Z,w$ are returned for the numerator estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.summary: The third amplitude coordinate stays controlled

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.text: For coordinates in the stated radius-$R$ box, $Z\ge1/2$ and inverse-square shear at most $\kappa$, both reciprocal denominators have size at most two and differ from $(1+x^2)^{-1/2}$ by at most $41R^2\kappa$. The proof establishes $\sqrt m\ge1/2$ and $n\ge1$. This algebraic lemma does not require $S\ne0$; physical callers impose positive shear separately.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.summary: Both coupling reciprocals remain bounded and close

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.text: With $R\ge4$, $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, bounded reference and actual wave coordinates, and forcing errors at most $\kappa\ge0$, the reference first numerator has size at most $6R$. Its actual change is at most $8R\kappa$. The parameters for the second numerator remain unrestricted because the first numerator does not use them.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.summary: The first coupling numerator has linear box bounds

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.text: Assume $a\ge1/2$, $a_0\ge1$ and $b\ge1$. If $a^{-1}$ differs from $a_0^{-1}$ by at most $d$ and $b^{-1}$ differs from one by at most $e$, then $|(ab)^{-1}|\le2$ and its reference error is at most $d+e$. The proof splits the reciprocal product difference.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.summary: Reciprocal products preserve the two denominator error budgets

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.text: Under the listed coordinate, forcing and reference bounds, $0\le\kappa\le1/2$ and $0\le r\le\kappa$, the reference second numerator is bounded by $6R^2$. Its change is at most $74R^2\kappa$. The independent parameter $r$ will be $S^{-2}$. Control of $z-z_0$ is supplied as the hypothesis $|z-z_0|\le8R\kappa$, rather than derived again in this lemma.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.summary: The second coupling numerator has quadratic box bounds

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.text: If a numerator changes by at most $74R^2\kappa$, its reference size is at most $6R^2$, and its reciprocal factor is bounded by two with error at most $41R^2\kappa$, then their product changes by at most $256R^4\kappa$. The assumptions $R\ge4$ and $\kappa\ge0$ absorb the smaller polynomial terms.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.summary: Combine numerator and reciprocal errors into one polynomial bound

_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.text: On $0\le\tau\le T$ with $T\ge2$ and $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, one has $4\le T^2$, $|x|\le T^2/2$ and $|\varepsilon\tau|\le T^2/2$. This chooses the box radius $R=T^2$ for the rational coupling estimates without any assumption on an actual perturbed wave.
_private.TorusEuler.GrowingCouplingCompa.summary: Reference wave coordinates fit a common time box

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: Evaluation of the half-Hölder field formed by summing the output blocks applied to $f$ gives the value of the continuous-function series of output blocks. This is a definitional identity after regularity has been established. Together with the theorem that evaluation commutes with the block sum, it allows either the continuous-function sum or the pointwise sum to be used in later Fourier and increment arguments.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: The constructed field evaluates to the continuous block sum

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: At any point $x$, evaluating the sum of continuous output blocks equals summing their values at $x$. Continuity of the evaluation linear map and the proved summability justify the interchange. The infinite sum therefore represents the actual convergent series here, rather than the value zero assigned to a nonsummable family.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Evaluation commutes with the convergent block sum

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: The constructed sum field has half-Hölder norm at most $14\,D.bound\,\|f\|$. Both the value and increment bounds follow from the dyadic series estimate. The numerical factor fourteen is an explicit sufficient bound from this construction, not an optimality claim about Fourier multiplier norms.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: The half Hölder norm is controlled by the block constant

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: Take the sum in the continuous-function space and package it as a half-Hölder field using the low/high block difference estimate. The constructed norm bound is $14\,D.bound\,\|f\|$. The half-Hölder regularity is proved for the resulting sum; it is not obtained by assuming the series converges in the full Hölder norm.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: The convergent block sum is a half Hölder field

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: The sequence $((2^j)^{-1/2})_{j\ge0}$ is summable. Rewriting it as the geometric sequence with ratio $2^{-1/2}$ gives a ratio strictly between zero and one. This elementary fact controls the continuous-function norms of the dyadic output blocks before any Hölder estimate for their sum is used.

Take the inverse Fourier kernel of a smooth compactly supported operator symbol, dilate it at scale $2^j$, and convolve with the half-Hölder input. The output is a continuous torus field, linear in the input. Cancellation and annular support are not required for this definition; they enter the later estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Dilate the inverse transform to form one dyadic output block

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: Bundle extraction of the continuous field as a real continuous linear map from half-Hölder fields, with norm bound one. Addition and scalar multiplication preserve the underlying values, and the supremum norm is bounded by the full half-Hölder norm. This map is used before Fourier coefficient extraction in the separate mean contribution.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: The forgetful map to continuous fields is bounded linear

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: If every Fourier coefficient of a Banach-valued spatial L² field is zero, the field itself is zero. Scalar functionals reduce the claim to scalar Fourier uniqueness. The proof explicitly uses the essentially separable range of a strongly measurable representative, avoiding an unjustified common null set over an uncountable family of functionals.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Vanishing Fourier coefficients force a Banach valued L² field to vanish

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: Map a target vector to the spatially constant half-Hölder field with that value. Its increments vanish, and its value norm gives a bound of one for the linear insertion map. This is the mechanism by which the separately prescribed zero-frequency symbol contributes to the full multiplier.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Insert a vector as a constant half Hölder field

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: For a frequency of norm at least one, the dyadically rescaled cutoff differences have sum one. The unit inner region and zero outer region make the sum telescope and eventually stop changing. This theorem proves that the series actually converges to one, so the later use of its sum does not rely on the value assigned to nonsummable families.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: The annular cutoff differences sum to one away from zero

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: A spatial L² field multiplied by any Fourier character is integrable under normalized Haar measure. Finite measure gives L²-to-L¹ inclusion, and the character has unit magnitude. This certificate permits applying continuous linear functionals to Banach-valued Fourier coefficients inside the uniqueness argument.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Fourier testing is integrable for spatial L² fields

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: Multiplying a continuous torus field by a fixed Fourier character gives an integrable field. Continuity and compactness of the torus provide the required integrability. This certificate is used when proving linearity of coefficient extraction and when moving bounded operators through Fourier coefficient integrals.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Character weighted continuous fields are integrable

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: A nonzero integer frequency vector, viewed in Euclidean three-space, has norm at least one because some coordinate has absolute value at least one. This elementary lower bound allows the annular partition indexed by nonnegative dyadic scales to cover every nonzero torus frequency without adding negative scale indices.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Every nonzero lattice frequency has norm at least one

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: The coefficient of the $j$th compact-symbol block at lattice frequency $k$ is the symbol evaluated at $2^{-j}k$ applied to the input coefficient. The Fourier transform of the dilated kernel gives the formula. This identifies the actual convolution block before its size and increment bounds are established.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: A dyadic block samples the symbol at the scaled frequency

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: The Fourier coefficient of the constant field with value $a$ is $a$ at zero frequency and zero at every other frequency. The proof realizes the constant as a one-term finite Fourier synthesis. This makes the separate mean contribution disjoint from all annular nonzero-frequency blocks.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: A constant field has only its zero Fourier coefficient

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: The Fourier coefficient of the embedded half-Hölder field equals that of its underlying continuous field. The proof compares the representatives inside the coefficient integral. This compatibility allows the same symbol formula to be used on the continuous/Hölder side and on the weak L² side of the construction.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Embedding into L² preserves every Fourier coefficient

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: If $\sigma(0)=0$, the continuous supremum norm of the $j$th block is bounded by the kernel’s half-moment times $\|f\|2^{-j/2}$. Kernel cancellation permits replacing the input by a spatial increment. The bound requires vanishing at zero; compact support and smoothness alone would not give this decay.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Cancellation gives square root decay of each block

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: The supremum norm of the underlying continuous field is at most its full half-Hölder norm. This follows from the value part of the bundled norm estimate. The direction of the inequality matters: uniform size alone does not control the spatial half-Hölder increments.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Forgetting regularity cannot enlarge the field norm

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: At every torus point, each lattice Fourier character has norm one. The proof lifts the point to Euclidean space and invokes the exponential-mode identity. This uniform bound controls Fourier coefficient integrals and ensures that multiplying by a character does not enlarge pointwise norms.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Every torus Fourier character has unit magnitude

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: The bounded map sending a vector to the corresponding constant half-Hölder field has norm at most one. The value bound is the vector norm and every increment is zero. This estimate ensures that adding the prescribed zero-frequency action costs at most the norm of that single operator.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Constant insertion has operator norm at most one

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: For a half-Hölder torus field, the difference between values at two Euclidean lifts is bounded by the field norm times the square root of the Euclidean separation. The torus distance bound transfers the original estimate. This is the cancellation input used to gain $2^{-j/2}$ from each dyadic kernel.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: The lifted field retains a Euclidean half Hölder increment bound

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: The norm of any Fourier coefficient of a continuous torus field is at most the field’s supremum norm. Unit character magnitude and normalized Haar mass one give the estimate. The bound is uniform in the frequency and is the continuity estimate needed to interchange coefficients with uniformly convergent dyadic sums.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Every coefficient is bounded by the spatial supremum norm

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: For an integrable operator kernel, convolve the underlying continuous field of a half-Hölder input and package the result as a real linear map into continuous functions. Linearity follows from justified integral addition and scalar multiplication. This definition does not yet supply the scale-dependent estimates required by a dyadic block family.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: One kernel defines a linear continuous output block

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: For a fixed lattice frequency, the character evaluated at the sum of two labels equals the product of its two values. This group-character identity permits Haar translation in the operator-convolution coefficient calculation. It is valid pointwise and requires no integrability or regularity hypothesis on any input field.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: A torus character converts addition into multiplication

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: The distance between the torus images of two Euclidean points is at most the norm of their difference. Coordinate quotient norms can only decrease, and the product torus norm is controlled by the Euclidean norm. This transfers a half-Hölder estimate on torus labels to the periodic Euclidean lift.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Torus distance is bounded by Euclidean lift distance

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: A continuous torus field with frequencies below $4\Lambda$ has increments bounded by $8\Lambda$ times the first kernel-derivative L¹ norm, its supremum norm, and torus distance. Positive scale and the normalized smooth cutoff are explicit. Bernstein bounds the Euclidean derivative, and close lifts contribute the extra factor two.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: A Fourier band bound gives a torus Lipschitz estimate

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: The coordinatewise quotient map from Euclidean three-space to torus labels is continuous. This local helper supplies continuity of lifted and translated fields inside operator-valued convolution. It uses the additive-circle quotient topology and does not require a global continuous choice of Euclidean representatives for torus points.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: Passing from Euclidean points to torus labels is continuous

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.text: The image of $-x$ under the torus quotient equals the negative of the image of $x$. The proof is coordinatewise on the additive circle. This identity is used when matching the negative-frequency character in the Fourier-transform convention with the convolution formula at the origin.

The image of a Euclidean difference is the difference of the two torus images. This exact homomorphism identity aligns translations in Euclidean kernel integration with translations of torus fields. It avoids choosing a fundamental-cell representative each time a convolution is evaluated.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderFourierMul.summary: The torus quotient respects spatial differences

_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderSpace.0.To.text: At a distinct pair, this continuous linear functional subtracts the normalized field difference from the stored candidate quotient. Its kernel enforces equality between the two. The denominator is the square root of distance, matching Hölder exponent one half; the metric and distinctness guarantee it is positive.
_private.TorusEuler.HalfHolderSpace.0.To.summary: The equation defining the half Hölder quotient

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyActualNorms.text: If all direction fields and both input fields are smooth, the derivative word applied to their sum equals the sum of the two derivative words. Smoothness is used at every inductive derivative step. This supplies the linearity needed for the triangle inequality of the measured finite-word norm.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyActualNorms.summary: Derivative words distribute over smooth sums

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyActualNorms.text: Applying any ordered list of directional derivatives to the zero function gives the zero function. The empty list is the identity case, while each additional letter differentiates a constant zero field. No regularity assumption on the direction fields is required for this particular zero identity.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyActualNorms.summary: Every derivative word annihilates the zero field

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyActualNorms.text: This bounded linear inclusion inserts a label-phase direction into the joint profile coordinates with zero time component. It is used to restrict the full slab derivative to a fixed time slice. The map acts on directions, so the fixed time value itself does not appear in it.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyActualNorms.summary: Hold time fixed when inserting label and phase directions

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyActualNorms.text: At any time in the slab, the fixed-time slice of a twisted profile is differentiable everywhere in label and phase. Its derivative is the joint derivative within the slab composed with the slice inclusion. The slice remains entirely inside the time domain, including when the fixed time is an endpoint.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyActualNorms.summary: The label-phase slice has the restricted joint derivative

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyCancellatio.text: Under the zero-endpoint conventions, transverse oscillations cannot act on the phase, and phase-independent means cannot be differentiated in that slot. Bilinearity therefore rewrites phase advection of the total velocity as completion and mean contributions over the index pairs $(i,j)$ with $2\le i\le P+1$ and $1\le j\le P+1$. The hypotheses explicitly require these annihilation properties for every profile.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyCancellatio.summary: Only completions and means differentiate the phase

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyCancellatio.text: Any bilinear map sends two finite sums to the sum of all pairwise interactions. The product of the index sets records both indices without imposing a hierarchy level. This is an algebraic expansion, with no differentiability or PDE hypothesis.

The sum of $f(p-1)$ over $2\le p\le P+1$ equals the sum of $f(p)$ over $1\le p\le P$. Only an additive commutative monoid is required. The explicit bijection handles $P=0$ as an empty sum and later aligns each oscillation with its divergence correction.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyCancellatio.summary: Shift the completion indices in a finite sum

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyCancellatio.text: For $P\ge1$, this splits a sum over $1\le p\le P$ into its first term and the sum over $2\le p\le P$. The hypothesis prevents an invalid first term when the interval is empty. It separates the prescribed wave from the recursively solved levels.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyCancellatio.summary: Separate the leading term from the corrections

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.text: This smooth profile is the input velocity minus its phase average. Centering makes the completion operator available on every periodic profile, including inputs whose mean does not vanish. On the admissible zero-mean subspace it leaves the input unchanged, allowing agreement with the manuscript’s original curl-completion formula.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.summary: Remove the phase mean before taking the periodic completion

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.text: The phase average of the centered completion input is the zero smooth profile. The proof uses linearity and idempotence of phase averaging. This equality holds in the profile space, whose representatives are zero outside the time slab, and supplies the mean condition required for a periodic potential.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.summary: Centering a profile removes its phase average

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.text: At every time in $[0,T]$ and every label, subtracting the phase average from a periodic profile leaves a one-periodic phase function. The mean is constant in phase and therefore unchanged by a unit shift. This is the periodicity input for constructing the normalized potential of arbitrary periodic data.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.summary: Centering preserves phase periodicity on every slab slice

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.text: Two vector fields smooth on the hierarchy profile slab have a cross product smooth on that same slab. The proof expands the three coordinates into sums and products of scalar components. It does not require nonvanishing or transversality; those properties enter the normalized potential separately.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.summary: Taking a cross product preserves smoothness on the slab

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.text: For positive slab length, smooth covector and velocity profiles yield a smooth wave potential provided the covector read at phase zero never vanishes on the slab. The definition freezes that covector in the phase variable before integrating. The conclusion is smoothness of every order on the slab, not global smoothness of the zero extension.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.summary: The normalized potential is smooth on the profile slab

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.text: At a time belonging to $[0,T]$ and a fixed spatial label, a smooth hierarchy profile is continuous as a function of phase. This follows by restricting its smooth label-and-phase slice along a constant-label inclusion. No assertion is made about regularity across the slab’s time boundary.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.summary: Every phase slice of a smooth profile is continuous

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.text: This continuous linear inclusion sends a spatial label increment to the corresponding joint increment with zero time and phase components. It identifies exactly which directions are differentiated by the label differential. The map is constructed from the standard left and right product inclusions.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.summary: The label direction inside the joint profile space

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.text: Under the same label, phase, and profile differentiability hypotheses as the graph chain rule, the physical divergence is the trace of the label derivative composed with the derivative $J$ of the label map, plus the covector paired with the phase derivative. The result concerns one point and makes no divergence-free assumption on the evaluated profile.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.summary: Graph divergence separates the slow trace from the fast term

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.text: Given derivatives $J$ of the label map $A$ and $\langle\kappa,\cdot\rangle$ of the phase map $\varphi$, and differentiability of the profile at their values, the derivative of the evaluated profile is the sum of its label derivative composed with $J$ and its phase derivative multiplied by the covector $\kappa$. This is the two-variable chain rule at one point.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteCom.summary: The graph derivative separates label and phase contributions

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteOpe.text: For positive slab length, averaging a vector profile over its unit-period phase produces a jointly smooth function of time, label, and phase on the slab. The averaged expression ignores the output phase coordinate. The proof uses the parameter-dependent phase integral, together with convexity and unique differentiability of the parameter domain.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteOpe.summary: Phase averaging preserves smoothness on the slab

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteOpe.text: At a time $t\in[0,T]$, the phase slice of a smooth profile is continuous on the whole real phase line. The argument composes on-slab continuity with the slice inclusion. This continuity supplies integrability and linearity properties for the phase mean.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteOpe.summary: Every fixed time-label phase slice is continuous

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteOpe.text: For an index $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, this is the Euclidean coordinate vector with component one at index $i$ and zero at the other two indices. The three-element index set rules out invalid coordinates. The basis is used to reconstruct a vector gradient from its three scalar directional derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteOpe.summary: The coordinate vectors for the physical gradient

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyConcreteOpe.text: This bounded linear map embeds a vector of labels into the joint time-label-phase space, with zero time and phase components. It is a coordinate inclusion used when the coframe converts a physical direction into a label direction. No differential or flow property is asserted.

This bounded linear coordinate inclusion sends a scalar to a direction with only a phase component. It is used after contracting an advecting velocity with the transported covector. The definition concerns the joint coordinate space, without imposing periodicity or a nonzero phase speed.

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyDepthAssemb.text: For any real seminorm $N$, the seminorm of a finite sum is bounded by the sum of the individual seminorms. The ambient object needs only an additive group and real module structure. This permits the hierarchy estimates to be assembled before choosing concrete weighted or unweighted function norms.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyDepthAssemb.summary: A seminorm of a finite sum obeys the triangle inequality

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyDepthTail.0.text: Membership of $(i,j)$ in the tail pairs at depth $P$ with offset $m$ implies bounds on each component: the first index lies from $m+1$ to $P+1$, and the second from one to $P+1$. This extracts only the rectangular range conditions, leaving the separate lower bound on the sum of indices to later exponent estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyDepthTail.0.summary: Every tail interaction stays inside the retained index range

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyDepthTail.0.text: If two nonnegative-budget quantities have bounds with parent powers $L^i$ and $L^j$, and $1+i+j\le6$, their product after one additional parent factor fits a common $L^6$ budget. The frequency is positive and $L\ge1$. The lemma adds the real frequency exponents while keeping the parent exponent independent of depth.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyDepthTail.0.summary: Two level estimates fit one fixed parent-loss budget

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyExponents.0.text: A pair in the tail with offset $m$ has first index at least $m+1$, interaction level at least $P+1$, and index sum equal to that level plus $m$. These inequalities follow from the finite-set membership conditions. They let the remainder estimate compare every omitted quadratic term with the first omitted level.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyExponents.0.summary: Tail interactions lie beyond the retained depth

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.text: If the coframe adjoint, strain, longitudinal projection, pressure, force and velocity are smooth, their reconstructed gradient profile is smooth in label and phase. Smoothness of the projection is an explicit premise, so possible singular behavior at a zero covector is not being disregarded. The pressure contribution uses one derivative of a smooth function.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.summary: The reconstructed pressure gradient is smooth

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.text: Assume the pressure, as a function of label and phase jointly, is differentiable at the selected point and its phase slice has derivative $b$. The full differential is then the sum of its label restriction and multiplication by $b$ in the scalar phase direction. The statement makes the chain rule usable without treating the two derivatives independently.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.summary: Split a pressure differential into label and phase parts

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.text: A finite family of differentiable scalar functions has a gradient equal to the sum of the individual gradients at every point. The differentiability assumptions are imposed only for indices belonging to the finite set. This permits the pressure-gradient reconstruction to be performed level by level before estimating the sum.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.summary: The gradient commutes with the finite pressure sum

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.text: This continuous linear map restricts a scalar differential on label-phase space to the label directions and then identifies that covector with a vector using the Euclidean inner product. It is the representation of the slow pressure gradient before a profile is read on the physical phase graph.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.summary: Extract the label part of a pressure differential

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.text: The label restriction of a differential is the inverse Euclidean dual map applied after composing with the inclusion of label directions. This definitional identity makes the vector representation explicit. It introduces neither a differentiability hypothesis nor an additional estimate; those belong to applications where the argument is a pressure derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.summary: Read the label restriction through the Euclidean dual

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.text: The operator norm of the map extracting the label-gradient vector is at most one. Restriction to the label inclusion and the Euclidean dual identification are both norm controlled. This bound prevents an additional coefficient from entering the estimate for the slow part of the pressure gradient.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.summary: Restricting a pressure differential does not increase its norm

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.text: If two smooth profiles satisfy the order-$n$ jet bound, every derivative of order at most $n$ bounded everywhere, with constants $A$ and $B$, their sum satisfies the same bound with constant $A+B$. The bound includes all derivative orders through $n$. This elementary calculus step is used to combine the slow and projected parts of the reconstructed pressure gradient.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.summary: Add bounds for derivatives of pressure profiles

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.text: Smooth operator and vector profiles with nonnegative bounds $A$ and $B$ through order $n$ give a bound $2^nAB$ for their pointwise application. The factor counts the product-rule contributions. This is the finite-order estimate for the coframe and projection factors in the reconstructed pressure gradient.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.summary: Control an operator coefficient acting on a vector profile

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.text: Multiplying a smooth profile by a constant scalar multiplies its order-$n$ jet bound constant by the scalar norm. The scalar is spatially and phase independent in this theorem, so no product derivatives appear. This accounts for numerical factors such as the factor two in the transverse pressure equation.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.summary: A scalar multiplies all pressure derivative bounds

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.text: For two smooth profiles with derivative bounds through order $n$, their difference has the sum of the two bounding constants as its bound. The estimate uses the triangle inequality for iterated derivatives. It is applied to the force minus twice the strain correction in the transverse pressure formula.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.summary: Subtract profiles while adding their derivative bounds

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.text: For nonzero label length $\ell$ and differentiable pressure, the scaled label-gradient profile equals $\ell^{-1}$ times the label restriction of the differential of the scaled pressure. The phase scale $h$ is arbitrary. Only a label derivative is extracted, so no inverse phase width enters this identity.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyHigherPress.summary: Scaling the label gradient produces one inverse length

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.text: Multiplying an existing bound by the nonnegative factor $KL\lambda^v$ adds one parent power and adds $v$ to the frequency exponent. Positive frequency justifies combining real powers. This records the cost of a solver or source operation without absorbing that cost prematurely.

Two pointwise upper bounds multiply to an upper bound with multiplied constants, added parent exponents, and added frequency exponents. The hypotheses give positive frequency and enough nonnegativity for monotone multiplication. This algebraic estimate is repeatedly applied to pairs of profile norms in source sums.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.summary: Combine constants, parent powers, and frequency powers

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.text: If $\lambda\ge1$, $L\ge1$, and $L^6\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, a product with at most six powers of $L$ and a frequency gap at least $1/12$ is bounded by the target frequency power alone. The nonnegative coefficient $a$ is retained. This is the uniform absorption step.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.summary: Spend the spare frequency power on parent losses

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.text: A pair $(i,j)$ contributing at level $p$ with offset $m$ has first index at least $m+1$, second index at least one, and total index $i+j=p+m$. The lemma unpacks the finite-set filter. These facts identify earlier levels and justify exponent identities in the quantitative hierarchy induction.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.summary: Identify the positive indices in a measured source

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.text: The scalar cap is $K\cdot s\cdot3A^2+K$, where $s$ is the number of slow pairs. It counts the three quadratic types contributing to each slow pair and adds the residual coefficient. This is a bookkeeping constant only; the corresponding source estimate still requires the recurrence, previous bounds, and parent-loss assumptions.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.summary: Count the three products in the mean source

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.text: This cap adds the relay contribution, the slow-pair contribution, and two fast-pair contributions, using the supplied bound $B$ for a mean factor. It is independent of frequency and parent scale as an expression. The induction supplies nonnegative inputs and proves that it bounds the measured transverse source.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.summary: Count relay and quadratic costs in the transverse source

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.text: When $K$ and $A$ are nonnegative, the explicit step cap is at least $A$. Every additional term in its definition is nonnegative, including the finite interaction counts. This supplies monotonicity of the recursively chosen constants without claiming they are minimal or sharply estimated.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.summary: The next finite constant dominates the previous one

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.text: At positive retained depth, the recurrence’s seed estimate and zero conventions give every one of the eight level bounds at level one. The common constant must dominate both $K$ and $K^2$, and one derivative order is reserved for completing the wave. The zero mean and source bounds come from the recurrence's seed conditions, which set the level-one sources, the level-one mean and the zeroth correction to zero.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.summary: Start the measured induction at the leading wave

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.text: The smallness condition $L^6\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$ absorbs all six parent factors in the mean estimate. It replaces the stronger mean exponent by the inductive mean exponent $-5/4-2(p-1)/3-1/2$, with the same nonnegative constant $a$. This produces the parent-factor-free mean bound used in the next transverse source.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.summary: Convert the strong mean bound into the propagated bound

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.text: With $\lambda\ge1$ and nonnegative coefficient and parent scale, replacing a frequency exponent by a larger exponent increases the resulting bound. This monotonicity is applied after exact exponent identities. It lets smaller terms fit the exponent used for their hierarchy level.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.summary: Weaken an estimate by increasing its frequency exponent

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.text: For nonnegative frequency, parent scale at least one, and ordered constants and natural exponents, increasing the coefficient and parent power weakens the upper bound. The frequency power remains fixed. The theorem is scalar bookkeeping used to place differently shaped estimates under one common parent-loss budget.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.summary: Enlarge a coefficient and its parent power

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.text: If every term of a finite sum is at most $M$, the sum is at most the cardinality of the index set times $M$. No sign condition is needed for this additive comparison. The lemma isolates pair-counting constants from the parent and frequency powers.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBounds.summary: Count the finitely many terms in a source

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: A globally smooth profile depending on a proper normed label space and a real phase has a globally smooth normalized phase primitive. The target space is complete for parameter integration. The proof rescales the variable integration interval and subtracts its average; phase periodicity is not needed for this smoothness assertion.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: The normalized primitive is jointly smooth in label and phase

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: For a one-periodic profile, translating the phase by any real number preserves its integral over one unit interval. The statement imposes no continuity hypothesis and concerns Lean’s interval-integral expression. It is used to identify the zero-mean normalization after moving the phase origin in derivative estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: A phase translation leaves the period average unchanged

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: The derivative operator associated with the concatenated word $wv$ equals the operator for $w$ applied to the operator for $v$. This follows directly from the recursive definition of an ordered derivative word. No smoothness is required for the identity, though later exchanges or estimates of such derivatives impose it.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: Appending words composes their derivative operators

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: For a continuous, one-periodic, zero-mean profile, shifting the input phase shifts its normalized primitive by the same amount. The zero-mean assumption ensures that the primitive itself is periodic. Uniqueness of the zero-mean antiderivative then removes the otherwise possible additive constant.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: The normalized primitive commutes with phase translation

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: Two smooth profiles with word bounds $A$ and $B$ have sum bounded by $A+B$ at the same order and scales. The proof treats them as a two-element finite family. This preserves separate velocity and forcing contributions when the normalized potential and pressure are assembled.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: Adding two profiles adds their derivative bounds

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: A derivative-word bound, a nonnegative $B$ bounding every admissible weighted derivative word at every time and point, supplies an explicit upper bound for each admissible derivative-value set used in the supremum norm. Its nonnegative bound controls the set’s inserted zero as well as all derivative norms. These boundedness facts are needed to use conditional real supremum inequalities correctly.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: Derivative bounds make every relevant supremum finite

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: For smooth factors with derivative-word bounds $A$ and $C$, a bounded bilinear map $B$ produces a word bound $2^n\|B\|AC$. Each derivative is distributed between the factors, with admissible subwords remaining within the same order. The theorem is uniform in the auxiliary parameter index and differentiates only labels and phase.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: A bilinear product obeys the weighted Leibniz estimate

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: Multiplying each smooth profile by a fixed real scalar $c$ changes its derivative-word bound from $B$ to $|c|B$. All label and phase derivatives commute with the constant scalar. The estimate allows zero and negative scalars; no condition on the time or parameter index is added.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: Multiplication by a scalar scales the derivative bound

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: A bound through order $n$ remains valid through any order $m\le n$, with any enlarged constant $C\ge B$. The proof uses inclusion of the admissible sorted words and transitivity of inequalities. It does not change the coordinate scales or the function being estimated.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: A derivative bound survives a lower order and larger constant

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: For smooth profiles, a word bound through order $n+1$ gives the same bound through order $n$ after taking one weighted coordinate derivative. The appended derivative is sorted using commutation of constant directions. There is no extra numerical factor for this single differentiation.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: One weighted derivative uses one additional available order

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: Smooth periodic zero-mean phase profiles with word bound $B$ have a primitive word bound equal to twice the number of admissible words times $B$. The estimate passes through the finite norm and therefore includes this counting factor. It keeps the derivative order unchanged and requires completeness of the target space.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: The primitive inherits a uniform derivative-word estimate

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: If every smooth term in a finite family has a derivative-word budget $B_i$, the sum has budget equal to the finite sum of those constants. The proof combines distribution of each word over the sum with the triangle inequality. Each individual budget also supplies the nonnegativity required of the resulting bound.

The identically zero profile has word bound zero at every finite order and for every pair of coordinate scales. All recursively defined directional derivatives vanish, including the empty word, which returns the function itself. This allows the potential to be treated as a two-input linear expression with a zero forcing input.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: The zero profile has a zero derivative budget

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: Scaling the first vector in a cross product scales its value by the same real number. There are no regularity or nonzero assumptions. This algebraic step is used when extracting the carrier frequency from the covector in the potential and its time-source formula.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: A scalar factor leaves the first cross-product slot

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: The continuous linear curl map applied to a derivative matrix is by definition the coordinate curl expression of that matrix. This bridge lets a normed linear-map chain rule be used for the curl expression appearing elsewhere in the construction. It introduces no additional equation or regularity hypothesis.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: The linear curl map agrees with coordinate curl

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: The inverse squared norm of $ra$ equals $r^{-2}\|a\|^{-2}$ under the convention that the inverse of zero is zero. The identity holds even when the scalar or vector vanishes. Subsequent frequency estimates impose positive frequency and, where genuine inverse-length estimates are needed, nonzero covectors.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: Inverse squared length separates under scalar multiplication

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: A weighted derivative word applied to a finite sum of smooth profiles equals the sum of that same word applied to each profile. Smoothness is required for the derivative-of-sum rules at every recursive stage. The theorem handles arbitrary finite index sets and retains the word’s order.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: Every derivative word distributes over a finite smooth sum

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: The normalized phase primitive commutes with multiplication by any real scalar. Both the anchored phase integral and its mean subtraction preserve this operation. This is a statement about the totalized integral expression and carries no continuity, integrability, periodicity, or mean-zero hypotheses on the input profile.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: A constant scalar passes through the phase primitive

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.text: Every three-dimensional Euclidean vector equals the sum of its three coordinate values times the corresponding coordinate direction. This unconditional finite-dimensional identity underlies the rank-one decomposition of a composed derivative. In the formalization the coordinates are indexed zero, one, and two.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyLinearRelay.summary: A vector is the sum of its coordinate components

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyParentGeome.text: Defines a torus-valued label field by choosing a Euclidean representative of each torus point and evaluating the supplied function there. The raw definition accepts any label field. Agreement with arbitrary representatives is only proved later under spatial periodicity on the time slab, so this is not an unconditional quotient-descent theorem.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyParentGeome.summary: Evaluate a label field through a chosen torus representative

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyParentGeome.text: At a time in the slab, evaluates the descended field at the torus image of $a$ as the original field at $a$. The chosen lift differs from $a$ by an integer lattice vector, and the periodicity hypothesis removes that difference. This is the representation-independence statement missing from the unrestricted definition.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyParentGeome.summary: Periodicity removes the chosen representative from evaluation

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyParentGeome.text: Shows periodicity of the Fréchet derivative by applying the derivative operator to the translated-function equality. This identity holds for arbitrary periodic functions under the totalized derivative convention. In the parent geometry construction the velocity is smooth, so the same equality concerns its ordinary analytic derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyParentGeome.summary: The derivative of a periodic field remains periodic

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyParentGeome.text: If a map changes by the same lattice translation when its argument is translated, its Fréchet derivative is spatially periodic. Differentiating the translated-function identity removes the added constant. No differentiability assumption appears: the totalized derivative identities also handle nondifferentiable points, while the actual flow application supplies smoothness.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyParentGeome.summary: The derivative of a lattice-equivariant chart is periodic

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyParentGeome.text: If a smooth profile agrees on the slab with a phase-independent field having a stated label-reflection sign, the stored profile has simultaneous reflection parity everywhere. On the slab this uses the value identity; off the slab both representative values are zero. The theorem does not claim a smooth time extension across the slab boundary.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyParentGeome.summary: Slab parity extends to the stored zero representative

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyParityPropa.text: Unpacks membership in the filtered interaction set with offset $m$: the first index is at least $m+1$, the second at least one, and their sum is $p+m$. These lower bounds justify eliminating the natural-number subtraction, which stops at zero, in the level formula. The result is used to show that each source only depends on permitted earlier levels.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyParityPropa.summary: An interaction at a fixed level has the required indices

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.text: Advection in the label directions is periodic when the coframe and both velocity profiles are periodic. The derivative of the second argument and the direction selected from the first repeat after a unit phase shift. This is a closure result for the concrete bilinear operator.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.summary: Label advection preserves the common phase period
