_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.text: The label gradient of a periodic scalar profile is periodic when its coframe G is periodic. Each coordinate derivative is periodic, and the coframe values repeat under the same translation. Positive slab length supports the concrete derivative construction, including evaluation at the time endpoints.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.summary: The coframe gradient preserves phase periodicity

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.text: The concrete material operator combines the time derivative within the slab with multiplication by the coefficient field M. Both preserve the unit phase period when the input and coefficients are periodic. This closure lemma justifies restricting that operator to periodic profiles; it proves no evolution equation.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.summary: The material operator preserves the phase period

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.text: Phase advection of one periodic profile by another stays periodic when κ is periodic. The contraction with the first field and the phase derivative of the second both repeat. This result only requires periodicity; cancellation of its average later needs stronger phase-independence assumptions.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.summary: Phase advection preserves the common phase period

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.text: The phase gradient is the scalar phase derivative multiplied by the transported covector. Periodicity of that derivative and of κ makes the resulting vector profile periodic. This establishes closure under the fast pressure operation for positive slab length, without requiring κ to be phase independent.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.summary: The fast pressure gradient preserves phase periodicity

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.text: With positive slab length and a fixed on-slab time, evaluating the derivative within the slab on the unit phase direction gives a continuous function of phase. Smoothness yields continuity of the joint derivative. This continuity is needed to integrate the phase derivative over a period.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.summary: The phase derivative varies continuously along its slice

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.text: For a fixed time in the closed slab and any label, the one-variable phase slice has derivative given by the joint derivative within the slab applied to the unit phase direction. The whole phase line stays inside the domain, so this is an ordinary derivative even at a time endpoint.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.summary: A phase slice differentiates by the slab derivative

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.text: If a smooth profile is invariant under one phase translation at every slab point, its whole representative is periodic. Outside the slab both translated and untranslated values are zero, since phase translation preserves membership. This proves global representative periodicity without assuming global smoothness.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.summary: Extend on-slab periodicity to the representative

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.text: The joint vector $(0,0,c)$ equals $c$ times the unit phase vector $(0,0,1)$. This elementary coordinate identity lets linearity of a Fréchet derivative factor the scalar phase speed out of a directional derivative. It is used for both phase-independence cancellation and transversality cancellation.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPeriodicPro.summary: Every fast direction scales the unit phase direction

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhaseIndepe.text: Any word in the four letters (three label directions and the phase) that omits the last letter, the phase, can be written as a word in the three label letters, mapped into the four-letter alphabet. This finite combinatorial fact separates genuine label words from words containing the phase direction. It supplies the indexing correspondence for equality of the two finite derivative norms.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhaseIndepe.summary: A word without phase letters is a label word

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhaseIndepe.text: If one direction field is identically zero and its letter occurs anywhere in a word, the derivative word evaluates to the zero function. No differentiability assumption is required for this total-derivative identity. It removes all words containing the phase letter when the profile depends only on labels.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhaseIndepe.summary: A zero direction annihilates the entire derivative word

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhaseIndepe.text: For a smooth label function pulled back along the first projection, a derivative word in constant label-phase directions equals the corresponding word in their label projections. The resulting function is again pulled back to label-phase space. This identifies how mixed words act on a profile that is genuinely independent of phase.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhaseIndepe.summary: Project each mixed direction onto the label space

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhaseIndepe.text: Mapping a word’s letters through a relabeling $e$ before applying the derivative-word operator is the same as replacing the direction family by its composition with $e$. This algebraic identity has no smoothness hypothesis. It is used when identifying the three label letters inside the four-letter mixed alphabet.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhaseIndepe.summary: Relabeling a word relabels its derivative directions

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalApp.text: For depth at least two, a smooth periodic odd divergence-free parent, even smooth periodic pressure, and its label flow, proves every one of the qualitative equations and symmetries of the approximate fields. The additional premise requires each selected mean solve to have zero total profile divergence. Reflection propagates through the hierarchy, curl completion handles transverse divergence, and graph identities give the exact residual.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalApp.summary: Assemble the physical equations from mean incompressibility

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalApp.text: At a point where both vector fields are differentiable, divergence of their sum is the sum of their divergences. The proof unfolds divergence into the trace expressed by a finite coordinate sum and uses additivity of the Fréchet derivative. The differentiability premises prevent relying on the total derivative convention at a nondifferentiable point.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalApp.summary: Divergence distributes over two differentiable vector fields

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalApp.text: A reflection identity verified on the profile slab $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ gives the reflection parity on the whole profile domain. The proof splits on membership in the slab. Outside it, both reflected and original profile values are zero by the smooth-profile representation, because reflection changes label and phase but preserves time.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalApp.summary: Reflection extends from the slab to the profile

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalApp.text: If the field, as a function of $(t,x)$, is smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, then its slice at any $t\in[0,T]$ is smooth on all of $\mathbb R^3$. The proof composes with the smooth inclusion $x\mapsto(t,x)$. No smoothness outside the time slab is inferred from this restriction argument.

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalGra.text: The sum of the three coordinate components times their Euclidean basis vectors equals the original vector. This finite-dimensional identity is unconditional. It converts the coordinate definition of the profile label gradient into the adjoint-coframe expression used by the physical pressure chain rule.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalGra.summary: Coordinate components reconstruct the gradient vector

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalGra.text: If the label component of a scalar profile’s derivative is represented by the vector $q_a$, then its encoded label gradient at a slab point equals the coframe adjoint applied to $q_a$. Positive slab length supplies the derivative operator. The statement identifies the representation rather than proving a pressure or flow equation.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalGra.summary: The encoded label gradient is the adjoint coframe gradient

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalGra.text: This continuous linear map sends a three-dimensional derivative operator to the trace of its underlying linear map. Additivity and real homogeneity come from trace. Finite dimensionality makes the linear map continuous, allowing it to act on smooth profile fields when defining the slow divergence.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalGra.summary: The matrix trace as a continuous linear map

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalGra.text: This continuous linear map embeds a spatial increment as a joint profile increment with time and phase components zero. It is used to separate the label part of a profile derivative from the time and phase parts. The construction uses product inclusions and is independent of the parent flow.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalGra.summary: The pure label direction in graph coordinates

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalGra.text: Any continuous linear map on the product of time, label, and phase equals the sum encoded by its three coordinate restrictions. Time and phase components are recovered by evaluation on unit directions; the label component is a composition with the pure-label inclusion. This identity is algebraic and imposes no differentiability assumption.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalGra.summary: A joint derivative separates into time label and phase parts

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalGra.text: A continuous linear map on time and space equals the coproduct of its value on the unit time direction and its restriction to spatial directions. The proof uses linearity and the product decomposition. This is applied to the inverse label map before identifying the time component through its transport equation.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalGra.summary: A time-space derivative splits into its two coordinate parts

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalIni.text: If the selected leading velocity vanishes at time zero, every retained transverse velocity profile has zero initial values and zero phase average. The proof separates the leading level from later levels selected by the zero-initial-data transverse solver. It says nothing about the mean profiles, whose endpoint problem may produce nonzero initial velocity.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalIni.summary: Every retained transverse profile has zero initial data

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalPre.text: This auxiliary linear map evaluates a smooth hierarchy profile on a specified physical phase graph at a fixed time and position. Linearity follows from pointwise addition and scalar multiplication of profiles. The definition accepts an arbitrary label map $A$, carrier $k$, time and position; geometric correctness and slab membership are hypotheses in subsequent uses.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalPre.summary: Graph evaluation is linear in the profile

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalPre.text: If each profile in the retained higher-level range is fixed by the hierarchy average, their finite sum is phase independent. The theorem first uses linearity of the average and then its concrete independence property. The empty range is allowed and gives the zero profile, which also has no phase dependence.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalPre.summary: A finite sum of means remains independent of phase

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalPre.text: The seminorm of a finite sum of profiles is no greater than the sum of their individual seminorms. This applies to both the selected means and their source profiles. The theorem is purely algebraic and includes empty sums; the quantitative level estimates are supplied when applying it.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalPre.summary: A seminorm of a finite mean sum is subadditive

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalPre.text: The gradient of the sum of two differentiable scalar pressure fields equals the sum of their gradients as a function. This helper is applied after the pressure increment has been decomposed into leading, higher and mean components. Differentiability is supplied by their smooth graph constructions.

A jointly smooth field on the closed slab has a smooth spatial slice at every slab time. This private helper is used for physical graph fields before differentiating their pressures. The entire spatial domain is available, so the derivative is ordinary spatial differentiation even when the selected time is an endpoint.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalPre.summary: The graph field has smooth spatial slices

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalPre.text: At a fixed spatial point and a time in the closed slab, joint smoothness implies differentiability of the time slice within that interval. This makes the temporal derivative in the physical momentum identity well defined at both endpoints. The theorem does not extend the field to an open time neighborhood.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalPre.summary: The graph field has a within-slab time derivative

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalVel.text: A jointly smooth field on the closed physical slab restricts to a smooth spatial function at each slab time. The proof composes with the constant-time map. This provides the spatial smoothness used in graph readout and Hölder estimates, without asserting smoothness for times outside the slab.

For nonnegative rate and $t<t_0$, the switch derivative is zero because the switch agrees with the constant zero function on a neighborhood of $t$. This version uses equality near $t$ and the strict inequality directly. The endpoint-inclusive version appears with the leading-input results.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalVel.summary: The activation derivative is zero strictly before the start

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalVel.text: If the inverse label map and the profile’s joint label-phase slice are smooth at a fixed time, their transported phase-graph readout is a smooth spatial field. The phase coordinate is the continuous linear functional given by the carrier dot product composed with inverse labels. No time derivative or time-smoothness conclusion is involved.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalVel.summary: Smooth profile slices stay smooth on the phase graph

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalVel.text: Given a decomposition $V=U+O+M$, half-Hölder regularity at order $P$, and scheduled bounds for the parent, oscillation, and mean, proves $1+\|V\|\le3\lambda^{2(P+1)}$. It requires $\mu\ge2$, a positive exponent parameter, and each prefactor at most $\mu$. The estimate is an arithmetic aggregation of supplied component bounds.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPhysicalVel.summary: Combine parent oscillation and mean at the full depth

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPrimaryPres.text: The closure of the interior of the centered fundamental cell is the entire closed cell. This geometric equality lets identities first proved away from the cell faces extend to the faces by continuity. It is needed because physical pressure derivatives must agree across the periodic construction, not only in an open representative cell.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPrimaryPres.summary: The closed label cell is determined by its interior

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPrimaryPres.text: For a regular seed and an active time, smoothness of the inverse-label map implies smoothness of the leading pressure coefficient. The regularity record supplies smooth strain, amplitude and an everywhere nonzero covector on the active slab. These conditions justify differentiating the reciprocal squared covector norm in the coefficient.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPrimaryPres.summary: The active pressure coefficient is smooth in space

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPrimaryPres.text: If a field is jointly smooth on a time set times the full spatial space, its fixed-time spatial slice is smooth for every time in that set. The statement is valid for any normed target space. It provides ordinary spatial calculus at times where the joint regularity is stated only on a slab.

The Euclidean gradient of an infinitely differentiable scalar function is infinitely differentiable. The proof views the gradient as the Fréchet derivative followed by the inverse inner-product dual map. This supplies continuity and further differentiability of Hessians when an identity is extended from the interior of a label cell.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyPrimaryPres.summary: A smooth scalar pressure has a smooth gradient

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyProductEsti.text: A finite list sum of smooth functions is smooth. The hypothesis supplies smoothness for every indexed function, and induction uses closure of smooth maps under addition. This general helper permits differentiation of the list of terms generated by the ordered Leibniz formula.

For a continuous bilinear map $B$ and functions $f,g$ differentiable at $x$, differentiating $B(f,g)$ in the direction $d(x)$ gives the derivative on the first factor plus the derivative on the second. Differentiability of $f$ and $g$ at $x$ suffices; no global smoothness or commutation of directions is required.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyProductEsti.summary: A directional derivative obeys the bilinear product rule

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyProductEsti.text: The directional derivative of a finite list sum equals the sum of the directional derivatives, assuming each summand is smooth. The direction field $d$ need not itself be smooth for this first derivative identity, because only its value at the evaluation point enters. It is used inside the word-product induction.

The set of quantities used to measure a word derivative is nonempty because its definition includes zero. This holds whether or not Hölder quotients are included and without regularity or boundedness assumptions on the field. Nonemptiness alone does not justify using its real supremum as a bound; later lemmas also require the set to be bounded above.

If every admissible word has a bounded jet-value set, the supremum for any one admissible word lies below the sum defining the finite norm. Zero belongs to each set, making all summands nonnegative. The boundedness hypothesis is essential for the conditional real supremum to behave as the intended norm.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyProductEsti.summary: One word supremum lies below the finite norm

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyProductEsti.text: The full Leibniz list equals the list of splits with nonempty first word followed by the unique pair consisting of the empty word and $w$. This is an equality of ordered lists, preserving multiplicities. It isolates the highest solution derivative before the remaining terms are estimated as coefficient commutators.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyProductEsti.summary: Separate the term with an undifferentiated coefficient

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyProductEsti.text: If every entry of a real-valued list is at most $M$, its sum is at most the list length times $M$. Nonnegativity is not assumed for this elementary addition inequality. The finite-word product estimates apply it after finding a common bound for all Leibniz terms.

The difference of two sums over the same list is the sum of the termwise differences. This is an additive identity requiring no analytic hypotheses. It aligns corresponding Leibniz terms at two spatial points before applying the bilinear difference estimate used for the half-Hölder seminorm.

The norm of $B(a,b)$ is at most $\|B\|\|a\|\|b\|$ for a continuous bilinear map represented as a nested continuous linear map. Applying the operator norm bound twice supplies each individual term in the finite-order product estimate. No differentiability hypotheses are involved in this inequality.

The difference $B(a,b)-B(a',b')$ is bounded by $\|B\|\|a-a'\|\|b\|+\|B\|\|a'\|\|b-b'\|$. The proof adds and subtracts the mixed value through bilinearity. This elementary estimate controls changes in either factor when proving the Hölder version of the product rule.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyProductEsti.summary: Split a bilinear difference between its factors

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyProductEsti.text: For a finite list, the norm of the sum of its values is bounded by the sum of their norms. The result requires only the normed additive structure of the target. It converts the exact ordered Leibniz expansion into a scalar sum of upper bounds, while retaining repeated terms.

For an admissible word, boundedness of all jet sets gives a pointwise derivative bound by the finite norm. When Hölder quotients are included, it also gives the corresponding square-root distance bound. The proof treats coincident points separately before clearing the positive denominator at distinct points.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyProductEsti.summary: A bounded finite norm controls values and differences

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayCofram.text: The norm of $A^*e_i$ is bounded by $\|A\|$. The proof uses preservation of the operator norm by the adjoint and the unit norm of the coordinate vector $e_i$. This coordinate estimate introduces no factor depending on the derivative order or on the selected coordinate.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayCofram.summary: A coframe row is bounded by the operator norm

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayCofram.text: The operator $w\mapsto v\times w$ has norm at most $|v|$. This follows from the Euclidean cross-product inequality applied to every vector in the definition of operator norm. The lemma converts a geometric row of the pulled-back curl into a continuous linear-map coefficient with an explicit bound.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayCofram.summary: Crossing with a vector has its norm bound

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayCofram.text: For smooth $G$, a fixed continuous linear map $P$ with norm at most $a_0$ sends an order-$j$ derivative bound $B$ to the bound $a_0B$ for $P\circ G$. The proof uses the iterated derivative of a linear composition. It supplies the common argument for both geometric row types.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayCofram.summary: A fixed linear map preserves a derivative bound

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayCofram.text: The continuous linear map from coframes to scaled curl rows has operator norm at most $|\ell^{-1}|$. The proof combines the cross-product bound and the adjoint-coordinate bound. Its estimate is valid for every real width, since the constructed map is zero when the totalized inverse is zero.

The map from a coframe to its scaled pressure row has norm at most $|\ell^{-1}|$. The scalar-to-vector map has norm equal to the length of its defining vector, so the adjoint-row estimate suffices. This keeps the pressure-gradient coefficient under the same geometric budget as the curl.

For a coordinate index $i$, this continuous linear map sends an endomorphism $A$ to $A^*e_i$. It composes the adjoint isometry with evaluation on the unit coordinate vector. These vectors supply the rows appearing in curl and pressure-gradient formulas after pulling derivatives back to label coordinates.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayCofram.summary: Extracting a coframe row through the adjoint

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayCofram.text: This packages $v\mapsto(w\mapsto v\times w)$ as a continuous linear map into the space of endomorphisms of $\mathbb R^3$. Additivity and scalar compatibility come from the cross product, and its continuity uses a norm bound of one. The construction supports derivative bounds by composition with coframe coefficients.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayCofram.summary: Cross product as a linear coefficient map

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayCofram.text: Applying the continuous linear curl-row map to $G$ gives by definition the geometric curl coefficient $\ell^{-1}(G^*e_i)\times\cdot$. The equality aligns a derivative-friendly linear-map representation with the coordinate formula used in the relay norm. It holds for every real width, including width zero, where $\ell^{-1}$ is assigned the value zero.

Applying the continuous linear pressure-row map to a coframe $G$ gives exactly the pressure coefficient $c\mapsto\ell^{-1}cG^*e_i$. This definitional equality connects the linear-map construction to the scalar-to-vector coefficient in the pressure-gradient sum. It imposes no invertibility or positivity assumptions; the analytic identities using the coefficient carry those assumptions separately.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayCofram.summary: The linear map is the pressure coefficient

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayPotent.text: This proposition records smoothness of each label slice, a nonnegative constant $C$, and derivative bounds $\|\partial_a^jf\|\le C\mathsf D^{16j+p}$ for all $j\le n$. The time index ranges over an arbitrary parameter set; no time derivative is included. The fixed slope sixteen allows a common width condition to absorb every label order.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayPotent.summary: Label derivatives with one fixed growth slope

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayPotent.text: The flipped evaluation map $(L,v)\mapsto Lv$ has norm at most one between the declared normed spaces. The estimate is the defining operator-norm inequality, expressed as a continuous bilinear map. It is used when combining strain, wave-vector, and scalar coefficient jets by bilinear operations.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayPotent.summary: Applying a linear operator has bilinear norm at most one

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayPotent.text: The operator-valued map $v\mapsto(v\times\cdot)$ has norm at most one. Applying the cross-product inequality first bounds the inner operator and then the outer operator. This fact lets the closure rule for contractive linear maps act on wave-vector jets without enlarging their derivative constant.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyRelayPotent.summary: The cross-product coefficient map has norm at most one

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySlowInterac.text: Restricting a full-slab norm to $[t_0,T]$ with weight one cannot increase it, provided $0\le t_0$. The assertion works whether or not the half-Hölder part is included. Its role is to replace unweighted factors on the active interval by quantities already measured on the whole parent slab.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySlowInterac.summary: The active interval has a smaller unweighted norm

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySlowInterac.text: A common upper bound $L$ for the norms of the three scaled coframe rows must be nonnegative, because any one of those norms is nonnegative. Hence $3Q_n^2L$ is nonnegative. This elementary fact legitimizes multiplying inequalities by the slow-interaction cost; it derives the sign from the assumed row bound instead of assuming it separately.

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceAssem.text: This private linear map sends a hierarchy profile to itself minus its phase average. It packages centering so finite sums can be manipulated using linear-map identities. At this algebraic level the abstract operator record supplies an averaging map; idempotence or a zero-mean conclusion is not built into this definition alone.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceAssem.summary: Subtract the phase average from a profile

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceAssem.text: Applying the centering map to $f$ gives $f-\langle f\rangle$ by definition, where $\langle\cdot\rangle$ is the supplied averaging map. This exposes the algebraic expression used when distributing centering across source sums. The identity is valid for any operator record and does not independently show that the output has zero average.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceAssem.summary: The centering map is subtraction of the average

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceAssem.text: If a real seminorm bounds each member of a finite family by the assigned scalar bound, it bounds the family sum by the sum of those scalars. The empty sum is included. This elementary inequality combines the separate product estimates in the mean and transverse hierarchy sources.

Membership of $(i,j)$ in the set of interaction pairs at level $p$, with depth $P$ and index shift $d$, is equivalent to explicit lower and upper bounds on both positive indices and the equation $i+j=p+d$. The first index starts at $d+1$, which excludes a nonexistent preceding completion in the fast sum. This finite-set description supports the change of index between fast and slow products.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceAssem.summary: Which pairs contribute to a hierarchy level

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.text: This private definition appends the direction index $i$ to a derivative word and sorts the resulting list. It represents the same multi-index with one extra coordinate derivative while retaining repeated letters. Its intended use is with already sorted admissible words, where insertion is injective and respects the order budget.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.summary: Insert one derivative into the sorted word

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.text: For a fixed direction $i$, insertion followed by sorting is injective on the admissible sorted words. Equal outputs have equal multisets after removing the added letter, and sortedness turns that multiset equality back into list equality. This prevents an extra combinatorial factor in the one-direction derivative estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.summary: Canonical insertion does not count words twice

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.text: An admissible sorted word of length at most $n$ remains admissible at order $n+1$ after inserting one index and sorting. The proof combines length preservation under sorting with the sortedness of merge sort. This maps the derivatives of a differentiated field into the next-order norm of the original field.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.summary: Inserted words fit the next derivative order

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.text: Sorting the word after appending the direction $i$ yields a permutation of the unsorted appended word. This purely combinatorial result does not identify the associated derivatives by itself. The later use combines it with commutation of constant directional derivatives on smooth fields to justify canonical sorted representatives.

For a smooth function, differentiating in two constant directions commutes. The proof identifies both sides with the second Fréchet derivative and uses its symmetry. Constancy of the directions matters: the theorem does not state commutation for spatially varying vector fields, whose derivatives introduce additional terms.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.summary: Constant directional derivatives commute on smooth fields

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.text: The finite word norm is nonnegative when all its jet-value sets are bounded above. Each such set contains zero, so its real supremum is nonnegative, and summing preserves that inequality. The explicit boundedness condition prevents treating an arbitrary conditional supremum as an automatically valid analytic norm.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.summary: Bounded jet ranges give a nonnegative finite norm

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.text: Smooth factors with bounded admissible jet sets have bounded jet sets after applying a continuous bilinear map. This establishes the analytic boundedness needed to interpret the product norm's real suprema. The bound is obtained from the wordwise Leibniz estimate and works for either the supremum or the half-Hölder choice.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.summary: Products retain bounded derivative and Hölder ranges

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.text: For smooth time-indexed fields and constant directions, the jet-value set of a word applied to one extra directional derivative equals the original field's jet-value set at the sorted extended word. The equality covers both sup values and optional Hölder quotients. It depends on permutation invariance of smooth constant-direction derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.summary: Differentiation shifts the canonical word range

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.text: For a word within the finite order budget, its pointwise derivative norms are bounded by the aggregate word norm, provided all jet ranges are bounded above. If the norm includes the half-Hölder part, the same norm bounds the half-Hölder difference. Coincident points are handled directly, while distinct points permit division by the positive square root of their distance.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.summary: Extract each derivative bound from the finite norm

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.text: The operator norm of a continuous linear map from $\mathbb R^3$ is at most the sum of its norms on the three standard coordinate directions. Expanding an arbitrary vector in that basis proves the bound. It converts coordinate derivative information into a full derivative norm for the Hölder interpolation argument.

A differentiable field bounded by $A$ with derivative bounded by $B$ satisfies $\|f(x)-f(y)\|\le\sqrt{2AB}\sqrt{\operatorname{dist}(x,y)}$, assuming $A,B\ge0$. The proof combines the global bound $2A$ with the Lipschitz bound $B\operatorname{dist}(x,y)$. This is the interpolation step behind the finite Hölder comparison.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.summary: Supremum and derivative bounds give half-Hölder control

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.text: The derivative indexed by the concatenation of two words $v$ and $w$ equals applying the derivative word $v$ to the function already differentiated by $w$. This follows from the recursive definition and has no smoothness hypothesis. It is a syntactic composition identity, not a claim that different derivative orders commute.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySourceBound.summary: Concatenated words compose their derivative operators

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyStageCoeffi.text: For a field smooth on the closed time slab, each fixed-time spatial slice is smooth on all of $\mathbb R^3$, provided the chosen time belongs to the slab. Composing with $x\mapsto(t,x)$ proves the result. No extension in time is constructed; only spatial variables are varied.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyStageCoeffi.summary: A smooth closed-slab field has smooth spatial slices

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySupportProp.text: At a time in the slab, the spatial derivative of a fixed-phase profile slice in direction $d$ is obtained by applying the full within-slab derivative to the direction $(0,d,0)$. Smoothness is built into the profile. The slice insertion stays in the slab for all labels, so this chain-rule identity does not require an ambient time extension.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySupportProp.summary: A label derivative is a direction of the full slab derivative

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySupportProp.text: If the two oscillatory blocks belong to the inactive submodule, the full label-advection product differs from the mean-mean product by an element of that submodule. Bilinearity expands the difference into terms with an inactive factor. No vanishing of the means is assumed, which is essential for the endpoint mean equation.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySupportProp.summary: Removing the mean product leaves an inactive oscillatory term

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySupportProp.text: Extracts the positive index bounds and exact sum relation from a filtered hierarchy interaction pair. These facts identify which lower levels appear in a source at level $p$. The truncated natural-number subtraction in the level function is justified by the lower bound on the first index before arithmetic reasoning is applied.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySupportProp.summary: Source interactions use the prescribed level relation

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySupportProp.text: From vanishing on the strict inactive region and $0<\tau$, obtains vanishing on the region including the activation slice. When time equals $\tau$, continuity from earlier slab times supplies the value. This strict positivity is material: a wave present at the initial time zero cannot be ruled out by an empty preactivation interval.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchySupportProp.summary: Continuity extends preactivation vanishing to a positive launch time

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTransverseB.text: For a smooth phase-independent coefficient with derivative growth $C\mathsf D^{16j+11}$, assume $\ell\le\mathsf D^{-30}$ and a nonempty admissible word through order $n$. The mixed derivative word is bounded by $C\mathsf D^{-3}$. Excluding the empty word is essential: the undifferentiated coefficient need not satisfy this small bound.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTransverseB.summary: Every positive-order coefficient word is small

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTransverseB.text: For a smooth label-only function and nonnegative label scale, every mixed label-phase word is bounded by $\ell^{|w|}$ times the ordinary derivative norm of that order. Words containing the phase direction vanish. The bound permits arbitrary phase scale because the function does not depend on phase.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTransverseB.summary: A mixed derivative word costs only label powers

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTransverseB.text: For a smooth function and $\ell\ge0$, the norm of its order-$j$ derivative after the map $a\mapsto\ell a$ equals $\ell^j$ times the original derivative norm at the scaled point. This exact scaling identity includes order zero and is used to absorb parent derivative powers into the envelope scale.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTransverseB.summary: Rescaling labels multiplies derivatives by the scale power

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTransverseB.text: Assume a smooth everywhere nonzero covector and positive carrier frequency. Jet bounds for the normalized covector and the reciprocal squared norm yield a jet bound for the pressure-source coefficient, with product factor $2^N$. The theorem also proves smoothness. Nonvanishing is required for the reciprocal coefficient, rather than supplied by the bound itself.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTransverseB.summary: Bound the normalized pressure source coefficient

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTransverseB.text: Assume derivatives through order $n$ are bounded by $C\mathsf D^{pj+q}$, with $C\ge0$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, and $\ell\mathsf D^p\le1$. The label-rescaled function then has a jet bound $C\mathsf D^q$ at all those orders. The estimate separates the derivative-dependent power, removed by scaling, from the fixed parent loss.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTransverseB.summary: A small label scale absorbs derivative-dependent parent powers

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTransverseN.text: Smooth strain and covector fields with a covector that is nonzero everywhere give smooth pressure-amplitude and pressure-source coefficient fields. The nonvanishing assumption protects the inverse squared norm in these coefficients. This regularity statement supplies product and derivative estimates for the pressure recovered from the transverse velocity.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTransverseN.summary: Nonzero covectors make the pressure coefficients smooth

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedComp.text: A smooth profile satisfying a given scalar reflection law on the slab satisfies that law globally as a representative function. Reflection preserves the time slab, and the profile is zero outside it. This is a support convention argument, not a claim that the representative is globally smooth across endpoint times.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedComp.summary: Reflection parity on the slab extends to its zero representative

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedComp.text: Subtracting the twisted profile’s phase average makes every phase slice have zero mean at every time in the slab. Idempotence of the underlying periodic averaging operator supplies the equality. The lattice twist remains in the surrounding profile type; the assertion itself is a fixed-label integral identity.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedComp.summary: A centered twisted profile has zero phase average

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedComp.text: If the input velocity is continuous, periodic, and zero mean, then the phase-reflected potential also has zero phase mean. The proof changes variables in the integral and uses periodicity to move the interval back to a unit period. This fixes the constant when identifying reflected normalized primitives.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedComp.summary: Reflecting a periodic potential preserves its zero mean

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedComp.text: For a continuous one-periodic zero-mean profile, translating its phase by a real number $b$ translates its normalized wave potential $-|\kappa|^{-2}\,\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V)$ by $b$. The proof compares derivatives and uses the zero-mean normalization to eliminate an additive constant. The covector $\kappa$ need not be nonzero for this algebraic integral identity.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedComp.summary: Shifting the phase shifts the normalized potential

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedFast.text: The finite derivative-word norm of a profile restricted to any set $A\subseteq[0,T]$ is bounded by its full-slab unweighted seminorm. The weight is the constant one and the norm is the supremum version without the half-Hölder part. The argument is monotonicity under restriction; no compactness or nonemptiness of $A$ is required.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedFast.summary: Restricting times decreases the unweighted norm

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedFast.text: For an unbundled function of label and phase, this definition averages the translates $f(x+(0,r))$ over one phase period. It allows derivative words with constant label or phase directions to commute with the same averaging operator. Periodicity is not part of the definition; it enters the identification with the bundled phase average.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedFast.summary: Averaging translations in the phase variable

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedFast.text: For a smooth function $f$ and any constant direction $d$ in label–phase space, differentiating the average of its phase translates equals averaging that directional derivative. The proof differentiates under the interval integral and then commutes evaluation of a continuous linear map with integration. The direction may include both label and phase components.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedFast.summary: A constant derivative commutes with phase averaging

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedFast.text: Any finite word in constant directions commutes with averaging phase translates of a smooth function. The proof inducts over the word and applies the single-derivative identity to the already differentiated smooth field. There is no sorting or derivative-order bound in this identity; those restrictions arise only when constructing a finite norm.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedFast.summary: Every constant derivative word commutes with averaging

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedFast.text: On a chosen time subset of the slab, the weighted slice of the bundled phase average equals the average of weighted phase translates of the original slice. Period one makes the integral independent of the starting phase. Since the weight $\tau$ depends only on time, it factors through the phase integral without requiring a time derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedFast.summary: Weighted phase averages as translated integrals

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.text: For positive slab length, the concrete label-advection operator preserves every carrier-dependent lattice shift when its inputs lie in the common twisted space. The proof checks that the derivative of the second field and the coframe direction selected by the first repeat under the same shift. This is a closure result, rather than an evolution or cancellation equation.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.summary: Label advection respects the carrier translation

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.text: For positive slab length, the concrete label gradient preserves every carrier-dependent lattice shift when its inputs lie in the common twisted space. The proof checks that the derivative of the scalar profile and the coframe G repeat under the same shift. This is a closure result, rather than an evolution or cancellation equation.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.summary: The label gradient respects the carrier translation

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.text: For positive slab length, the concrete material operator preserves every carrier-dependent lattice shift when its inputs lie in the common twisted space. The proof checks that its time derivative and multiplication by M repeat under the same shift. This is a closure result, rather than an evolution or cancellation equation.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.summary: The material operator respects the carrier translation

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.text: For positive slab length, the concrete phase-advection operator preserves every carrier-dependent lattice shift when its inputs lie in the common twisted space. The proof checks that the phase derivative of the second field and the contraction of κ with the first repeat under the same shift. This is a closure result, rather than an evolution or cancellation equation.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.summary: Phase advection respects the carrier translation

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.text: For positive slab length, the concrete phase gradient preserves every carrier-dependent lattice shift when its inputs lie in the common twisted space. The proof checks that the phase derivative of the pressure and the covector κ repeat under the same shift. This is a closure result, rather than an evolution or cancellation equation.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.summary: The fast gradient respects the carrier translation

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.text: For a unit-periodic vector function, replacing the phase by its negative leaves the phase mean unchanged. Reversing the integration interval and then shifting it by one period gives the same integral. The result supports propagation of joint label-phase reflection symmetry through the averaging operator.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.summary: A complete phase average is invariant under reversal

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.text: For a unit-periodic vector function, translating the phase argument by any real $b$ leaves its phase mean unchanged. The proof translates the interval integral and uses equality of integrals over intervals of length one. This is the step that removes carrier-induced phase offsets from averaged profiles.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.summary: A complete phase average ignores the starting phase

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.text: If a periodic profile satisfies every carrier-dependent lattice translation identity on the slab, its whole representative satisfies those identities. Outside the slab both sides vanish, since the shifts leave time fixed. This supports packaging solver outputs whose geometric properties are proved only on the time domain.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.summary: Extend the twisted identity beyond the slab

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.text: If a period direction $d$ is negated by the joint reflection and $f$ is periodic with period $d$, then composing $f$ with the reflection is still periodic with that period. The proof uses invariance under subtracting a period. This applies to both pure phase periods and twisted lattice shifts.

A smooth profile satisfying the reflection identity on the slab satisfies it everywhere as a representative. Reflection preserves time, so both sides are zero at off-slab points. This lets later symmetry proofs work on the domain where derivatives and coefficient identities have their physical meaning.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProf.summary: Extend an on-slab reflection law to the representative

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.text: Fixing a label $a$ in a smooth twisted profile gives a function continuous on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$ in time and phase. The proof composes the profile’s slab continuity with the insertion of the fixed label. This is the domain needed for differentiating the phase primitive with respect to time.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.summary: A fixed-label profile is continuous in time and phase

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.text: If two vector-valued functions are continuous on a set $S$, their pointwise cross product is continuous on $S$. The proof expands the three coordinate formulas into products and differences. This supplies continuity of the potential-time integrand before differentiating its phase integral on a closed time interval.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.summary: Cross products preserve continuity on a set

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.text: At a fixed label and phase zero, a smooth profile is continuous as a function on the time–phase product slab, even though the displayed phase coordinate is unused. This is a convenient common domain for coefficient and profile integrands. It follows by inserting the fixed label and phase into the slab-continuous field.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.summary: The phase-zero coefficient is continuous in time

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.text: If $f$ is differentiable at $(a,s)$, the label part of its derivative there is exactly the derivative of $b\mapsto f(b,s)$ at $a$. The proof decomposes the derivative on the product space into its label and phase parts. It translates between the mixed-coordinate potential and the ordinary derivative used in a pulled-back curl.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.summary: The label jet is the fixed-phase derivative

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.text: If $\kappa\cdot F=0$ at every label and phase, the normalized pressure profile agrees with the pressure obtained by replacing $F$ with zero. Only the forcing contribution to the pressure slope vanishes. The velocity-dependent term remains, so the conclusion does not assert that the pressure itself is zero.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.summary: A transverse force contributes no phase-pressure slope

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.text: For continuous velocity and forcing slices, the potential-time profile decomposes into its zero-forcing part plus the ordinary normalized wave potential of the force $F$. This follows by separating the integrand’s two linear coefficient terms and adding their phase primitives. No transverse condition is needed for this identity; transversality is used when simplifying pressure.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.summary: The forcing contributes its own potential

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.text: For continuous functions into a complete real normed space, the centered phase primitive of their sum is the sum of the two primitives. Continuity supplies integrability on every finite interval and continuity of the resulting indefinite integrals. These hypotheses justify the additivity needed to split forcing from homogeneous relay terms.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.summary: Adding continuous inputs adds their phase primitives

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.text: Multiplying an input by a real constant $r$ multiplies its centered phase primitive by the same constant. The proof distributes scalar multiplication through both interval integrals and through subtraction of the phase mean. This algebraic identity applies without an extra continuity assumption; it does not claim that the primitive differentiates to an arbitrary input.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.summary: A constant passes through the centered phase primitive

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.text: An existing smoothness and derivative-word bound for a relay coefficient with allowance $A$ remains valid with any $B\ge A$. Smoothness is unchanged, and both the allowance’s nonnegativity and each word estimate are enlarged by the same inequality. This lemma combines separately obtained potential and geometric bounds into one shared budget.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedRela.summary: A larger coefficient allowance preserves every derivative bound

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSlow.text: For two bundled profiles $L$ and $f$, evaluation of their pointwise application at a slab point is ordinary application of $L(x)$ to $f(x)$. The result is valid for arbitrary real normed spaces of the declared types. It is an encoding identity used to expose scalar contractions inside divergence estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSlow.summary: Applying a profile of linear maps pointwise

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSlow.text: For arbitrary smooth twisted coefficients and profiles, the abstract label-advection operator equals the sum of its three coordinate contributions. The proof expands the label vector $Gz$ in the Euclidean basis and uses linearity of the slice derivative. The identity uses $T>0$ to identify slab and fixed-time derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSlow.summary: Summing coordinate contributions gives slow advection

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSlow.text: This helper multiplies the $i$th component of $Gz$ by the $i$th label derivative of $g$. Both operations are built from bundled continuous linear maps and pointwise application. Summing the three coordinates recovers label advection; the definition itself makes no claim about a numerical bound or amplitude weight.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSlow.summary: A single coordinate contribution to slow advection

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSlow.text: At a slab time, the helper is $(Gz)_i$ times the derivative of the fixed-time slice of $g$ in direction $(e_i,0)$. The statement unfolds the bundled derivative and application operations. It fixes exactly which profile is differentiated, preventing the coefficient or advector from being mistaken for the derivative’s target.

For nonzero label width, one coordinate of slow advection has its order-$n$ weighted norm bounded by two product constants, the scaled-row norm, the order-$n$ norm of the advector, and the order-$(n+1)$ norm of the differentiated profile. Separate bounded time weights $r$ and $q$ multiply to the output weight.

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.text: For positive slab length, a phase-independent twisted profile is fixed by the concrete average operator. This converts a value-level independence statement into the algebraic identity required by hierarchy construction. The period has length one, so averaging a constant phase slice returns that same slice.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.summary: A phase-independent profile equals its average

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.text: At any label and any time in the closed slab $[0,T]$, the phase slice $s\mapsto f(t,a,s)$ of a smooth hierarchy profile is continuous. This auxiliary statement is made directly for smooth profiles on the slab, so the completion integration argument need not introduce twisted periodicity at this step. It supplies regularity for integrals rather than a source identity.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.summary: The completion calculation has continuous phase integrands

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.text: The value of the twisted fast-advection profile built from $C$ and $Y$ is the scalar product $\kappa\cdot C$ times the within-slab phase derivative $\partial_sY$. The time is required to lie in the slab. This exposes the concrete integrand to which periodic integration by parts is applied in the completion cancellation.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.summary: Evaluate fast advection as a phase derivative

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.text: For a twisted profile and a time in the slab, the label derivative at a fixed label is a continuous function of phase. The proof obtains this regularity from the smooth label-phase slice. It provides the integrability required when the average acts on operator-valued derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.summary: The label derivative varies continuously with phase

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.text: Fix a label and a time belonging to the closed slab. Smoothness carried by the twisted-profile type implies continuity of the remaining phase function. This allows the period integral to be used at endpoint times as well as interior times; it makes no claim about values outside the slab.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.summary: A fixed label has a continuous phase slice

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.text: This private abbreviation asserts phase independence of the underlying smooth profile carried by a lattice-twisted profile. It concerns equality of values on the profile slab, not the absence of a phase variable from the function type. It lets mean profiles be recognized even when their stored representation still accepts a phase argument.

If the twisted hierarchy average fixes a profile, then its underlying smooth function is phase independent on the slab. The proof uses the concrete definition of phase averaging. This is the direction needed to treat selected mean profiles and the parent residual as label fields.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.summary: A profile equal to its average has no phase dependence

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.text: At a time in the closed slab, applying the within-slab Fréchet derivative in the direction $(0,v,0)$ gives the ordinary derivative of the fixed-time, fixed-phase label slice in direction $v$. Spatial labels are unrestricted, which permits an ordinary label derivative even at a temporal endpoint.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.summary: The slab derivative agrees with the label derivative

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.text: For a phase-independent twisted profile, the label derivative at any phase equals the derivative at phase zero. The equality follows by identifying the two entire label functions before taking the derivative. It does not require an additional regularity estimate, and its time is restricted to the profile slab.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.summary: The derivative of a mean is independent of phase

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.text: For a twisted profile whose operator average is zero, the unit-period integral $\int_0^1f(t,a,s)\,ds$ of its values vanishes at each label and each time in the slab $[0,T]$, $T>0$. The coefficient fields $G$, $M$ and $\kappa$ parameterize the operators but do not change this integral. The conclusion translates the algebraic average into the analytic phase mean.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.summary: The abstract zero average is the actual phase integral

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.text: Assume every label slice of the fixed-time profile has zero phase mean. The mean of the operator-valued label derivative then vanishes. Smoothness and completeness justify differentiation of the phase integral. This is stronger than checking a single label direction and supports cancellation after applying phase-independent matrices.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.summary: The label derivative of an oscillation averages to zero

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.text: If the phase mean vanishes at every time and label on a positive closed slab, the mean of the within-slab time derivative also vanishes there. The proof differentiates the parameter integral using the profile regularity. Positive slab length supplies the unique within-derivative behavior at both temporal endpoints.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.summary: Time differentiation preserves a vanishing phase average

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.text: The product of the slow divergence of the zero profile with any second profile is zero. The conclusion is equality of twisted vector profiles, so all representation layers are included. It removes the artificial zero level when reindexing the completion contribution in the hierarchy average.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.summary: A zero first profile contributes no divergence product

_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.text: The time slice at fixed label and phase has a derivative within the closed interval, given by the full profile derivative in direction $(1,0,0)$. This formulation includes both endpoints without imposing an extension beyond them. It is the time-derivative identity used when differentiating a zero phase mean.
_private.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedSour.summary: The profile time derivative is taken inside the slab

_private.TorusEuler.InductionAmplificati.text: For nonnegative $C$, natural exponent $n$, and positive real exponent $\alpha$, the inequality $C(\log\mu)^n\le\mu^\alpha$ holds for all sufficiently large real $\mu$. The statement is eventual as $\mu\to\infty$; no explicit numerical threshold is claimed. It supplies the asymptotic absorption behind the induction budgets.
_private.TorusEuler.InductionAmplificati.summary: Every fixed logarithmic power is absorbed by a positive frequency power

_private.TorusEuler.InductionBudget.0.To.text: For all sufficiently large real $x$, $(\log x)^6\le x^{1/16}$. The proof specializes the standard little-o comparison between logarithmic and positive power growth and then removes absolute values on an eventually nonnegative domain. This converts the logarithmic gain bound into a decaying induction interval length.
_private.TorusEuler.InductionBudget.0.To.summary: A small positive power dominates six logarithms

_private.TorusEuler.InductionBudget.0.To.text: When $\mu\ge1$, $C\le\mu$, and both $b$ and $n$ are positive integers, the statement bounds $C(\mu^9)^{bn}$ by $\mu^{10bn}$. The positive product $bn$ absorbs the extra factor $\mu$. This is the arithmetic step used before converting a derivative-order cost into a small power of the new frequency.
_private.TorusEuler.InductionBudget.0.To.summary: Parent powers and a constant fit into one exponent

_private.TorusEuler.InductionBudget.0.To.text: For $b\ge1$, every scheduled exponent $K(q)=320b(q+1)$ is at least $320$. The integer formula already contains the positive factor $q+1$, so no additional lower bound on $q$ is needed. This estimate supplies generous numerical margins in the parent and residual frequency budgets.
_private.TorusEuler.InductionBudget.0.To.summary: Every scheduled frequency exponent is at least 320

_private.TorusEuler.InductionChildEstima.text: With $\mu\ge2$ and $b\ge1$, the child frequency is at least $2\mu$ and $2^{12}$, and the following frequency is at least the child frequency. Both frequencies are explicit powers with scheduled exponents. These bounds supply positivity and separation needed in later real-power estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.InductionChildEstima.summary: Three lower bounds for successive scheduled frequencies

_private.TorusEuler.InductionChildEstima.text: For $\mu\ge1$, $b\ge1$, and $n\le320$, the scheduled child frequency $\mu^{K(q)}$ dominates $\mu^n$. The lower bound follows from the factor $320b(q+1)$ in the exponent. No monotonicity of an entire frequency sequence is needed.
_private.TorusEuler.InductionChildEstima.summary: The child frequency absorbs every fixed low power

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveParentGeome.text: Assume $f\ge1$, $K\ge0$, $2K\le f$ and $f^2\le g$. Then $Kf^5g^{-3}\le1/2$. This converts the Fourier differentiation factor and next-frequency residual decay into the bound $|\nabla R|\le1/2$ required of the restricted parent. Positivity of the denominators follows from the hypotheses; it is not supplied by the convention $x/0=0$.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveParentGeome.summary: The residual derivative fits the half-unit budget

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveParentGeome.text: If $\lambda_0\ge4$, every later frequency satisfies $\lambda_j\ge\lambda_0$. Each next frequency satisfies $\lambda_{j+1}\ge2\lambda_j$ and $\lambda_{j+1}\ge\lambda_j^2$. These inequalities follow from the recurrence $\lambda_{j+1}=\lambda_j^{K(q_{j+1})}$ of the parameter schedule and make the fixed numerical residual and coercivity budgets valid at every stage.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveParentGeome.summary: The stage frequencies dominate their predecessors and squares

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveProfileBoun.text: For any physical approximation over the given parent geometry and pressure, proves that its stored parent residual equals the slab's residual profile. Both have the same pointwise momentum-residual value on the slab, so profile extensionality identifies them. This prevents the recurrence from using estimates for a different residual witness.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveProfileBoun.summary: The hierarchy residual equals the actual parent residual

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveProfileBoun.text: If the parent scale is at least one, increasing both a nonnegative coefficient and its natural exponent increases their product. This small inequality is used repeatedly when several analytic losses are placed under one chosen parent power. It is independent of any Euler equation, profile construction or frequency schedule.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveProfileBoun.summary: Increasing a nonnegative coefficient and parent exponent preserves bounds

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.text: Reads the central amplitude from each positive-index generated tip and inserts zero at index zero. The exported stage or central-wave record uses the positive indices fixed by its formulas. This is bookkeeping for the same recursively selected waves; it does not claim that the genuine first wave or its data vanish.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.summary: The central amplitudes of the generated sequence

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.text: Reads the time cutoff from each positive-index generated tip and inserts zero at index zero. The exported stage or central-wave record uses the positive indices fixed by its formulas. This is bookkeeping for the same recursively selected waves; it does not claim that the genuine first wave or its data vanish.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.summary: The switching functions of the generated sequence

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.text: Reads the central derivative-error operator from each positive-index generated tip and inserts zero at index zero. The exported stage or central-wave record uses the positive indices fixed by its formulas. This is bookkeeping for the same recursively selected waves; it does not claim that the genuine first wave or its data vanish.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.summary: The central gradient errors of the generated sequence

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.text: Identifies the activation attached to the older member of the $n$th generated pair with the global activation $t_n$. The proof separates the zero-index case from successor indices. This equality supplies the identification of types needed to compare the older stage object with the globally retained stage.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.summary: The older stage uses its original activation

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.text: Extracts the practical velocity equality from the generated tip and retained-stage definitions. It is used when exporting correction and gradient-splitting fields, whose formulas initially refer to the local older stage. The equality identifies actual functions and therefore allows the same derivative and residual expressions to be reused.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.summary: The older and retained velocities are the same function

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.text: Reads the oscillatory velocity increment from each positive-index generated tip and inserts zero at index zero. The exported stage or central-wave record uses the positive indices fixed by its formulas. This is bookkeeping for the same recursively selected waves; it does not claim that the genuine first wave or its data vanish.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.summary: The oscillatory increments of the generated sequence

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.text: Reads the central wave vector from each positive-index generated tip and inserts zero at index zero. The exported stage or central-wave record uses the positive indices fixed by its formulas. This is bookkeeping for the same recursively selected waves; it does not claim that the genuine first wave or its data vanish.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.summary: The central wave vectors of the generated sequence

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.text: Proves that the Leray-projected momentum expression of the time-independent shear is identically zero, for every real parameter and time. The time derivative is zero and the shear advects itself trivially. This supplies the base stage’s residual identity; no forcing term is introduced by the chosen closed-slab derivative convention.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.summary: The stationary shear has zero projected momentum

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.text: For a shear parameter of absolute value at most one and $C\ge1+4\pi$, certifies the actual two-time stationary shear flow on the unit time slab. Explicit inverse-flow and Jacobian formulas establish the derivative bounds. The hypotheses are quantitative; the theorem does not cover arbitrary large shear parameters with the same constant.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageConstr.summary: The stationary flow satisfies the stage deformation bound

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStagePressu.text: For a smooth velocity with first and second derivatives bounded by $R\mathsf D^j$, where $R\ge0$ and $\mathsf D\ge1$, proves the gradient has order-zero half-Hölder norm at most $3R\mathsf D^2$. The first jet bounds the supremum and the second supplies variation. This is a Euclidean estimate and does not require converting the field to a torus Fourier representation.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStagePressu.summary: Two velocity jets control the gradient Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStagePressu.text: Restricts a jointly smooth field on a closed time slab to a fixed time belonging to that slab. Since the spatial domain is all of Euclidean space, the result is globally smooth in the spatial variable. This supplies ordinary spatial derivatives in the pressure estimates, including at the temporal endpoints.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStagePressu.summary: A smooth slab field has smooth spatial slices

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStagePressu.text: If each field at a retained mean level is fixed by the hierarchy's averaging operator, then their finite sum is phase independent. Linearity of the average first shows that the sum is also fixed; the phase-independence theorem then applies. The statement remains valid for an empty level set, where the sum is zero.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStagePressu.summary: A finite sum of mean fields stays phase independent

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageProfil.text: For positive retained depth, a closed envelope set, and a leading input inactive before $t_0$ or outside that set, the centered finite velocity profile is zero at every slab time strictly before activation. The proof expands it as the finite sum of oscillations and completions and applies their inherited inactivity. The phase-independent mean is removed before this conclusion is asserted.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageProfil.summary: The full centered profile vanishes before activation

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageProfil.text: Given an order-$m$ inverse-coframe bound and a profile seminorm bound $A\mathsf D^q\lambda^{\alpha}$, with nonnegative costs, $\mathsf D\ge1$, and positive frequency $\lambda$, the scaled coframe-applied slice has order-$m$ phase jets bounded by the coframe cost times $A\mathsf D^{q+1}\lambda^{\alpha}$. The proof combines the finite product estimate with the conversion from mixed-word norms to scaled Fréchet jets.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageProfil.summary: A coframe consumes one parent power in the jet bound

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageProfil.text: At a slab time, pulling the finite velocity profile back by the inverse parent coframe sends its phase average to the average part and its centered profile to the oscillatory part. The proof moves the phase-independent linear map through the period integral. The statement concerns the case in which the additional Eulerian correction is zero; the phase mean need not vanish.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageProfil.summary: The uncut pullback preserves the phase decomposition

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageProfil.text: The preceding pointwise average and oscillation identities are promoted to equalities of functions of label and phase at a fixed slab time. The proof uses function extensionality twice and contains no new averaging argument. These equalities permit rewriting the functions inside scaled phase-jet bounds for the same finite velocity profile.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageProfil.summary: The pullback identities hold as full label–phase functions

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageProfil.text: On a positive time slab, the unweighted order-$m$ seminorm of a linear-map profile applied to a vector profile is bounded by the product constant for four directions times their two seminorms. Evaluation of a continuous linear map is bilinear with operator norm at most one. The estimate is applied to the inverse coframe, but the linear-map profile need not be invertible or an actual inverse coframe.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageProfil.summary: Applying a coframe obeys the finite product estimate

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageProfil.text: If every value of the parent coefficient-cost function is nonnegative, the coframe cost is nonnegative at each order. The proof combines positivity of $4^m$, the finite product constant, and the coefficient-order sum. This arithmetic helper justifies multiplying inequalities in the subsequent scaled-jet estimates; it does not bound the inverse coframe itself.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageProfil.summary: Nonnegative coefficient costs give a nonnegative product budget

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageVeloci.text: Takes the coframe order constant at order $P+1$ for depth $P$. That extra spatial derivative is needed when the finite hierarchy is evaluated on the physical graph and then placed in a Hölder norm at the cutoff depth. The definition does not itself prove any coframe estimate; the corresponding stage coefficient certificate supplies it.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageVeloci.summary: The inverse-flow coefficient is read at one extra order

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageVeloci.text: Multiplies the common level bound by the number $P$ of retained levels $\{1,\dots,P\}$. This scalar estimates finite sums when individual profile bounds are converted into a bound for the assembled field. At zero depth the index set is empty; physical stage estimates later require a nonempty hierarchy of depth at least two.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageVeloci.summary: The retained levels contribute their number times one bound

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageVeloci.text: Adds the scalar factors for the first derivative at the origin of the higher oscillatory remainder and the mean correction. The constants $96$ and $24$ retain the two distinct derivative estimates. This prefactor is then placed inside the common step budget used to bound the central-gradient error.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageVeloci.summary: The two central corrections have a common scalar cost

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageVeloci.text: Combines the coframe constant, retained-level count and chain-rule factors into the oscillatory velocity prefactor at the selected depth. Frequency and parent powers are kept outside this scalar. It is subsequently included in the common step cost, allowing the schedule to dominate all fixed-depth constants before any inductive stage is chosen.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageVeloci.summary: The oscillatory graph has an explicit cutoff-depth cost

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageVeloci.text: For nonnegative integers with $a\le b$ and $c\le b$, proves $a(P+1)+c\le b(P+2)$. This arithmetic inequality absorbs the derivative-dependent parent loss and one further fixed loss into a uniform expression linear in depth. It is used in the full-depth graph estimate and carries no analytic hypotheses.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageVeloci.summary: Two derivative losses fit one larger parent exponent

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageVeloci.text: Assumes a parent scale at least one, nonnegative scalar costs, a recurrence loss bounded by $\mathsf D^\rho$, and sufficient exponent and prefactor budgets. It then bounds both oscillatory and mean graph factors by $\Gamma\mathsf D^{b(P+2)}$. The two cases use squared and sixth-power recurrence losses respectively; this lemma only performs their numerical absorption.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStageVeloci.summary: Both graph estimates fit the chosen parent power

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStepNumeric.text: If the frequency $\lambda$ is at least one and $C\le\lambda^{1/32}$, then $C\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$. The proof compares with the combined exponent $-5/96$. Nonnegativity of $C$ is unnecessary because the multiplying real power is nonnegative.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveStepNumeric.summary: The step rate beats the negative twelfth power

_private.TorusEuler.InductiveVorticityBo.text: The cross product of two scaled vectors equals the product of the scalars times the original cross product. This private bilinearity identity is used to express a preceding wave’s curl in its normalized moving frame. It has no nonzero or orthogonality assumptions, because the algebraic identity holds for all vectors.
_private.TorusEuler.InductiveVorticityBo.summary: Scaling both vectors scales their cross product

_private.TorusEuler.IntegratedLimit.0.To.text: Continuous curves converging uniformly on $[0,T]$ have integrals from zero to any slab time converging to the integral of the continuous limit. The proof bounds the integral of the difference by the interval length times the uniform error. This helper needs no derivative convergence and is used for the nonlinear term and vanishing residual separately.
_private.TorusEuler.IntegratedLimit.0.To.summary: Uniform convergence passes through a time integral

_private.TorusEuler.LabelFlowGeometry.0..text: At the common start and target time $t$, differentiating the starting-time variable $u$ of $X(u\to t)x$ gives $-U(t,x)$. The hypotheses supply a uniform velocity bound $|U|\le C$, a spatial Lipschitz bound with constant $K$, and time continuity at the fixed spatial point. The derivative is taken within the closed slab.
_private.TorusEuler.LabelFlowGeometry.0..summary: Reversing the start time negates velocity

_private.TorusEuler.LabelFlowGeometry.0..text: If the velocity is uniformly bounded by $C$ at every spatial point and allowed time, a particle moves by at most $C\lvert t-s\rvert$ between any two times $s,t$ of the slab.
