The result applies differentiation under an integrable operator kernel using the previously proved kernel integrability. Periodicity is not required here; it is one later way to obtain the global bounds.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: A pressure block preserves bounded smooth inputs

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: If cutoff and velocity are continuous on a set $S$, their far quadratic tensor is continuous there. Continuity of the bounded bilinear tensor map and scalar multiplication gives the result. On the compact far source set this supplies the integrability required by the actual kernel pressure estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Continuous cutoff and velocity give a continuous far density

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: For a complex scalar field of class $C^2$ on Euclidean space, each coordinate Hessian entry is continuous. Differentiation and evaluation in the fixed direction $e_j$ first give a $C^1$ scalar field, whose derivative evaluated at $e_i$ is continuous. These hypotheses justify the compact-cell Hessian integrals.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Twice continuous differentiability makes each mixed partial continuous

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: The coordinate Hessian entry first differentiates in direction $e_j$, then differentiates that scalar function in direction $e_i$. The scalar field may be complex, with both derivatives taken over the real spatial domain. Later $C^2$ hypotheses ensure these expressions are the classical mixed partial derivatives used by periodic integration by parts.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Differentiate a scalar field in two coordinate directions

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: For a smooth periodic velocity and smooth periodic cutoff supported off the lattice, full dyadic pressure equals the sum of the near dyadic pressure and far kernel pressure on any target set separated from the far source. The identity descends both tensor pieces to half Hölder fields, applies multiplier linearity, then uses separated kernel agreement.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Full pressure splits into near multiplier and far kernel

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: For a smooth periodic field and any finite derivative order, a nonnegative real number bounds that jet at every Euclidean point. Continuity bounds the jet on the compact centered cell, and derivative periodicity moves every point into that cell. The bound may depend on the field and the derivative order.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Smooth periodic jets have global uniform bounds

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: If the operator kernel is integrable and the multilinear jet field is continuous with global norm bound $M$, their output composition is integrable. The proof supplies strong measurability and dominates the integrand by $\|K(y)\|M$. This is the integrability certificate used before differentiating the pressure convolution.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: An integrable kernel times a bounded continuous jet is integrable

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: This private field multiplies the quadratic complex velocity tensor by the scalar cutoff $\chi$. The intended cutoff is one near the target and vanishes near the singular lattice. Its support allows a velocity smooth only off the lattice to produce a globally smooth tensor field for the near pressure multiplier.

The order-$d$ pressure-block jet is bounded by $(2M_d+M_{d+1})$ times its half moment. Smoothness and global bounds on every input jet justify differentiation under the integral. Zero kernel mean subtracts the jet at $x$, and the adjacent derivative bound converts this difference into a square-root distance factor.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Cancellation bounds each block by two adjacent input jets

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: For two fields smooth off the lattice, their bilinear tensor jet of order $d$ at an off-origin point is bounded by $\|B\|2^dPQ$ when all input jets through $d$ are bounded there by $P,Q$ and $P\ge0$. The binomial Leibniz coefficients sum to $2^d$. No global bound or periodicity is assumed.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: A bilinear tensor jet has a finite Leibniz bound

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: The norm of the jet obtained by applying a complex operator to its output is at most the product of the operator and jet norms. This follows from the standard composition estimate and invariance under scalar restriction. No completeness, integrability or spatial regularity assumption is needed for this algebraic estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Output composition costs the product of the two norms

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: A globally $C^1$ field bounded by $M$ with derivative bounded by $D$ satisfies $\|f(x)-f(y)\|\le(2M+D)\sqrt{\|x-y\|}$. For short distances use the mean-value estimate, and for long distances use the two value bounds. The hypotheses themselves force $M,D\ge0$; these signs are not extra inputs.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: A value bound and derivative bound imply half Hölder control

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: This private complex linear functional selects entry $(i,j)$ from a pressure tensor. It makes coordinate extraction commute with tensor integrals and preserves smoothness of the selected spatial component. These facts allow the physical double-divergence equation to be compared with the Fourier pressure symbol component by component.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Extract a tensor component for periodic integration by parts

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: This bounded real bilinear map applies a complex-linear operator to the output of a real multilinear spatial jet. Restricting scalars preserves the operator norm, and composition leaves the spatial arguments unchanged. It is the integrand map for differentiating the operator-valued convolution kernel against a smooth complex tensor field.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: An operator acts on the output of a spatial jet

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: Every iterated Fréchet derivative of a spatially periodic function is spatially periodic. Translation by a fixed lattice vector has identity derivative, so differentiating the equality of translated functions preserves each jet. The statement does not require smoothness: it is an identity of the totalized derivative expressions, with regularity supplied by callers.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Spatial derivatives retain integer periodicity

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: The block at scale $2^j$ convolves the input tensor with the inverse Fourier kernel of the annular pressure symbol. This is a scalar complex field on the Euclidean lift. Its kernel is integrable and has zero mean; bounded smooth inputs later allow differentiation and a summable half-moment estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: One dyadic pressure block acts by Euclidean convolution

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: This nonnegative real number integrates the operator-kernel norm weighted by $\sqrt{\|y\|}$. It records exactly the moment needed after replacing a bounded Lipschitz jet by its half Hölder difference bound. Scaling makes these moments decay geometrically with the dyadic index, so their series is finite.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: The half moment measures one dyadic pressure block

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: The integrand defining the block mass is a product of a norm and the nonnegative square root of a norm, so its integral is nonnegative. This estimate needs no strict positivity. It is used when summing block bounds and constructing an everywhere positive denominator for the uniform convergence estimate.

The inverse Fourier transform of the annular pressure symbol is a Schwartz kernel, hence integrable. Dilation by the positive factor $2^j$ preserves integrability with the dimensional normalization $2^{3j}K(2^jx)$ of the rescaled kernel. This establishes a property of the kernel alone; input-dependent integrability is proved separately.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Every dyadic pressure kernel is integrable

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: Every dyadic pressure kernel has integral zero because its compact Fourier symbol vanishes at frequency zero. The positive scale normalization preserves that integral identity. This cancellation permits subtracting the input jet at $x$ inside convolution and is the source of the extra decaying half-moment factor.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: The annular pressure kernel has zero integral

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: For two smooth periodic tensor inputs, the pressure lift of their difference equals the difference of their pressure lifts. The proof descends both to half Hölder torus fields, uses the multiplier agreement theorem and its linearity, then lifts back. These hypotheses ensure that raw infinite sums and integrals represent the genuine linear operator.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Pressure subtraction follows from bounded multiplier linearity

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: If both cutoff and velocity are spatially periodic, the cutoff quadratic tensor is spatially periodic. The statement follows by replacing each translated input with its unshifted value. It is independent of the support and smoothness conditions needed to use this source in the pressure convergence argument.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Periodic cutoff and velocity give a periodic near source

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: Integer periodicity of velocity gives integer periodicity of its pressure tensor pointwise. Both factors are evaluated at the same translated point, so the equality follows directly from the input periodicity. No differentiability, incompressibility or Fourier expansion is needed for this property.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: The quadratic pressure source is spatially periodic

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: The block mass equals the fixed Schwartz half moment multiplied by $(\sqrt2)^{-j}$. The scaling formula for weighted kernel integrals gives this equality, and the ratio is strictly between zero and one. Thus cancellation supplies an absolutely summable majorant for pressure blocks at every derivative order.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Dyadic half moments form a summable geometric sequence

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: For a smooth periodic tensor field, the complex values of its pressure blocks are summable at every spatial point. Compact periodicity supplies the input bounds at orders zero and one; the order-zero block estimate dominates the terms by a summable half-moment sequence. This is used to identify the dyadic sum by uniqueness of limits.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Smooth periodic data have a convergent pressure block series

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: For a fixed smooth cutoff supported off the lattice, convergence of every velocity jet on every compact off-origin set yields convergence of all near tensor jets on the centered cell. The proof first forms tensor jets on the compact intersection with the cutoff support, then extends convergence across the cell using cutoff multiplication.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Compact local velocity limits give near tensor limits on the cell

_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.text: On a compact source set, uniformly convergent continuous velocities with continuous limit give convergence to zero of the integral norm of the far tensor difference, provided $0\le\chi\le1$. This isolated lemma imposes no measurability on $\chi$, so its conclusion concerns the totalized integral expression. The later pressure application assumes a continuous cutoff and proves genuine integrability.
_private.TorusEuler.OffOriginPressureAss.summary: Uniform velocity convergence controls the cutoff norm integral

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.text: A jointly smooth family on $[l,r]$ times a full parameter space gives a smooth parameter function at each time in the interval. Composing with the constant-time inclusion proves the claim. The helper permits spatial or label derivatives of coefficients and solutions while retaining within-time derivative conventions at the endpoints.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.summary: Parameter slices of a smooth slab family are smooth

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.text: A within derivative at $t+c$ transfers to the time-translated function at $t$, provided translation maps the new set into the old one. The derivative value is unchanged because translation has derivative one. This helper shifts an arbitrary launch interval to an interval starting at zero.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.summary: Translate a within derivative to another time interval

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.text: For a positive scalar weight $g$, if each vector in a finite list has norm divided by $g$ at most $C$, then the norm of their sum divided by $g$ is at most the list length times $C$. The proof is repeated triangle inequality; the empty list contributes zero.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.summary: A weighted sum is bounded by its term count

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.text: For a smooth parameter function and positive constant $g$, the norm of a constant-direction word applied to $g^{-1}$ times the function equals the original differentiated norm divided by $g$. The weight is constant with respect to the differentiated parameters. This explicitly matches the manuscript’s convention of dividing by the time weight after differentiation.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.summary: A positive time weight divides the differentiated norm

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.text: For two smooth functions and a list of constant parameter directions, the iterated directional word applied to their sum equals the sum of the two word values. Induction on the list uses additivity of the Fréchet derivative at each step. Smoothness is required so that the derivative operation is additive on the intermediate functions.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.summary: Constant directional words distribute over a sum

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.text: If two functions agree on a neighborhood of a point, then their corresponding directional-word functions agree on some neighborhood there for any finite word. The directions may depend on position in this lemma. Induction uses locality of the Fréchet derivative, enabling derivative vanishing outside a closed support from local equality with zero.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.summary: Local equality survives repeated directional differentiation

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.text: A word of constant directional derivatives applied to the zero function is zero, including the empty word. The proof proceeds by induction on the list. This is used for zero initial data and for localized solutions outside their support, where every derivative of the identically zero field vanishes.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.summary: Every directional word annihilates the zero function

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.text: Multiplying a scalar phase function by a fixed real scalar before taking its mean-corrected primitive is the same as multiplying the primitive afterward. The proof unfolds phase oscillation and uses linearity of the interval integral and phase mean. It is an algebraic helper in the normalized-pressure estimate, without smoothness or nonzero-scalar assumptions.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryDerivativ.summary: Scalar multiplication commutes with the normalized phase primitive

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryHierarchy.text: At a time where the wave vector is nonzero, its adjoint transport equation and the projected amplitude equation imply that the derivative of $\langle\kappa,V\rangle$ is zero. The identity is local and does not assume that the pairing is already zero. A separate uniqueness argument propagates a transverse initial condition across an interval.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryHierarchy.summary: The coupled equations preserve the transverse pairing

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryHierarchy.text: This continuous linear functional sends a bounded continuous profile on $\mathbb R$ to its integral over one unit interval. Its norm is bounded by one because the interval has length one. Periodicity is not required to define the map; it becomes a phase average in applications to periodic profiles.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryHierarchy.summary: Average a bounded continuous phase profile

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryHierarchy.text: Applying a continuous linear operator to a bounded continuous profile before phase averaging gives the same result as applying it to the average. The operator is independent of phase, and continuity guarantees integrability on the unit interval. This identity turns the average of the forced phase ODE into an ordinary homogeneous ODE.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryHierarchy.summary: Averaging commutes with a fixed linear operator

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryHierarchy.text: This continuous linear map sends a linear operator on the target space to its pointwise action on bounded continuous phase profiles. The action has norm at most the operator norm. It allows a phase-independent time-varying coefficient to define a linear ODE in the Banach space of entire phase profiles.

At each phase value, the lifted operator acting on a bounded continuous profile evaluates to the original operator applied to that profile value. This definitional equality links the Banach-space ODE to its pointwise-in-phase version. It carries no assumptions about periodicity, means, transversality or the time evolution.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryHierarchy.summary: The profile action agrees with pointwise evaluation

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryHierarchy.text: If the forcing and velocity profiles are continuous, periodic of period one and have zero phase mean, their pressure slope has the same properties. The strain and wave vector are fixed in phase. No nonzero-wave-vector assumption is needed for this algebraic statement: the slope is zero at $\kappa=0$ under total real division.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryHierarchy.summary: The pressure slope inherits periodicity and zero mean

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: Smooth strain, nonvanishing wave vector, forcing and velocity profiles give a jointly smooth normalized phase pressure. The proof first differentiates the explicit pressure slope and then uses regularity of the phase primitive. This lemma drops the finite-dimensional assumptions and does not itself prove periodicity, zero mean, transversality or the momentum equation.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: The pressure primitive is jointly smooth on the slab

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: On a positive closed time slab, joint smoothness of a parameterized field gives joint smoothness of its ordinary parameter derivative. The proof restricts the joint within-derivative to the parameter direction. Positivity of the slab supplies unique differentiability at its endpoints; the conclusion remains relative to the same closed time domain.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Spatial differentiation preserves smoothness on the closed slab

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: Smooth strain and wave-vector fields on a parameter domain yield smooth amplitude and transverse-projection operators, provided the wave vector never vanishes there. The reciprocal squared norm is the only potentially singular scalar factor. The statement is algebraic in the supplied fields and does not assume the wave-vector transport equation.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Nonvanishing wave vectors give smooth transverse operators

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: Data jointly continuous on the compact time slab times the parameter set yield a map continuous within that parameter set into the uniform path space. This upgrades pointwise-in-time continuity using the compact time domain. The zero extension outside the parameter set does not enter the conclusion and need not be globally continuous.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Joint continuity gives uniform path continuity within the domain

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: For a convex time set, a jointly continuous family and its supplied continuous time derivative on the unit phase interval may be averaged before differentiation. The resulting within-time derivative is the phase mean of the derivative field. This justifies the mean ODE even at time-domain boundary points, without assuming periodicity.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Differentiate the phase average within the time domain

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: On a convex parameter set, jointly continuous data and jointly continuous supplied parameter derivatives give the within-set derivative of the curried path map. The candidate derivative sends a direction to the path of pointwise derivatives. Convexity controls the remainder uniformly in time, upgrading pointwise differentiability to differentiability in the uniform path norm.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: A continuous derivative field differentiates the path-valued map

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: At a slab point, a jointly continuous time-derivative field and the specified parameter derivative combine into a joint within-slab Fréchet derivative. The time derivative is assumed along every parameter trajectory, while the parameter derivative is needed at the chosen time and point. The proof separates the time increment from the parameter increment without extending beyond the slab.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Combine the time derivative with the parameter derivative

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: For phase-independent continuous operators, a jointly continuous forced ODE solution starting from zero inherits period one and zero phase mean from its forcing. The proof applies uniqueness to the phase-shift difference and to the averaged solution. It allows nonnegative duration and concludes these properties at a specified time of the closed slab.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Zero-start dynamics preserve periodicity and zero phase mean

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: Two profiles that agree on the closed unit interval have equal phase averages. This is an interval-integral congruence, with no continuity or periodicity hypothesis. It is used to compare an actual profile with a clamped continuous-path representative that may have unrelated values outside that interval.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Only the values on one interval determine the average

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: A continuous path of linear maps from the parameter space to the target gives one continuous linear map sending a fixed direction to its time path of images. Its norm is bounded by the uniform norm of the operator path. This is the form of the derivative of a curried time-path family.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: An operator path acts on a fixed parameter direction

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: The construction that turns an operator-valued path into a linear map with path-valued output is continuous linear, with norm at most one. This packages the change in argument order as a bounded operator. It allows regularity of the pointwise derivative field to imply regularity of the derivative in the uniform path space.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Currying operator paths is itself continuous linear

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: At a slab time $t$, the path obtained by applying a continuous operator path $A$ to a fixed direction $p$ equals $A(t)p$. This definitional identity identifies the candidate derivative of a path-valued map with the original pointwise derivative. It requires no differentiability or parameter-domain hypotheses beyond continuity of the operator path.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Evaluate the operator path on its fixed direction

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: This bounded linear map integrates a continuous path on $[0,1]$, using its clamped extension to express the phase-average operation. Its norm is at most one. The compact domain supplies the uniform norm, and the map is used to transfer derivatives through phase averaging.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Integrate a continuous profile on the unit interval

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: If a continuous unit-interval path agrees there with an ordinary real-domain profile, integrating the path gives that profile's phase average. The proof uses equality only on $[0,1]$. It therefore permits the two objects to differ arbitrarily elsewhere and does not require a globally continuous or periodic extension of the profile.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: The path integral equals the original phase average

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.text: If the original generator, weight $g$ and specified weight derivative $g'$ are continuous on $I$, and the weight is strictly positive there, the transformed generator is continuous. Only continuity and positivity are used in this lemma; $g'$ is not yet required to be an actual derivative. The result prepares the weighted linear-ODE existence and comparison arguments.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.summary: A positive differentiable weight gives a continuous generator

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.text: A solution of the homogeneous transformed equation becomes a solution of $x′=Ax$ after multiplication by the positive weight. The derivative witness for the weight supplies the cancellation of its logarithmic rate. This converse lets the assumed weighted stability of the original equation control ordinary norms for the transformed equation.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.summary: Multiplying by the weight restores the original equation

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.text: If $x′=Ax+f$ and the positive weight $g$ has derivative $g'$, then $x/g$ solves the transformed equation with generator $A-(g'/g)I$ and forcing $f/g$. All identities are within the same set $I$ at the point $t$. The strict positivity hypothesis rules out division by a vanishing amplitude weight.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.summary: Dividing a forced solution changes its generator

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.text: For a positive real weight $g$, the norm of $g^{-1}x$ is $|x|/g$. Positivity removes the absolute value in the scalar norm. This identity converts ordinary norm estimates for the normalized solution back into the weighted ratios used throughout the seed comparison.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.summary: A positive scalar weight divides the norm

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.text: Defines the transformed linear generator $A-(g′/g)I$ for the normalized unknown $x/g$. The inputs are the value $g$ and its proposed derivative $g'$ at a time. The definition itself does not assert that $g'$ is a derivative or that the weight is positive; those assumptions enter the transformation theorems.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.summary: The generator after dividing by the amplitude weight

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.text: Assume every homogeneous solution of $x'=Ax$ satisfies the given weighted forward estimate with constant $K$. Then every solution of the transformed generator satisfies the corresponding unweighted norm estimate. The weight is positive and has the stated within derivative throughout the interval, so multiplying back by it and cancelling its values is legitimate.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.summary: Weighted stability becomes ordinary stability after normalization

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatorySolveSymm.text: For a continuous operator coefficient on a nonnegative closed time slab, two solutions of the same inhomogeneous linear equation with equal initial values agree throughout the slab. Subtraction removes the forcing and reduces the claim to homogeneous uniqueness. The theorem allows a zero-length slab, where the conclusion is only equality at the initial point.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatorySolveSymm.summary: Equal initial data give the same forced linear trajectory

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatorySolveSymm.text: The formula for the oscillatory pressure slope is linear in the forcing and velocity when the matrix and covector are fixed. Negating those two inputs therefore negates the scalar slope. This algebraic equality remains valid under Lean’s total division convention and is used inside the separately nondegenerate oscillatory solve.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatorySolveSymm.summary: Negating velocity and forcing negates the pressure slope

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S53.Lib.text: The scaled derivatives of the wave profile are bounded by $Ch$, obtained from Lemma 3.1 through the wave-profile bounds, which replace the original constants $1/2$ and the library bounds. This is a finite derivative estimate for the localized leading profile. The phase width is positive and at most one, and the spatial envelope is kept separate from the central amplitude weight.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S53.Lib.summary: Weighted profile derivatives have size proportional to the width

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S53.Lib.text: With unit label scale, an Appendix D label direction is exactly the corresponding Euclidean coordinate vector. The adjacent statement proves reconstruction of a vector by its coordinate sum; the comment written above this statement in the formalization describes that different identity.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S53.Lib.summary: Unit label directions are the coordinate vectors

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S53.Lib.text: Coordinate vectors reconstruct every spatial vector. The bridge converts between coordinate word norms in Appendix D and Fréchet derivative bounds used by the fixed-plane construction. The conversion changes constants depending on the order, not the absolute parent exponent.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S53.Lib.summary: Coordinate vectors reconstruct every spatial vector

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S5a.Lib.text: Difference bound for a label-dependent field from its first jet. The first label derivatives of the parent coefficients make the fixed-plane ODE a small perturbation of its value at the origin. A common envelope exponent controls both amplitude comparison and positivity of the physical coupling.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S5a.Lib.summary: A first derivative bound controls differences between labels

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: Let $J_m$ be continuous curves in complete normed spaces, and suppose each satisfies an integrated equation driven by a bounded bilinear map applied to the curve of index $r(m)$. On a positive closed interval, every curve is smooth in time. Induction differentiates the integral at successively higher indices; no uniform bound on the derivative loss $r$ is assumed.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Integrated quadratic evolution gives every time derivative

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For a family of smooth periodic velocities, continuity of its compatible jet tuple through order two on $[0,S]$ implies continuity of the projected quadratic momentum at each fixed spatial point. The product estimate (5.59), a hypothesis, supplies the bounded bilinear map. The conclusion here is continuity in time for the chosen point, not a separate uniform spatial convergence statement.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Continuous second-order jets give a continuous momentum term

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: The inclusion of the range of smooth jet tuples through order $m$ has dense range in the space of compatible jets of order $m$. This follows from defining that space as the topological closure of the range. It asserts density in this particular closed subspace, not density of smooth jets in the entire ambient space of arbitrary derivative tuples.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Smooth jet tuples are dense in the chosen completion

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: This continuous linear map evaluates the zeroth compatible jet at a spatial point and converts its zero-argument multilinear value into a vector. The construction is purely an evaluation map; it asserts no Euler equation or regularity of a time-dependent field. It lets uniform jet convergence imply convergence of the actual nonlinear term at that point.

For smooth periodic $u$ and $v$, evaluate the order-zero output of the completed projected momentum map of order $0$ at $x$. The result is the projected momentum $-\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(u\otimes v)(x)$. This combines the smooth-input compatibility theorem with the identity for the zeroth iterated derivative, connecting Banach-space convergence to the pointwise Euler equation.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Zeroth momentum evaluation returns the physical nonlinear term

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: A continuous spatially periodic function into a normed additive group has a real uniform bound on its norm over all of $\mathbb R^3$. The proof descends it to the compact torus and pulls the compactness bound back. This supplies boundedness of each smooth spatial derivative before it is packaged as a bounded continuous jet.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: A continuous periodic field has a global bound

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: A linear isometry $e:E\to H$ with dense range lets every continuous linear map from $E$ into a complete space $F$ extend to $H$. This definition bundles extension itself as a continuous linear operation on maps. Density gives uniqueness and the isometry controls the norm, preparing the completion argument for periodic momentum on spatial jets.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Extend operators across a dense isometric inclusion

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: Given a bounded bilinear map on $E$, a linear isometry with dense range from $E$ into $H$, and a complete target $F$, this definition extends the operation to two inputs in $H$. It extends in both variables using continuous linear maps. The resulting map agrees with the original operation on the dense domain, as the following theorem records.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Extend a bilinear operation to compatible limiting jets

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: Evaluating the extended bilinear map on $e(x)$ and $e(y)$ returns exactly $B(x,y)$. Both uses of continuous extension are reduced using density and the isometric inclusion. This compatibility identity is what later identifies the completed momentum map with the actual projected tensor divergence for smooth velocity inputs.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The extended operation agrees on original inputs

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: At a fixed point $x$, assume uniform convergence of velocities and second-order compatible jets, continuity of the stage and limit quantities, uniformly vanishing residuals, and the actual stage derivative equation. With the product estimate (5.59), the limit satisfies both the integrated projected equation and its within-time derivative identity on the positive closed prefix. Integration is performed before taking the limit.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The integrated stage equation passes to the limit

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: If $f$ has spatial Hölder regularity $C^{m,1/2}$ and $j\le m$, then the norm of $D^jf(x)$ is at most the $C^{m,1/2}$ norm of $f$. The boundedness witnesses in the regularity hypothesis justify taking the suprema, and each seminorm is nonnegative. The theorem therefore applies to genuine Hölder fields, not to arbitrary functions for which the norm expression is merely defined.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The Hölder norm controls each lower derivative

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For a smooth periodic velocity, each derivative of order $i\le m$ at any point is bounded by the norm of its order-$m$ compatible jet tuple. The estimate combines evaluation in the bounded-function norm with the product norm. This supplies uniform derivative bounds before converting tuple control into Hölder control.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The tuple norm bounds each spatial derivative

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: Multiplying a smooth periodic field by a real scalar commutes with its periodic Hölder Leray lift. The proof represents the field as a bounded half-Hölder field on the torus and uses linearity of the bounded Leray operator there. This verifies homogeneity on genuine smooth inputs rather than relying on how the lift is defined for unsuitable functions.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The Leray projection respects scalar multiplication

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For two smooth periodic velocities, this constructs the smooth periodic field $\operatorname{div}(u\otimes v)$. It differentiates their tensor product and contracts the derivative with the tensor divergence. Smoothness and periodicity are proved and stored with the output. No divergence-free hypothesis is imposed on either input.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The tensor divergence remains a smooth periodic field

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: This packages $(u,v)\mapsto\operatorname{div}(u\otimes v)$ as an algebraic bilinear map on smooth periodic fields. The product’s bilinearity and linearity of differentiation prove additivity and scalar compatibility in each variable. This declaration supplies no operator-norm estimate; boundedness is established later after the fields are represented by finite jet tuples.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Tensor divergence is linear in each smooth input

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: At a spatial point, the constructed momentum-divergence field is the contraction of the derivative of the tensor product. This definitional equality removes the smooth-field wrapper. It is used to establish additivity and homogeneity without losing the identification with the tensor divergence appearing in the projected Euler equation.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Evaluate the tensor divergence by its defining contraction

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: The pointwise tensor product $u\otimes v$ of two smooth periodic velocity fields is spatially smooth. This follows from the continuous bilinearity of the momentum tensor $(u,v)\mapsto u\otimes v$, applied to the two smooth functions. The statement itself is a regularity fact; the following constructions add tensor divergence and the Leray projection to obtain the Euler momentum.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The tensor product of smooth velocities is smooth

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: Composing tensor divergence with the negative Leray projection gives an algebraic bilinear operation on smooth periodic velocity fields. On the diagonal it is the nonlinear term in the projected Euler evolution. This map is defined before selecting a finite-jet norm; its continuity and derivative loss are supplied by later estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The projected Euler momentum is bilinear on smooth fields

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: After forgetting the smoothness and periodicity data, the bundled bilinear momentum of $u$ and $v$ equals the projected momentum $-\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(u\otimes v)$. The equality holds by definition. It connects the algebraic construction used in jet spaces to the actual negative Leray projection of tensor divergence, preventing an abstract bilinear estimate from standing in for an unidentified evolution operator.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The bundled momentum is the actual projected tensor divergence

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: A smooth periodic velocity has Hölder regularity through order $m$, and its Hölder norm is at most $3(m+1)$ times its compatible jet norm through order $m+1$. The proof bounds each derivative and its half-Hölder increment from the next derivative. This is one source of the two-order loss in the later momentum estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: One extra bounded derivative controls the Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For $i\in\{0,\dots,m\}$, this continuous linear map extracts the order-$i$ bounded spatial jet from a tuple in the space of compatible jets of order $m$. The finite index enforces the available range of derivative orders. The map is used to pass integrated evolution and time regularity from whole tuples to individual derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Read one derivative from a compatible tuple

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: This embeds the range of the smooth velocity jet map isometrically into its topological closure, the space of compatible jets of order $m$. The inclusion does not alter the tuple or its norm. The target contains compatible limits of smooth periodic jets, which is the domain needed for a complete-space evolution argument.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Include smooth jet tuples in their closure

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: The finite jet map is followed by the inclusion of its range into the completed compatible jet space. This gives a real-linear map from smooth periodic velocities to the space of compatible jets of order $m$. It preserves the actual derivative tuple; the definition performs no limiting process on the velocity itself.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Place a smooth velocity in the compatible jet space

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: This real-linear map sends a smooth periodic field to minus its periodic Leray projection. The output remains smooth and periodic, with its proofs supplied by Hölder estimates at every order. The minus sign is the sign in $u_t=-\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)$; this declaration is not itself an evolution equation.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The negative Leray projection on smooth periodic fields

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For order $m$ and a smooth periodic velocity $v$, this packages $D^mv$ as a bounded continuous multilinear-valued function on $\mathbb R^3$. Smoothness gives continuity and periodicity gives a uniform bound. The chosen bound is used only to place the field in the space of bounded functions; evaluation still returns the actual iterated derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: A smooth spatial derivative as a bounded continuous field

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: This linear equivalence identifies smooth periodic velocities with the range of their finite jet map. Injectivity comes from the zeroth derivative, and membership in the range supplies a preimage. The equivalence is algebraic; it does not assert a normed-space equivalence on the whole completion or reconstruct a smooth field from an arbitrary limiting tuple.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Recover the velocity from a tuple in the smooth range

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: The bounded-function representation of the order-$m$ jet evaluates at $x$ to the $m$th iterated derivative $D^mv(x)$. This is an equality by definition rather than an approximation or convergence statement. It ensures that the subsequent Banach-space estimates remain statements about the original smooth velocity and its derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Evaluating a jet gives the actual spatial derivative

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For a smooth periodic velocity, the derivative of its order-$m$ bounded jet is the order-$(m+1)$ jet, read as a map of one further direction. The result is a derivative identity at every spatial point. This compatibility between adjacent derivative orders permits differentiation of the integrated zeroth-order velocity equation in the proof of Proposition 8.1.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Differentiating one spatial jet gives the next

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For every finite order $m$, the map from a smooth periodic velocity to its tuple of derivatives through order $m$ is injective. The zeroth component already recovers the original function. The proof evaluates that component, avoiding any claim that higher derivatives alone determine the velocity.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: A finite jet tuple still determines the velocity

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For a smooth periodic velocity field $v$, this theorem extracts invariance under every lattice translation. The smoothness proof stored alongside it is not needed for this projection. Later helpers combine both properties to obtain bounded spatial derivatives on the torus and to define the projected momentum of two such fields.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The chosen velocity type carries spatial periodicity

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: A smooth periodic velocity field is a function together with proofs of smoothness and periodicity. This theorem extracts the smoothness component, infinite differentiability on $\mathbb R^3$. It concerns a single spatial field, with no time variable or Euler equation, and supports the derivative identities used to construct compatible velocity jets.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The chosen velocity type carries spatial smoothness

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: If a function is spatially periodic, each of its iterated Fréchet derivatives is spatially periodic as well. The declaration allows a general real normed codomain and imposes no smoothness assumption. Translation invariance of the total derivative operation proves the equality; separate regularity hypotheses are used when these derivatives are interpreted as smooth jets.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Every spatial derivative retains the period lattice

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: Suppose $U_n$ converges uniformly to $u$ on a closed interval, and $u$ is continuous there. Every bounded bilinear map $B$ then sends the diagonal pairs $(U_n,U_n)$ to a sequence converging uniformly to $B(u,u)$. Compactness bounds the limiting inputs; the estimate controls the two factors separately. The result is generic and imposes no Euler or periodicity assumptions.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: A bounded quadratic operation preserves uniform convergence

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAffineStatement.text: Two solutions on $J$ of the wave equations (2.1), $\kappa'=-D^T\kappa$ and $\mathbf a'=-D\mathbf a+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot D\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$, with the same initial wave vector and amplitude at $t_0$ agree on $J$, provided $J$ is order connected, contains $t_0$, and $D$ is continuous there. One hypothesis requires the second wave vector to stay nonzero on $J$. Linear ODE uniqueness first identifies the wave vectors, then their amplitude coefficients. No nonzero amplitude assumption is required.

If two reference slopes agree on the nonnegative half-line, their exponential integral factors agree there as well. For a nonnegative evaluation time, the entire integration interval lies inside that half-line, so interval-integral congruence suffices. No differential equation or continuity hypothesis is used by this lemma; those enter when identifying the slopes in its callers.

The Euclidean norm of the three-vector with coordinates $u$, $v$ and $z$ is bounded by $|u|+|v|+|z|$. The vector is placed in Euclidean space, with its Euclidean norm, unlike the maximum norm on a plain product. This elementary inequality converts the coordinatewise wave-vector error into the vector error used by the older additive-comparison statement.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAffineStatement.summary: The Euclidean norm is at most the coordinate sum

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAffineStatement.text: There is an absolute threshold $N\ge240$. For $C_0\ge N$, a valid amplification window, positive carrier scale, both smallness conditions, the supplied wave equations and prescribed initial data, this theorem identifies that wave with the constructed growing wave. The supplied Y must solve the Riccati equation on the nonnegative half-line with $Y(0)=1$. It gives nonzero transverse data, logarithmic norm comparison, a positive first coupling and late-time coupling-ratio control. ODE uniqueness transfers the estimates to the supplied functions.

Given a physical amplification window with $T\ge2$, threshold $C_0\ge240$, an admissible clock, both smallness assumptions, supplied wave equations and the two initial equalities for the wave vector and amplitude, the rescaled functions have the required normalized initial data and satisfy the wave equations on $[0,T]$. The proof uses the clock value at zero to identify the initial frame and applies the chain rule to both wave equations. This bridge does not itself derive amplitude or coupling estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAffineStatement.summary: Moving the initial data to normalized time

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: If $e$ is a continuous linear equivalence equal to the compression of $B$ by an idempotent projection $\Pi$, then $e^{-1}f$ solves $\Pi(Bv)=f$. The second conclusion identifies every competing vector in the fixed space $\{v:\Pi v=v\}$ with that preimage. The fixed-space restriction is essential: uniqueness is not asserted for arbitrary ambient vectors.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: The compressed equivalence solves and determines the equation

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: Given an actual continuous linear equivalence $e$, this converts the assumed operator bound on $e^{-1}$ into a bound for every $v$ by $\|ev\|$. Positivity of $\mu$ and nonnegativity of $M$, $S$ and $L$ justify enlarging the polynomial base. The exponent is the concrete value $145$, and the prefactor gains $2^{145}$.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: A pointwise bound from the inverse operator bound

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: For positive coercivity $\mu$ and nonnegative size bounds $S,L$, the base $4+\mu^{-1}+S+L$ is at most twice $2+\mu^{-1}+S+L$. This elementary inequality changes the concrete inverse estimate to the paper’s preferred scale. It gives no inverse or regularity statement by itself.

For an already supplied compressed equivalence $e$, positive coercivity, and an orthogonal translation-compatible projection, order-$N$ coefficient regularity yields a constant bounding $e^{-1}$ in the same lifted Hölder norm. The constant is chosen before the datum, so it is uniform in the forcing. It may depend on the coefficient, inverse, projection, and order; this lemma does not assert a universal higher-order polynomial.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Bound the higher norm of the compressed inverse

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: A bounded torus operator $P$ commuting with line derivatives and an order-$n$ half-Hölder coefficient $B$ give a higher Hölder bound for $P(Bv)$ on admissible fields $v$ in the fixed space $\{v:Pv=v\}$. The constant is chosen independently of $v$, using the coefficient product estimate and operator norm. Neither idempotence nor coercivity is assumed for this forward bound.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Bound the forward coefficient operator on fixed fields

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: This lemma restricts order-$(n+1)$ half-Hölder regularity to order one. Both differentiability and boundedness of the required lower derivative quotients are retained. It prepares the first-order coefficient input to the order-zero freezing equivalence before that equivalence is shown bounded in the higher Hölder norm.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Extract first-order control for the inverse

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: The total Fréchet derivative of a spatially periodic function is spatially periodic. Equality of the translated functions gives equality of their derivative expressions. The theorem has no differentiability premise, so its conclusion concerns periodicity only; subsequent Hölder assumptions ensure these expressions represent genuine derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Lattice translations preserve the derivative expression

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: Order $n+1$ half-Hölder regularity implies order-one regularity of the same lifted field. The proof restricts both the smoothness order and the finite family of uniform and increment bounds. This is used to obtain a Lipschitz coefficient before applying the higher inverse theorem; it adds no quantitative estimate of its own.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Retain first-order regularity from a higher order

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: With positive coercivity and nonnegative factors, the polynomial using $S+2M$ is bounded by $2^{145}$ times the polynomial using $S+M$. This absorbs the factor two in the torus Lipschitz estimate into the absolute prefactor. The declaration is a real inequality and contains neither a regularity assertion nor an inverse construction.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Absorb the derivative conversion into the constant

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: This function evaluates a half-Hölder torus field at the image of a Euclidean point under the quotient map $\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3$. It is the periodic Euclidean lift used to compare coordinate derivative words with the usual Fréchet-derivative Hölder class. The definition itself introduces no new differentiability claim.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: The periodic lift of a half-Hölder field

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: Starting from a spatially periodic field, any finite word of coordinate derivative operations remains periodic. Induction applies periodicity of the Fréchet derivative at each step and then evaluates a coordinate direction. No regularity is assumed, so this alone does not prove that the derivative word has the analytic meaning or bounds required later.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Every coordinate derivative word is periodic

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: The lift of a half-Hölder torus field is invariant under integer lattice translations. This follows from the quotient map alone and needs no differentiability assumption. It is the periodicity input used when the derivatives of a lifted field are descended back to torus Hölder fields.

If coefficient $B$ and field $v$ both have lifted order-$n$ half-Hölder regularity, applying a derivative-commuting torus operator to their product $Bv$ preserves that class. The proof combines the bilinear product estimate with the projection lift theorem. It assumes neither coercivity nor invertibility and supplies the forward-map half of the higher isomorphism.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Compression preserves the coefficient product’s regularity

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: If $f$ has order-$n$ half-Hölder regularity and a coordinate word $l$ has length at most $n$, the resulting derivative has order $n-|l|$ and no larger Hölder norm. The length bound $|l|\le n$ matters because subtraction of natural numbers stops at zero. Each coordinate direction has unit norm, giving the contraction estimate used in the induction.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: A derivative word consumes its order of regularity

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: Ordinary lifted order-$n$ half-Hölder regularity supplies a family of torus fields representing all coordinate derivative words through that order. This implication discards the quantitative bound furnished by the companion estimate on the norms of those word fields and keeps the derivative relations. It is one direction of the equivalence used to restate the higher freezing inverse.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Convert Hölder regularity into derivative words

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: A family of half-Hölder torus fields representing all coordinate derivative words through order $n$ yields order-$n$ half-Hölder regularity of the Euclidean lift. The successor step reconstructs a Fréchet derivative from the three continuous coordinate derivatives and then applies induction to their remaining words. The hypothesis uses actual torus-line derivatives, which prevents arbitrary named fields from being treated as a derivative hierarchy.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Recover Hölder regularity from actual derivative words

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: The correction list for a derivative word of length $n$ contains exactly $2^n-1$ entries, counted with multiplicity. The missing entry is the term with no derivative on the coefficient. This list count, rather than a count of distinct word pairs, controls the finite sum in the triangular derivative estimate.

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAInvers.text: A first-derivative bound on an endpoint coefficient, with constants $C_0$ for values and $C_1$ for first derivatives, gives a half-Hölder norm cap $C_0+2C_1$ and a torus Lipschitz cap $2C_1$ for every time in the normalized slab. The hypothesis includes differentiability, nonnegative constants, and the pointwise derivative bound. This conversion prepares the coefficient sizes needed by the integrated inverse.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAInvers.summary: Convert derivative bounds to Hölder coefficient bounds

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAInvers.text: If two coefficient curves agree on the normalized interval, their coefficient-times-velocity primitives agree at every time in that interval. The integration segment is contained in the interval by the hypothesis on $t$, so pointwise equality suffices. No assertion is made about primitives outside the slab or about agreement of the coefficient extensions there.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAInvers.summary: Equal coefficients give equal integrated moments

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAInvers.text: Starting from an integrated solution whose label velocity is already jointly smooth, smooth coefficient and source lifts imply smoothness of its displacement, constant field, and represented remainder $G$. An equality hypothesis identifies that remainder from the integrated momentum; its pressure-gradient interpretation belongs to later results. This lemma transfers smoothness to the remaining outputs and assumes the smooth velocity construction.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAInvers.summary: Recover smooth displacement constant and momentum remainder

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.text: For a fixed finite set of coordinate words of length $m$, chooses one nonnegative constant before the real value space, scale and function. The sum of derivative suprema is bounded by $C\Lambda^m\|g\|$ when $\Lambda\ge1$ and the Fourier band is $4\Lambda$. The constant may depend on the chosen words and cutoff symbol.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.summary: Bernstein constants for selected coordinate words

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.text: A real function in the finite real span of the Fourier modes of frequency at most $R$ has an infinitely smooth lift along the quotient map $\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3$. Membership in the finite span is the essential hypothesis. The proof proceeds through the span operations and smooth Fourier characters; it does not claim that an arbitrary torus function becomes smooth merely by being lifted.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.summary: Real Fourier polynomials have smooth lifts

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.text: Assumes every continuous real linear measurement of $g$ belongs to one finite-dimensional scalar function space $W$. It then writes $g$ in the fixed basis of $W$ with coefficients in the original normed value space. Separation by continuous linear functionals proves equality. Completeness of that value space is not required by the statement.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.summary: Recovering a vector field from scalar coordinates

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.text: Restricts point evaluation at $z$ to a real linear subspace $W$ of scalar functions. The output lies in the algebraic dual of $W$, the space of all real linear functionals on it. No topology or continuity of evaluation is claimed here; finite dimensionality is introduced only when later expressing arbitrary dual elements by evaluations.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.summary: Point evaluation on a space of scalar functions

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.text: For a finite-dimensional subspace $W$ of real functions, every algebraic dual element is a finite linear combination of point evaluations. The finitely supported coefficient function $c$ records both the selected points and their weights. This is a representation theorem for the dual; it does not choose a canonical sampling set.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.summary: Dual elements are combinations of evaluations

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.text: If the continuous real linear functional $l$ has operator norm at most one, its complex-valued scalarization of the continuous torus function $g$ has supremum norm at most that of $g$. The complex embedding preserves absolute value. This transports scalar Fourier estimates back to real normed-space-valued functions.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.summary: Scalarization by a norm-one functional is contractive

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.text: For an integer frequency $k$ with $|k|\le R$, selects the real part of the complex character $e^{2\pi ik\cdot x}$ when a binary flag is true and the imaginary part otherwise. These scalar functions span the real finite Fourier space. The definition concerns the torus variable alone and imposes no positivity assumption on the band radius.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.summary: Real and imaginary parts of Fourier characters

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.text: Takes the real linear span of the sine and cosine components indexed by the finite frequency band. It is a submodule of all real functions on the torus, not a space completed in a norm. Its finite dimensionality lets the Bernstein proof recover vector-valued functions from finitely many real scalar measurements.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.summary: The real space of bounded Fourier frequencies

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.text: If the continuous real normed-space-valued function $g$ has Fourier band $R$, every continuous real linear functional $l$ sends it into the finite real span of the Fourier modes of frequency at most $R$. This supplies a finite-dimensional scalar target without complexifying the entire value space. The functional need not have norm at most one for this membership statement.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.summary: Scalar measurements stay in the Fourier band

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBLInfin.text: A continuous scalar function times an integrable vector-valued function is integrable on the compact torus. The scalar field may be real or complex. Compactness supplies a finite bound for the multiplier; this helper justifies passing bounded linear maps through the cutoff’s vector-valued integral.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBLInfin.summary: A continuous multiplier preserves torus integrability

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBLInfin.text: The coordinatewise complexification of a real vector in $\mathbb R^3$ has exactly the same Euclidean norm. No function-space assumption is involved. This identity pairs with the real-part contraction to transfer the complex cutoff’s integral estimate to real velocity fields without introducing a dimension factor.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBLInfin.summary: Complexifying a velocity preserves its norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBLInfin.text: The real-part projection from complex Euclidean three-dimensional space $\mathbb C^3$ to $\mathbb R^3$ is contractive. The proof compares squared coordinate norms. This finite-dimensional estimate ensures that converting the complex Fourier cutoff back to a real velocity field does not enlarge the operator bound.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBLInfin.summary: Taking real parts cannot increase the norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixD.0.Tor.text: For $i\le n$ and a table whose entries are at least one, bounds $C_i$ by one plus the sum $\sum_{j\le n}C_j$. The proof uses inclusion of the $i$th term and nonnegativity of the rest. This collects finitely many order-dependent coefficient constants without changing the power of the parent parameter.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixD.0.Tor.summary: Each coefficient cost fits the cumulative budget

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixD.0.Tor.text: If every entry of the coefficient-cost table is at least one, then one plus its sum $\sum_{j\le n}C_j$ through order $n$ is at least one. Only nonnegativity of the summands is needed in the proof. This elementary estimate supplies an admissible enlarged constant for the coefficient calculus.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixD.0.Tor.summary: A finite coefficient budget is at least one

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDCoordi.text: For a continuous $m$-linear map on copies of $\mathbb R^3$, bounds its operator norm by the sum of norms of its values on all coordinate tuples. Expanding each argument in the coordinate basis proves the estimate. This comparison accounts for ordered words and allows later coefficient bounds to preserve the exponent of $D$.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDCoordi.summary: Coordinate values control a multilinear operator

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDCoordi.text: Every vector $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is the sum $v_1e_1+v_2e_2+v_3e_3$ of its three scalar coordinates times their coordinate directions. This exact identity supplies the multilinear expansion used to compare operator norms with coordinate evaluations. There are no smoothness, scale or boundedness assumptions because the statement is finite-dimensional linear algebra.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDCoordi.summary: Expanding a vector in coordinate directions

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.text: Defines a function on the label-phase product by averaging $f(x+(0,r))$ over $r$ in one phase period. Keeping the phase translation inside the integrand makes differentiation commute directly with averaging. The definition itself does not assume that $f$ is periodic; identifying it with the label-only phase average requires a separate periodicity theorem.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.summary: Averaging translates in the phase variable

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.text: For an infinitely smooth field and a fixed direction $d$ in label-phase space, differentiation of the translated average equals the translated average of the directional derivative. The direction is constant, which is material to the commutation. This is the first-order ingredient for the phase-operator estimates of Lemma D.1.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.summary: Averaging commutes with a constant directional derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.text: If each label slice of $f$ has period one in the phase, averaging the translated phase interval equals averaging the unshifted phase function at that label. The conclusion holds at every label-phase point. This identifies the smooth translated average used in the proof with the paper’s phase-independent average.

If $f$ is infinitely smooth on the label-phase space, its translated phase average is infinitely smooth as well. Integration occurs over a fixed compact phase interval, permitting derivatives under the integral. This result concerns the translated average without yet assuming period one or reducing it to a label-only field.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.summary: Smoothness of the translated phase average

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.text: For smooth $f$, every finite word of constant directional derivatives commutes with the translated phase average. The proof iterates the first-order commutation and preserves smoothness at each step. This moves averaging past arbitrary mixed label and phase derivatives before their supremum bounds are taken.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.summary: Averaging commutes with a derivative word

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.text: For smooth directional fields and smooth function slices, the finite word quantity of $cf$ equals $|c|$ times that of $f$. A true-or-false parameter decides whether difference quotients are included. This is a scaling identity for the defined quantity; it does not independently supply boundedness of all derivative-value sets.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.summary: Constant scaling of a finite derivative norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.text: If $L_0$ intertwines each input derivative $D^E_i$ with the output derivative $D^F_i$, it also intertwines every derivative word. Induction on the word proves the equality. This isolates the constant principal part of the linear equation before the proof expands derivatives falling on variable coefficients.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.summary: A commuting linear operator passes through every derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.text: Interchanges a finite sum over the coefficient index with a list sum over derivative correction pairs. Only the additive structure and finiteness of the coefficient index are used. The identity lets the differentiated equation collect all coefficient contributions under one correction-pair sum before taking seminorms.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.summary: Interchanging the coefficient and correction sums

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.text: The finite derivative quantity obtained by summing a seminorm over admissible ordered words is nonnegative. Each summand is nonnegative by the seminorm axioms. No derivative commutation or analytic regularity is needed for this algebraic fact; those assumptions enter when relating arbitrary words to the chosen ordered representatives.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.summary: Nonnegativity of the finite derivative sum

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.text: For a finite index set, the seminorm of its sum is at most the sum of the seminorms. This is the finite-set counterpart of the preceding list lemma. It is used to bound the coefficient-index sum inside each differentiated forcing correction before the derivative-order recursion is applied.

The seminorm of the sum of a mapped finite list is at most the list sum of the individual seminorms. Induction applies the triangle inequality one term at a time. This handles repeated Leibniz correction pairs without requiring the list to contain distinct elements.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.summary: A seminorm bounds a list sum by the termwise sum

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.text: If the linear derivative maps commute, the seminorm of any word of length at most $n$ is bounded by the finite derivative norm of order $n$. Sorting the word preserves its value and places it among the admissible summands. The assumptions include a finite, linearly ordered set of directions.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.summary: Every derivative word fits the finite order norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDMultiI.text: For a smooth coefficient slice, the directional operator word associated with a finite coordinate tuple equals the corresponding evaluation of its iterated Fréchet derivative. The label scale is fixed to one. The proof handles the list length and index casts explicitly, providing the bridge between word and multi-index coefficient encodings.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDMultiI.summary: Coordinate words evaluate the full derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDMultiI.text: At scale one, the hierarchy's label direction fields are exactly the family of constant coordinate directions $e_1,e_2,e_3$. The equality is an immediate scalar-multiplication simplification. It lets the multi-index conversion compare the hierarchy’s weighted directional notation with ordinary spatial derivatives in the unscaled coefficient norm.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDMultiI.summary: Unit label scale gives coordinate directions

_private.TorusEuler.PaperFlowBounds.0.To.text: A jointly smooth vector field on the closed time slab has a smooth spatial slice at any time belonging to that slab. The proof composes with the map sending $x$ to $(t,x)$ and then uses smoothness on the whole spatial space. No differentiability in time outside the slab is asserted.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperFlowBounds.0.To.summary: Slices of a jointly smooth field are smooth

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.text: The Hessian of a constant scalar multiple of a scalar spatial field equals that scalar times its Hessian. The statement has no differentiability hypotheses: it uses the total Fréchet derivative’s constant-scalar rule over the field. Later analytic applications separately establish pressure smoothness before interpreting these Hessians as classical derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.summary: A constant scalar factors out of the Hessian

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.text: For $T>0$ and a jointly smooth field on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, its ordinary spatial derivative is jointly smooth on the same slab. Unique differentiation of the product identifies the spatial restriction of the within derivative with the usual spatial derivative. The positive-duration hypothesis matters at the time boundary.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.summary: Spatial derivatives vary smoothly throughout the slab

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.text: Any jointly smooth field on the closed slab has an infinitely smooth spatial slice at a slab time. Composition with the fixed-time inclusion proves the assertion. This local helper is used when taking the ordinary spatial gradient and Hessian of the generic pressure, independently of the within-time derivative convention.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.summary: Smooth spatial pressure slices on the slab

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.text: If the approximation’s leading data equal the constructed paper-cutoff input, the slice of its leading and completion switch terms equals the cutoff derivative times the primary activation wave for that same seed and coframe. The identity holds at every slab time and label-phase point. It is an exact source formula before any norm estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.summary: The full activation slice is the derivative times the primary wave

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericSwitchCo.text: Proves that derivatives within the closed centered label cell $[-1/2,1/2]^3$ are uniquely determined at every point, by its convex geometry and nonempty interior. This supplies uniqueness of derivatives even at the cell faces. It is the necessary justification for differentiating an equality known on the closed cell when computing the curl completion of a wrapped profile.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericSwitchCo.summary: The closed centered cell has unique differentiation

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericSwitchCo.text: Multiplying the phase velocity by a real scalar multiplies its normalized wave potential by the same scalar. The covector and phase point are fixed. The proof uses linearity of the phase primitive and cross product; no nonzero covector hypothesis is needed for this algebraic identity of totalized expressions.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericSwitchCo.summary: A scalar passes through the phase potential

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericSwitchWe.text: A raw field smooth on the active time slab has a smooth label-phase slice at any active time. The proof composes with the fixed-time map and uses that the whole label-phase space is included. This helper provides the spatial derivatives required for the weighted amplitude seminorm, without differentiating the time multiplier.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericSwitchWe.summary: Smoothness of a spatial and phase seed slice

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: If an even-reflection profile agrees on the slab with a label-only function $f$, then $f(t)$ is even for every slab time. Setting the phase to zero converts simultaneous label-phase reflection into ordinary label reflection. This extracts parity of the physical strain and transported covector from the parent-geometry profiles.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Even phase independent profiles give even label fields

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: If a property of time, label and phase is preserved by the specified twisted lattice shifts and holds on the centered cell at every slab time, then it holds throughout the profile slab. The property is arbitrary. The proof moves each label to its centered representative and transports the assertion by the corresponding phase shift.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A centered-cell property extends by lattice shifts

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: Two twisted profiles are equal if their values agree on the centered label cell for every slab time and phase. Twisted lattice periodicity extends the equality to all labels, and both profiles vanish outside the slab. This extensionality result explains why later identities can be proved only on the closed cell.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Equality on the centered cell determines a profile

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: Wraps a raw phase-periodic field by centered twisted periodization and then regards it as a twisted profile on the closed time slab. Smoothness of the periodized field is supplied as a hypothesis; it is not deduced for arbitrary raw input. The resulting profile has exact phase and lattice compatibility, with the zero extension outside the slab used by the profile space.
