_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Wrapping a smooth profile on the parent cell

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: At a time in $[0,T]$, the wrapped profile evaluates to the centered twisted periodization of its raw input. The theorem explicitly unwraps the nested profile structures. It says nothing about evaluation outside the slab, where the smooth-profile construction uses zero; nor does it remove the spatial periodization on an arbitrary label.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Evaluating the wrapped profile inside the slab

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: Defines the scalar leading pressure with its normalized pressure coefficient and phase primitive, but without the radial envelope. The strain, covector and amplitude are evaluated at the same time and label. Factoring out the envelope later makes the support and centered-cell smoothness arguments share the same spatial cutoff.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: The leading pressure before applying the envelope

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: A regular seed has smooth bare pressure on $[t_0,T]$ in time, label and phase. The proof uses smooth strain, covector and amplitude, and the explicit nonzero covector field before dividing by its squared norm. Valid phase-width bounds provide a smooth primitive. Smoothness outside the active slab is not asserted.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: The bare pressure is smooth on the active slab

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: Let $t_0<T$, let $\widetilde\chi$ be smooth on $[0,T]$ and zero there for $t<t_0$, and let $f(t,a,s)$ be smooth on $[t_0,T]\times\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, with values in a real Banach space. The formal statement proves that $\widetilde\chi(t)f(t,a,s)$ is smooth on the whole closed slab $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. The function $f$ is defined at earlier times but may have arbitrary values there; multiplication by the zero cutoff removes them. No extension of the cutoff to a globally smooth function and no bound $0\le\widetilde\chi\le1$ are assumed. This supplies the smoothness step in (3.7), including the case $t_0=0$, where no vanishing at the initial time is required.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: The vanishing cutoff removes arbitrary earlier values of the profile

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: Multiplying the seed’s leading wave by a smooth scalar time function that vanishes before activation produces a smooth raw profile on the entire slab. The seed's hierarchy regularity supplies the active wave regularity and $t_0<T$. The preceding extension lemma handles the activation seam; no arbitrary values of the raw seed before activation affect the product.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A cut-off leading wave is smooth on the slab

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: For a seed with hierarchy regularity, the product of its amplitude and the phase wave profile is smooth on the active time slab. The seed regularity supplies amplitude smoothness and the valid phase width. The spatial envelope and the time cutoff are deliberately absent from this intermediate field.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Smoothness of the unenveloped leading oscillation

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: For the valid phase width supplied by a regular seed, the wave-pressure primitive is even. The proof uses its normalized phase construction and symmetry. This parity is needed with the even label coefficients to show that the leading pressure is unchanged under simultaneous reflection of label and phase.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: The normalized pressure primitive is even

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: The seed’s leading pressure equals its radial envelope $g(a)$ times the bare pressure, the same pressure formula without the envelope. This is an algebraic identity valid for arbitrary time, label and phase arguments. It separates the compact spatial localization from the smooth active pressure coefficient, allowing the periodization and multiplier lemmas to be applied uniformly.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Factoring the radial envelope from the pressure

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: For a regular seed, the leading wave is zero at any label whose norm is at least twice the envelope radius. The identity holds at arbitrary time and phase because the radial envelope is the factor that vanishes. It establishes spatial support, without claiming the seed amplitude itself is zero there.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: The leading wave vanishes outside its envelope

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: For a phase-periodic raw field whose phase mean is zero at every label, centered twisted periodization also has zero phase mean at every label. The wrapping changes the phase by a label-dependent translation, and integration over one period is invariant under that translation. No spatial derivative estimate is involved.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A wrapped zero-mean phase field still has zero mean

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: Builds the normalized leading pressure profile with a smooth time multiplier vanishing before activation. It factors out the radial envelope, periodizes the smooth supported active pressure, and restricts to the slab. The carrier is the supplied $k$; smoothness and periodicity are proved from the regular seed rather than assumed for arbitrary raw pressure.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A multiplied pressure as a twisted profile

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: At a slab time, the pressure-multiple profile evaluates to the scalar time factor multiplied by the centered periodization of the leading pressure. The formula exposes the underlying field while retaining the spatial wrapping. It does not identify the raw and wrapped values away from the centered-cell support argument.

The leading pressure of a regular seed vanishes at labels of norm at least twice the envelope radius. Its scalar coefficient may remain defined there, but the radial cutoff is zero. The conclusion holds at every time and phase and supplies the same support gap used for the leading velocity’s centered-cell periodization.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: The leading pressure vanishes outside its envelope

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: On the closed slab, the time derivative of the cutoff times the leading seed, plus strain and phase-pressure terms, equals the cutoff derivative times the seed. The proof separates times before activation from the active interval and extends the identity to the seam. The pressure is multiplied by the same time cutoff.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Differentiating the cutoff gives the raw activation equation

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: If a twisted profile has the stated reflection parity at all slab points, then it has that parity as a globally represented function. Reflection preserves the time slab, and outside it both sides vanish by the profile convention. This extension is algebraic; it makes no claim of time smoothness outside the slab.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Reflection on the slab determines global profile parity

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: Builds the twisted velocity profile from $c(t)$ times the localized leading seed. The scalar multiplier is smooth on the slab and zero before activation; seed regularity gives a small supported envelope and a valid periodic phase profile. Centered periodization followed by slab restriction supplies the final profile representation.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A multiplied velocity as a twisted profile

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: The wrapped leading velocity multiplied by a smooth active scalar has zero profile phase average. The proof uses the seed’s zero-mean wave profile, invariance of phase integration under wrapping, and zero extension outside the slab. The multiplier may vary in time but not in the phase being averaged.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A time multiple of the leading wave has zero average

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: At every time in the slab, the velocity-multiple profile equals the scalar time factor times the centered twisted periodization of the leading seed. This is an evaluation identity for the wrapped object. The time factor is independent of label and phase, which allows it to be pulled outside periodization.

If the seed amplitude is even in the label on the active slab, its wrapped leading velocity multiplied by a smooth active scalar is odd under simultaneous label-phase reflection. The phase wave is odd and the radial envelope is even. Before activation the multiplier is zero, so no amplitude parity outside the active interval is required.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A time multiple of the velocity has odd reflection parity

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: If the bundled covector profile agrees with the seed’s covector on the slab, the time-multiplied leading velocity is orthogonal to it at every profile point. The proof uses the seed’s transverse amplitude and handles the pre-activation region by zero. The covector identification is an explicit assumption.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A time multiple remains transverse to the covector

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: If a raw field vanishes outside radius $2\ell$ and that radius fits strictly inside the centered cell, its centered twisted periodization equals the raw value on the closed cell. The proof treats wrapped boundary representatives using the support gap. This avoids requiring equality only in the cell interior when later taking spatial derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Periodization agrees with a supported field on the cell

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: If a function is zero at every slab time before $t_0$, its within-slab derivative is zero at any time strictly before $t_0$. The theorem asserts that zero is a derivative within the slab there, using local equality with zero. Strict inequality is essential: it does not by itself identify the derivative exactly at the activation time.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A field vanishing before activation has zero derivative there

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGraphReadout.0..text: A smooth spatial slice of the label map $A$ turns a twisted profile into a smooth Eulerian graph readout at a time in $[0,T]$. Time membership is explicit because the profile’s regularity is bundled only on that slab. The conclusion is spatial smoothness at the chosen time, not a new jointly smooth flow.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGraphReadout.0..summary: Graph readouts of smooth slices are smooth

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyDepth..text: For a real loss scale $L\ge1$ and natural exponent $r\le6$, the power $L^r$ is bounded by $L^6$. This elementary monotonicity step places different recurrence losses under the common sixth power used in Theorem 5.6. It supplies no frequency smallness condition by itself.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyDepth..summary: All smaller losses fit the sixth parent power

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyInvers.text: At a launch time in a positive slab, and with $\gamma(t_0)>0$, the launch seminorm controls every word of the frozen initial profile after division by its launch amplitude. The conclusion is a relay word bound that is constant in later time. No positive label or phase width is required for this representation-level inequality; the amplitude denominator is explicitly guarded.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyInvers.summary: Launch data enter the weighted word bound

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyInvers.text: Assumes nonzero label and phase widths, a positive multiplier $c$, nonnegative jet bound $B$, positive amplitude weight and smooth active slices. Scaled jet bounds for $cf$ then bound $c$ times the weighted finite-word norm by the number of admissible words times $B$. The nonzero widths permit conversion from rescaled derivatives back to the original profile.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyInvers.summary: Scaled jets control the weighted raw profile norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyLeadin.text: For a seed and a phase width satisfying $0<h\le1$, differentiating its leading pressure in phase gives the radial envelope times the wave profile times the oscillatory pressure slope. The time and label are arbitrary here. This explicit identity connects the normalized pressure primitive to the leading transverse momentum equation.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyLeadin.summary: The phase derivative of the leading pressure

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: For the actual parent geometry, a regular seed and representatives agreeing with its unswitched velocity and pressure on the active interval, proves transversality and zero leading material-plus-phase-pressure momentum on that interval. The proof first works on the centered cell, uses within-interval time derivatives, then transfers by twisted periodicity. It does not extend the homogeneous equation to earlier times where the representatives were freely extended.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: The actual unswitched wave satisfies homogeneous active momentum

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: If a typed profile and a raw field agree on the active interval, their weighted finite mixed derivative norms agree at every order. The interval lies in the parent slab, and its amplitude weight is continuous and strictly positive. The proof rewrites equal time slices before differentiating in labels and phase; it does not need the two fields to agree outside the active interval.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: The typed amplitude norm equals the raw active norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: Builds a twisted hierarchy profile from a smooth coefficient and a smooth phase function of period one, after inserting the radial envelope. The positive radius and cell-margin proofs establish smoothness, while periodization supplies the lattice twist. The constructor retains these properties in its output type; it does not assert that the profile solves a wave equation.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: A smooth periodic coefficient produces a wrapped profile

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: For a positive terminal time and the same smooth periodic zero-mean phase function, the typed phase average of the wrapped vector profile equals the zero profile. It promotes the pointwise phase-mean calculation to equality of hierarchy profiles by extensionality on the slab. The conclusion concerns the average, not the original oscillating field itself.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: The wrapped vector profile has zero averaged field

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: At every time in the closed hierarchy slab, evaluation of the constructed profile equals the explicit twisted periodization of the enveloped coefficient and phase function. The coefficient and phase function satisfy the same smoothness, periodicity and radius conditions as the constructor. This is a value identity on the slab, without an assertion about the representative at arbitrary outside times.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: The wrapped profile has its stated slab values

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: If the periodic scalar phase function has zero mean, then every label slice of the wrapped profile also has zero phase mean on the closed slab. The proof writes periodization as a phase translation depending on the centered label. Integrating a periodic function over any unit interval preserves its mean, while the coefficient and envelope remain fixed during that integration.

A globally smooth coefficient and globally smooth scalar phase profile give a smooth twisted periodization after multiplication by the radial envelope. Positive envelope radius and the strict margin $2\ell<1/2$ keep the support away from the centered cell boundary. The conclusion is smoothness on the hierarchy slab, sufficient to build the typed representative.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: The localized twisted periodization stays smooth on the slab

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: For a function vanishing whenever the label norm is at least $2\ell$, its twisted periodization agrees with the original function on the centered cell, provided $2\ell<1/2$. The theorem needs only a zero value in the target type. The support gap provides a collar near every cell face where changing representatives cannot change the value.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: Periodization leaves the supported central cell values unchanged

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.text: Defines a function on time and torus labels by evaluating $f$ at a chosen Euclidean representative of the label. The function is defined for arbitrary $f$; periodicity is not built into the definition. The following lemma proves agreement with the intended Euclidean lift only when the relevant time slice is spatially periodic.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.summary: Choose a Euclidean representative for each label

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.text: For a periodic time slice, descending by a chosen representative and then evaluating at the torus point of $a\in\mathbb R^3$ recovers $f(t,a)$. Two representatives differ by an integer lattice vector, and the periodicity hypothesis removes that difference. This supplies the exact coefficient identities when the parent’s Euclidean deformation data are packaged on torus labels.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.summary: Periodic data are independent of the chosen representative

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.text: If translating the input by a lattice vector translates the output by that same vector, the Fréchet derivative is lattice-periodic. This is the correct symmetry for a flow lift, which is equivariant rather than periodic as a position map. The conclusion concerns the total derivative expression; existence of actual flow derivatives is supplied by separate smoothness results.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.summary: The derivative of an equivariant flow is periodic

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.text: A periodic vector field has a periodic total Fréchet derivative, by differentiating the equality of its lattice translates. This private lemma prepares the parent velocity gradient for descent to the torus. No differentiability premise occurs in the lemma; the flow adapter separately has the smoothness needed to interpret the derivative analytically.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.summary: The derivative of periodic velocity is periodic

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..text: On a positive slab, any integrated solution yields a mixed field representing its velocity, fixed by the mixed projection and solving the projected equation. Continuous coefficients and source, exact path-action identities for the kinetic coefficient $K$ and the vorticity coefficient $\Omega$, and the source representation are required. This transfers a candidate solution into the uniqueness domain of the mixed inverse.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..summary: An integrated solution has a mixed representative

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..text: Continuous coefficient curves $K$, $\Omega$, a continuous source and a continuous solenoidal velocity $g$ give continuity of the integrated momentum on the closed slab. The primitive term is treated in the Banach Hölder space, using continuity of coefficient multiplication. This establishes regularity of the expression before it is projected or identified with a pressure gradient.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..summary: The integrated momentum is continuous in time

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..text: For $T>0$, a continuous solenoidal velocity with zero terminal primitive has every mixed representation fixed by the mixed Leray projection. Continuity and the representation hypothesis connect the time-path representative with its spatial slices. The terminal condition becomes zero time mean, while solenoidality supplies the spatial constraint; neither is inferred from the representation alone.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..summary: The represented velocity satisfies both projections

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..text: If a continuous field has the same spatial projection $c$ at every time, then the mixed projection of its represented path is zero. The proof tests against fields with zero time mean and solenoidal spatial slices. Positive slab length and the representation hypothesis are explicit, so this is an identification of the concrete projections on the correct function spaces.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..summary: The mixed projection removes a solenoidal constant

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..text: Two mixed fields solving the same projected equation coincide if both are fixed by the mixed projection and the supplied map is the corresponding compression equivalence. The proof sends each field to the same projected source and uses injectivity. Coercivity is not a direct hypothesis here because existence of the actual equivalence has already been supplied.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..summary: Two projected velocities agree in the fixed space

_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalCutoff..text: If both scalar pressure fields are $C^2$, the Hessian of their difference is the difference of their Hessians at every spatial point. The proof first subtracts gradients and then differentiates that identity. The regularity assumptions ensure this is the classical subtraction rule used in the physical cutoff argument.

Restricts joint smoothness on a closed time slab to spatial smoothness at a specified slab time. This supplies the differentiability needed to compare the pressure of a smooth approximation with its frequency-truncated child. No Fourier or pressure estimate is proved by this fixed-time composition lemma.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalCutoff..summary: Smooth spatial slices for physical truncation

_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.text: A physical parent on a positive closed slab has finite nonnegative bounds for its kinetic and vorticity coefficients and their first spatial derivatives. The proof uses joint smoothness, spatial periodicity, and compactness after passage to the torus. The constants depend on the supplied parent and duration; this is not a uniform estimate over all parents.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.summary: The smooth parent has finite coefficient bounds

_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.text: For a smooth mean solution at a slab time, differentiating $Kv$ in time gives $\Omega v+F^*f-\nabla q$. The proof combines the physical label momentum equation with the deformation ODE and the inverse identity. The derivative is taken within the closed interval, so endpoints are included without claiming differentiability of an arbitrary external extension.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.summary: Differentiate the kinetic momentum along a label

_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.text: Joint smoothness on the closed time slab gives a globally smooth spatial slice at any time belonging to the interval. The proof composes with the fixed-time inclusion and removes the universal spatial domain. The membership assumption on $t$ is required; the result says nothing about slices outside the prescribed time interval.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.summary: Spatial slices of a jointly smooth field are smooth

_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.text: Joint smoothness on the product of the closed time interval with all spatial labels yields smoothness, within that interval, of the curve at each fixed label. The conclusion is smoothness relative to the interval, retaining the endpoint-sensitive domain. It is used when differentiating the mean equation and applying the fundamental theorem of calculus.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.summary: Time curves of a jointly smooth field are smooth

_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.text: For any time-dependent function on torus labels, its Euclidean evaluation through the quotient map $\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3$ is periodic at a fixed time. The codomain is arbitrary and no continuity is needed. This supplies periodicity of the deformation and gradient lifts when smooth coefficient representations are built for the physical mean inverse.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.summary: Label evaluation gives a periodic physical lift

_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalParentI.text: For a smooth spatial velocity, $D\ge1$ and $R\ge0$, bounds on its first two derivatives by $RD^j$ imply a half-Hölder bound for its gradient, with norm at most $3RD^2$. The first derivative controls the supremum and the second controls spatial increments. This is a local analytic estimate, independent of Fourier truncation once the jet bounds are supplied.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalParentI.summary: Two derivative bounds control the parent gradient Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperSequenceStateme.text: For every natural $j$, proves $t_{j+2}<t_{j+3}$. The next crossing lies after completion of a switch interval of positive length, since its physical rate is positive. The statement deliberately begins at the second activation: the first two wave activation times are both zero.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperSequenceStateme.summary: Activation times strictly increase after the second wave

_private.TorusEuler.PaperSequenceStateme.text: Identifies the velocity stored as the older stage in tip $j$ with the sequence velocity $U_j$. The proof checks the initial and successor index cases directly. This index correspondence is needed when the central crossing's coupling ratio is rewritten in the notation of the paper's common-sequence conclusions.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperSequenceStateme.summary: The preceding tip uses the correct older sequence velocity

_private.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalStateme.text: For inductive stage data whose initial frequency is at least two, every next frequency is at least the square of the current one. The proof uses monotonicity and the stored power recurrence, whose exponent is at least two. This is the growth estimate supplied to the terminal convergence construction; it does not itself prove convergence or divergence of a physical norm.

_private.TorusEuler.PaperTruncatedHierar.text: If $D\ge1$, $0\le A\le B$ and natural exponents satisfy $q\le r$, then $AD^q\le BD^r$. Both coefficient and exponent are enlarged using nonnegative powers. This arithmetic helper lets the lengthy truncated-hierarchy estimate combine several compatible coefficient bounds under one selected parent loss.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperTruncatedHierar.summary: Enlarging a coefficient and its parent power

_private.TorusEuler.ParentCoframeEstimat.text: A velocity jointly smooth on the closed slab is smooth in space at any fixed time $t$ belonging to that slab. Composition with $x\mapsto(t,x)$ removes the time variable. The statement concerns spatial smoothness on all of $\mathbb R^3$ and does not assert an extension in time beyond the slab.

If $i\le n$ and all $C_j$ are nonnegative, then $C_i$ is bounded by $1+\sum_{j=0}^{n} C_j$. The proof inserts the chosen index into the finite sum. It allows one derivative-order constant to control all lower orders in the parent composition and inverse estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentCoframeEstimat.summary: The common constant bounds every included derivative

_private.TorusEuler.ParentCoframeEstimat.text: For a nonnegative sequence $C$, the quantity $1+\sum_{j=0}^{n} C_j$ is at least one. The nonnegativity hypothesis applies to every index. This inequality supplies positive common constants when several derivative orders are combined in the proof of the parent coefficient bounds.

_private.TorusEuler.ParentPressureParity.text: Derives evenness of the Fréchet derivative from oddness of a vector field, using composition with the linear negation map. The equality is valid without a differentiability hypothesis under the derivative’s total convention. In the physical use, smoothness already holds, so it describes the ordinary velocity gradient.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentPressureParity.summary: The derivative of an odd vector field is even

_private.TorusEuler.ParentResidualEstima.text: The standard coordinate vector $e_i$ in $\mathbb R^3$ has norm one for each of the three indices $i$. This normalization removes the product of direction norms when evaluating an iterated Fréchet derivative on coordinate vectors. It is a geometric helper for converting full derivative bounds into derivative-word bounds.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentResidualEstima.summary: Each coordinate direction has unit length

_private.TorusEuler.ParentResidualEstima.text: Embedding a real three-vector into the complex Euclidean space preserves its norm exactly. The proof uses the componentwise equality between the complex norm of a real number and its real absolute value. This allows Fourier estimates on the complexified parent residual to retain the original real amplitude bound.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentResidualEstima.summary: Complexification preserves the parent vector norm

_private.TorusEuler.ParentResidualEstima.text: The continuous linear map taking coordinatewise real parts has operator norm at most one. Each real component is bounded by the norm of its complex component, and the Euclidean sum preserves the inequality. This transfers the complex Fourier derivative estimates back to real-valued residuals without enlarging their constants.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentResidualEstima.summary: Taking real parts does not increase the norm

_private.TorusEuler.ParentSeedJetBudgets.text: For any real constant $C$, chooses a natural exponent $A\ge30$ such that every $D\ge2$ and positive radius $\ell\le D^{-A}$ satisfy $2\cdot C\cdot \ell\cdot D^{30}\le1$. The proof uses an Archimedean power bound at base two. The exponent depends on the fixed constant, while the resulting inequality is uniform in $D$ and the radius.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentSeedJetBudgets.summary: One radius exponent absorbs the fixed coframe constant

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: This private definition forgets the quantitative half Hölder bound and retains the underlying continuous real vector field on the torus. Evaluation is unchanged. The conversion allows the Fourier band predicate, which is formulated for continuous maps, to be applied to inputs and outputs of the bounded Leray projection.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: The continuous representative of a half Hölder field

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: A finite sum of torus characters multiplied by arbitrary vector coefficients is continuous. The coefficient space is a complex normed space; no decay condition is needed because the frequency set $s$ is finite. This supplies the continuity hypotheses needed when products of parent Fourier expansions are integrated term by term.

A continuous field on the compact torus with values in a complex normed space remains integrable after multiplication by the conjugate Fourier character $e^{-2\pi ik\cdot x}$. Compactness supplies integrability from continuity. This result justifies finite sum manipulations under the integral defining the parent Fourier coefficients.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Continuous fields have integrable Fourier coefficients

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: For finitely many continuous fields with values in a complete complex normed space, the Fourier coefficient of their sum equals the sum of the coefficients. Continuity is required only for indices belonging to the finite index set $s$. The proof establishes integrability of each character weighted term before interchanging the finite sum and integral.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Fourier coefficients distribute over finite sums

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: The Fourier coefficient at $k$ of one character at frequency $a$ times a vector $e$ vanishes when $k\ne a$. The proof integrates the product of the two characters and uses their orthogonality. This is the local calculation behind the finite frequency support argument.

For the product of a scalar finite Fourier sum and a vector finite Fourier sum, the coefficient at $k$ vanishes if $k$ is unequal to every sum $j+l$ from their supports. Expanding the product gives the convolution rule directly. The hypothesis concerns membership in the finite supports, without imposing a radius or symmetry.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Products cannot create unrelated Fourier frequencies

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: For a $C^2$ velocity with nonnegative uniform bounds $M$, $B$, and $H$ on its value, first derivative, and second derivative, the supplied advection field has half Hölder norm at most $2(BM+B^2+HM)$. The hypothesis that the supplied field represents the advection $(u\cdot\nabla)u$ is essential. The proof combines a Lipschitz estimate at short distances with a supremum estimate at long distances.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Velocity and two derivatives bound half Hölder advection

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: The supremum norm of the underlying continuous torus field is no larger than the bundled half Hölder norm. The result reads off the value bound contained in the half Hölder norm. It allows estimates for the Leray projection in the stronger space to serve as amplitude inputs to the parent Bernstein estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Forgetting Hölder control decreases the norm

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: For a $C^2$ spatial velocity, the derivative of $u\cdot\nabla u$ is bounded by $\|Du\|^2+\|D^2u\|\|u\|$ at the chosen point. The product rule differentiates both the velocity and its gradient. This private estimate supplies the Lipschitz part of the later half Hölder bound.

If each of the three coordinate columns of a continuous linear map has norm at most a nonnegative number $M$, its operator norm is at most $3M$. The proof expands an arbitrary vector in the coordinate basis and applies the triangle inequality. It deliberately uses a convenient dimensional constant rather than an optimal one.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Coordinate bounds control the full gradient

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: The map from an integer frequency triple to its Euclidean vector preserves addition. This private coordinate identity makes the frequency arithmetic in products of finite Fourier sums compatible with the Euclidean norm used for the parent band. It contains no assertion about the fields or their regularity.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Integer frequencies add as Euclidean vectors

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: The Euclidean length of the sum of two integer frequencies is bounded by the sum of their lengths. The preceding embedding identity reduces the claim to the triangle inequality. This is the geometric step that turns two input bands of radius $2\Lambda$ into an output band of radius $4\Lambda$.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: A product frequency lies in the summed band

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: For a smooth periodic time family, continuity of its completed jet tuple through order two implies time continuity of the signed quadratic momentum at each fixed point. This follows by continuity of the bounded bilinear extension and the bounded zeroth evaluation map. The conclusion is on the supplied closed time slab.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: Continuity of two spatial orders controls the momentum value

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: This bounded linear map extracts the zeroth component of a completed order zero tuple, evaluates it at $x$, and identifies the zero argument multilinear map with a vector. It lets convergence of completed momentum tuples imply convergence of the actual momentum at a fixed spatial point.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: The zeroth completed jet evaluates to a vector

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: Evaluating the extended order zero momentum tuple of two smooth inputs returns their actual signed projected momentum at $x$. The two inputs are taken through order two. The proof combines the agreement of the extension on smooth tuples with the canonical interpretation of the zeroth derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: Zeroth jet evaluation recovers the momentum value

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: At a fixed spatial point, uniform convergence of velocities, order two jet tuples, and residuals to zero passes the stage equation to the limit. Continuity assumptions justify integration. The result gives both the limiting integral identity and its within time derivative on the closed positive slab, with no remaining forcing term.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: The residual disappears from the integrated momentum equation

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: The finite spatial Hölder norm is nonnegative when $f$ is $C^m$ with bounded derivatives and bounded half-Hölder increment quotients through order $m$. The proof uses the boundedness premises to justify each real supremum and the zero increment to bound the seminorm below by zero. This premise matters because the norm formula still returns a value outside its intended domain.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: Admissible Hölder data have a nonnegative norm

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: Restricting a jointly smooth field on a closed time slab to any time in that slab gives a smooth function of space. The proof composes with the map sending $x$ to $(t,x)$. It uses no derivative in time and therefore does not require a strict inequality between the two interval endpoints.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: A jointly smooth slab restricts to a smooth spatial slice

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: Joint smoothness on a closed slab ensures that each fixed spatial value has, as its derivative within the slab, the value of the within time derivative. The theorem simply restricts the smooth field along a time line. It does not compute the derivative by an Euler formula; that identification comes from the projected momentum hypotheses.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: A smooth slab supplies its within time derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: A velocity jointly smooth on the half open preterminal slab has smooth spatial slices at every time belonging to that slab. The proof restricts the joint function to a fixed time. This private lemma supplies the ordinary spatial smoothness needed for advection and pressure recovery.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: Preterminal smoothness restricts to every spatial slice

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: For a bounded bilinear map $B$, uniform convergence of $U_j$ to a continuous limit on the compact interval implies uniform convergence of $B(U_j,U_j)$. Compactness supplies a uniform bound for the limiting curve. The proof controls the two factors separately, rather than treating a quadratic map as globally uniformly continuous.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: Uniform convergence passes through a bounded quadratic expression

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The momentum operation is transported to the range of genuine smooth jet tuples through order $m+2$, with values in the completed space at order $m$. Injectivity recovers each velocity from its tuple, and the explicit norm inequality makes the resulting bilinear map continuous. The domain remains the exact range at this step.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The momentum estimate gives a bounded map on genuine jets

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: A continuous tower in complete normed spaces becomes smooth in time when each entry satisfies an integrated equation with a bounded bilinear map from a finite higher level. This variant uses general spaces $X_m$, allowing the closed spaces of compatible periodic jets. Induction on the number of time derivatives handles the finite loss function $r$.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Completed jet spaces admit the same time bootstrap

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The inclusion of the smooth jet range into its closure has dense range. This is the topological fact needed by the extension theorem for bounded bilinear maps. It does not assert that every element of the closure is already a smooth jet tuple.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The original jet range is dense in the completed space

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: A continuous periodic field on the Euclidean lift is uniformly bounded. The proof descends it to the compact unit torus, obtains a bound there, and pulls it back. The conclusion gives an unspecified real upper bound, which is enough to bundle actual derivatives as bounded continuous functions.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Continuity and periodicity provide a global bound

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: For a dense linear isometry $e:E\to H$ and complete target $F$, this construction sends each bounded linear map on $E$ to its continuous extension on $H$. The construction itself is a bounded linear operator of norm at most one. Density and isometry provide the extension agreement used later.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Bounded operators extend from a dense isometric subspace

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: A bounded bilinear map on a dense isometric subspace is extended to the ambient space in each argument. Completeness of the target ensures the extensions exist. This is how the momentum map reaches completed compatible jets while retaining bilinearity, without assuming a formula for arbitrary collections of unrelated derivative fields.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: A bounded bilinear map extends in both inputs

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: Evaluating the extended bilinear map at $e(x)$ and $e(y)$ returns $B(x,y)$ exactly. The proof applies the continuous linear extension agreement theorem in each argument. This identity ensures that the completed momentum operator computes the original analytic expression on smooth periodic velocities.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The extended map agrees on original inputs

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The explicit coefficient used for the momentum jet estimate is nonnegative at every natural order. This follows from nonnegativity of operator norms, the square root, and positive numerical factors. It supplies the sign assumptions needed to package the subsequent bilinear map as a bounded operator.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The chosen momentum constant is nonnegative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: If $f$ belongs to $C^{m,1/2}$, with bounded derivatives and bounded half-Hölder increment quotients through order $m$, each actual derivative of order at most $m$ is bounded by the full spatial Hölder norm. The premise supplies boundedness for the real suprema and nonnegativity of every summand. The theorem would not follow merely by evaluating the norm formula, which returns a value for every field, on an arbitrary field.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: A Hölder norm bounds every stored pointwise derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: For two smooth periodic velocities, the completed norm of their signed projected momentum through order $m$ is bounded by the stated constant times the product of their norms through order $m+2$. Tensor differentiation costs one order and the passage from uniform jets to half Hölder control costs another. This is a sufficient boundedness estimate, not an optimal loss claim.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Momentum loses two orders in the uniform jet estimate

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The norm of an actual derivative at any spatial point is at most the completed tuple norm, provided its order is among the stored components. The proof combines evaluation boundedness with the finite product supremum norm. This gives the pointwise inputs for subsequent Hölder and momentum estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Every pointwise derivative is controlled by the tuple norm

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The periodic Leray lift of a real scalar multiple of a smooth periodic field equals the same multiple of its projection. The proof represents the field in the torus half Hölder space and uses the concrete bounded projection there. This domain restriction prevents the raw lift’s fallback branch from obscuring linearity.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Projection commutes with real scaling on smooth fields

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The divergence of the tensor product of two bundled velocities is packaged as another smooth periodic velocity. Smoothness follows by differentiating their smooth tensor; periodicity follows because differentiation commutes with lattice translations. This object is defined before Leray projection and does not require either input to be divergence free.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Tensor divergence remains a smooth periodic field

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The tensor divergence construction is bundled as an algebraic bilinear map on smooth periodic fields. Linearity in each slot uses the derivative rules for sums and scalar multiples of smooth tensors. No operator norm is asserted at this stage; a finite derivative estimate is supplied later on jet tuples.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Tensor divergence is bilinear on smooth periodic velocities

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: Evaluating the constructed smooth periodic momentum divergence returns the contraction of the actual derivative of the pointwise tensor. This definitional equality connects the bundle to the expression used by the projected Euler equation. It remains a tensor divergence formula without a divergence-free premise on the inputs.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The bundled divergence has the expected tensor formula

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: This nonnegative scalar collects the operator norms of Leray projection, tensor divergence, and the momentum tensor, together with the finite product and Hölder comparison constants. It depends on the target order $m$. Its purpose is to prove boundedness of momentum from jets through $m+2$ to jets through $m$.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: An explicit constant for the finite jet momentum estimate

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The pointwise tensor formed from two bundled smooth periodic velocities is smooth in space. The proof uses the continuous bilinear tensor map and smoothness of both inputs. Periodicity is not part of this theorem’s conclusion, although it is established in the following divergence construction.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Two smooth velocities have a smooth momentum tensor

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: Composing tensor divergence with negative Leray projection gives a bilinear map on smooth periodic velocities. This package records that the output remains in the same smooth periodic submodule. Its later bounded extension uses finite jet norms; the present definition itself asserts algebraic bilinearity rather than a no-loss estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The smooth momentum operation is an algebraic bilinear map

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: For smooth periodic inputs, forgetting the bundle on the algebraic momentum map yields exactly $-\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(u\otimes v)$, the signed projected momentum of $u$ and $v$. This is a definitional equality. It is the bridge from estimates proved for packaged smooth fields back to the explicit signed projected tensor divergence used in the limit equation.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The bundled operation equals the raw momentum expression

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: On the completed tuples of two smooth periodic velocities, the extended momentum map equals the completed tuple of their smooth momentum field. The proof reduces the extensions to their agreement on the dense source. This rules out any change of the intended formula when completion is introduced.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Completion preserves the original smooth momentum calculation

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm of a smooth periodic velocity is at most $3(m+1)$ times the norm of its jet tuple through order $m+1$. Uniform value and derivative bounds yield the half Hölder increment estimate. This is one source of the finite derivative loss in the completed momentum construction.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: One extra uniform derivative controls the Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: This continuous linear map extracts a single bounded spatial jet from a completed compatible tuple. It first forgets the closed subspace membership and then projects onto the chosen finite coordinate. The coordinate index ensures that only an order stored in the tuple can be requested.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: One derivative order is a bounded coordinate projection

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: This linear isometry includes the range of smooth velocity jets in its topological closure. Norms are inherited from the same ambient tuple space, so preservation of norm is definitional. The map supplies the embedding along which the momentum operator will be extended by continuity.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Smooth jet tuples sit densely in their closure

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: This linear map first identifies a smooth periodic velocity with its exact finite jet tuple and then includes that tuple into the closure. It preserves the actual derivative values. The construction is algebraic at this stage; a norm on the original smooth velocity space is not being introduced.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The velocity map into completed compatible jets

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The negative periodic Leray projection is a linear map from smooth periodic fields to themselves. Higher Hölder estimates prove smoothness of the output; Fourier periodicity supplies its lattice invariance. The sign is chosen so composition with tensor divergence gives the right hand side of the Euler evolution.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Negative Leray projection preserves the smooth periodic domain

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The order $m$ derivative of a bundled smooth periodic velocity is continuous and periodic, hence uniformly bounded. This definition packages it as a bounded continuous function. The auxiliary chosen bound is used only to establish boundedness; the underlying function remains the actual iterated Fréchet derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Actual derivatives become bounded continuous jet fields

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: Injectivity of the finite jet map identifies the algebraic space of smooth periodic velocities with its range of tuples. This linear equivalence lets the momentum formula be transported from functions to genuine jet tuples before any completion. Its inverse recovers the unique velocity represented by a range element.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: A velocity is equivalent to its exact jet tuple

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The bounded jet constructed from a smooth periodic velocity evaluates exactly to its iterated Fréchet derivative. This is a definitional identity, so the choice of a uniform bound has no effect on values. It is repeatedly used to compare operator estimates in jet spaces with pointwise differential expressions.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Evaluating the bundled jet returns the actual derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The derivative of the order $m$ bounded jet field equals the order $m+1$ jet of the same smooth velocity, read as a linear map into order $m$ multilinear maps. The proof invokes its actual Taylor series. This compatibility is necessary for joint regularity; boundedness and continuity of separate tuple entries alone would not establish it.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Successive smooth jets have the required derivative relation

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: Two smooth periodic velocities with identical finite jet tuples are equal, for every order $m$. The proof evaluates their zeroth components and uses the canonical identification of zero argument multilinear maps with vectors. No derivative order above zero is needed for injectivity.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The zeroth jet recovers the whole velocity

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: This private projection extracts the periodicity proof from a smooth periodic velocity. It permits derivatives and tensor expressions to be moved to the compact torus when bounds are needed. The predicate concerns invariance under all integer lattice translations of the Euclidean lift.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Bundled velocities carry spatial periodicity

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: An element of the smooth periodic velocity submodule carries a proof of smoothness of its underlying function. This private projection extracts that proof. The conclusion concerns a single spatial field and says nothing about time dependence, divergence, parity, or the Euler equation.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Bundled velocities carry spatial smoothness

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The iterated Fréchet derivatives of a spatially periodic function are spatially periodic at every order. Translation commutes with the totalized derivative operator, so no smoothness hypothesis is needed for this identity. Smoothness is supplied separately when these derivatives are used to define the actual periodic jet spaces.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Every spatial derivative retains periodicity

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: The complex Laplacian of a real $C^2$ pressure, viewed as complex-valued, equals the complex inclusion of the divergence of its real gradient. The proof compares each diagonal coordinate derivative and sums them. This prevents a sign or coordinate convention from being hidden in the transition to Fourier Poisson uniqueness.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: The complexified Laplacian is the real pressure divergence

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: For a $C^2$ real velocity, double divergence of its complex pressure tensor equals the complex inclusion of the divergence of its real momentum tensor divergence. The proof expands both coordinate sums and uses commutation of complex inclusion with mixed derivatives. No incompressibility is needed for this representation identity; it is used later to identify tensor divergence with advection.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: The complex source equals real momentum double divergence

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: For a real $C^2$ scalar field, its complex inclusion has coordinate second derivatives equal to the complex inclusion of the original mixed partials. The proof applies the first-derivative compatibility twice, using $C^2$ regularity to make the first coordinate derivative $C^1$. This transfers the real pressure equation to complex coordinates.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: Complex inclusion preserves the mixed coordinate derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: For a $C^2$ field valued in momentum tensors, stored as three column vectors in $\mathbb R^3$, component $i$ of its tensor divergence is the sum over $j$ of the derivative of entry $i$ of column $j$ in direction $e_j$. Coordinate projection commutes with differentiation by the chain rule. The explicit ordering matches the momentum tensor’s column representation.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: Tensor divergence is the sum of coordinate derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: At a point where a real scalar field is differentiable, the real Fréchet derivative of its complex inclusion evaluated on a vector is the complex inclusion of its real derivative. This is the chain rule for the real-linear inclusion $\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$. The differentiability premise rules out reading the default value of an undefined derivative as a classical derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: Complex inclusion commutes with a real spatial derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: If a smooth periodic vector field is fixed by the periodic Leray lift, its divergence vanishes everywhere. The proof descends the field to the bundled half Hölder space, interprets the fixed point as solenoidality, then uses the smooth gradient-pairing characterization. Smooth periodicity ensures the raw lift is operating on its valid analytic domain.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: A smooth periodic fixed point of Leray is divergence free

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: A jointly smooth field on the half-open Euler slab has a smooth spatial slice at every time in that slab. The proof composes with the map $x\mapsto(t,x)$ and uses that the spatial domain of the joint smoothness is all of $\mathbb R^3$. The time may be zero, since no ambient time differentiation is used here.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: Joint smoothness restricts to a smooth spatial slice

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: For an Euler solution and a time in $[0,T)$, the spatial divergence of its within-time velocity derivative is zero. A nondegenerate closed prefix containing the time allows differentiating the Leray fixed-point relation, including at time zero. Joint smoothness and periodicity of the derivative then convert its fixed-point property to pointwise zero divergence.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: The within-time derivative remains divergence free

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerUniquen.text: For a classical Euler solution $(U,p)$ on $[0,T)$, choose a positive $S$ strictly below $T$. The within-time derivative is continuous jointly in time and space on $[0,S]\times\mathbb R^3$. The proof compares the derivative on this closed prefix with the solution’s half-open time derivative, including the initial face rather than discarding it.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerUniquen.summary: The Euler time derivative is continuous on strict prefixes

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerUniquen.text: If $(U,p)$ is a classical Euler solution on $[0,T)$ and $r\in[0,T)$, then the spatial pressure function $p(r)$ is smooth to every order. This follows by composing joint smoothness with the fixed-time inclusion. The conclusion is full spatial smoothness, not only continuity.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerUniquen.summary: Every preterminal pressure slice is smooth

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerUniquen.text: At a time $t\in[0,T)$, the Euler equation satisfied by the classical solution $(u,p)$ gives $u_t=-Du\,u-\nabla p$ pointwise. The theorem only rearranges the existing momentum identity. It is used when subtracting the two Euler equations in the classical uniqueness energy estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerUniquen.summary: The time derivative equals the negative Euler momentum

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.text: This private abbreviation names the three-dimensional unit additive torus used by the higher Leray estimates. It fixes the domain of the Hölder fields and their translations. It adds no regularity, mean-zero condition, or divergence constraint; those belong to the field types, projections, and hypotheses that follow.

For periodic order-zero half-Hölder data, the lifted action of $P$ remains in that class and has norm at most $2\sqrt{2}\|P\|$ times the input norm. The constants come from the two conversions between torus and Euclidean-lift norms. This base case does not need derivative commutation, because no spatial derivative is taken.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.summary: Bound the projected field in the base Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.text: The half-Hölder increment quotient of the iterated derivative of $Df$ equals the quotient at the next derivative order of $f$. The proof uses the linear isometry identifying a $(j+1)$-linear map with a $j$-linear map into linear maps, including its preservation of differences. It does not assert that either quotient is bounded; later regularity hypotheses provide that fact.

The norm of the order-$j$ derivative of $Df$ equals the norm of the order-$(j+1)$ derivative of $f$. This is an equality of real-valued functions, using the isometric identification of iterated Fréchet derivatives of $Df$ with those of $f$. It carries no regularity or boundedness assumption and supplies only the algebraic norm identification.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.summary: Successive derivative norms agree under the multilinear identification

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.text: If $f$ is invariant under integer lattice translations, its Fréchet derivative, taken with its default value where it does not exist, is invariant under those translations too. The proof uses translation of the derivative and equality of the translated functions. No differentiability assumption appears here: this is periodicity of the derivative expression, not an assertion that an actual derivative exists.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.summary: A periodic function has a periodic derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.text: The quotient map from Euclidean space to the unit torus sends a vector sum to the sum of its images. This coordinatewise quotient identity lets a Euclidean line be read as a translated torus line. No regularity or periodicity assumption on a field is involved.

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: Abbreviates the unit three-torus used when comparing bundled quotient half-Hölder fields with periodic Euclidean lifts. The quotient carries the coordinate product metric, while $\mathbb R^3$ carries its Euclidean norm. The later comparison constants account for this difference; the abbreviation itself asserts no equivalence of norms.

The distance between two quotient labels is at most the Euclidean norm of the difference of their lifts. The proof combines the circle quotient bound with the coordinate-to-Euclidean norm inequality. This provides one direction of the metric comparison used to transfer half-Hölder increment estimates from the torus to the lift.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: The quotient distance is bounded by the lifted distance

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: The quotient of a Euclidean sum equals the sum of the quotient labels. This additive identity expresses a lifted spatial line as a translated torus line. It is used to transport derivative relations between the Euclidean field and its descended half-Hölder representative.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: Translations pass through the quotient map

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: The quotient label of $x-y$ equals the difference of the quotient labels of $x$ and $y$. The proof is coordinatewise additivity of the circle quotient. This identity is used to compare torus distances with distances between Euclidean representatives when relating the two Hölder norms.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: Differences pass through the quotient map

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: The first iterated derivative is identified with the Fréchet derivative through the standard one-variable multilinear currying equivalence. The equality holds as an identity of total derivative operators, without a differentiability assumption. It lets norm comparisons move between the paper’s first spatial derivative and Lean’s iterated-derivative representation.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: The first iterated derivative is the curried Fréchet derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: The strong spatial Leray projection commutes with every torus translation on half-Hölder vector fields. The proof uses its exact complex Fourier coefficient law, where translation contributes a scalar phase that commutes with each mode projection. This supplies the invariance needed to pass spatial derivatives through the projection.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: The torus Leray operator commutes with translations

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: The half-Hölder quotient formed from the first iterated derivative equals the quotient formed from the Fréchet derivative. The currying equivalence preserves differences and their norms. This is an encoding identity for the derivative field; it does not independently prove existence or continuity of a classical derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: First-derivative increments have the same Hölder quotient

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: The half-Hölder quotient of the zeroth iterated derivative equals that of the original field. Lean stores a zeroth derivative as a zero-argument multilinear map, and the standard currying equivalence preserves norms of differences. This identity removes that encoding when comparing the order-zero lift norm with ordinary field bounds.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: The zeroth derivative preserves Hölder quotients

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.text: This private abbreviation names the frequency type consisting of three integer coordinates. It is used uniformly for mode insertion, coefficients, and longitudinal generators in spatial $L^2$. There is no nonzero restriction, so every construction must handle the constant frequency explicitly.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.summary: Three integer indices for spatial Fourier modes

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.text: Pairing the complex frequency vector with the complexified real velocity gives the real Euclidean frequency contraction cast into complex numbers. The integer frequency entries are real, so conjugation in the first inner-product slot changes nothing. This identity connects the two solenoidal-space definitions.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.summary: Complex longitudinal pairing equals the real contraction

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.text: The complex $L^2$ pairing of two inserted modes equals their coefficient inner product when the frequencies agree, and zero otherwise. The proof uses character orthogonality after replacing representatives almost everywhere. This identifies which longitudinal directions must be removed by the all-field Leray projection.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.summary: Hilbert modes have orthogonal frequency components

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.text: Every spatial $L^2$ field is integrable on the probability torus, and multiplication by a Fourier character preserves integrability because its modulus is one. The lemma justifies the Bochner integral defining each coefficient. It applies to arbitrary $L^2$ inputs, with no smoothness assumption.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.summary: Multiplying an L2 field by a character remains integrable

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.text: This private coefficient is the integer frequency embedded in complex Euclidean space. It spans the longitudinal direction for that mode and is inserted into spatial $L^2$ to generate gradient directions. At frequency zero it is the zero vector, leaving constant velocity coefficients unconstrained.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.summary: The frequency vector as a longitudinal coefficient

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.text: This submodule is the complex linear span of all longitudinal mode insertions. A span means finite algebraic linear combinations; it is not declared closed. Its orthogonal complement is nevertheless closed and supplies the solenoidal $L^2$ space used for the orthogonal Leray projection.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.summary: Finite linear combinations of longitudinal Fourier modes

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: This abbreviation names complex scalar L² over the torus Haar measure. It lets the proof use scalar Fourier density coordinate by coordinate before returning to complex vector fields. There is no zero-mean condition, smoothness condition, or prescribed Fourier support in the type itself.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Scalar square integrable Fourier fields on the torus

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: For any lattice frequency, complex amplitude, and bounded real-linear functional, the Euclidean lift of the scalarized Fourier wave is smooth of all orders. Smoothness comes from the exponential Fourier mode and linearity of the functional $L$. This prepares the classical integration-by-parts argument for its weak solenoidal membership.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: A scalarized torus wave has a smooth lift

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: For a fixed coordinate $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, project a complex vector-valued spatial $L^2$ field to scalar $L^2$. The map is complex-linear and continuous because the Euclidean coordinate projection is bounded. It is used to reduce vector Fourier density to the scalar Fourier density theorem.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Extract one coordinate of a complex spatial field

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: The divergence of the Euclidean lift is $L$ applied to the Fourier mode multiplied by the divergence symbol $\sum_i 2\pi ik_ia_i$. Differentiating each coordinate supplies its frequency factor, and their sum is the divergence symbol. The formula holds before transversality is assumed, so the next lemma can set this contraction to zero.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: The wave divergence is its frequency contraction

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: The real $L^2$ inner product of the real part of $u$ with $v$ equals the real part of their complex $L^2$ inner product after embedding $v$. The proof moves the real-part linear map through the integral and uses the vector identity almost everywhere. This is the Hilbert-space compatibility needed for orthogonal projections.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Spatial inner products commute with taking real parts

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: For a complex vector $u$ and real vector $v$, pairing the real part of $u$ with $v$ equals the real part of the complex inner product of $u$ with the complexification of $v$. This coordinate identity transfers orthogonality from the complex Fourier space to the real velocity space.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Real pairing equals the real part of complex pairing

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: Insert a scalar spatial $L^2$ field into the $i$th coordinate of a three-component complex field, leaving the other coordinates zero. The map is obtained from scalar multiplication by the corresponding Euclidean basis vector. Together with coordinate extraction it reconstructs arbitrary vector fields as a finite sum.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Place a scalar field in one vector coordinate

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: If the real part of $-iu$ is zero, then complexifying the real part of $u$ recovers $u$. The assumption is exactly vanishing of the imaginary component as an $L^2$ class. This reconstruction criterion permits a real-valued conclusion without requiring matching pointwise representatives everywhere.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: A field without imaginary part equals its real embedding

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: Define the complex submodule generated by all torus Fourier waves with arbitrary complex three-vector amplitudes. Elements are finite complex linear combinations of these waves. Density in the whole vector L² space is a later theorem, rather than a property built into the definition.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Finite linear combinations of vector Fourier waves

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: The topological closure of the complex span of all vector Fourier modes is the entire complex spatial L² space. Scalar Fourier density is transferred through coordinate insertion, and the three coordinate components are recombined. This supplies the density step that extends modewise projection identities to arbitrary L² input.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Vector Fourier waves are dense in spatial L²

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: A real continuous linear functional $L$ on complex spatial $L^2$ vanishes everywhere if it vanishes on every vector Fourier mode. Arbitrary complex amplitudes ensure vanishing on complex scalar multiples, despite $L$ being only real-linear. Density of the mode span and continuity finish the argument.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: A continuous functional is determined by its Fourier modes

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: For an amplitude $a$ in the transverse mode space $\{a\in\mathbb C^3:\ a\perp k\}$, the real part of its vector Fourier mode lies in the weak real solenoidal space. The theorem translates the subspace membership into zero frequency contraction and identifies the representative with a real scalarized wave. It bridges the complex coefficient and real test-function definitions.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Real parts of transverse modes are weakly solenoidal

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: The real part of $-i$ times a complex spatial L² field agrees almost everywhere with its coordinatewise imaginary part. This formula expresses the imaginary projection using the already-defined real-part map. Its representative-level conclusion is enough to show later that a projected embedded real field has no imaginary component.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Multiplication by minus i reveals the imaginary part

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: Complexify a real spatial L² field, multiply it by $-i$, and take the real part: the result is zero. The statement is an L² equality and formalizes vanishing imaginary component of a real embedding. It is used to prove that the complex Leray projection preserves the embedded real subspace.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: An embedded real field has zero imaginary part

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: For a real continuous linear functional $L:\mathbb C\to\mathbb R$, apply $L$ to each coordinate of a Fourier character times its complex amplitude. The result is a continuous real vector field on the torus. Choosing real or imaginary part gives the real waves used in weak divergence tests.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Real scalarizations of a complex Fourier wave

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: At torus point $z$ and coordinate $i$, the scalarized mode is exactly $L(e^{2\pi ik\cdot z}a_i)$. This definitional identity exposes the ordinary complex Fourier wave underneath the real Euclidean-space representation. It is used for subsequent smoothness and divergence calculations on the Euclidean lift.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Each scalarized coordinate is the expected Fourier expression

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: If the frequency contraction $\sum_ik_ia_i$ of amplitude $a$ vanishes, the scalarized Fourier mode, embedded in spatial $L^2$, belongs to the weak solenoidal subspace. The proof computes its classical divergence and applies periodic integration by parts. At zero frequency the contraction is automatically zero, so constant fields are retained.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Transverse Fourier waves satisfy the weak divergence condition

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: Extract each of the three scalar coordinates of $u$, insert it back into its coordinate position, and sum: the resulting $L^2$ class is $u$. The proof combines representative identities with the finite Euclidean basis expansion. This avoids assuming vector-valued Fourier density as an independent library fact.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Summing the coordinate fields reconstructs the vector field

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicMultiplierBo.text: The complex Euclidean inner product with the frequency vector in the first slot equals the algebraic frequency contraction. This works because integer frequency entries are real and unchanged by conjugation. The identity reconciles the coordinate Leray formula with the orthogonal-projection implementation.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicMultiplierBo.summary: Hermitian pairing reproduces the frequency contraction

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicMultiplierBo.text: The integral inner product of two single Fourier terms is the coefficient inner product if their frequencies agree, and zero otherwise. The target is any complex Hilbert space. This transfers scalar character orthogonality to vector or path coefficients before proving finite Parseval identities.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicMultiplierBo.summary: Orthogonality holds for Hilbert valued Fourier terms

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicMultiplierBo.text: The square of the complex Euclidean norm of the embedded frequency is $|k|^2=\sum_ik_i^2$. The calculation uses the reality of integer casts and the sum-of-squares norm formula. It provides the denominator identification needed to compare the explicit Leray coefficient with a singleton-span projection.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicMultiplierBo.summary: The Euclidean coefficient norm matches frequency length

_private.TorusEuler.PhaseJetBounds.0.Tor.text: Every scalar coordinate selected from a label-phase pair has absolute value at most the norm of that pair.
