_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentPoiss.text: Computes the coordinate formula of the real-part conversion map from complex vectors in $\mathbb C^3$ to $\mathbb R^3$: its $i$th real component is the real part of the original $i$th complex component. This identity holds by definition and fixes the normalization when translating complex Fourier derivatives into the real Euclidean operators used by the pressure theorem.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentPoiss.summary: The conversion takes each coordinate real part

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentPoiss.text: For a complex scalar function differentiable at the evaluation point, identifies the real gradient of its real part with the converted complex gradient. Testing coordinates against the Euclidean basis proves the equality. This is the scalar companion to the divergence conversion used in the finite Poisson calculation.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentPoiss.summary: Real parts commute with the scalar gradient

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentPoiss.text: Identifies the gradient of the negative of a scalar function with the negative gradient, as an equality of functions. This identity uses the negation rule for the totalized Fréchet derivative and does not assume differentiability. It supplies the sign of the negative Fourier pressure potential.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentPoiss.summary: Negation commutes with the scalar gradient

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentPoiss.text: Moves the finite-product norm conversion through a finite Fourier sum. The equality holds for every finite frequency set, every complex vector coefficient family and every torus point. It is an algebraic continuous-linear-map identity, needed because the Fourier and Euclidean differential libraries use different presentations of the same vector space.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentPoiss.summary: Fourier synthesis respects the product representation

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentPoiss.text: For an arbitrary function on the label torus, proves spatial periodicity after composition with the quotient map. The target can be any type; continuity and differentiability are unnecessary. The proof uses equality of quotient points under integer translation, so it is a representation fact rather than an analytic estimate.

Restricts a jointly smooth function on a closed time slab to a fixed time belonging to that slab, producing an all-order smooth function on the entire spatial space. The target is any real normed vector space. This restriction needs slab membership but no positive interval length.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentPoiss.summary: Joint slab smoothness gives every spatial slice

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentProje.text: A jointly smooth field on a closed time slab is smooth in all spatial variables at every time belonging to that interval. The proof composes with the fixed-time inclusion. No strict inequality between the slab endpoints is required for this restriction; the conclusion concerns only a slice already inside the specified domain.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentProje.summary: Restrict closed slab smoothness to a spatial slice

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentProje.text: A coordinate of the total gradient expression equals the total Fréchet derivative applied to the corresponding basis vector. The identity is valid for an arbitrary scalar function because the gradient is defined by inner-product duality from that derivative expression. Actual differentiability of pressure is required separately before this can be read as a derivative statement.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentProje.summary: Identify a gradient coordinate with the Fréchet derivative

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentProje.text: If each slice inside the closed interval is continuous and periodic, there exists a time-indexed family of continuous torus fields agreeing with those slices. Each slice is descended separately, and the construction uses zero outside the interval. This theorem promises pointwise representation on the slab, not continuity of the family as a curve in a function space.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentProje.summary: Choose torus representatives of the periodic slices

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentProje.text: If every time slice on the closed interval is spatially periodic, its total within-interval time derivative is spatially periodic at each interval time. This follows from equality of the translated curves on the differentiation set. The lemma assumes neither differentiability nor distinct endpoints; later results supply actual derivative witnesses and interval nondegeneracy.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentProje.summary: The total time derivative retains spatial periodicity

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: Abbreviates a three-column array of complex Euclidean vectors. It is the complex target in which the real momentum tensor can undergo Fourier synthesis. The abbreviation carries no symmetry, positivity or divergence condition; those properties belong to particular fields and separate analytic statements.

For a continuous bilinear map $B$, the field $x\mapsto B(f(x),g(x))$ is $C^m$ when both input fields are $C^m$. The statement gives regularity only, without a size estimate. It supplies the differentiability prerequisite for the later quantitative Leibniz bounds on momentum tensors.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: A continuous bilinear product preserves finite smoothness

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: The uniform tail constant at any input order is nonnegative. Its definition is a nonnegative natural-number factor times one plus a sum of nonnegative absolute moments. This simple sign check permits multiplication of the tail estimate by embedding, projection and tensor-contraction norms in the residual bound.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: The common cutoff-tail constant is nonnegative

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: Defines a continuous real-linear map that complexifies every column of a real momentum tensor. It preserves the column indexing used by tensor divergence and supplies complex-valued data for Fourier synthesis. The map does not alter the tensor-product convention or require the tensor to arise from a velocity.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: Complexifying the momentum tensor column by column

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: Defines a continuous real-linear map from complex momentum tensors to real tensors by taking each column’s coordinatewise real part. The map is used after complex Fourier synthesis. It is a projection onto real data and need not be injective on arbitrary complex tensors.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: Taking real parts of momentum-tensor columns

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: Taking real parts after complexifying a momentum tensor returns that tensor exactly. This follows column by column from the real-vector identity. It supplies the retraction hypothesis of the abstract tensor tail estimate, ensuring that the cutoff error there refers to the original real momentum tensor.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: Real momentum tensors survive the complex detour

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: If all derivatives of the inputs $f$ and $g$ through order $j\le m$ are bounded at $x$ by $A$ and $D$ respectively, with $A\ge0$, then the $j$th derivative of the bilinear product is bounded by $\|B\|2^mAD$. The factor $2^m$ bounds the sum of binomial coefficients. The theorem is pointwise and assumes sufficient $C^m$ regularity for the product rule.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: Leibniz terms give an exponential derivative bound

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: If a field is $C^m$ with bounded derivatives and bounded half-Hölder quotients through order $m$, its spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm is nonnegative. The proof sums the nonnegative derivative-level contributions rather than relying on an unconditional property of real suprema. This sign is needed throughout the product, tail and projected residual estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: The finite Hölder norm is nonnegative

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: An order-$(m+1)$ half-Hölder field has a derivative field $Df$ that is half-Hölder of order $m$, with $\|Df\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le\|f\|_{C^{m+1,1/2}}$. The isometric identification of derivatives of $Df$ with derivatives of $f$ of one higher order matches each derivative level with the next level of the original field. Removing the nonnegative zeroth level gives the norm inequality used before contracting a tensor derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: A spatial derivative costs one Hölder order

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: An order-$m$ half-Hölder field is half-Hölder of order $n$ whenever $n\le m$, and its $C^{n,1/2}$ norm is no larger. The definition sums all levels through the specified order, so the proof restricts regularity and removes nonnegative summands. This lets high-order tail information supply the first and second orders used in the residual.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: Lowering derivative order cannot increase this Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: Negating a half-Hölder field preserves its regularity and leaves the full finite-order norm unchanged. The proof uses negation of iterated derivatives and invariance of norms of both values and increments. This permits the cutoff tail estimate for $V-u$ to be used with the paper’s velocity error $u-V$.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: Changing the sign preserves the Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: If a $C^m$ field has all derivative norms through order $m$ bounded by $A$ and all corresponding increments bounded by $B\sqrt{|v|}$, with $B\ge0$, it has order-$m$ half-Hölder regularity and $C^{m,1/2}$ norm at most $(m+1)(A+B)$. The result proves boundedness of the quotient ranges explicitly before summing the levels.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: Uniform level bounds assemble a Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: At positive scale, the real cutoff of an order-$m$ half-Hölder field retains that regularity and has norm bounded by $2(m+1)(1+C_m)$ times the input norm, where $C_m$ is the uniform tail constant of the cutoff kernel at order $m$. The proof writes the cutoff as the original field minus its zero-loss tail. The bound is uniform in the cutoff scale, with dependence only on the fixed symbol and order.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: The real cutoff is bounded at each Hölder order

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: Every derivative through order $m$ has increments bounded by the full $C^{m,1/2}$ norm times $\sqrt{|v|}$. The theorem first uses the corresponding derivative seminorm, then compares that seminorm with the whole norm. It supplies the difference estimate for the product-rule argument, alongside the separate pointwise derivative bound.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: Derivative increments are controlled by the full norm

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: For $j\le m$, the pointwise norm of the $j$th full derivative is bounded by the full $C^{m,1/2}$ norm. The regularity hypothesis ensures the relevant supremum is a genuine upper bound. This is the basic estimate used to control each Leibniz term in products and residual tensors.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: Every spatial derivative is bounded by the full norm

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: For a field with order-$m$ half-Hölder regularity, any level $j\le m$, that is $\sup|D^jf|+[D^jf]_{1/2}$, contributes at most the full norm. Each other summand is nonnegative under the boundedness hypotheses supplied by that regularity. The lemma turns order-specific supremum and increment bounds into estimates using a single input budget.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: One derivative level is bounded by the full Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.text: For an order-$m$ half-Hölder field, the sum of the supremum and seminorm at any derivative level $j\le m$ is nonnegative. The regularity hypothesis supplies boundedness of both real-supremum ranges. This permits derivative levels to be discarded or added when comparing the various finite-order norms.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncatedParentResid.summary: Every bounded derivative level contributes a nonnegative amount

_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.text: A continuously differentiable Euclidean lift of a continuous torus vector field has a coordinate derivative represented by a continuous torus field. Periodicity of the derivative allows quotient descent, and its continuity follows from the assumed first-order regularity. This constructs the actual derivative data required by the cutoff commutation lemma.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.summary: Descend a continuous coordinate derivative to the torus

_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.text: At a point where $f$ is differentiable, the derivative of its composition with a continuous real linear map $L$ is $L$ composed with the derivative of $f$. The differentiability hypothesis ensures both derivative expressions represent actual derivatives. This chain rule is used for tensor columns and coordinate projections.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.summary: Differentiate after a bounded linear map

_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.text: If $d$ is a continuous torus field whose lift equals one coordinate derivative $\partial_i$ of the continuously differentiable lift of $g$, then differentiating the finite cutoff of $g$ in that coordinate gives the cutoff of $d$. The result holds for arbitrary real symbol and scale. It concerns a finite synthesis and requires no decay estimate or limiting exchange.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.summary: Differentiate a finite vector Fourier cutoff

_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.text: For a differentiable momentum-tensor field at a point, differentiating its selected column in the corresponding coordinate direction equals evaluating the derivative tensor in that direction and then selecting the column. This is the bounded evaluation-map chain rule. Summing these identities produces the physical tensor-divergence formula.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.summary: Differentiate a tensor column by evaluation

_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.text: The Fourier coefficient of the sum of two continuous torus fields is the sum of their Fourier coefficients. Completeness of the complex target and compactness of the torus ensure that the integrands are integrable before additivity is applied. This supports the real cutoff’s linearity and the momentum rearrangement.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.summary: Fourier coefficients add for continuous fields

_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.text: For a continuous torus field with values in a complete complex normed space, applying a continuous complex linear map commutes with taking a Fourier coefficient. Continuity on the compact torus supplies Bochner integrability. This is the integral identity behind the cutoff formulas for vector components and tensor columns.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.summary: Fourier coefficients commute with bounded complex maps

_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.text: The real scalar cutoff of two added continuous torus functions equals the sum of their cutoffs. Integrability comes from continuity, and the proof distributes through Fourier coefficients, finite summation, and real-part extraction. No symmetry or positivity assumptions on the symbol or scale are needed for this linear identity.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.summary: The real scalar cutoff preserves addition

_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.text: Taking a coordinate of the real vector cutoff gives exactly the real scalar cutoff of that coordinate field. The identity holds for every real symbol and cutoff scale. It reconciles the componentwise scalar Fourier construction with the bundled vector construction before their derivatives are assembled into a divergence or gradient.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.summary: Scalar cutoff agrees with each vector coordinate

_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.text: Applying the real scalar cutoff to a finite sum of continuous functions equals the finite sum of their cutoffs. The theorem includes the empty sum and arbitrary symbol and scale. Its role is to pass the cutoff through the three coordinate terms in the divergence of a vector field.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.summary: The real scalar cutoff preserves finite sums

_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.text: For every symbol and real scale, applying the real vector Fourier cutoff to the zero continuous field gives the zero field. Every Fourier coefficient and every term of the finite sum vanish. The result is used when a divergence-free field is truncated; it does not require an analytic cutoff bound.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.summary: The real vector cutoff sends zero to zero

_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.text: A bounded complex linear map can be moved through the finite Fourier cutoff of a continuous torus field. The result follows term by term from coefficient commutation and linearity. It holds for any real symbol and cutoff scale; smoothness, support, symmetry, and positivity assumptions are unnecessary for this algebraic identity.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.summary: The finite cutoff commutes with bounded complex maps

_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.text: Composing any function on the torus $\mathbb T^3$ with the quotient map $\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3$ produces a field on $\mathbb R^3$ invariant under all integer translations. The target is arbitrary, and no regularity is asserted or required. This supplies the periodicity needed to descend coordinate derivatives and compare the Fourier cutoff with physical differential operators.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.summary: Pull back a torus function periodically

_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.text: Packages one coordinate of a continuous torus vector field as a continuous real torus function. The index belongs to the three-coordinate type, so evaluation always selects a valid coordinate. This lets the scalar cutoff lemmas express the components of the vector cutoff without changing the underlying field.
_private.TorusEuler.TruncationFourierCom.summary: View a vector coordinate as a scalar field

_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletion.0.Tor.text: For a continuous phase profile $V$ and fixed vector $\kappa$, proves continuity of $-\|\kappa\|^{-2}(\kappa\times V(s))$. The wave vector may be zero because the scalar coefficient is constant in phase and Lean defines its inverse there. Nonzero $\kappa$ is required later for curl inversion, not for this continuity statement.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletion.0.Tor.summary: The potential integrand is continuous in phase

_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionBounds.text: For a nonzero covector $\kappa$, the vector $-|\kappa|^{-2}\kappa\times v$ has norm at most $|v|/|\kappa|$. Transversality of $v$ is not needed for this upper bound. The nonzero hypothesis makes division by the covector length legitimate and exposes the inverse-frequency gain used by completion.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionBounds.summary: The normalized cross product gains inverse covector length

_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionBounds.text: For a continuous phase profile $V$ and a fixed continuous linear map $A$, averaging $A(V)$ over one period gives $A$ applied to the average of $V$. This only uses integrability supplied by continuity on the integration interval. Periodicity is not required for the averaging identity.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionBounds.summary: A fixed linear map commutes with phase averaging

_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionBounds.text: With strain $M$ and covector $\kappa$ fixed, the time source $S(v,f)=|\kappa|^{-2}(M^{\mathsf T}\kappa\times v+\kappa\times Mv-\kappa\times f)-2\langle\kappa,M\kappa\rangle|\kappa|^{-4}\,\kappa\times v$ can be written $Av+Bf$ for two continuous linear maps. No nonzero-covector hypothesis is needed for this algebraic decomposition, since the formula is defined at $\kappa=0$ through the convention $x/0=0$. The representation is used to transfer continuity, periodicity, and zero phase mean from the inputs.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionBounds.summary: The potential time source is linear in velocity and forcing

_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionRelay..text: If $f$ is jointly continuous on $[a,b]\times\mathbb R$ with $a\le b$, its anchored phase integral $(t,s)\mapsto\int_0^sf(t,\sigma)\,d\sigma$ is continuous on the same set. Time is clamped to the closed slab to build a continuous extension. This auxiliary extension does not assert any differentiability beyond the slab.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionRelay..summary: Phase integration preserves continuity on a closed time slab

_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionRelay..text: Joint continuity of $f(t,s)$ implies continuity of the integral $\int_0^sf(t,\sigma)\,d\sigma$ from zero to the variable phase endpoint. The proof rescales that interval to $[0,1]$ and uses continuity of a parameter integral. The target is a real normed space; no periodicity or zero-mean assumption is needed.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionRelay..summary: The anchored phase integral depends continuously on its parameters

_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionRelay..text: The cross product changes sign when its first argument is negated. This algebraic identity holds for arbitrary three-dimensional vectors and needs no transversality or nonvanishing assumption. It is used when differentiating the transported covector, whose evolution has a minus sign.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionRelay..summary: Negating the covector negates the cross product

_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionRelay..text: The cross product $k\times(rk)$ of $k$ with any scalar multiple of $k$ vanishes. This includes the zero vector and zero scalar. In the potential time derivative, the pressure contribution lies in the covector direction and is removed by this identity, so no pressure derivative enters the final source.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionRelay..summary: A vector has zero cross product with its multiples

_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionRelay..text: For a fixed first vector, taking a cross product is linear in the second vector and therefore preserves subtraction. The identity is unconditional. It separates the forcing, strain, and longitudinal-pressure pieces of the transverse velocity equation during the time differentiation of the curl potential.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveCompletionRelay..summary: The cross product distributes over a difference

_private.TorusEuler.WaveDivergence.0.Tor.text: If every coordinate satisfies $-1/2\le x_i<1/2$, the centered representative is the original point. The half-open upper bound matters because points on a positive face are represented on the corresponding negative face. This identifies local profile values away from the periodization seams.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveDivergence.0.Tor.summary: The representative fixes the half open centered cell

_private.TorusEuler.WaveDivergence.0.Tor.text: If each shifted coordinate $x_i+1/2$ has strictly positive fractional part, then near $x$ the centered representative map is subtraction of one fixed integer lattice vector. The floor values are locally constant under this hypothesis. This local identity permits smoothness of a profile to pass through periodization away from seams.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveDivergence.0.Tor.summary: Away from cell seams the representative is a fixed translation

_private.TorusEuler.WaveDivergence.0.Tor.text: For a collar width $\delta$ with $0<\delta\le1/2$, assume one shifted coordinate $x_i+1/2$ has zero fractional part at $x$. Nearby representatives have that coordinate within the collar $|a_i|>1/2-\delta$ of a cell face. The result handles both sides of the jump in the fractional-part representative.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveDivergence.0.Tor.summary: Near a seam the representative stays inside a boundary collar

_private.TorusEuler.WaveDivergence.0.Tor.text: This private real linear map sends a vector-valued derivative matrix to its coordinate curl vector. Additivity and scalar compatibility are supplied by earlier calculations. Since the spaces are finite dimensional, it can subsequently be viewed as continuous and composed with the derivative of a potential.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveDivergence.0.Tor.summary: Curl extraction as a linear map on derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.WavePressureCenter.0.text: A $C^2$ scalar function on three-dimensional Euclidean space has a differentiable gradient. The proof obtains differentiability of the derivative and identifies it with a vector through the inner product. This supplies the derivatives needed to compute the actual pressure Hessian, rather than an expression that takes the value zero where no derivative exists.
_private.TorusEuler.WavePressureCenter.0.summary: Twice differentiable pressure has a differentiable gradient

_private.TorusEuler.WavePressureCenter.0.text: For $0<h\le1$, differentiates the pressure $-c(x)P_h(\phi(x))$ at a point with specified coefficient and phase gradients. The result separates the fast term $-cF_h\kappa$ from the slow term $-P_h\nabla c$. It assumes only those pointwise gradient witnesses; the full Hessian calculation later requires $C^2$ regularity.

Bounds the operator norm of the nonleading Hessian terms by two mixed coefficient-gradient factors, one phase-Hessian factor and the coefficient-Hessian remainder. The statement is algebraic for arbitrary scalars and vectors, with no sign assumptions. It uses the norm of a rank-one operator and the triangle inequality before any frequency scales are substituted.
_private.TorusEuler.WavePressureCenter.0.summary: Bound the geometric Hessian terms by separate factors

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: The distance from a real phase to the integer $\lfloor s+1/2\rfloor$ is at most one half. This follows from the two floor inequalities. The estimate ensures that every phase lies in a centered unit cell and that its local bump copy can be selected consistently.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: Nearest integer reduction stays within half a unit

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: If a scalar function $f$ has derivative $f'(s)$ at every real point $s$ and that derivative function is infinitely smooth, then the original function is infinitely smooth. This general calculus lemma is used twice, first for the wave profile and then for its pressure primitive.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: A function with a smooth prescribed derivative is smooth

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: The concrete bump formed by composing the smooth transition with $1-64s^2$ is infinitely differentiable. The polynomial inner function is globally smooth. This establishes the regularity input for scaling, periodization, and uniform derivative bounds in the construction of the phase profile.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: The chosen compact bump is infinitely smooth

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: Under the admissible scale assumptions, the periodic bump is smooth, and subtracting its phase mean and dividing by a constant preserves smoothness. The result establishes infinite differentiability of the normalized slope as a phase function. Positivity of the denominator is proved separately for its quantitative use.

For each order $n$, there is a positive constant uniformly bounding the norm of the bump’s $n$th derivative over the real line. Compactness bounds it on a fixed quarter interval; outside that interval the bump is locally zero. The constant depends on order and is not supplied numerically.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: Every fixed derivative of the compact bump is bounded

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: For $0<h\le1$, the $n$th derivative of the periodic bump equals $h^{-n}$ times the corresponding derivative of the original bump at the centered scaled phase. Local translation agreement legitimizes differentiating across seams. The floor value is frozen locally in this calculation rather than differentiated.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: Each phase derivative contributes an inverse width factor

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: For positive derivative order $n>0$ and admissible width $0<h\le1$, differentiating the normalized slope gives the corresponding derivative of the periodic bump divided by the same constant denominator, one minus the phase mean of the bump. The phase mean disappears because it is constant. The order restriction excludes the value itself, where the subtraction still matters.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: Positive slope derivatives ignore the subtracted mean

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: For $0<h\le1$ and phase in the closed interval $[-1/2,1/2]$, the periodic bump equals the original bump evaluated at $s/h$. The equality includes both boundary points because the bump vanishes there. It allows the phase mean to be estimated directly from the scaled support.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: The periodic bump matches the scaled bump on the closed cell

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: For $0<h\le1$, if phase $s$ lies within distance $3/4$ of an integer $z$, the periodic bump equals the bump scaled around that integer. If the nearest integer differs, both candidate bumps vanish. This overlap agreement removes the apparent discontinuity introduced by the floor function.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: A nearby bump copy agrees with the periodic definition

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: Under $0<h\le1$, reversing phase leaves the periodic bump unchanged. The proof compares copies centered at opposite integers and uses evenness of the original bump. The collar where copies vanish handles half-cell boundary choices, where the nearest-integer representative itself is not odd.

Under $0<h\le1$, the periodic bump agrees near any phase with one fixed translated and scaled copy of the original bump. The integer center is chosen from the floor value at that phase. This local identity is stronger than a pointwise formula and allows all derivative orders to transfer.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: Every phase has a smooth local bump formula

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: The periodic bump has value at most one at every scale and phase. This follows from the range of the smooth transition and remains true even outside the intended width range. Together with its support length, the bound controls the mean removed in the phase-profile construction.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: The periodic bump is bounded above by one

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: The periodic bump is nonnegative for every real scale and phase because the underlying smooth transition is nonnegative. This value bound does not rely on admissible scale or smoothness across seams. It enters the lower estimate for the normalized mean-free slope.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: The periodic bump is everywhere nonnegative

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: The normalized slope is one-periodic for every real scale because its phase dependence comes only from the periodic bump. Subtracting a fixed mean and dividing by a fixed scalar do not change the period. This includes degenerate scales, although the intended normalization requires the later positive-width hypotheses.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: Subtracting the mean preserves slope periodicity

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: For $0<h\le1$, the phase mean of the periodic bump is at most $h/4$. The proof shifts integration to the centered cell and restricts it to the support interval of length $h/4$, where the bump is at most one. This supplies a positive lower bound for slope normalization.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: The bump mean is at most one quarter of its width

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: For an admissible width, the normalized slope has zero mean over one period. The numerator subtracts exactly the bump’s own mean, and division by a constant preserves zero mean. This is the condition that makes the integral based at zero a periodic wave profile rather than a function with linear drift.

The chosen bump takes the same value at $s$ and $-s$. Its argument depends only on $s^2$, so the identity is exact for all real inputs. Evenness is preserved through the permitted scaled periodization and later makes the integrated normalized slope into an odd wave profile.

For positive $h$, the scaled bump at $s/h$ vanishes whenever $|s|\ge h/8$. Positivity is used to translate the support inequality through division. This locates the narrow active region within each unit phase cell and underlies the upper bound on its mean.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: Scaling the bump scales its support radius

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: If $|s|\ge1/8$, the bump vanishes. The chosen quadratic argument is then nonpositive, where the smooth transition is zero. The support is narrower than the paper’s allowed quarter interval, leaving a generous zero collar for the periodic copies to fit together smoothly.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: The bump vanishes outside the inner eighth interval

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: At every phase and for $0<h\le1$, the slope lies between $-h/2$ and one. The lower bound uses the small bump mean and the denominator lower bound; the upper bound uses the bump’s value at most one. These are concrete constants for the inequalities in Lemma 3.1.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: The slope has a small negative part and unit upper bound

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: For $0<h\le1$, one minus the bump’s phase mean is strictly positive. The preceding mean bound gives a value at least $3/4$, though this lemma states only positivity. It is the guard allowing division to normalize the slope and cancellation at phase zero.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: The normalized slope has a positive denominator

_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.text: For $0<h\le1$, the normalized slope is even in phase. The bump is even and its mean and denominator are phase-independent scalars. Integrating this even slope from zero will therefore produce an odd profile, which is the symmetry needed for the localized Euler velocity.

For $0<h\le1$, the slope at phase zero is exactly one. The bump value there is one, so numerator and denominator agree; their common value is nonzero by the positivity lemma. This verifies the normalization that prescribes the central gradient of the localized wave.
_private.TorusEuler.WaveProfile.0.TorusE.summary: The normalized slope equals one at the origin

TorusEuler.Paper.Text.eq_5_13.text:
Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$ and $\lambda\ge1$. The parent $U$ is a smooth odd divergence-free field on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, with Fourier support $|\xi|\le2\mathsf D$ and flow $X$. The bounds $\|\nabla U\|_\infty,\|D_aX\|_\infty,\|(D_aX)^{-1}\|_\infty\le\mathsf D$ hold. For a smooth periodic pressure $p_U$, set $R_U=U_t+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla p_U$; require $R_U$ odd, supported in $|\xi|\le4\mathsf D$, $\|R_U\|_\infty\le\lambda^{-5/2}$, and $D^2p_U-\nabla R_U\le I$ as quadratic forms. The formal statement imposes these conditions directly. The paper selects the zero-mean Poisson pressure; the formal statement permits any pressure meeting the displayed conditions, without separately requiring $\operatorname{div}R_U=0$.

Set $F=D_aX$, $M=(\nabla U)\circ X$, $K=F^TF$ and $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. Fix a nonnegative integer $C_A$. For a sufficiently large integer $a$, put $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$, and choose any number $A$ with $0<A\le\mathsf D^{C_A}$. For every integer $m\ge1$, the formal statement asserts finiteness of the coefficient Hölder norms and gives $\ell_*^m(|K|_{m,1/2}+|\Omega|_{m,1/2})\le C_m\mathsf D^C\ell_*^{1/2}\le C_m/A$.

Here $|\cdot|_{m,1/2}$ sums the half-Hölder norms of the order-$m$ label derivatives, uniformly over $[0,T]$; the half-Hölder norm is the maximum of the supremum and seminorm. The lower threshold for $a$ may depend on $C_A$. After $a$ is fixed, $C$ and the sequence $C_m$ are chosen before the parent and $A$, and $C$ is independent of $m$.

The paper uses the particular endpoint inverse bound $A$ from (4.10). The formal statement admits every positive $A$ with the prescribed polynomial bound, so it includes that case once the bound for the endpoint inverse has been supplied. It does not prove that bound as part of (5.13). The parent pressure can also be more general as above. Positivity of $A$ is explicit, so the division in $C_m/A$ has its ordinary meaning. No conclusion at $m=0$ is stated.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The statement applies to every positive polynomially bounded $A$, including the endpoint inverse bound established in the mean-equation argument.

TorusEuler.Paper.Text.eq_5_14.text:
Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$ and $\lambda\ge1$. The parent $U$ is a smooth odd divergence-free field on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, with Fourier support $|\xi|\le2\mathsf D$ and flow $X$. The bounds $\|\nabla U\|_\infty,\|D_aX\|_\infty,\|(D_aX)^{-1}\|_\infty\le\mathsf D$ hold. For a smooth periodic pressure $p_U$, set $R_U=U_t+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla p_U$; require $R_U$ odd, supported in $|\xi|\le4\mathsf D$, $\|R_U\|_\infty\le\lambda^{-5/2}$, and $D^2p_U-\nabla R_U\le I$ as quadratic forms. The formal statement imposes these conditions directly. The paper selects the zero-mean Poisson pressure; the formal statement permits any pressure meeting the displayed conditions, without separately requiring $\operatorname{div}R_U=0$.

Let $F=D_aX$, $M=(\nabla U)\circ X$ and $\mathbf d=F^{-T}\nabla_a$. Suppose smooth phase-independent periodic fields satisfy $B_t+MB+\mathbf d\bar q=\bar f$ and $B=Fz_t$, with a smooth periodic displacement $z$ obeying $z(0)=z(T)=0$ and $\operatorname{div}_a z_t=0$. Write $v=z_t=F^{-1}B$ and $g=F^T\bar f$.

For sufficiently large fixed $a$ and $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$, the formal statement gives $\|v\|_{[n],1/2}\le C_n\mathsf D^C\|g\|_{[n],1/2}$ at every nonnegative integer order $n$. The scaled norm sums the half-Hölder norms of label derivatives through order $n$, with weights $\ell_*^{|\alpha|}$ and uniformity over $[0,T]$. Finiteness of the source norm is an explicit premise, and finiteness of the velocity norm is part of the conclusion. Smooth periodic data on the closed slab supply the bounded quantities in the paper's application.

The derivative order is the same on both sides, as in (5.14). The later estimate (5.12) loses one derivative when converting to scaled supremum norms. The formal statement allows any smooth periodic representative $v$ satisfying $B=Fv$; invertibility of $F$ identifies it with $z_t$. Once $a$ is fixed, the exponent $C$ and constants are chosen before the parent and source, with $C$ independent of $n$. The broader pressure class above explains the stronger verdict; the explicit finiteness condition is not a claim that an unbounded source norm is controlled.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The explicit finiteness requirement holds for the smooth periodic source. The same-order Hölder estimate is retained before conversion to the one-derivative-loss bound.

TorusEuler.Paper.Text.eq_5_59.text:
Fix a nonnegative integer $m$. Let $E,F,G$ be real normed spaces, let $B:E\times F\to G$ be a continuous bilinear map, and let $f:\mathbb R^3\to E$ and $g:\mathbb R^3\to F$ belong to $C^{m,1/2}$ with finite global norm. The formal statement concludes that $x\mapsto B(f(x),g(x))$ also belongs to $C^{m,1/2}$ and that $\|B(f,g)\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le C_m\|B\|\|f\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\|g\|_{C^{m,1/2}}$.

The constant $C_m\ge0$ is chosen before the three spaces, the bilinear map and the fields. The norm sums the supremum and half-Hölder bounds of the derivatives through order $m$, using operator norms for the multilinear derivatives. Periodicity is not a hypothesis; periodic lifts give the application on $\mathbb T^3$.

The paper writes (5.59) for the products needed in its estimates. Scalar multiplication, the tensor products and contractions used there are special cases of this bilinear statement. The factor $\|B\|$ is necessary when the product itself is allowed to vary, and can be absorbed in the constant for a fixed product. The stronger verdict records the arbitrary target spaces and products and the explicit regularity conclusion. It does not remove the requirement that the two input norms be finite.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The general bilinear Hölder estimate includes all products and contractions used in the cutoff argument. Its operator-norm factor is absorbed into the constant for each fixed product.

TorusEuler.Paper.Text.eq_D_2.text: For $0<\ell_*\le1$, let $c(t,a)$ be smooth in $a\in\mathbb R^3$, with derivatives uniformly bounded over a specified time set through the next required order. The formal statement proves the exact-order inequality and both comparisons in (D.2), including $\|c\|_{[n]}\le\|c\|_{[n],1/2}$, and establishes the necessary Hölder finiteness. Each spatial multi-index is counted once. The Hölder norm is the maximum of the uniform norm and half-Hölder seminorm, and the constant is explicitly four. The paper does not fix that internal convention or the absolute constant; using the customary sum changes the constant by at most a factor two. The cost is still exactly one additional spatial derivative and $\ell_*^{-1/2}$. The result holds for any chosen time domain and any real normed target, with no time differentiability assumption.

TorusEuler.Paper.Text.section8_setting.text: The opening paragraph of Section 8 selects a common construction and then derives a continuous field $w$ with uniform velocity convergence on $[0,T_\infty]\times\mathbb T^3$. The formal statement at this link asserts only existence of parameters, a construction and constants satisfying Theorem 7.1, including the positive common time and activation-time limit. It contains neither $w$ nor a convergence conclusion. A separate supplied theorem proves the continuous closed-interval limit and also identifies it with the Euler solution before $T_\infty$; that theorem takes the Proposition 8.1 conclusions as an additional input for the identification. The link to the previously unlinked convergence sentence has therefore been supplied separately. The weakness belongs to this particular statement link, not to the available Section 8 development as a whole.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. Selection of the common construction and construction of its continuous closed-interval velocity limit are separate results, and both are supplied.

TorusEuler.Paper.corollary_8_3.text: The final conclusions agree: $T_*=T_\infty>0$, the constructed Euler solution has no smooth continuation, and both integrals in (1.2) are infinite. The formal conclusion also identifies the same lifespan for every maximal solution of finite lifespan from the same datum. The explicit implication has a different preceding input: its version of Proposition 8.2 includes a uniform lower bound $c\lambda_{j-1}^{1/8}-C\lambda_{j-1}^{1/32}-C$ on every sufficiently late activation interval. The proof combines that bound with lower estimates for the crossing durations. The paper instead invokes the periodic Beale–Kato–Majda criterion after identifying the maximal time. The quantitative input is established earlier in the formal construction; it is not an unproved extra condition on the final example. This declaration proves the construction-specific corollary without proving the general continuation criterion. The integrals are nonnegative Lebesgue integrals over $[0,T_\infty)$, with essential suprema over one spatial period and operator norm for the gradient.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The corollary's endpoint conclusions agree; the formal proof integrates quantitative vorticity bounds over crossing intervals for the selected solution.

TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_1_3.text: Let $b\ge1$ be an integer and $K(s)=320b(s+1)$. Assume $\mathcal B(s)>0$ and $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$ for $s\ge1$, $q_1=1$, $\lambda_0\ge\mathcal B(1)$, $\lambda_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{K(q_j)}$, and $q_{j+1}=\max\{1\le s\le q_j+1:\mathcal B(s)\le\lambda_{j-1}\}$ for $j\ge1$. The formal statement proves $q_j\le q_{j+1}\le q_j+1$, $q_j\to\infty$, and $4\log\lambda_{j+2}\le(\log\lambda_{j-1})^2$ for every $j\ge1$. The last formula is exactly (1.15), since $L_i=4\log\lambda_{i+1}$. The maximum is the greatest admissible integer. In the paper, $\mathcal B$ is also nondecreasing and dominates the fixed-order analytic constants, and $b$ is fixed by the later construction. The formal statement does not assume these two conditions; it proves the same three assertions from $\mathcal B(s)>0$ and the lower bound (1.13) alone. Frequencies are real, while derivative orders and the exponents $K(s)$ are nonnegative integers; the hypotheses force the relevant frequencies to be positive.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The arithmetic lemma proves the required schedule conclusions under fewer hypotheses.

TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_1.text:
Let $J$ be an interval on which relative time derivatives are unique. The formal statement assumes a differentiable spatial linear map $D(t)$ with $\operatorname{tr}D=0$ and symmetric $D'+D^2$, together with $k'=-D^Tk$ and $\mathbf a'=-D\mathbf a+2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$. For differentiable $F$ and any primitive $P'=F$, it proves that $u(t,x)=D(t)x+\mathbf a(t)F(k(t)\cdot x)$ is divergence free and satisfies the Euler momentum equation on $\mathbb R^3$ whenever $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$ throughout $J$. The pressure is exactly $-x\cdot(D'+D^2)x/2-p_{\rm w}P(k\cdot x)$. The needed time and spatial differentiability of the velocity and spatial differentiability of the pressure are included. If $k,\mathbf a$ are nonzero and perpendicular at one $t_0\in J$, these properties persist at every $t\in J$, including times before $t_0$.

The paper assumes smooth $D$, a smooth odd one-periodic profile with $F'(0)=1$, and a primitive of zero phase average. The formal statement does not require those additional profile properties or the higher regularity of $D$. It also extends the Euler-identity part to $k=0$, where the coefficient is assigned zero by the convention that division by zero is zero. The persistence part still explicitly requires nonzero initial data. These are precise extensions of the quoted lemma, not a change from periodic Euler dynamics to an affine torus flow: this lemma concerns the local affine model on $\mathbb R^3$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The affine Euler calculation remains valid under the paper’s smoother, nonzero data.

TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_2.text:
For nonzero perpendicular paths $k,\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $k\prime=-B^Tk$ and $\mathbf a\prime=-B\mathbf a+2(k\cdot B\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ on a time set $J$, with $\operatorname{tr}B=0$, define $E_1=k/|k|$, $E_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, $E_3=E_1\times E_2$, $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$, and $\sigma=|k||\mathbf a|$. The formal statement gives an orthonormal frame and precisely the four identities $E_1'=-B_{12}E_2-B_{13}E_3$, $E_2'=B_{12}E_1-B_{32}E_3$, $E_3'=B_{13}E_1+B_{32}E_2$, and $(\log\sigma)'=B_{33}$. The three frame positions correspond in order to the paper’s subscripts $1,2,3$. Nonvanishing and perpendicularity are explicit hypotheses at every time in the set under consideration; a defined normalized triple alone would not guarantee orthonormality.

The paper assumes a smooth background $B$ on an interval. The formal statement does not require any time regularity of $B$ beyond the prescribed derivatives of $k$ and $\mathbf a$, and it permits relative derivatives on an arbitrary time set. On the paper’s interval these are the ordinary interior derivatives and the appropriate one-sided endpoint derivatives. No symmetry assumption on $B'+B^2$ appears. The stronger verdict refers to these weaker background and domain hypotheses with all four conclusions retained. It does not mean that the separate logarithmic derivatives of $|k|$ and $|\mathbf a|$, displayed inside the proof, are also conclusions of this declaration.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The complete moving-frame identities contain the individual calculations needed downstream.

TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_3.text:

Put $E_1=k_p/|k_p|$, $E_2=\mathbf a_p/|\mathbf a_p|$, $E_3=E_1	imes E_2$, $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$, $\sigma_p=|k_p||\mathbf a_p|$, $\sigma=\sigma_p(t_0)$, $

e0$ and $\Pi=[2\zeta_2\alpha_1+(\zeta_1+\varepsilon\zeta_3)\alpha_2]/[\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2]$. 

For each fixed $\varepsilon,T$ and every tolerance $e>0$, it chooses one $S_0$ before the physical configuration, wave frequency, activation time and evaluated time. Every model wave with $S\ge S_0$ satisfies $|\zeta-(\varepsilon	au^2/2,-\varepsilon	au,1)|\le e$ in Euclidean norm, and every entry of its amplitude matrix is within $e$ of the corresponding entry of $- igl( egin{smallmatrix}\varepsilon	au\sin2\varphi&\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon	an\varphi)\1&0\end{smallmatrix} igr)$, where $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon	au^2/2)$. These estimates hold throughout $[0,T]$.

The statement additionally includes $\zeta_3
e0$ beyond that common threshold. It permits continuous background data on a compact physical set containing the active interval, rather than requiring the smooth background on precisely that interval used in the paper. The result concerns a limit with $\varepsilon,T$ fixed; it does not claim a polynomial shear threshold in $T$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The complete model theorem supplies the stated limit, with its fixed-parameter quantifiers.

u-1|+\sup_I|B_{32}/\eta-1|+\sup_I\|B\|/r+\sup_I\|E_c\|/

The comparison with the printed lemma concerns three specific choices. First, the formal statement permits continuous $B,E_c$ on a compact set containing the active interval. When that set is larger, the error suprema are also taken there and the smallness assumption must be checked there. Second, continuity of the common amplitude error and the bound for $\sigma_p/\sigma$ are conclusions that the paper obtains in its proof but omits from the lemma statement. Third, the formal statement fixes Euclidean operator norms for the physical matrices and the maximum norm on pairs for the amplitude error; the paper leaves its matrix norms unspecified. The real coefficient and natural exponent can be absorbed into the paper’s $CT^C$ notation by enlarging an absolute constant because $T\ge2$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The full additive comparison supplies every bound needed by the amplitude and coupling arguments.

TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5.text: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, let $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ and consider $Y'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)Y-Y^2$, $Y(0)=1$, on $[0,\infty)$. There is a unique solution on that half-line, with $|Y|\le1$ and $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)/4$ for one function $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$. Its amplitude $a_{\rm ref}=\exp\int_0^\tau Y$ equals $\sqrt{\cos\varphi}\exp\int_0^\tau(1+e)\cos\varphi$. It has its global maximum at the unique zero $\tau_m$ of $Y$, with $2\le\varepsilon\tau_m\le3$, positive $Y$ before and negative $Y$ after, and $\log a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)\ge\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1$. The formal statement therefore retains all the conclusions of Lemma 2.5. It makes uniqueness on $[0,\infty)$ explicit, matching the paper’s reference to “the solution,” and uses one common deviation $e$ in both representations. The equation, bounds and uniqueness concern only $\tau\ge0$, with a right derivative at zero; negative-time values are unrestricted. The statement does not assert that the perturbed amplitude has its maximum at the reference turning time.

TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_6.text:
Let $B,E_c$ be continuous on compact $I\supset[t_0,t_0+T/r]$, with $\operatorname{tr}B=0$ and nonzero perpendicular preceding wave data satisfying $k_p\prime=-B^Tk_p$, $\mathbf a_p\prime=-B\mathbf a_p+2(k_p\cdot B\mathbf a_p)k_p/|k_p|^2$. Set $E_1=\widehat{k_p}$, $E_2=\widehat{\mathbf a_p}$ and $E_3=E_1	imes E_2$; $B_{ij}=E_i\cdot BE_j$. Physical derivatives are relative to $I$; for interval $I$, endpoint derivatives are one-sided. u$. Assume $T\ge2$ and $C_0\varepsilon\le1$, $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$ for sufficiently large integer $C_0$. In physical time, the new wave solves $k'=-M^Tk$, $\mathbf a'=-M\mathbf a+2(k\cdot M\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$, $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$, with $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$, $k(t_0)=\lambda E_3(t_0)$, $\lambda>0$, and $\mathbf a(t_0)=-E_1(t_0)/S+E_2(t_0)$. Use $	au=r(t-t_0)$, $\alpha_1=S\mathbf a\cdot E_1$, $\alpha_2=\mathbf a\cdot E_2$, $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon	au^2/2)$, and $a_{m ref}=\exp\int_0^	au Y$ with $Y\prime=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon	an\varphi)-\varepsilon	au\sin(2\varphi)Y-Y^2$, $Y(0)=1$, on $[0,\infty)$. The formal statement gives $\alpha_2>0$, $|\alpha_1/\alpha_2+Y|\le CT^p\delta$, $\alpha_2\le|\mathbf a|\le(1+CT^p\delta)\alpha_2$, and $|\log(|\mathbf a|/a_{m ref})|\le\varepsilon$ at every $	au\in[0,T]$. It also supplies an invertible linear propagator from $k(	au_1)^\perp$ onto $k(	au_2)^\perp$ for $0\le	au_1\le	au_2\le T$, agreeing with every transverse amplitude solution and satisfying $\|\Phi\|\le252\exp(1)S|\mathbf a(	au_2)|/|\mathbf a(	au_1)|$ in the Euclidean operator norm. These retain all conclusions of Lemma 2.6 and specify its propagator constant. The generalization is from smooth $B$ on the physical interval to continuous $B$ on a compact set containing it. For a larger set, the four suprema defining $\delta$ are also taken over that set, so the smallness condition must still be checked there. The absolute factor $C$, integer exponent $p$ and integer threshold for $C_0$ are chosen before the wave data. The paper’s $CT^C$ notation is recovered by enlarging an absolute constant for $T\ge2$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The full finite comparison retains amplitude positivity, logarithmic gain comparison and transverse transport bounds.

TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_7.text:
Let $B,E_c$ be continuous on compact $I\supset[t_0,t_0+T/r]$, with $\operatorname{tr}B=0$ and nonzero perpendicular preceding wave data satisfying $k_p\prime=-B^Tk_p$, $\mathbf a_p\prime=-B\mathbf a_p+2(k_p\cdot B\mathbf a_p)k_p/|k_p|^2$. matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The rigorous coupling bound uses the reference angle and retains the constants required for the crossing argument.

TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_3_1.text: The formal theorem proves Lemma 3.1 for one specified family, whereas the paper asserts existence of a suitable family. For every $0<h\le1$, the constructed $F_h$ is smooth, odd and period one; its normalized primitive $P_h$ is smooth, period one and has zero phase mean, with $P_h'=F_h$. There is one $C>0$, chosen before $h$, such that $F_h'(0)=1$, $-Ch\le F_h'\le1$ and $\|F_h\|_\infty\le Ch$. For each integer $j\ge2$, there is $C_j>0$, chosen before $h$ and the phase, such that $\|\partial_s^jF_h\|_\infty\le C_jh^{1-j}$. The exponent uses integer subtraction, so it is negative for $j\ge2$, exactly as in the paper. The specified bump is supported in $[-1/8,1/8]$, inside the interval allowed by the proof. Phase mean means integration over $[0,1]$; the primitive is normalized by subtracting that mean, not by fixing its value at zero. The formula is defined outside the admissible width range, but the theorem asserts these properties only for $0<h\le1$. The stronger verdict concerns the identified family and its uniform estimates; it does not assert spatial periodicity after evaluation at an arbitrary real wave vector.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The named profile family is proved to satisfy the entire existential property list.

TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_4_1.text:
Let $0<T\le1$, let $u$ be a smooth divergence-free velocity on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, and let $X$ be its flow with $X(0,a)=a$. Write $F=D_aX$, $M=(\nabla u)\circ X$, $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$, $K=F^TF$ and $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. Suppose $w\cdot H^\#(t,a)w\le|w|^2$ for every $t,a,w$; symmetry of $H^\#$ and an Euler equation for $u$ are not assumed.

For every label $a$ and every $z\in H^1_0([0,T];\mathbb R^3)$, put $\xi=Fz$. Both statements give $\int H^\#\xi\cdot\xi\le\tfrac12\int|\xi_t|^2$ and $\int(Kz_t\cdot z_t+\Omega z_t\cdot z)\ge\tfrac12\int|\xi_t|^2$. The factor $1/2$, the sign of the $\Omega$ term and the test class agree.

The formal statement uses periodic lifts to $\mathbb R^3$ for the torus and represents $z$ by $z(t)=\int_0^t v(s)\,ds$, with $v\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^3)$ and $\int_0^T v=0$. This is exactly the space of Sobolev paths with both endpoints zero; it does not restrict the test paths to smooth ones. It writes $\xi_t=M\xi+Fv$, an almost-everywhere identity sufficient for these integrals. The bound on $H^\#$ is one-sided, not an absolute matrix-norm bound.

TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_10.text:
Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$ and $\lambda\ge1$. The parent $U$ is a smooth odd divergence-free field on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, with Fourier support $|\xi|\le2\mathsf D$ and flow $X$. The bounds $\|\nabla U\|_\infty,\|D_aX\|_\infty,\|(D_aX)^{-1}\|_\infty\le\mathsf D$ hold. For a smooth periodic pressure $p_U$, set $R_U=U_t+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla p_U$; require $R_U$ odd, supported in $|\xi|\le4\mathsf D$, $\|R_U\|_\infty\le\lambda^{-5/2}$, and $D^2p_U-\nabla R_U\le I$ as quadratic forms. The formal statement imposes these conditions directly. The paper selects the zero-mean Poisson pressure; the formal statement permits any pressure meeting the displayed conditions, without separately requiring $\operatorname{div}R_U=0$.

Write $F=D_aX$, $M=(\nabla U)\circ X$ and $\kappa=F^{-T}k_*$, where $k_*\ne0$. Choose $0\le t_0<T$ with $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda$. At the origin take a nonzero transverse solution $\mathbf a$ of $\mathbf a_t=-M\mathbf a+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$. Put $\gamma(t)=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|$. For every transverse homogeneous solution $\mathbf b$ and $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$, assume $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$, and assume $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$ at the origin. The formal normalization is $0<\gamma\le1$; the paper additionally requires $\max\gamma=1$. Fix $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$ for a sufficiently large integer $a$, and $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$.

The finite expansion is selected as follows. Extend the seed to all labels by its transverse equation with $\mathbf a(t_0,a)=(I-P_{\kappa(t_0,a)})\mathbf a(t_0,0)$. Use the fixed smooth radial envelope $g$, equal to one on $|a|\le\ell_*$ and zero on $|a|\ge2\ell_*$, and the fixed one-periodic zero-mean phase profile $F_h$ of Section 3. The time cutoff $\widetilde\chi$ is smooth on $[0,T]$, lies in $[0,1]$, and is zero for $t<t_0$. This permits $\widetilde\chi\equiv1$ when $t_0=0$. On the centered label cell set $A_1=g\mathbf aF_h$, $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$ and $\mathsf p_1=\widetilde\chi\mathsf p[A_1]$, where $\mathsf p[A_1]$ has zero phase mean and $A_{1,t}+MA_1+\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p[A_1]=0$. Set $B_1=\bar q_1=C_1=0$ and $C_{p+1}=C[V_p]$. Here $C[V]=\mathbf d\times(-\kappa\times\partial_s^{-1}V/|\kappa|^2)$, $\mathbf d=F^{-T}\nabla_a$, and $\partial_s^{-1}$ is the zero-mean phase primitive. Higher transverse velocities have zero phase mean, are perpendicular to $\kappa$ and satisfy $V_p(0)=0$. The means have $B_p=Fz_{p,t}$, $\operatorname{div}_a z_{p,t}=0$ and $z_p(0)=z_p(T)=0$. Use the recursive sources in (5.27)–(5.28), including $-R_U\circ X$ at mean level two. Mean pressures have zero spatial mean and transverse pressures zero phase mean. The terminal convention is $V_{P+1}=B_{P+1}=0$. All profiles are smooth on $[0,T]$, one-periodic in phase, and satisfy $f(t,a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=f(t,a,s)$ for $n\in\mathbb Z^3$.

The recursive equations can be stated without referring to another result. Write $Y_i=V_i+C_i$, $Z_i=Y_i+B_i$ and $S=\widetilde\chi'A_1$. For $2\le p\le P$, define

$H_p=(\partial_t+M)C_p+\mathbf d\mathsf p_{p-1}-\mathbf1_{p=2}C[S]+\sum_{i+j=p}(Z_i\cdot\mathbf d)Z_j+\sum_{i+j=p+1,\,i\ge2}(C_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_j$,

where all summation indices are positive integers. Set $\bar f_p=-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R_U\circ X$, $f_p=-(H_p-\langle H_p\rangle_s)$ and $f_p^S=-\sum_{i=2}^p(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_{p+1-i}$. The mean equation is $B_{p,t}+MB_p+\mathbf d\bar q_p=\bar f_p$ with $B_p$ and $\bar q_p$ independent of phase. The transverse equation is $V_{p,t}+MV_p+\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p_p=f_p+f_p^S$, with $\kappa\cdot V_p=0$, zero phase mean and $V_p(0)=0$. The new mean is therefore fixed before the current transverse source is determined. The subtraction at level two removes the differentiated cutoff from the leading curl correction. Its remaining contribution to the full equation is $R_{\widetilde\chi}=S+C[S]$.

With $V_{P+1}=B_{P+1}=0$, the remainder is

$R_P=(\partial_t+M)C_{P+1}+\mathbf d\mathsf p_P+\sum_{1\le i,j\le P+1,\,i+j\ge P+1}(Z_i\cdot\mathbf d)Z_j+\sum_{1\le i,j\le P+1,\,i+j\ge P+2}(Z_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_j$.

These are finite sums; there is no passage to an infinite expansion. The stored correction of $V_p$ carries the paper index $C_{p+1}$. At unused index zero, natural-number predecessor is zero, so the bare reindexing gives $C_0=C_1$; the expansion separately imposes $C_1=0$.

Let $P\ge2$ and take the resulting finite expansion. Set $W=\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)$, $\mathsf P=\sum_{p=1}^P(\mathsf p_p+\bar q_p)$, $V=U+W^\natural$ and $\Pi=p_U+\mathsf P^\natural$. The notation $f^\natural(t,x)$ means $f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ at $a=X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(x)$. Choose $C_{\rm step}=\Gamma_P\mathsf D^b$ sufficiently large and assume $C_{\rm step}\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$. The exponent $b$ is independent of $P$, whereas $\Gamma_P$ may depend on $P$ and the fixed profiles.

Let $v$ be a smooth periodic divergence-free perturbation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$ with $\sup_{t,x}\|D_x^jv(t,x)\|\le\lambda^{-5/2}$ for each integer $0\le j\le2$. The formal statement supplies a flow $Y$ of $V+v$ and proves $\sup_{t,a}\|D_aY(t,a)\|\le C_{\rm step}\lambda^{1/4}$ and the same bound for the derivative of the inverse flow. It also asserts these bounds for every flow solving the stated initial-value problem on $[0,T]$.

The paper assumes the single norm bound $\|v\|_{C_tC^2}\le\lambda^{-5/2}$. The formal hypotheses bound each of the three derivative orders separately in operator norm; the paper's norm bound implies these inequalities. In addition, the formal statement allows the broader parent-pressure class and a nonzero central seed whose peak need not reach $\lambda^{-3/4}$. These are enlargements of the admitted data, while the two bounds in (5.53) are retained.

The inverse derivative means the derivative of the transition from time $t$ back to time zero. At the particle position $Y(t,a)$ it is $(D_aY(t,a))^{-1}$; the bounds over all positions are equivalent because the flow is bijective. The formal fields are periodic lifts to $\mathbb R^3$, and their flows commute with integer translations. Smoothness and the flow conclusions concern the closed interval $[0,T]$, not an unspecified continuation beyond it. All thresholds are fixed before the parent and perturbation.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The paper’s summed $C^2$ bound implies the separate derivative bounds. The formal flow theorem therefore covers its perturbations and also supplies flow existence.

TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_3.text:
Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$ and $\lambda\ge1$. The parent $U$ is a smooth odd divergence-free field on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, with Fourier support $|\xi|\le2\mathsf D$ and flow $X$. The bounds $\|\nabla U\|_\infty,\|D_aX\|_\infty,\|(D_aX)^{-1}\|_\infty\le\mathsf D$ hold. For a smooth periodic pressure $p_U$, set $R_U=U_t+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla p_U$; require $R_U$ odd, supported in $|\xi|\le4\mathsf D$, $\|R_U\|_\infty\le\lambda^{-5/2}$, and $D^2p_U-\nabla R_U\le I$ as quadratic forms. The formal statement imposes these conditions directly. The paper selects the zero-mean Poisson pressure; the formal statement permits any pressure meeting the displayed conditions, without separately requiring $\operatorname{div}R_U=0$.

Write $F=D_aX$, $M=(\nabla U)\circ X$ and $\kappa=F^{-T}k_*$, where $k_*\ne0$. Choose $0\le t_0<T$ with $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda$. At the origin take a nonzero transverse solution $\mathbf a$ of $\mathbf a_t=-M\mathbf a+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$. Put $\gamma(t)=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|$. For every transverse homogeneous solution $\mathbf b$ and $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$, assume $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$, and assume $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$ at the origin. The formal normalization is $0<\gamma\le1$; the paper additionally requires $\max\gamma=1$. Fix $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$ for a sufficiently large integer $a$, and $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$.

For a profile $f(t,a,s)$, the norm $\|f\|_{[n]}$ sums $\ell_*^{|\alpha|}h^j\sup|\partial_a^\alpha\partial_s^j f|$ over $|\alpha|+j\le n$ on $[0,T]$. The weighted norm $\|f\|_{[n],\gamma}$ uses $[t_0,T]$ and divides by $\gamma(t)$; it differentiates only labels and phase. Each multi-index is counted once. The profiles are smooth on the closed time slab, one-periodic in $s$, and satisfy $f(t,a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=f(t,a,s)$ for $n\in\mathbb Z^3$. Their stipulated zero values outside the time slab do not assert smoothness across its endpoints.

Use the particular fixed smooth radial envelope $g$, equal to one on $|a|\le\ell_*$ and zero for $|a|\ge2\ell_*$. Extend the seed from the origin by solving its linear equation with $\mathbf a(t_0,a)=(I-P_{\kappa(t_0,a)})\mathbf a(t_0,0)$. For $|a|\le2\ell_*$ the formal statement gives $|\mathbf a(t,a)|\le2|\mathbf a(t,0)|$ and the strict inequality $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a>0$ on $[t_0,T]$. For a transverse solution $V_t=-(I-2P_\kappa)MV+(I-P_\kappa)f$, whose initial value and source vanish outside the repeated envelope support, it gives $\|V\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^C(\gamma(t_0)^{-1}\|V(t_0)\|_{[n]}+\|f\|_{[n],\gamma})$.

For the transverse momentum equation $V_t+MV+\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p=f$, the formal estimate is $\|V\|_{[n],\gamma}+\lambda\|\mathsf p\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^C\|f\|_{[n],\gamma}$. It assumes a full-interval solution with $V(0)=0$, $V\perp\kappa$, and zero phase means of $V,f,\mathsf p$; the source vanishes before $t_0$ and outside the envelope. For $A_1=g\mathbf aF_h$ and its zero-mean wave pressure it gives the same left-hand side bounded by $C_n\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/4}$.

The numerical powers, initial-value term and pressure factor agree with (5.19)–(5.22). The scope changes in both directions: part (i) of the numbered formal statement takes profiles smooth on $[0,T]$, while the paper permits data given only on $[t_0,T]$; a smooth extension is needed to apply that statement to such data. The parent pressure and the central normalization are less restrictive as described above. Part (ii) is an estimate conditional on a solution; its existence and uniqueness are separate results. The constants are chosen before the parent and derivative order, after fixing $a$.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The full-interval regularity requirement is satisfied by the constructed hierarchy, and the separate transverse existence theorem supplies its solutions.

Set $\mathbf d=(D_aX)^{-T}\nabla_a$ and $C[V]=\mathbf d\times Q[V]$, where $Q[V]=-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V/|\kappa|^2)$ and $\partial_s^{-1}$ takes the zero-mean periodic primitive. For $V\perp\kappa$ on $[t_0,T]$ with zero phase mean, the formal statement gives $\|C[V]\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-1}\|V\|_{[n+1],\gamma}$. The differential equation, transversality and pressure normalization are required only on $[t_0,T]$. Thus an arbitrary field given on the active interval is not an input until an appropriate extension has been supplied. This restriction accompanies the weaker pressure and seed-normalization assumptions above, which explains the verdict different.

For the leading field $A_1=g\mathbf aF_h$, the formal statement itself supplies smooth profiles on $[0,T]$ that agree with $A_1$ and its pressure on the active interval within the centered label cell; elsewhere they obey the stated coupled translation law. They satisfy the homogeneous equation throughout the active interval. The source term then vanishes in the second estimate. One exponent $C$ works at every derivative order after the envelope exponent is fixed, and all constants are chosen before the parent. Nonvanishing of $\kappa$ and positivity of $\gamma$ make every division used in these conclusions ordinary division.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The hierarchy is smooth and centered on the full interval. For the unswitched leading wave, the lemma itself supplies the smooth representative needed to apply the estimate.

Their stipulated zero values outside the time slab do not assert smoothness across its endpoints.

Let $g_0$ be such a profile with values in a real normed space, independent of phase outside the repeated support of the envelope. Define its physical field by $g_0^\natural(t,x)=g_0(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ with $a=X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(x)$. The transformation rule of the profile ensures periodicity in $x$ even when $k_*\notin\mathbb Z^3$. The formal spatial derivative sum in the conclusion ranges over all ordered coordinate sequences of length $m$; the paper's sum ranges over multi-indices. Their multiplicities are bounded in terms of $m$ and absorbed into $C_m$. This physical derivative sum is distinct from the finite profile norm on the right, which counts each multi-index once.

The paper's smooth continuation across cell faces is represented by the globally defined profile and its transformation law. The formal statement also allows arbitrary real normed target spaces, asserts the Hölder regularity explicitly, and uses the broader parent and seed hypotheses above. The envelope exponent is fixed first, followed by $C$ and the sequence $C_m$, before the parent and target space. The integer $C$ is independent of derivative order and no expansion depth enters this estimate.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The coupled translation law represents smooth continuation of the cell profile. The broader target spaces and norm convention retain the graph bounds needed by the construction.

TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_8.text:
Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$ and $\lambda\ge1$. The parent $U$ is a smooth odd divergence-free field on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, with Fourier support $|\xi|\le2\mathsf D$ and flow $X$. The bounds $\|\nabla U\|_\infty,\|D_aX\|_\infty,\|(D_aX)^{-1}\|_\infty\le\mathsf D$ hold. For a smooth periodic pressure $p_U$, set $R_U=U_t+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla p_U$; require $R_U$ odd, supported in $|\xi|\le4\mathsf D$, $\|R_U\|_\infty\le\lambda^{-5/2}$, and $D^2p_U-\nabla R_U\le I$ as quadratic forms. The formal statement imposes these conditions directly. The paper selects the zero-mean Poisson pressure; the formal statement permits any pressure meeting the displayed conditions, without separately requiring $\operatorname{div}R_U=0$.

Write $F=D_aX$, $M=(\nabla U)\circ X$ and $\kappa=F^{-T}k_*$, where $k_*\ne0$. Choose $0\le t_0<T$ with $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda$. At the origin take a nonzero transverse solution $\mathbf a$ of $\mathbf a_t=-M\mathbf a+2\kappa(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$. Put $\gamma(t)=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|$. For every transverse homogeneous solution $\mathbf b$ and $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$, assume $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$, and assume $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|\kappa||\mathbf a|$ at the origin. The formal normalization is $0<\gamma\le1$; the paper additionally requires $\max\gamma=1$. Fix $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$ for a sufficiently large integer $a$, and $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$.

The finite expansion is selected as follows. Extend the seed to all labels by its transverse equation with $\mathbf a(t_0,a)=(I-P_{\kappa(t_0,a)})\mathbf a(t_0,0)$. Use the fixed smooth radial envelope $g$, equal to one on $|a|\le\ell_*$ and zero on $|a|\ge2\ell_*$, and the fixed one-periodic zero-mean phase profile $F_h$ of Section 3. The time cutoff $\widetilde\chi$ is smooth on $[0,T]$, lies in $[0,1]$, and is zero for $t<t_0$. This permits $\widetilde\chi\equiv1$ when $t_0=0$. On the centered label cell set $A_1=g\mathbf aF_h$, $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$ and $\mathsf p_1=\widetilde\chi\mathsf p[A_1]$, where $\mathsf p[A_1]$ has zero phase mean and $A_{1,t}+MA_1+\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p[A_1]=0$. Set $B_1=\bar q_1=C_1=0$ and $C_{p+1}=C[V_p]$. Here $C[V]=\mathbf d\times(-\kappa\times\partial_s^{-1}V/|\kappa|^2)$, $\mathbf d=F^{-T}\nabla_a$, and $\partial_s^{-1}$ is the zero-mean phase primitive. Higher transverse velocities have zero phase mean, are perpendicular to $\kappa$ and satisfy $V_p(0)=0$. The means have $B_p=Fz_{p,t}$, $\operatorname{div}_a z_{p,t}=0$ and $z_p(0)=z_p(T)=0$. Use the recursive sources in (5.27)–(5.28), including $-R_U\circ X$ at mean level two. Mean pressures have zero spatial mean and transverse pressures zero phase mean. The terminal convention is $V_{P+1}=B_{P+1}=0$. All profiles are smooth on $[0,T]$, one-periodic in phase, and satisfy $f(t,a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=f(t,a,s)$ for $n\in\mathbb Z^3$.

The recursive equations can be stated without referring to another result. Write $Y_i=V_i+C_i$, $Z_i=Y_i+B_i$ and $S=\widetilde\chi'A_1$. For $2\le p\le P$, define

$H_p=(\partial_t+M)C_p+\mathbf d\mathsf p_{p-1}-\mathbf1_{p=2}C[S]+\sum_{i+j=p}(Z_i\cdot\mathbf d)Z_j+\sum_{i+j=p+1,\,i\ge2}(C_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_j$,

where all summation indices are positive integers. Set $\bar f_p=-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R_U\circ X$, $f_p=-(H_p-\langle H_p\rangle_s)$ and $f_p^S=-\sum_{i=2}^p(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_{p+1-i}$. The mean equation is $B_{p,t}+MB_p+\mathbf d\bar q_p=\bar f_p$ with $B_p$ and $\bar q_p$ independent of phase. The transverse equation is $V_{p,t}+MV_p+\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p_p=f_p+f_p^S$, with $\kappa\cdot V_p=0$, zero phase mean and $V_p(0)=0$. The new mean is therefore fixed before the current transverse source is determined. The subtraction at level two removes the differentiated cutoff from the leading curl correction. Its remaining contribution to the full equation is $R_{\widetilde\chi}=S+C[S]$.

With $V_{P+1}=B_{P+1}=0$, the remainder is

$R_P=(\partial_t+M)C_{P+1}+\mathbf d\mathsf p_P+\sum_{1\le i,j\le P+1,\,i+j\ge P+1}(Z_i\cdot\mathbf d)Z_j+\sum_{1\le i,j\le P+1,\,i+j\ge P+2}(Z_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_j$.

These are finite sums; there is no passage to an infinite expansion. The stored correction of $V_p$ carries the paper index $C_{p+1}$. At unused index zero, natural-number predecessor is zero, so the bare reindexing gives $C_0=C_1$; the expansion separately imposes $C_1=0$.

Let $P\ge2$ and take the resulting finite expansion. Set $W=\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)$, $\mathsf P=\sum_{p=1}^P(\mathsf p_p+\bar q_p)$, $V=U+W^\natural$ and $\Pi=p_U+\mathsf P^\natural$. The notation $f^\natural(t,x)$ means $f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ at $a=X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(x)$. Choose $C_{\rm step}=\Gamma_P\mathsf D^b$ sufficiently large and assume $C_{\rm step}\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$. The exponent $b$ is independent of $P$, whereas $\Gamma_P$ may depend on $P$ and the fixed profiles.

The formal statement says that $V$ is smooth, periodic, odd and divergence free on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, and that $\Pi$ is smooth and periodic there. Its exact momentum residual is $R_V=R_P^\natural+R_{\widetilde\chi}^\natural$, where $R_P$ is the remainder of the finite expansion and $R_{\widetilde\chi}=\widetilde\chi'(A_1+C[A_1])$ is the activation error. The parent residual has already been canceled in this identity.

With $\bar W=\sum_{p=2}^PB_p$ and $W_{\rm osc}=W-\bar W$, the bounds are $\|W_{\rm osc}^\natural\|_{C_tL^\infty}\le C_{0,P}\mathsf D^b\lambda^{-5/4}$, $\|W_{\rm osc}^\natural\|_{C_tC^{m,1/2}}\le C_{m,P}\mathsf D^{b(m+2)}\lambda^{3(m+1)/2-5/4}$ and $\|\bar W^\natural\|_{C_tC^{m,1/2}}\le C_{m,P}\mathsf D^{b(m+2)}\lambda^{-5/2}$. The residual satisfies $\|R_V\|_{C_tC^{1,1/2}}\le C_{\rm step}\lambda^2(\lambda^{-2P/3}+\|\widetilde\chi'\gamma\|_{\infty,[t_0,T]})$. All three time norms of fields use $[0,T]$; only the last cutoff supremum uses $[t_0,T]$.

The powers, parity, divergence assertion and activation factor agree with (5.46)–(5.48). Pointwise bounds uniform in time represent the displayed time suprema; Hölder regularity is also asserted. The formal statement permits the larger pressure and seed class specified above. After fixing $a$, it chooses thresholds $b_0,\Gamma_{0,P}$ and constants $C_{m,P}$ before the parent, then allows every $b\ge b_0$ and $\Gamma_P\ge\Gamma_{0,P}$ satisfying the corresponding smallness assumption. These constants do not change when $b$ or $\Gamma_P$ is enlarged. No vanishing of the mean correction before activation is concluded.

matters.line: Does this affect Theorem 1.1? No. The physical estimates retain the paper’s powers, parity and divergence conclusions, including the separate activation error. The enlarged parent and seed class does not weaken them.
